blueprints.name: Static site: S3 private bucket behind CloudFront with OAC, ACM cert in us-east-1, Route 53 alias
blueprints.forWho: A marketing site, docs site, landing page, portfolio, or a client-side SPA whose data comes from a third-party API. Content changes by redeploying files, not by a user writing to a database. One or two people deploy it from a Git push.
blueprints.scale: Effectively unbounded for a brochure site. 10k-100k visits/month is nothing; the same architecture serves millions. Practical limit is your build/deploy process, not AWS. CloudFront soft default is 250,000 requests/second per distribution and 1 Tbps; a single distribution supports 100 alternate domain names and 25 cache behaviors by default.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $0.50-$2/month at 10k visits, and still roughly $1-$3/month at 100k visits. Route 53 hosted zone is the floor: $0.50/month, fixed, plus ~$0.40 per million DNS queries. CloudFront pay-as-you-go now gives 1 TB/month data transfer out and 10 million requests/month free permanently, so a 100k-visit brochure site (say 2 MB/visit, 40 requests/visit = 200 GB and 4M requests) lands inside the free allowance. S3 storage for a 50-500 MB site is $0.001-$0.012/month at $0.023/GB, and S3-to-CloudFront origin fetches are free. ACM public certificates are free. Cost drivers: large uncompressed media (video pushes you past 1 TB), and a badly-tuned cache that turns every viewer request into an origin fetch.

components.service: Amazon S3
components.role: Origin. Holds the built HTML/CSS/JS/images. Not a website endpoint - a plain private bucket accessed via the REST endpoint.
components.why: Not an EC2 instance running nginx. A t4g.nano is ~$3/month plus an EBS volume plus an Elastic IP plus you patching the OS, rotating certs, and being the single point of failure; S3 is 11-nines durable, has no capacity to size, no kernel to patch, and no instance to fall over at 3am. Not a Lightsail instance for the same reason. The only thing nginx buys you here is server-side redirects and rewrites, and CloudFront Functions do those for $0.10 per million invocations without a server. Also NOT the S3 static website endpoint: that endpoint is HTTP-only, cannot be locked to CloudFront, and forces the bucket public - the only reason to use it is its built-in index-document-per-directory behaviour, which CloudFront Functions replicate.
components.config: Block Public Access all four settings ON. Bucket policy grants s3:GetObject only to the CloudFront service principal, conditioned on AWS:SourceArn = your distribution ARN. Default encryption SSE-S3. Versioning on (it is your rollback and it is nearly free at this size). No lifecycle rule needed under ~1 GB; add noncurrent-version-expiration at 30 days if you deploy many times a day. Set Cache-Control on upload: hashed asset filenames get `public,max-age=31536000,immutable`; index.html and any unhashed HTML gets `public,max-age=0,must-revalidate` (or `max-age=60`).

components.service: Amazon CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC)
components.role: The only public front door. TLS termination, global edge cache, compression, security headers, SPA routing.
components.why: OAC rather than a public bucket or the legacy OAI. Public bucket means anyone can bypass your CDN, hit S3 directly, run up your origin bill, and read your object listing if you ever misconfigure a list permission - and your access logs then have two front doors. OAC signs origin requests with SigV4, works with SSE-KMS and with buckets in every region, and is what AWS now recommends over OAI (OAI is legacy). Rather than serving from the bucket directly: CloudFront gives you HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, a free ACM certificate on your own domain, edge caching so 100k visits mostly never touch S3, and the free 1 TB/10M-request allowance. There is no crossover point where the public-bucket option wins - OAC costs nothing extra.
components.config: Origin: the bucket REST endpoint (bucket.s3.region.amazonaws.com), origin access = OAC with signing behaviour 'Sign requests'. Viewer protocol policy Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Compress objects automatically ON. Default root object index.html. Cache policy CachingOptimized (managed, id 658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6) - do NOT forward cookies or all query strings, that shatters your cache hit ratio. Response headers policy SecurityHeadersPolicy (adds HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, frame options, referrer policy) - this is the difference between a site that passes a security scan and one that does not. Price class: use PriceClass_100 (US/EU/IL) if your audience is regional - it cuts per-GB cost; use All if you have real global traffic. Attach a CloudFront Function (viewer-request) for SPA/pretty-URL rewrites: append index.html to directory paths. For a client-routed SPA, add a custom error response mapping 403 and 404 to /index.html with response code 200 - but only for a true SPA, because it also turns real missing assets into 200s and hides broken links.

components.service: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
components.role: Free public TLS certificate for example.com and www.example.com, auto-renewed.
components.why: Rather than Let's Encrypt on a server, or a paid cert: ACM is free, renews itself, and you never run certbot. The trap: a certificate used by CloudFront MUST be issued in us-east-1 regardless of where anything else lives. If you provision with CloudFormation/CDK, the whole CloudFront stack is easiest to keep in us-east-1 for this reason - AWS's own secure-static-site template requires it.
components.config: Request in us-east-1. SANs: example.com and *.example.com (or just www). DNS validation, with the CNAME created in the same Route 53 hosted zone - DNS validation renews silently forever; email validation does not.

components.service: Amazon Route 53
components.role: DNS. Alias A and AAAA records at the apex and www pointing to the distribution.
components.why: Alias records rather than a CNAME: a CNAME is illegal at the zone apex, so without alias records you cannot serve example.com at all without an HTTP-redirect hack. Route 53 alias queries to a CloudFront distribution are free and resolve to the nearest edge. Keeping DNS at your registrar (Cloudflare, Namecheap) is a legitimate choice and saves the $0.50 - do that only if you never need ACM DNS validation automated or Route 53 health checks. Do not split: registrar-DNS plus AWS certs plus manual CNAMEs is how certificates silently fail to renew.
components.config: One public hosted zone, $0.50/month. A + AAAA alias at apex and www. Keep TTLs default; alias records ignore TTL in the useful sense. Add a CAA record for amazon.com so no other CA can issue for your domain.

components.service: Deployment: GitHub Actions with OIDC, `aws s3 sync` then targeted invalidation
components.role: Build, upload, bust the cache.
components.why: Rather than AWS Amplify Hosting: Amplify is genuinely good and is the right call if you want zero pipeline work, PR preview environments and built-in SSR for Next.js. But its free allowance is much smaller - 15 GB/month data transfer out then $0.15/GB, versus CloudFront's 1 TB free then ~$0.085/GB. At 100 GB/month Amplify is roughly $13 and this stack is roughly $1. Amplify also owns the CloudFront distribution, so you cannot attach your own WAF rules, response-headers policy or Lambda@Edge without leaving. Choose Amplify when developer time is the scarce resource and traffic is small; choose this when the site is long-lived, media-heavy, or you need control of the edge. Rather than long-lived IAM access keys in CI: OIDC federation gives short-lived credentials and there is no key to leak.
components.config: `aws s3 sync ./dist s3://bucket --delete` with two passes: first sync hashed assets with `--cache-control 'public,max-age=31536000,immutable'`, then sync HTML with `--cache-control 'public,max-age=0,must-revalidate'`. Then invalidate ONLY `/index.html` and `/` - not `/*`. Invalidations: first 1,000 paths/month free, then $0.005 per path; a wildcard counts as one path, so `/*` is also free-tier-cheap but it dumps your entire edge cache and re-pulls everything from origin. With immutable hashed filenames you rarely need to invalidate at all. The 1,000 free paths are per AWS account across all distributions, not per distribution.

blueprints.ceiling: The architecture does not break on traffic. It breaks on requirements. Exact ceiling: the moment you need (a) to store something a visitor typed - a contact form, a signup, a comment; (b) per-user content or a login; (c) server-side rendering of content that changes per request; (d) a secret that must not be in the browser bundle (any API key with write scope); or (e) server-side redirect logic more complex than a CloudFront Function's 10 KB / ~1 ms CPU budget and no-network limit. Quantitatively, CloudFront Functions cap at 10 KB of code, 2 MB memory, sub-millisecond execution and cannot make network calls or see the request body; the first time you need to call an API from the edge you are on Lambda@Edge (~$0.60/million plus GB-seconds, and multi-region deploy lag), and at that point you should be asking whether this is still a static site.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Not capacity - the cache hit ratio and the deploy. Two real failure shapes. (1) Cache-busting: you ship a change, index.html is still cached at the edge with a long max-age, and some visitors see the old site for hours while you insist it is deployed. Symptom: it works in incognito in one city and not another. (2) Origin storm: someone sets a cache policy that forwards all query strings or cookies (analytics params like ?utm_source= are the classic), hit ratio collapses from ~95% to near zero, every request becomes an S3 GET, and page load gets slower after you added the CDN. Watch the CloudFront `CacheHitRate` metric - below ~85% on a static site means you have misconfigured the cache policy, not that your content is unusual.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Machine-checkable: (1) the repo contains a form that POSTs anywhere, or any `fetch` with a method other than GET to an origin you own; (2) the build injects any credential into the client bundle that is not publishable (anything other than a publishable/anon key); (3) CloudFront CacheHitRate sustained below 80% because content is genuinely per-request; (4) you have added more than ~3 CloudFront Functions or any Lambda@Edge; (5) product requires a login. Any one of these means blueprint 2. Note that (1) alone does NOT require it - a single form can go to a Lambda Function URL or a form service and leave the rest static.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build a VPC. This architecture touches no VPC at all - S3, CloudFront, ACM and Route 53 are all outside it. A NAT gateway is ~$32/month per AZ plus $0.045/GB processed; two AZs of NAT is ~$65/month, i.e. thirty times the cost of this entire site, to route traffic for a site that has no servers. Do not add AWS WAF: $5/month per web ACL plus $1 per rule plus $0.60 per million requests, and a static site behind CloudFront has no injectable surface - add it only when you have a specific attack or a compliance requirement naming it (CloudFront's own DDoS protection via Shield Standard is already on, free). Do not add Origin Shield ($0.0075-0.016 per 10k requests) - it earns its keep when you have many edge locations thrashing one origin, not at 100k visits. Do not add real-time logs ($0.01 per million lines) or a logging pipeline; standard access logs to S3 are free apart from storage and you will not read them. Do not add multi-region replication - S3 is already multi-AZ and CloudFront is already global. Do not add a CI/CD product (CodePipeline, ~$1/month per pipeline plus CodeBuild minutes) when a GitHub Actions workflow of 20 lines does it. Do not buy a paid TLS certificate. Typical waste from ignoring this: $70-$120/month on infrastructure for a site whose real cost is $1.

plain.plainName: A website that just shows information
plain.problem: You need a site for your business, your docs, or your portfolio. Nobody logs in. You change it by uploading new files when the prices or the words change.
plain.answer: Keep the files in S3, which is AWS storage, and put CloudFront in front of it so the pages load fast everywhere.
plain.money: About $0.50 to $2 a month at 10,000 visits, and still about $1 to $3 a month at 100,000 visits. The domain name record costs a fixed $0.50 a month.
plain.holdsUpTo: This does not run out. 10,000 to 100,000 visits a month is nothing, and the same setup serves millions. The limit is how fast you can publish new files, not AWS.
plain.whatBreaks: Not the traffic. Two things go wrong. You publish a change and some visitors keep seeing the old site for hours, so it works in one city and not another. Or someone changes a setting so every visit goes back to the storage instead of the fast copy, and the bill and the load jump.
plain.timeToMove: Move on the day you need to store something a visitor typed, like a contact form or a signup, or you need logins, or you need a secret key that must not sit in the browser.
plain.dontYet: Do not build a private network. This setup does not use one at all. The gateway people add for that costs about $32 a month for one, and about $65 a month for the usual pair, which is thirty times the cost of this whole site, for a site that has no servers. Do not add the AWS firewall either. That is $5 a month per rule set plus $1 per rule plus $0.60 per million visits, and there is nothing here to attack.
plain.pitch: I just need my business online and nobody will be logging in.

blueprints.name: Small dynamic app to ~1,000 users: one right-sized compute choice + managed Postgres + Secrets Manager + CloudWatch, no VPC heroics
blueprints.forWho: A real product with logins, a database and background work, serving up to roughly 1,000 registered users (realistically 50-200 concurrent at peak, single-digit to low-tens of requests per second). One to three engineers, no dedicated ops person, runway measured in months. Downtime of a few minutes during a deploy is survivable; losing a day of data is not.
blueprints.scale: 1,000 users, peak ~10-30 req/s, database under ~20 GB, under ~2,000 write transactions/minute. A single 2 vCPU / 4 GB app instance serves this with headroom on almost any stack. Serverless equivalent: ~5-20 million requests/month.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $25-$120/month depending on which option below, excluding domain. Honest per-option numbers, us-east-1, on-demand: (A) Single EC2 t4g.small (2 vCPU, 2 GB, Graviton) ~$12/mo + 30 GB gp3 ~$2.40 + Elastic IP ~$3.60 (IPv4 is now charged at $0.005/hr whether attached or not) ≈ $18-20, plus RDS db.t4g.micro single-AZ 20 GB ~$12-15 → ~$32/mo all-in, or ~$20/mo if you run Postgres on the same box (see the honest caveat below). (B) Lightsail: $5-12/mo instance bundle (the $12 bundle is 2 GB / 2 vCPU / 60 GB SSD / 3 TB transfer) plus $15/mo managed database bundle (1 GB, 40 GB) → ~$27/mo, with bandwidth included rather than metered. (C) ECS Express Mode on Fargate: 0.25 vCPU/0.5 GB Fargate task ~$9/mo plus an ALB at $0.0225/hr ≈ $16.43/mo plus LCU charges → ~$27-35/mo for the first service; the ALB is the floor and it is shared by up to 25 Express services in the same networking config, so service #2 through #25 cost only their Fargate time. (D) Elastic Beanstalk: no charge for Beanstalk itself, you pay the EC2 + ALB it provisions → ~$30-45/mo for a single-instance environment (no ALB) or ~$50/mo with a load balancer. (E) Serverless (Lambda + API Gateway HTTP API + DynamoDB on-demand): at 5M requests/month, HTTP API is $1.00/million ≈ $5, Lambda at 200 ms/512 MB ≈ $8-10, DynamoDB on-demand for a light workload $3-10 → ~$15-25/mo, and genuinely near $0 at low traffic, but see the ceiling. Add to all of them: Route 53 $0.50, CloudFront free tier, ACM free, Secrets Manager $0.40 per secret/month, CloudWatch Logs $0.50/GB ingested, S3 backups a few cents.

components.service: Compute: pick ONE — ECS Express Mode (containerised team) or a single EC2/Lightsail instance (non-containerised team)
components.role: Runs the application process.
components.why: The landscape changed in 2026 and the honest answer changed with it. **App Runner is out**: AWS closed it to new customers on 30 April 2026 and moved it to maintenance mode - security and availability investment only, no new features - and explicitly points migrants at ECS Express Mode. Do not start anything on App Runner now, whatever older guides say. **ECS Express Mode** is the successor: one `create-express-gateway-service` call gives you a Fargate service, an ALB with target groups and health checks, autoscaling, networking and a URL, at no charge for Express Mode itself. Choose it over raw ECS+CDK because you skip several hundred lines of infrastructure code; choose it over EC2 when you already build a container image. **Elastic Beanstalk** rather than Express Mode only if you are not containerised and want zip-deploy of a Rails/Django/Node app with a managed platform - it is stable and supported, but it is the oldest of these, it provisions and hands you real EC2 instances and an ALB (so you pay for both and still own the AMI lifecycle), and its configuration surface is idiosyncratic enough that you end up learning Beanstalk instead of learning AWS. **Lightsail** rather than EC2 when predictable flat billing and bundled bandwidth matter more than growth path - $5-12/mo, 1-3 TB transfer included, a console you can understand in ten minutes. Its real cost is the exit: Lightsail lives outside your VPC, its managed database is not RDS, and 'graduating' to EC2/RDS later is a migration, not a resize. **A single EC2 instance** is the least fashionable and the most defensible answer for a small team that knows Linux: t4g.small Graviton, systemd unit, Caddy or nginx in front for automatic TLS, deploy by `git pull && systemctl restart`. It is the cheapest, has no cold starts, no per-request billing surprise, and you can attach a debugger to the actual process. Its cost is that you own patching and the reboot. **The one a small team regrets least: ECS Express Mode if your app is already a container, otherwise a single Lightsail or EC2 instance with an AMI/snapshot you have actually restored once.** The regret in all directions is real but asymmetric: teams that picked a single instance regret an afternoon of downtime; teams that picked Kubernetes or a hand-rolled VPC+ALB+ASG regret a quarter.
components.config: ECS Express Mode: `aws ecs create-express-gateway-service --primary-container '{image, containerPort, environment}' --health-check-path /health --scaling-target '{"minTaskCount":1,"maxTaskCount":4}' --monitor-resources`, with `ecsTaskExecutionRole` and `ecsInfrastructureRoleForExpressServices`. 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB is the sane starting task size; 0.25/0.5 is enough for a light API and will OOM a Rails or JVM app. Provisioning takes 3-5 minutes. EC2 path: t4g.small, Amazon Linux 2023, gp3 30 GB, IMDSv2 required, no SSH key at all - use SSM Session Manager - security group open only on 80/443, Caddy for automatic ACM-free TLS via Let's Encrypt (or put CloudFront in front and use an ACM cert). Lightsail path: $12 bundle, enable automatic snapshots, attach a static IP.
components.alternative_named: AWS App Runner (closed to new customers, 30 Apr 2026); raw ECS on Fargate with hand-written CDK; EKS.

components.service: Database: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, db.t4g.micro or db.t4g.small, SINGLE-AZ
components.role: The system of record.
components.why: Managed Postgres rather than Postgres on the app instance: the instance is the thing you will rebuild, resize and accidentally fill with logs, and a database on it turns every one of those into a data-loss event. RDS gives you automated backups, point-in-time recovery to any second in the retention window, and a one-click minor-version patch. Single-AZ rather than Multi-AZ at this stage: Multi-AZ roughly doubles the bill (~$12-15 becomes ~$25-30) to buy automatic failover in 60-120 seconds. At 1,000 users the honest question is whether 10 minutes of downtime during an AZ event costs you more than $15/month for 12 months - usually it does not, and single-AZ RDS still restores from backup. Relational rather than DynamoDB for an MVP: your access patterns are not known yet, and DynamoDB forces you to commit to them in the key schema - a new query pattern means a new GSI or a migration, whereas in Postgres it means a new index and sometimes not even that. Use DynamoDB when the access pattern genuinely is key-value at known keys (sessions, idempotency records, feature flags, event logs) - it is excellent there and effectively free at this scale. Aurora Serverless v2 rather than RDS: only once you have real idle periods AND real spikes; its floor is 0 ACUs with auto-pause now, but the complexity and the per-ACU-hour pricing are not worth it under 1,000 users.
components.config: db.t4g.micro (2 vCPU burstable, 1 GB) for read-light apps, db.t4g.small (2 GB) if you have any ORM with eager loading. 20 GB gp3, storage autoscaling ON with a max you set (this prevents the 3am disk-full outage). Automated backups retention 7 days minimum (0 is the default in some paths - check it; 0 means no PITR). Deletion protection ON. Publicly accessible OFF; reach it from the app's security group only, and from your laptop via SSM port forwarding, never a public endpoint with a password. `performance_insights` ON (7-day retention is free) - it is how you will find the slow query. Set `max_connections` awareness: db.t4g.micro lands around 50-60 usable connections, so pool accordingly.
components.alternative_named: DynamoDB on-demand; Postgres co-located on the app instance; Aurora Serverless v2; Multi-AZ RDS.

components.service: Connection pooling: PgBouncer sidecar or RDS Proxy — but only if you went serverless
components.role: Keeps the database from being the ceiling.
components.why: This is the single most common way a small AWS app dies, and it is worth its own line. A long-running app process (EC2, Fargate, Beanstalk) holds a small pool - 10-20 connections - and never exhausts a t4g.micro. Lambda does not: every warm concurrent execution wants its own connection, so 100 concurrent Lambdas means 100 connections against a ~60-connection limit and you get `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved` under exactly the traffic spike you wanted to survive. RDS Proxy fixes it (~$0.015 per vCPU-hour of the database instance, ~$11-15/month for a small instance) but that is often more than the database. This is the concrete reason Lambda + RDS is a worse MVP pairing than Lambda + DynamoDB, and the concrete reason a single always-on process is easier than serverless at this size.
components.config: Always-on compute: set the ORM pool to 10-15 per process and confirm total (pool x processes x tasks) stays under 60% of `max_connections`. Serverless + relational: either RDS Proxy, or Aurora DSQL / Data API, or reconsider and use DynamoDB.
components.alternative_named: No pooling at all (the default, and the trap).

components.service: Edge + TLS: CloudFront in front of the app, ACM certificate in us-east-1, Route 53 alias
components.role: HTTPS on your domain, static asset caching, one place to add WAF later.
components.why: CloudFront in front of the ALB or instance rather than terminating TLS at the origin: it caches your static assets and any cacheable GETs so they never reach the app, it gives you HTTP/3 and Shield Standard free, and it means your origin can later move (EC2 to Fargate) without a DNS change. The crossover: below a few hundred requests/second of purely dynamic, uncacheable traffic CloudFront saves you little latency - its value at MVP scale is the free certificate on your apex, the asset offload, and the fact that you are not re-architecting when traffic arrives. If your app is entirely an API with no cacheable responses and you already have an ALB with an ACM cert, skipping CloudFront is defensible and saves nothing but complexity. ACM rather than Let's Encrypt when a load balancer or CloudFront terminates TLS (free, auto-renewing, no renewal cron to fail); Caddy/Let's Encrypt when you terminate on a single instance with no ALB.
components.config: ACM cert in us-east-1 for CloudFront (mandatory region), or in your app's region for an ALB. Cache policy: CachingDisabled on the default behaviour for an API, plus an explicit `/static/*` or `/_next/static/*` behaviour on CachingOptimized. Origin protocol policy HTTPS only. Forward the Host header if your framework generates absolute URLs.

components.service: Secrets: AWS Secrets Manager (or SSM Parameter Store SecureString)
components.role: Database password, API keys, signing keys.
components.why: Secrets Manager ($0.40 per secret per month + $0.05 per 10,000 API calls) rather than environment variables baked into a task definition or an .env on the box: environment variables show up in `describe-task-definition`, in CloudFormation events, in CI logs and in every screenshot someone pastes into Slack, and rotating one means redeploying. Secrets Manager also does managed rotation for the RDS password. SSM Parameter Store SecureString rather than Secrets Manager when budget genuinely matters - standard parameters are free, KMS decrypt is free-tier-covered, and the only things you give up are managed rotation and cross-account sharing. At five secrets that is $2/month versus $0 - take Parameter Store if you are counting, but never take the .env file.
components.config: One secret per environment, not one per key, to keep the count down. Grant the task/instance role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on that ARN only. ECS injects them via the `secrets` block in the task definition so they never appear in `environment`. Cache the fetch in-process; do not call on every request.

components.service: Backups + a proven restore
components.role: Recovery.
components.why: RDS automated backups with 7-day retention rather than nothing, and a nightly `pg_dump` to a versioned S3 bucket with Object Lock or at minimum a lifecycle rule, rather than relying on RDS snapshots alone. Two different mechanisms because they fail differently: RDS snapshots die with the RDS instance if someone deletes it (deletion protection ON is why), and a logical dump survives an account-level mistake and can be restored to a laptop. The rule that matters: a backup nobody restored is not a backup. Restore the dump to a throwaway instance and diff row counts before you call this done.
components.config: RDS: backup retention 7 days, backup window outside your peak, deletion protection ON, final snapshot on delete. Nightly dump: a scheduled ECS task or a cron on the instance running `pg_dump -Fc` to `s3://backups/` with versioning ON, lifecycle to Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days, expire at 180. Test restore monthly; put the date of the last successful restore somewhere a human sees.

components.service: Minimum viable monitoring: CloudWatch Logs + 5 alarms + one synthetic check
components.role: Knowing it is broken before a user tells you.
components.why: Five alarms rather than a dashboard: dashboards are read when you already suspect a problem; alarms wake you when you do not. And a synthetic canary hitting `/health` from outside rather than only internal metrics, because every internal metric can look healthy while DNS, the certificate or the security group is the thing that is broken - the classic silent failure. Do not install Datadog/New Relic at this stage; the agent cost and the per-host pricing exceed your infrastructure bill. Do not build a logging pipeline to OpenSearch (an OpenSearch domain starts around $25-50/month, more than your whole app) - CloudWatch Logs Insights queries the same data at $0.50/GB ingested and ~$0.005 per GB scanned.
components.config: Structured JSON logs to stdout, picked up by the awslogs/awsfirelens driver; log group retention set to 30 days (the default is Never Expire, which is how a $0.50/GB bill becomes a $40 bill). The five alarms: (1) 5xx rate > 1% over 5 min; (2) p95 latency > 2s over 5 min; (3) RDS FreeStorageSpace < 20%; (4) RDS CPUUtilization > 80% for 15 min AND CPUCreditBalance falling (the burstable-credit death spiral); (5) DatabaseConnections > 70% of max. Plus a CloudWatch Synthetics heartbeat canary every 5 minutes against `/health` (~$0.0012 per run, a few dollars a month) and an alarm on it. All alarms to one SNS topic to one email/phone. Every scheduled job writes a last-run timestamp somewhere queryable and has an alarm on staleness - a cron that silently stops is the failure you find six weeks late.

blueprints.ceiling: Concrete numbers, in the order you will actually hit them. (1) **Database connections first, almost always.** A db.t4g.micro (1 GB) tops out near 50-60 usable Postgres connections; a db.t4g.small near 120. With a 15-connection pool per process you get 3-4 app processes before you are at the wall, and you hit it as a wall, not a slope - latency is fine, then everything returns connection errors at once. (2) **Burstable CPU credits second.** t4g/t3 instances and db.t4g databases accrue CPU credits; a t4g.small earns 24 credits/hour and sustains ~20% CPU baseline. Run above baseline for hours and the balance hits zero and you are throttled to baseline - the app does not crash, it just gets slow and stays slow, which is far harder to diagnose. Watch `CPUCreditBalance`, and if it trends to zero daily you need a non-burstable size (m7g.medium), not a bigger t-instance. (3) **Single-instance throughput.** A 2 vCPU / 4 GB instance running a typical Python/Node/Rails app with a database-backed request at 50-100 ms serves roughly 200-500 requests/second of simple work, and far less - 30-80 req/s - once requests do real ORM work. Treat 500 req/s on one small instance as the optimistic bound, not the plan. (4) **The deploy itself.** With one instance, every deploy is downtime; at some traffic level that stops being acceptable, and that is a business ceiling, not a technical one. For the serverless variant the ceiling is different: Lambda's default account concurrency is 1,000 (a soft limit you can raise), API Gateway HTTP API's default is 10,000 requests/second per account per region, and the real ceiling is cost-per-request crossing over against an always-on instance somewhere around 10-20 million requests/month plus whatever a cold start does to your p99.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The database connection pool saturates first, and it looks like this: everything is fine at 8 req/s, you get a launch mention, concurrency triples, every new request tries to check out a connection, the pool is exhausted, requests queue, the queue exceeds the request timeout, and the app returns 500s across the board while CPU on both the app and the database sits under 30%. Every metric you are watching looks healthy, which is why people restart the app instead of fixing the pool. The second-most-common break is the burstable CPU credit balance hitting zero after a sustained busy day - silent, gradual, and it persists after the traffic leaves. The third is CloudWatch log-group retention set to Never Expire quietly becoming the largest line on the bill.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Machine-checkable signals: (1) `DatabaseConnections` sustained above 70% of `max_connections`, or any occurrence of `remaining connection slots are reserved` in the logs; (2) `CPUCreditBalance` reaching zero more than once a week, or CPU above 70% for more than an hour a day; (3) p95 latency above 1s with database CPU under 50% (means you are queueing, not computing); (4) deploy downtime is now being mentioned by users, or you need a deploy more than once a day during business hours; (5) RDS `FreeStorageSpace` trending to exhaustion inside 60 days; (6) an AZ-level outage would cost more than ~$200 (the annualised delta to Multi-AZ). Signal 1 means add a pooler or a bigger instance class. Signals 1+3 together mean the read path needs a cache or a read replica. Signal 4 is what actually justifies a second instance behind a load balancer - and that, not user count, is when this tier ends.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: This is where small teams burn a quarter's runway. **Do not build a custom VPC with public/private subnets and NAT gateways.** A NAT gateway is $0.045/hour ≈ $32.85/month each, plus $0.045 per GB processed; the textbook two-AZ layout is ~$66/month before a single byte, which is two to three times the entire rest of this architecture, to give private-subnet tasks outbound internet they mostly use for `apt` and one API call. Use the default VPC, put the app in a public subnet with a tight security group, and put the database in a subnet group with no public accessibility. If you genuinely need private subnets, VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are gateway endpoints and are free - use those before you use a NAT. **Do not enable Multi-AZ RDS** yet: it doubles the database bill to cut a 10-minute recovery to 60-120 seconds. Cost of skipping: one bad AZ day. Cost of adding: ~$180/year, every year, from day one. **Do not run Kubernetes.** EKS is $0.10/hour ≈ $73/month for the control plane alone before any node, plus the engineer-weeks to learn ingress controllers, and it solves a scheduling problem you do not have with one service and one database. This is the single most expensive premature decision on this list - reckon $73/month plus 2-6 engineer-weeks, call it $15-30k in the first year. **Do not build microservices.** Two services means two deploys, two sets of credentials, a network boundary where a function call was, and distributed-tracing work - for an app one person can hold in their head. **Do not add a message queue, Redis/ElastiCache, or a search cluster on speculation.** ElastiCache smallest useful node is ~$12-25/month and a Postgres index usually beats it at this size; OpenSearch starts at $25-50/month and Postgres full-text search is adequate to well past 1,000 users. SQS is the exception - it is genuinely near-free (1 million requests/month always free) and worth adding the moment you have a real background job, but add it for a job you have, not a job you imagine. **Do not set up multi-account Control Tower / Organizations with four accounts**; two (prod and non-prod) is the most a team of three should run. **Do not add auto-scaling groups with sophisticated policies** for a workload whose peak is 30 req/s - `minTaskCount 1, maxTaskCount 4` on Express Mode covers it. **Do not adopt a service mesh, a feature-flag platform, or an APM vendor.** Total avoidable spend commonly seen at this stage: $150-250/month in infrastructure plus the far larger cost of the engineering time, against a real need of $30-60/month.

plain.plainName: A real app with logins for your first 1,000 users
plain.problem: You have a product with logins, a database, and some work that runs in the background. Up to about 1,000 signed up users. A few minutes down during a release is fine. Losing a day of data is not.
plain.answer: Run the app on one right sized server or one ECS service, keep the data in managed Postgres, keep passwords in Secrets Manager, and watch it with CloudWatch.
plain.money: About $25 to $120 a month, not counting the domain. A small server is about $18 to $20 a month, and the managed database on top of that.
plain.holdsUpTo: About 1,000 users, 10 to 30 requests a second at peak, a database under 20 GB and under 2,000 writes a minute. One machine with 2 CPUs and 4 GB does this with room to spare.
plain.whatBreaks: You get a mention somewhere, three times as many people show up at once, and every page starts returning errors at the same moment. The confusing part is that the CPU on both the app and the database is under 30 percent, so every chart you are looking at says everything is fine.
plain.timeToMove: When the database connections sit above 70 percent of the limit, or the small server runs out of its CPU credit more than once a week, or slow pages happen while the database is under half busy, or users start complaining about downtime during releases.
plain.dontYet: Do not build a custom private network with gateways. Each gateway is about $32.85 a month plus $0.045 per GB, so the standard pair is about $66 a month before you send a single byte. That is two to three times the cost of everything else here, to give your app an internet exit it mostly uses for software updates and one API call. Use the default network with tight rules instead.
plain.pitch: I have paying users and logins, and I cannot afford an ops person yet.

blueprints.name: Two AZs, an ALB in front of a small auto scaling group, and a Multi-AZ managed database
blueprints.forWho: You have one EC2 box (or one Lightsail/Heroku dyno) running the app and the database side by side. Revenue is real, maybe 1,000-10,000 users, a few hundred thousand requests a day. A reboot or a bad deploy is a visible outage and someone emails you about it. Two to four engineers, nobody is a full-time SRE.
blueprints.scale: 1k-20k registered users, 50-300 req/s steady with peaks to ~600 req/s, DB under ~500 GB, under 1 TB/month egress
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $450-900/mo. Roughly: ALB $20-35 (LCU-driven), 2x t3.large or m7i.large app $120-150 on a 1-yr Compute Savings Plan, RDS db.m7g.large Multi-AZ ~$250-300 with 200 GB gp3, 1 NAT gateway $33 + ~$0.045/GB processing, S3+CloudFront $20-60, CloudWatch logs $20-50. The two things that actually drive the bill: the Multi-AZ RDS (doubles DB cost) and NAT data processing.

components.service: Application Load Balancer
components.role: Single public entry point, TLS termination with an ACM certificate, health checks that actually remove bad instances
components.why: Rather than an Elastic IP on one EC2 instance with nginx. The EIP approach means every deploy and every instance replacement is a DNS-or-downtime event, and there is no health check. ALB also gives you per-target-group blue/green for free later. Not NLB: you want HTTP health checks, host/path routing and HTTP/2 termination. Not CloudFront alone: CloudFront is not a load balancer and will happily cache-miss straight into a dead origin. ALB pricing is LCU-based; one LCU covers 25 new connections/sec, 3,000 active connections/min, 1 GB processed/hour, 1,000 rule evaluations/sec, and you pay the highest dimension. With keep-alive on, the new-connections dimension almost never dominates — processed bytes does.
components.config: internet-facing, 2 public subnets in 2 AZs; idle timeout 60s (must be LONGER than your app server's keep-alive timeout or you get random 502s); deregistration delay 30s; health check path a real /healthz that checks the DB, interval 15s, healthy 2 / unhealthy 3; access logs to S3; HTTP->HTTPS redirect rule; TLS 1.2+ policy

components.service: EC2 Auto Scaling group
components.role: 2-6 app instances across 2 AZs behind the ALB
components.why: Rather than jumping straight to Fargate. At this size EC2 with a 1-year Compute Savings Plan is materially cheaper for steady-state load — a 4 vCPU/16 GB workload is roughly $98/mo on m7i.xlarge with a 1-yr CSP versus roughly $128/mo for the equivalent Fargate task with a Fargate CSP, and the EC2 Savings Plan discount ceiling is higher (up to ~66% vs ~50%). Fargate wins when your containers run well under ~20 hours a day, when you have spiky or batch load, or when you have no one willing to patch AMIs. Fargate's real price is paid in engineer-hours saved, not dollars — be honest about which one you are short of. Rather than a fixed pair of instances: the ASG is what gives you automatic replacement of a failed instance, which is most of the availability win. The scaling is a bonus.
components.config: min 2, max 6, desired 2; target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget (pick a number you measured, e.g. 120 req/target) NOT on CPU — CPU lags and hides I/O-bound saturation; health check type ELB with 300s grace; instance refresh with MinHealthyPercentage 100 for deploys; AMI baked in CI (Packer or EC2 Image Builder) so boot time is under 90s; IMDSv2 required; no SSH keys, use SSM Session Manager

components.service: VPC: 2 public + 2 private subnets, one NAT gateway
components.role: App instances and RDS in private subnets; ALB in public; egress for package installs, webhooks and third-party APIs
components.why: One NAT gateway, not two, at this stage. Two NATs (one per AZ) is the textbook answer and costs another $33/mo plus removes a cross-AZ dependency — but for a 2-8 person team the far bigger win is killing NAT data-processing charges. NAT processing is $0.045/GB on top of the $0.045/hr. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB costs nothing — no hourly, no per-GB — and typically removes 50-80% of NAT bytes on its own once you add ECR interface endpoints too. The cheap alternative people reach for, a t4g.nano NAT instance (fck-nat, ~$3-4/mo, ~5 Gbps burst, no per-GB fee), is a real option and saves real money, but it is a single box you now own and patch; take it only if someone on the team will treat it as production infrastructure. Do not put app instances in public subnets with security groups as the only control — one misconfigured SG is then internet exposure, not a lateral-movement problem.
components.config: /16 VPC, /20 per subnet; S3 + DynamoDB gateway endpoints on day one (free); NAT in AZ-a only; route private subnets to it; VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch with a 14-day retention so you can actually find what is generating NAT traffic

components.service: Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL or MySQL), Multi-AZ
components.role: The primary datastore, on gp3 storage, in private subnets
components.why: Multi-AZ stops being optional the moment an unplanned reboot costs you money — Well-Architected is explicit that production workloads run in at least two AZs and that for managed data services you enable Multi-AZ so an AZ impairment is detected and failed over without you. Single-AZ RDS has a real, observed failure mode: a hardware event puts you down for the length of a restore-from-snapshot, which on 200 GB is tens of minutes to hours. Multi-AZ failover is typically 60-120 seconds. Multi-AZ instance (two-node) rather than Multi-AZ DB cluster (three-node) at this size: the cluster gives you faster failover and two readable standbys but costs ~50% more and adds a second endpoint concept. Rather than self-managing Postgres on EC2: you would be buying a part-time DBA job to save ~$80/mo. Do NOT use a burstable db.t3/t4g class as the production primary once you are past ~50 req/s of real query load — CPU credit exhaustion looks exactly like a database that has mysteriously become 10x slower, and it happens at the worst moment.
components.config: db.m7g.large (2 vCPU/8 GiB) or db.r7g.large if working set is memory-bound; Multi-AZ ON; gp3 200 GB with 3,000 baseline IOPS (raise IOPS explicitly, do not rely on gp2 size-coupled IOPS); automated backups 7-14 days; deletion protection ON; Performance Insights ON with 7-day free retention; parameter group with log_min_duration_statement = 500ms (Postgres) so slow queries land in CloudWatch; a read-only user separate from the app user

components.service: Connection pooling in the application (PgBouncer/HikariCP/pgx pool), not RDS Proxy yet
components.role: Keep total DB connections well under max_connections as the ASG scales
components.why: This is the first bottleneck almost everyone hits and it is not CPU. Postgres max_connections on RDS is derived from instance memory — LEAST(DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392, 5000) — which is ~341 on a 4 GiB db.t3.medium and ~680 on an 8 GiB db.m7g.large. Six app instances x a 30-connection default pool is 180 connections doing almost nothing, each costing the server memory and scheduler time. Fix it in the app pool first (pool size ~= 2-4 x vCPU per instance, so 8-10, not 30). Reach for RDS Proxy rather than app-side pooling only when you have Lambda or many short-lived processes, or when you want the proxy to hold connections through a Multi-AZ failover. RDS Proxy costs ~$0.015/vCPU-hour of the DB instance (~$22/mo on a 2 vCPU class), adds a few ms of latency, and its benefit collapses if your workload pins connections (session state, prepared statements in some modes, SET statements). PgBouncer on your own box is the other option: more debuggable, more flexible, and free, at the cost of being one more thing you run.
components.config: per-instance pool max = 10, min = 2, connection max-lifetime 15 min, acquire timeout 3s (fail fast, do not queue forever); alarm on DatabaseConnections > 60% of max_connections; if you do add RDS Proxy: MaxConnectionsPercent at least 30% above observed peak (AWS's floor is 20 for db.t3.medium-and-above, 30 for db.t3.small), watch DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency

components.service: S3 + CloudFront
components.role: Static assets, and all user uploads; CloudFront in front of both the asset bucket and the ALB
components.why: Rather than serving static files and uploads from the app instances. Two reasons, and cost is the smaller one: (1) every asset request served by your app is a request your ASG has to scale for, and static assets are typically 60-80% of request count; (2) files on instance disk do not survive an ASG instance replacement — you will lose user uploads, and this is the single most common data-loss incident at this stage. On cost, origin-to-CloudFront transfer from S3/ALB/EC2 is $0.00/GB, and CloudFront's first 1 TB/month plus 10M requests is free, so putting CloudFront in front of the ALB removes roughly $0.085/GB of ALB egress — about $77/mo saved on a 1 TB workload, which pays for the whole setup. Rather than making the bucket public: use Origin Access Control and presigned URLs/POSTs for uploads so the browser uploads straight to S3 and never through your app.
components.config: one distribution, two origins (S3 via OAC for /assets/* and /uploads/*, ALB for everything else); cache policy CachingOptimized for assets with content-hashed filenames and max-age 1 year; CachingDisabled for the app origin until you know what is safe to cache; forward Host to the ALB origin; S3 Block Public Access ON, versioning ON, lifecycle to move old versions to Glacier IR at 90 days; presigned POST with a content-length-range condition so nobody uploads a 5 GB file

components.service: SQS + a small worker ASG (or the same AMI with a different role)
components.role: Email, PDF generation, webhook delivery, image processing, anything over ~300ms that the user does not have to wait for
components.why: Rather than doing it inline in the web request, and rather than a cron-driven DB-table queue. Inline work is what turns a third-party outage into your outage: their 30s timeout becomes your 30s response time becomes your ALB 504. A DB-backed queue works until it doesn't — polling it is write load on the primary and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED contention at a few hundred jobs/sec. SQS is effectively free at this scale (first 1M requests/month free, then $0.40/M). Rather than Lambda for workers at this stage: your worker probably shares the app's code, ORM and connection pool, and running it on the same AMI means one deploy path instead of two. Lambda wins when the job is spiky and stateless.
components.config: standard queue (not FIFO unless you truly need ordering — FIFO caps at 300 msg/s without batching); visibility timeout = 6x your p99 job duration; maxReceiveCount 5 then a dead-letter queue; CloudWatch alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage > 300s (age, not depth — depth tells you nothing about whether you are keeping up); separate queues per job class so a slow PDF job cannot starve password-reset emails

components.service: CI/CD: GitHub Actions (or CodePipeline) -> build AMI/artifact -> deploy to staging -> manual approval -> production
components.role: One deploy path for code, migrations, and config
components.why: Rather than SSH-and-git-pull, and rather than a hand-rolled script on a laptop. The thing that matters is not the tool, it is that there is exactly one path and it runs migrations in a defined order. Use OIDC federation to assume an IAM role rather than long-lived access keys in CI — a leaked CI key is the most common way small teams lose an AWS account. Staging that actually matches production means the same AMI, the same Terraform/CDK modules with different variable values, and a production-shaped (not production-sized) database seeded from a sanitised snapshot.
components.config: GitHub OIDC -> IAM role with a narrow trust policy scoped to your repo AND branch; ASG instance refresh or CodeDeploy blue/green; migrations run as a separate, idempotent, expand-then-contract step BEFORE the new code rolls (never a destructive migration in the same deploy as the code that needs it); a real rollback command that is tested quarterly

components.service: Secrets Manager (or SSM Parameter Store SecureString) + CloudWatch Logs + a small set of alarms
components.role: Config, logs, and being told when it breaks
components.why: Parameter Store SecureString is free for standard parameters and is the right first choice; Secrets Manager costs $0.40/secret/month and earns it only when you want automatic RDS credential rotation or cross-account sharing. Rather than environment variables baked into the AMI or a .env in the repo. For logs: CloudWatch Logs agent on the instances with structured JSON, rather than a third-party log SaaS on day one — CloudWatch Logs Insights is adequate up to a few hundred GB/month and you already pay for it. Watch ingestion cost ($0.50/GB) and set retention explicitly; the default is forever.
components.config: Alarms that actually page: ALB 5xx rate > 1% for 5 min, ALB TargetResponseTime p99 > 2s for 5 min, UnHealthyHostCount >= 1, RDS FreeStorageSpace < 20%, RDS CPUUtilization > 80% for 15 min, RDS DatabaseConnections > 60% of max, SQS oldest-message-age, and a heartbeat alarm that fires when a scheduled job has NOT reported in. Log retention 30 days on app logs, 90 on audit. Everything to one SNS topic -> one on-call channel. Fewer than 10 alarms or nobody reads them.

components.service: Backups you have restored
components.role: Automated RDS snapshots plus a quarterly restore drill
components.why: Automated backups are a setting; a backup is a thing you have restored. Rather than trusting the console's green tick: restore the latest automated snapshot into a throwaway db instance in the staging account, run a row-count and checksum comparison on your five biggest tables, and record the wall-clock time it took. That number IS your RTO for the data-loss case, and it is usually 3-5x longer than people guess. Also enable AWS Backup with a separate vault if you want copies that a compromised production IAM role cannot delete.
components.config: RDS automated backups 14 days + PITR; one monthly manual snapshot copied to a second region; S3 versioning + MFA delete on the uploads bucket; a written runbook with the actual restore command and the measured restore time; drill on the calendar, quarterly

blueprints.ceiling: Roughly 300-600 req/s of dynamic traffic and a database working set that still fits in the RDS instance's RAM (about 6 GiB usable on a db.m7g.large). The app tier itself will go much further — you can add instances — but the single writer database is the wall.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The database, and it breaks in one of two ways, in this order. (1) Connection exhaustion: you scale the ASG under load, each new instance opens its pool, and you cross max_connections (~680 on 8 GiB). Symptom: 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already' / 'Too many connections' in the app logs, ALB 5xx spikes, and the DB's own CPU looking fine — which is why people misdiagnose it and scale the app tier, making it worse. (2) Read saturation: buffer cache hit ratio falls below ~95%, ReadIOPS climbs toward your provisioned 3,000, and p99 query time goes from 5ms to 200ms with no change in query count. Performance Insights will show you waiting on IO:DataFileRead. The second-order failure to watch for: when the DB slows, requests queue, keep-alive connections pile up on the ALB, and your target response time alarm and your unhealthy-host alarm fire together — the instances are not sick, they are blocked.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Any of these, measured, not felt: RDS CPUUtilization sustained above 70% for a week of business hours; DatabaseConnections above 60% of max_connections at peak; BufferCacheHitRatio below 95%; ALB TargetResponseTime p95 above 500ms while target CPU is below 50% (that means you are waiting on the DB, not on compute); ReadIOPS within 20% of provisioned; ASG scaling to max more than twice a week; or deploys taking longer than 10 minutes because instance boot dominates.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add Kubernetes. EKS is $73/mo for the control plane before a single pod runs, and the real cost is that one of your 2-8 engineers becomes a part-time cluster operator — call it 20-30% of a salary, which is $30-60k/yr to save maybe $100/mo of compute. Do not add read replicas yet: a replica costs a full instance and solves nothing until you have actually proven your load is read-heavy AND your code can tolerate replication lag; adding one before that just gives you a second place for data to be stale. Do not add ElastiCache yet — an unindexed query is not a caching problem, and cache-before-index is how teams end up with a fast wrong answer. Do not add a service mesh, multi-region anything, or a data warehouse. Do not shard. Do not add a second NAT gateway before you have added the free S3 gateway endpoint. Do not buy a 3-year Savings Plan on an instance family you have been running for six weeks.

plain.plainName: Two copies of everything so one reboot is not an outage
plain.problem: You run the app and the database on one box. Revenue is real, maybe 1,000 to 10,000 users. A reboot or a bad release is a visible outage and someone emails you about it.
plain.answer: Put a load balancer in front of a small group of servers that grows and shrinks, and move the database to a managed one that keeps a standby copy in a second data centre.
plain.money: About $450 to $900 a month. The two things that drive the bill are the standby database copy and the network gateway, not the servers.
plain.holdsUpTo: About 1,000 to 20,000 signed up users, 50 to 300 requests a second with peaks near 600, a database under 500 GB and under 1 TB of traffic out a month. The app side can keep growing. The single database that accepts writes is the wall.
plain.whatBreaks: The database. Under load you add more app servers, each one opens its own set of connections, and you cross the limit. The app logs fill with too many clients messages and users see errors, while the database CPU looks fine, which is exactly why people add more app servers and make it worse.
plain.timeToMove: When the database CPU stays above 70 percent for a week of work hours, or connections sit above 60 percent of the limit at peak, or pages take over half a second while the servers are under half busy, or the server group hits its maximum more than twice a week.
plain.dontYet: Do not add Kubernetes. It is $73 a month before a single thing runs, and the real cost is that one of your two to eight engineers becomes a part time cluster operator, roughly 20 to 30 percent of a salary, which is $30,000 to $60,000 a year to save maybe $100 a month. Do not add a read only copy of the database until you have proved your load is mostly reads and your code can live with that copy being slightly behind.
plain.pitch: One bad reboot takes my whole business offline and customers notice.

blueprints.name: Containers on Fargate, a read replica and ElastiCache, with real CI/CD and a staging that matches
blueprints.forWho: The database has become the visible bottleneck and deploys have become the scary part. 10,000-100,000 users. You have more than one service now, or you want to. Four to eight engineers, and at least one of them is spending a day a week on infrastructure they did not want to spend.
blueprints.scale: 10k-100k users, 500-2,000 req/s with peaks, 100-500 GB hot data, 1-10 TB/month egress
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $1,800-5,000/mo. Roughly: Fargate 6-12 tasks at 1 vCPU/2 GB with a Fargate Compute Savings Plan $250-600; ALB $40-80; RDS db.r7g.xlarge Multi-AZ ~$700-800 + 500 GB gp3 with provisioned IOPS $80-150; one read replica ~$350; ElastiCache Valkey/Redis cache.r7g.large replication group ~$300; NAT $70-200 depending on how much you killed with endpoints; CloudFront $100-500; CloudWatch + logs $150-400. The surprise line items are almost always NAT data processing and CloudWatch Logs ingestion.

components.service: ECS on Fargate
components.role: The web service and the worker service as separate ECS services, same image, different command
components.why: Now Fargate beats EC2, and the reason is not the sticker price — it is that you have stopped wanting to own AMIs, patch cycles, and the bin-packing problem. The honest arithmetic: EC2 with a 1-yr Compute Savings Plan is still ~20-25% cheaper per vCPU-hour than Fargate with a Fargate CSP, and the gap widens if you can bin-pack 10+ containers per instance or run Spot. So EC2 stays cheaper if your load is flat, your utilisation is above ~70%, and someone will own the capacity provider. Fargate wins when load is spiky (you pay per second for exactly the task size), when you have several services with different shapes, or when your engineer-hours are the scarce resource. Pick ECS over EKS: ECS control plane is $0, EKS is $73/mo plus a Kubernetes operator's attention. Pick ECS over App Runner because App Runner is being wound down and you need VPC-level control anyway. Right-size the task before you buy a Savings Plan — Fargate charges vCPU and GB separately, and an over-provisioned 2 vCPU/4 GB task that uses 0.4 vCPU is the most common waste at this stage.
components.config: awsvpc networking in private subnets; 1 vCPU / 2 GB per web task as a starting point, then right-size from Container Insights; ARM64/Graviton tasks (~20% cheaper, and your image probably builds for it); service auto scaling on ALBRequestCountPerTarget with min 4 / max 20; deployment circuit breaker with rollback ON; health check grace 60s; ECS Exec enabled for debugging instead of SSH; separate task definition and service for workers, scaled on SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible per task via a target-tracking custom metric

components.service: RDS primary (larger, Multi-AZ) + one read replica
components.role: Writes and read-your-writes go to the primary; reporting, search, exports and analytics-shaped reads go to the replica
components.why: Vertical first, then a replica. Doubling the primary (r7g.large -> r7g.xlarge) is the cheapest, lowest-risk capacity you will ever buy and it buys you roughly 2x — take it before you take on replication complexity. Add the read replica rather than more caching when the load is genuinely read-heavy AND the reads are long or scan-heavy (reports, exports, admin dashboards) — those are exactly the queries that poison the buffer cache for everyone else, and moving them is a bigger win than caching them. Do NOT route general application reads to the replica by default: RDS async replication lag is typically sub-second but spikes to seconds under write bursts or during vacuum, and 'user saves a form and the next page does not show it' is a bug class you will spend months on. Route by intent (an explicit read-only session/connection for known-safe endpoints), not by a global read/write splitter. Rather than Aurora: Aurora is genuinely better here (faster failover, storage that grows itself, up to 15 low-lag replicas) and costs roughly 20-30% more plus I/O charges unless you use Aurora I/O-Optimized; migrating is a real project, so take it at a planned moment, not during an incident.
components.config: primary db.r7g.xlarge (4 vCPU / 32 GiB) Multi-AZ, gp3 with explicitly provisioned IOPS (do not let 3,000 baseline be your ceiling) and provisioned throughput; one replica of the same class in the third AZ; alarm on ReplicaLag > 30s; Performance Insights with 7-day retention and the top-SQL view checked weekly; RDS Proxy in front of the primary if you now have Lambda or short-lived tasks in the mix

components.service: ElastiCache (Valkey or Redis OSS), replication group with automatic failover
components.role: Cache the three or four things you measured, plus sessions and rate-limit counters
components.why: Cache what Performance Insights says is expensive, not what feels expensive. In practice the first four wins are: (1) the permissions/feature-flag/tenant-config lookup that runs on literally every request, (2) the homepage or dashboard aggregate that takes 200ms+ and changes once a minute, (3) session data, so you can stop hitting the DB for auth, (4) rate-limit and idempotency counters, which do not belong in a relational DB at all. Use lazy loading (cache-aside) as the default — only requested data gets cached, and a cache node failure degrades rather than breaks — and add write-through only for the small set of reference data you can afford to keep permanently warm. AWS's own guidance is that write-through is almost always implemented alongside lazy loading, not instead of it. Rather than in-process memory caching: with 4-20 tasks you get 4-20 different answers and no way to invalidate. Rather than caching at CloudFront for logged-in pages: per-user content at the edge is how you leak one user's data to another.
components.config: cache.r7g.large, cluster-mode disabled, 1 primary + 1 replica in another AZ, automatic failover ON, Multi-AZ ON; encryption in transit and at rest; maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for the cache keyspace; explicit TTLs on everything (no TTL is a memory leak with extra steps); a separate cluster or at least separate DB index for sessions, because you never want to flush sessions to clear a cache; alarm on Evictions > 0 and on CPUUtilization > 60% (Redis is single-threaded per shard — 60% is the real ceiling, not 90%)

components.service: SQS + dead-letter queues + worker autoscaling, with backpressure discipline
components.role: All async work, with queues separated by job class and by tenant where one tenant can flood
components.why: At this size the queue itself becomes a failure mode. The AWS Builders' Library point is the one to internalise: a backlog can become insurmountable — if consumers drain slower than producers fill, you do not have a delay, you have an outage that gets worse while you watch. Their mitigations are the ones to copy: separate workloads into separate queues, shuffle-shard so one noisy tenant hits only a subset, and sideline excess traffic to a side queue you process later rather than letting it block the main line. Rather than one big queue with priority fields: priority-in-a-single-queue does not work, because the low-priority messages are still ahead of you in the poll. Rather than scaling workers on queue depth: scale on backlog-per-task (messages visible / running tasks) targeting a number derived from your job duration and your acceptable latency.
components.config: one queue per job class; DLQ on every queue with maxReceiveCount 5 and an alarm on DLQ depth > 0 (a message in a DLQ is a bug, always); visibility timeout 6x p99 duration; ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage alarm per queue; a documented, tested drain procedure; idempotency keys on every handler, because SQS standard delivers at-least-once and your worker WILL process a message twice

components.service: S3 + CloudFront with an upload pipeline
components.role: All user uploads via presigned POST direct to S3; processing triggered by S3 event -> SQS -> worker
components.why: Rather than uploads flowing through your app tasks. A 50 MB upload through a Fargate task holds a vCPU hostage for the duration and counts against your task concurrency; direct-to-S3 makes it someone else's problem. Trigger processing from S3 events into SQS rather than S3 -> Lambda directly, so you get the DLQ, the retry policy and the backpressure you already built. Use CloudFront with signed URLs for private user content rather than making objects public or proxying every download through the app.
components.config: presigned POST with content-length-range and content-type conditions, 5-minute expiry; separate buckets for raw uploads and processed derivatives; S3 event notification -> SQS (not directly to the worker); Intelligent-Tiering on the derivatives bucket; CloudFront signed URLs with short expiry for private objects; Block Public Access ON at the account level

components.service: CI/CD with a real staging environment and an approval gate
components.role: Build once, promote the same image through staging to production
components.why: Build the image once and promote the digest — rather than rebuilding per environment, which means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped. Staging matches production in shape, not size: same VPC layout, same service topology, same IAM structure, same migration path, a smaller RDS class, and a database seeded from a sanitised production snapshot so your query plans are realistic. A staging DB with 500 rows will never show you the sequential scan that takes production down. The approval gate is a human, and the sequence is never batched: deploy to staging, someone other than the author verifies, then the go-ahead, then production.
components.config: immutable image tags by git SHA, never :latest; ECR lifecycle policy keeping the last 30 images; ECS rolling deploy with circuit breaker, or CodeDeploy blue/green with a 10-minute bake and automatic rollback on the 5xx alarm; migrations as a standalone ECS run-task that must succeed before the service update; a smoke-test job that hits real endpoints after deploy and fails the pipeline

components.service: Centralised logging, metrics and traces
components.role: Structured JSON logs to CloudWatch, Container Insights on, and X-Ray or an OTel collector for traces
components.why: Traces earn their keep at exactly this point, when a request crosses ALB -> web task -> cache -> DB -> queue -> worker and 'it's slow' has four possible owners. Rather than reading logs across services by hand. Keep CloudWatch as the alarm and metric backbone (it is already integrated with every alarm you need), and be deliberate about log ingestion cost at $0.50/GB — a debug-level log line per request at 1,500 req/s is about 4 TB/month if you are careless. Sample traces (5-10%) rather than tracing everything.
components.config: structured JSON with a request ID propagated end to end and into the queue message; log retention 30 days hot; metric filters for the handful of business events you alarm on; Container Insights enabled; X-Ray/ADOT sampling at 5% plus 100% of errors; one dashboard per service that a new engineer can read at 3am

blueprints.ceiling: Roughly 2,000-4,000 req/s and a single-writer database. You can keep growing the app tier almost indefinitely on Fargate; you cannot keep growing writes. The wall is write throughput and the working set on one primary — on a db.r7g.4xlarge with well-provisioned gp3 or io2 you are looking at low thousands of write transactions per second before checkpoint and WAL behaviour dominate.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Write contention on the primary, and lock contention before raw IOPS. The pattern: a hot table (a counter, a jobs table, a tenant row updated on every request) starts showing lock waits in Performance Insights, p99 write latency climbs while CPU and IOPS both look fine, and connections pile up waiting. Second failure mode: replication lag on the read replica spikes during your nightly batch, and any endpoint you routed to the replica starts serving stale data — usually discovered as a customer support ticket, not an alarm. Third, and the one that catches teams: cache stampede. A popular key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests all miss, all hit the DB with the same expensive query, and the DB falls over — the cache you added to protect the database is now the mechanism that kills it. Fix with a lock-on-miss or probabilistic early expiry before you need to.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Write TPS on the primary above 60% of what you measured it can sustain; lock-wait events appearing in the Performance Insights top-waits list; the biggest table past ~500 GB or past the point where an ALTER TABLE is a multi-hour event; replication lag regularly above 10s; one tenant's traffic able to degrade every other tenant; or your team saying out loud that they are afraid to run a migration. Also: the moment a compliance question arrives (SOC 2, a customer security review), which pushes the account separation below.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not shard the database. Sharding is a year of engineering, it removes cross-shard joins and transactions from your vocabulary, and almost everyone who did it at this scale could have bought two more instance sizes and an archiving job instead. Do not go multi-region active-active — you will pay cross-region data transfer, double the infrastructure, and inherit conflict resolution, to solve an availability problem you have not actually had. Do not add EKS to get 'portability' you will never exercise. Do not adopt a service mesh for 4-8 services; ECS Service Connect covers service discovery and you do not need mTLS between two services you own. Do not build a microservice per team boundary before the monolith is demonstrably the constraint — the distributed version of your bug is much harder to find. Do not buy an observability SaaS at $30k/yr before you have tried CloudWatch Logs Insights and found it wanting for a named reason.

plain.plainName: Containers, a spare copy of the data, and releases that are not scary
plain.problem: The database is now the obvious bottleneck and releasing new code has become the scary part of the week. 10,000 to 100,000 users. You have more than one service, and one engineer is losing a day a week to infrastructure they never wanted.
plain.answer: Run the app as containers on Fargate, add one read only copy of the database and an ElastiCache memory cache, and build a real release pipeline with a staging copy that matches production.
plain.money: About $1,800 to $5,000 a month. The main pieces are the containers at $250 to $600, the main database around $700 to $800, the read copy about $350 and the cache about $300.
plain.holdsUpTo: About 10,000 to 100,000 users, 500 to 2,000 requests a second with peaks, and 100 to 500 GB of hot data. You can keep adding containers almost forever. You cannot keep adding writes. The wall is around 2,000 to 4,000 requests a second.
plain.whatBreaks: One popular row or table, like a counter or a jobs table, gets written by everyone at once. Writes start taking much longer for a small share of users while the CPU and disk both look fine. Separately, the read only copy falls behind during the nightly batch, so anything reading from it shows people stale data.
plain.timeToMove: When writes pass 60 percent of what you measured the database can take, or your biggest table passes about 500 GB and a schema change becomes a multi hour event, or the read copy is regularly more than 10 seconds behind, or one customer's traffic can slow down every other customer, or your team says out loud that they are afraid to run a migration.
plain.dontYet: Do not split the database into shards. It is about a year of engineering and you lose the ability to join or transact across the pieces. Almost everyone who did it at this size could have bought two bigger instances and an archiving job instead. Do not go multi region, and do not add Kubernetes for portability you will never use.
plain.pitch: The database is the bottleneck and I dread every deploy.

blueprints.name: Separate production account, shared services, and the blast-radius work you should have done earlier
blueprints.forWho: Everything above is running in one AWS account, and that has started to be the risk. Someone can run terraform destroy against production from a laptop. A staging load test has throttled production's API quota. A customer's security questionnaire asks how environments are isolated and the honest answer is 'IAM policies, mostly'. This is an organisational blueprint layered onto either of the two above, not a replacement for them.
blueprints.scale: Applies from about 10k users or the first enterprise customer, whichever comes first; typically 4-8 engineers and 2-4 environments
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $50-250/mo incremental. AWS Organizations, Control Tower's core machinery, IAM Identity Center and SCPs cost nothing. The real costs are: duplicated baseline infrastructure per account (a NAT gateway per account at $33/mo is the big one, plus a second ALB for staging ~$20), CloudTrail data events and Config if you enable them ($50-150), and the engineering time — budget 1-2 weeks of one person to do it properly, and do it BEFORE you have 40 hand-made resources per environment.

components.service: AWS Organizations with a Production OU and a Non-Production OU
components.role: A hard boundary between environments, not a policy one
components.why: An AWS account is the only real blast-radius boundary AWS gives you — it is a natural security, access, quota and billing boundary, and AWS's own best-practice guidance is to separate production workloads from test/dev workloads into separate accounts and to organise OUs by business purpose and a common set of controls, not by your org chart. The alternative people try first is tag-based IAM conditions in one account: it works on paper and fails in practice, because every new service adds a resource type someone forgets to tag, and a single Deny gap is full production access. The other thing account separation buys you that IAM cannot: service quotas and API rate limits are per-account, so a staging load test literally cannot exhaust production's Lambda concurrency or EC2 API throttle budget. And it makes cost per environment a fact rather than a tagging exercise.
components.config: Management account runs NOTHING except Organizations, billing and Identity Center; Security OU (log archive + security tooling accounts); Infrastructure OU (shared services, CI/CD, ECR); Workloads OU with Prod and Non-Prod children; production account has its own VPC, its own RDS, its own everything. Group email address for every root account, root credentials removed via centralised root access management, MFA everywhere.

components.service: IAM Identity Center (SSO) with permission sets
components.role: How humans get access, everywhere, with no long-lived keys
components.why: Rather than IAM users with access keys per account, which is how you end up with 30 keys nobody can attribute and a leaked one in a git history. Permission sets give you time-bound, role-based, logged access, and offboarding is one action in one place. Production gets a read-only permission set by default and a break-glass admin set that is loud — alarmed on assumption, not merely logged.
components.config: ReadOnly + Ops + BreakGlass permission sets; production admin requires MFA and fires a CloudWatch alarm to the team channel on assumption; session duration 1-4 hours, not 12; no IAM users at all except a documented break-glass one with credentials in a sealed store

components.service: Service Control Policies
components.role: Guardrails that even an account admin cannot escape
components.why: SCPs are the only control that a compromised or careless account-level administrator cannot override, which is exactly the class of mistake you are trying to prevent. Rather than relying on IAM policies alone — those are editable by the person making the mistake. Keep the SCP set small and boring at first; a clever SCP that breaks a deploy at 2am teaches everyone to distrust guardrails.
components.config: Deny leaving the organisation, deny disabling CloudTrail/GuardDuty/Config, deny deleting log-archive buckets, deny regions you do not operate in (this alone kills most crypto-mining abuse), deny root user actions. In the Non-Prod OU additionally deny expensive instance families. Test every SCP in a sandbox OU first.

components.service: Cross-account CI/CD from a shared services account
components.role: The pipeline lives in one account and assumes a deploy role in each target account
components.why: Rather than a pipeline per account, or a pipeline in production. The deploy role in production is the only path into production, it is assumable only by the pipeline's role, and it is scoped to the resources it deploys. This is also what lets you keep one ECR registry — build the image once in the shared account, grant pull access to the workload accounts by repository policy, and promote the same digest. Rather than copying images between accounts: same artifact, cross-account pull.
components.config: CodePipeline or GitHub Actions in the shared account; sts:AssumeRole into prod-deploy-role with an ExternalId or a branch-scoped OIDC trust; ECR repository policy granting pull to the Organization; artifact bucket with a KMS key shared to the workload accounts (the KMS grant is the step everyone forgets and the error message is unhelpful)

components.service: Centralised logging to a log archive account
components.role: CloudTrail (organisation trail), VPC Flow Logs and application logs land in an account nobody can write to
components.why: Rather than logs in the same account as the workload. If an attacker or a mistake takes the production account, logs in that account are gone or forged. An organisation-wide CloudTrail delivering to a separate log archive account, with a bucket policy that allows write-but-not-delete, is the difference between an incident you can investigate and one you can only speculate about. This is also the artifact an enterprise security review actually asks for.
components.config: organisation trail, management + selected data events; S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the archive bucket for the retention you claim; lifecycle to Glacier after 90 days; the retention number in your security documentation must match the lifecycle policy — go and check, because if the document and the bucket disagree the document is wrong

components.service: Per-account cost visibility and budgets
components.role: Each environment's bill is a number, not an estimate
components.why: Consolidated billing gives you one invoice with per-account lines, which turns 'what does staging cost us' from a tagging archaeology project into a Cost Explorer filter. Budgets with alerts on non-production accounts catch the forgotten load-test cluster within a day instead of at month end. This is the argument that usually gets the account separation funded.
components.config: a budget per account at 120% of trailing average with alerts at 80/100/120%; Cost Anomaly Detection on; a monthly 15-minute review; Compute Savings Plans bought at the organisation level so coverage applies across accounts

blueprints.ceiling: This structure holds well past 100,000 users and into hundreds of accounts; the ceiling is organisational, not technical. It stops being enough when you need per-customer or per-region isolation (dedicated accounts per enterprise tenant), or when the number of accounts outgrows manual provisioning and you need Control Tower Account Factory plus a real platform team.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The shared-services seam.
