The three things that go wrong, in order of likelihood: (1) cross-account KMS grants — the pipeline can read the artifact bucket but cannot decrypt, and the error says AccessDenied with no mention of KMS; (2) VPC peering or Transit Gateway added reflexively between environments, which quietly rebuilds the network path you just spent a week removing and undoes most of the isolation; (3) an SCP that blocks a service the deploy needs, discovered during a production incident. Also expect the NAT gateway line on the bill to multiply by the number of accounts — add the free S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints in every account as part of the baseline, not later.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: You need a dedicated account per large customer; you are operating in more than two regions; account provisioning is manual and happening more than monthly; or compliance requires evidence of controls you are enforcing by convention. Then: Control Tower with Account Factory, an account baseline as code, and a named owner for the landing zone.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not create fifteen accounts on day one. Start with four — management, log archive, production, non-production — and add shared-services and security accounts when you feel the specific pain. Every account is a VPC, a NAT gateway, a set of baseline resources and a place for drift to hide. Do not adopt Control Tower before you have four accounts; it imposes a structure you should first understand by hand, and un-enrolling is unpleasant. Do not write clever SCPs — a deny policy you cannot explain in one sentence will cost you an outage. Do not peer the environment VPCs together 'for convenience'; if staging needs production data, that is a sanitised snapshot pipeline, not a network route. Do not run any workload in the management account, ever, including the 'temporary' one.

plain.plainName: Keeping production separate so one mistake cannot wipe it
plain.problem: Everything runs in one AWS account and that is now the risk. Someone can delete production from a laptop. A test under load slowed down real customers. A customer asks how your environments are separated and the honest answer is not good.
plain.answer: Split into separate AWS accounts under AWS Organizations, sign in through IAM Identity Center, and fence off what each account may do with service control policies.
plain.money: About $50 to $250 a month extra. The accounts, the sign in system and the policies cost nothing. The extra money is duplicated basics per account, mainly a $33 a month network gateway in each one and about $20 for a second load balancer for staging.
plain.holdsUpTo: Well past 100,000 users and into hundreds of accounts. The limit is your organisation, not the technology.
plain.whatBreaks: The joins between accounts. Most often a release pipeline can read a file from another account but cannot unlock it, and the error just says access denied with no hint about the key. Or someone reconnects the networks between environments and quietly undoes the separation you just spent a week building.
plain.timeToMove: When you need a dedicated account for a single large customer, or you run in more than two regions, or you are creating accounts by hand more than once a month, or an auditor wants evidence of rules you are only enforcing by habit.
plain.dontYet: Do not create fifteen accounts on day one. Start with four, which are management, log archive, production and non production, and add more when you feel the specific pain. Every account is another network, another gateway and another place for things to drift. Do not adopt Control Tower before you have four accounts, and do not write clever deny policies you cannot explain.
plain.pitch: Someone could delete production from a laptop and nothing would stop them.

blueprints.name: One region, three AZs, one modular monolith, one Aurora cluster, everything slow pushed off the request path
blueprints.forWho: 100k–1M users, 10–40 engineers, a transactional product where five minutes down is a customer email and an hour is a refund. You have paying customers and an on-call rota but no platform team yet. Most teams who say 'we need to scale' are actually here, and most of them skip this tier for no reason.
blueprints.scale: 100k–1M registered, 20k–150k DAU. 2,000–8,000 req/s peak reads, 200–800 writes/s. 1–10 TB in the primary DB. p99 API target 300ms.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $12k–$45k. Order of drivers: Aurora writer + 2 readers on r7g.4xlarge (~$4.5k–7k before I/O), app tier on ECS Fargate or EC2 (~$3k–10k), ElastiCache (~$800–2.5k), NAT Gateway plus cross-AZ transfer (~$1k–4k, almost always unbudgeted), CloudWatch Logs ingest at $0.50/GB (easily $2k+ if you log full request bodies). Cost per MAU lands $0.20–$0.60 — start tracking it now, it is the number that tells you whether growth is profitable.

components.service: CloudFront in front of an ALB
components.role: TLS termination, cacheable-GET offload, absorbs bot long tail.
components.why: Rather than serving everything from the ALB. The ALB never caches and is billed in LCUs on connections, bytes and rule evaluations, so every cacheable GET it serves burns an app thread and a DB connection for nothing. Crossover is roughly a few hundred cacheable GETs/sec or ~1 TB/month of static egress; below that the ALB alone is fine and CloudFront is just another cache to invalidate.
components.config: Cache policy keyed on path plus an explicit allowlist of query params and headers — never CacheKey=all-headers, which gives a ~0% hit rate. Origin Shield on in the origin's region. Compress objects. Separate behaviour for /api/* with caching disabled so you never cache a logged-in response by accident.

components.service: ALB + ECS Fargate (or an EC2 ASG), one service, three AZs
components.role: Runs the modular monolith. Horizontal, stateless, autoscaled.
components.why: Rather than decomposing into 12 microservices now. At this tier a modular monolith with enforced internal module boundaries gives you the same design discipline without a network hop, a deploy pipeline and a failure mode per boundary. Prime Video's own team rebuilt a Step Functions + Lambda + S3 pipeline back into a single process and cut cost ~90% because the orchestration transitions and the S3 round-trips between stages dominated. Decompose when a module has genuinely different scaling or on-call shape, not when the diagram gets big.
components.config: Minimum 6 tasks (2 per AZ) so losing an AZ removes a third, not a half. 1 vCPU / 2 GB is a normal starting task. ALB deregistration delay 30s, target group health check 10s interval / 2 healthy / 2 unhealthy. Autoscale on ALB RequestCountPerTarget, not CPU — CPU lags by a scaling cycle. Cap DB connections per task explicitly (e.g. pool of 10) so max tasks × pool stays below the Aurora max_connections.

components.service: Aurora PostgreSQL, writer + 2 readers across AZs, behind RDS Proxy
components.role: System of record. Reads split onto the reader endpoint, writes to the writer.
components.why: Rather than RDS Multi-AZ on plain PostgreSQL. Aurora's shared storage layer makes a reader promotion roughly 30 seconds rather than a multi-minute Multi-AZ failover, replica lag is typically tens of milliseconds rather than seconds, and adding a reader takes minutes with no rebuild. RDS Proxy rather than PgBouncer on a box: it survives failover by holding the client connection while the backend flips, which is the whole point. Aurora gives you 15 read replicas per cluster and that is a hard, non-adjustable quota — know it before you plan on it.
components.config: Start r7g.2xlarge writer. Readers in the other two AZs, autoscaled on reader CPU. Backtrack or PITR on. Enable Performance Insights and Enhanced Monitoring at 1s from day one — you cannot diagnose the saturation retroactively. Explicitly route reads: a `useReplica` flag per query path, defaulting to the writer, so read-after-write correctness is opt-out and visible in code review.

components.service: ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis), cluster mode disabled, 1 primary + 1 replica
components.role: One cache layer only: hot object cache and session/rate-limit counters.
components.why: Rather than adding a second in-process cache too. The Builders' Library's caching article is blunt about this: caches create modal behaviour, and the day the cache is empty your service meets a load it has never handled. An external cache at least gives you coherence across hosts; a local in-process cache gives you N different views of the truth and a cold start on every deploy. Only cache where hit rate will exceed ~80% — below that you have added a failure mode and a latency hop to save almost nothing.
components.config: Soft TTL / hard TTL pair: refresh at the soft TTL, keep serving up to the hard TTL if the origin is failing. Jitter every TTL by ±10% so keys do not expire in a convoy. Request coalescing (single-flight) on cache miss or the first miss on a hot key becomes a thundering herd on Aurora. Cache negative results with a short TTL. Emit hit rate, miss rate and origin-request rate as first-class metrics. Run a scheduled game day with the cache flushed — if the service falls over, the cache is load-bearing and you should size the DB for cold.

components.service: SQS standard queues + a separate worker service, fed by a transactional outbox table
components.role: Everything the user does not wait for: email, webhooks, PDF generation, search indexing, analytics fan-out.
components.why: Rather than publishing to the queue inline in the request handler. That is a dual write: commit succeeds, publish fails, and the downstream never learns — or publish succeeds, transaction rolls back, and you charge a card for a booking that does not exist. The outbox table written in the SAME transaction as the business row, drained by a poller, is AWS's own prescribed fix. SQS rather than a DB-backed job table because the visibility timeout, DLQ and at-least-once redelivery are already built and tested.
components.config: Outbox row carries an event id, aggregate id, sequence number and timestamp. Poller batches 10, SendMessageBatch, deletes only on a successful send. Consumers MUST be idempotent — dedupe on the event id in a table with a TTL, do not rely on FIFO to save you. Visibility timeout = 6× p99 handler time. maxReceiveCount 5 then DLQ. Alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, not queue depth: depth tells you volume, age tells you whether you are keeping up.

components.service: CloudWatch + a structured log pipeline, with a heartbeat per scheduled job
components.role: Observability and proof that background work actually ran.
components.why: Rather than relying on error alerts alone. A job that stops running emits no errors. Every cron, poller and integration writes a last-success timestamp and you alarm on its staleness. Use metric filters / EMF for counters rather than paying to query logs for numbers you could have emitted as metrics.
components.config: RED metrics per endpoint (rate, errors, duration) at p50/p90/p99 — never average latency, which hides exactly the tail that hurts. Alarm on p99 and on error rate, plus a composite alarm so a dependency blip does not page three people. Log retention 30 days hot in CloudWatch, everything older exported to S3.

blueprints.ceiling: The writer instance. On an r7g.8xlarge Aurora PostgreSQL writer you will typically hold 3,000–6,000 writes/s of small OLTP transactions and maybe 15,000–25,000 simple reads/s spread across readers, before one of three things bites. In practice teams hit the wall between 500 and 2,000 req/s per app instance depending on how many queries a request makes — a request that issues 30 queries saturates the pool at a twentieth of the traffic of one that issues 1.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Almost always the connection pool, not CPU. Symptom: p99 climbs while writer CPU sits at 40%, and application logs fill with pool-acquire timeouts. Cause: tasks × pool size exceeded what the writer will serve, and every extra connection makes Postgres slower, not faster. Second most common: autovacuum on your largest table cannot keep up, bloat grows, and IOPS flatlines at the instance's EBS ceiling — Figma names exactly this pair (vacuum reliability impact and the IOPS ceiling) as what pushed them off a single instance. Third: a single hot partition of a hot table, where one tenant's rows dominate and no amount of instance size helps.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: (1) Writer CPU sustains >60% at daily peak, or writes/s have doubled in a quarter. (2) You have added your 5th read replica — you are treating replicas as a fix for a write problem. (3) Replica lag exceeds 1s at peak and you have started seeing read-after-write bugs in support tickets. (4) Your largest table exceeds ~500 GB and vacuum no longer completes inside the low-traffic window. (5) Deploy blast radius: a bad deploy takes 100% of customers down and you have had two such incidents. (6) Cost per MAU has risen two quarters in a row while MAU grew — you are scaling sub-linearly in the wrong direction.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not go multi-region. AWS's own multi-region fundamentals guidance says start multi-AZ and be honest about whether the requirement is real: multi-region roughly doubles infrastructure, adds cross-region transfer, and buys you a failover path you will not test often enough to trust. A multi-region active-active build at this tier typically costs 2–2.5× and consumes a senior engineer for two quarters, to protect against an event rarer than your own deploy-induced outages. Do not shard the database. Figma got a 100x runway out of vertical partitioning and replicas first and did not ship their first horizontal shard until 2023 — sharding before you have exhausted vertical, replicas and purpose-built stores buys you a distributed transaction problem you did not have. Do not adopt Kubernetes for six services; you will spend a headcount on the cluster. Do not build a service mesh. Do not add a second cache tier. Do not split into microservices along org-chart lines — you are converting in-process function calls that cannot fail into network calls that can, and you now need retries, timeouts, circuit-breaking and distributed tracing to get back to where you were.

plain.plainName: One well built app in three data centres in one region
plain.problem: 100,000 to 1,000,000 users and 10 to 40 engineers. Five minutes down is a customer email and an hour is a refund. You have an on call rota but no platform team. Most teams who say they need to scale are actually here.
plain.answer: Run one well organised app across three data centres behind CloudFront and a load balancer, put the data in one Aurora cluster with two read copies, and push everything slow onto SQS queues and background workers.
plain.money: About $12,000 to $45,000 a month. The order of spend is the database at $4,500 to $7,000, the app at $3,000 to $10,000, the cache at $800 to $2,500, network transfer at $1,000 to $4,000 which is almost always unbudgeted, and logs at $0.50 per GB which easily reaches $2,000 if you log full requests.
plain.holdsUpTo: 100,000 to 1,000,000 registered users, 20,000 to 150,000 daily actives, 2,000 to 8,000 reads a second at peak and 200 to 800 writes a second, with 1 to 10 TB of data. The one writing database typically holds 3,000 to 6,000 writes a second before it bites.
plain.whatBreaks: Not the CPU. Pages get slow for the unlucky few while the database CPU sits at 40 percent, because the app is queueing for a free database connection. Adding more connections makes it slower, not faster. The other common one is background cleanup falling behind on your biggest table until disk activity flatlines.
plain.timeToMove: When the writing database stays above 60 percent CPU at daily peak, or writes have doubled in a quarter, or you are adding your fifth read copy, or the read copies fall more than a second behind and support tickets show people not seeing what they just saved, or your biggest table passes about 500 GB and cleanup no longer finishes overnight.
plain.dontYet: Do not go multi region. AWS's own guidance says start with multiple data centres in one region and be honest about whether you really need more. Multi region roughly doubles your infrastructure, adds cross region transfer, and gives you a failover path you will not practise enough to trust. At this size it costs 2 to 2.5 times as much and eats a senior engineer for two quarters, to protect against an event rarer than your own bad releases. Do not shard the database.
plain.pitch: An hour of downtime means refunds, and I have no platform team.

blueprints.name: One region, N independent cells, shuffle-sharded tenants, read path and write path split apart
blueprints.forWho: 1M–10M users, or any multi-tenant platform where a single bad deploy or one poisonous tenant currently takes down every customer. 40–150 engineers with a platform team. The trigger is not raw load — it is that your blast radius is 100% and your board has noticed.
blueprints.scale: 1M–10M users, 200k–2M DAU. 20,000–150,000 req/s aggregate. Tens of TB of primary data. Availability target 99.95%+ with a real error budget.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $80k–$400k. Cells are the dominant driver: 4 cells each with their own Aurora cluster, cache and compute costs roughly 4× the per-cell fixed floor, so the fixed floor per cell is the number to attack. Second: data transfer and the streaming tier (Kinesis at $0.015/shard-hour plus PUT payload units, or EventBridge at $1.00 per million events). Third: observability, which at this scale becomes a top-3 line item and is why you sample. Cost per MAU should be FLAT or falling — if it rises as you add cells, your cell is sized too small.

components.service: A thin cell router (Route 53 / CloudFront Function / API Gateway) plus a control plane
components.role: Maps a partition key to exactly one cell and presents one endpoint. Nothing else.
components.why: Rather than an ALB doing smart routing, or the app deciding. AWS calls this the 'thinnest possible layer' for a reason: the router is the one shared component, so anything it does beyond lookup-and-forward becomes a correlated failure across every cell and you have thrown away the isolation you just paid for. Keep auth, rate limiting, enrichment and retries OUT of it. The control plane (provisioning, migrating tenants, draining cells) is a separate system with a separate deploy — a control-plane failure must not stop the data plane serving.
components.config: Partition key must be present in essentially every API call: tenant id, org id, or user id. Not a value you have to look up first, because that lookup is a shared dependency. Mapping stored in a cheap, highly available store (DynamoDB or a static config distributed to edge) with a long TTL and a stale-is-fine read. Start with 2–4 cells and grow deliberately; the common path is few large cells first, then smaller cells as your automation improves.

components.service: The cell: a complete, independent copy of the stack (compute + DB + cache + queues)
components.role: Serves a fixed subset of tenants. Shares no state with any other cell.
components.why: Rather than one big fleet with more redundancy. Redundancy protects against a host dying. It does not protect against a bad deploy, a poison-pill request, a corrupt cache entry or a schema migration — those travel with your code and your data and go everywhere at once. With 10 cells, a failure that would have been 100% is 10%. Cell-based architecture does not necessarily mean more hosts: 30 hosts in one fleet can become 30 hosts in 6 cells plus a router.
components.config: Size each cell by what you can TEST at 100% of its stated maximum, and keep that maximum comfortably below your per-account service quotas — cells exist partly so no single cell can hit an account limit. Write the cell's contract down: max TPS, max tenants, max GB. Load test to that number and beyond every release. Deploy cell-by-cell with bake time between: cell 1, wait, cells 2-3, wait, the rest. That staged rollout is most of the value.

components.service: Shuffle sharding on top of the cells (or on the worker/queue tier)
components.role: Gives each tenant a near-unique combination of workers so that two tenants rarely share their full set.
components.why: Rather than plain sharding. With 8 workers split into 4 fixed shards of 2, a bad tenant takes out 25% of the service. With shuffle sharding — each tenant assigned a virtual shard of 2 out of those same 8 workers — there are 28 possible combinations, so scope of impact is 1/28th: seven times better for zero extra hardware. Route 53 runs 2,048 virtual name servers with 4 assigned per domain, giving ~730 billion combinations, enough that no two customer domains share more than two name servers. AWS Lambda applies the same trick to queues: a fixed pool, each customer hashed to a small subset, enqueue into whichever of those has the fewest messages.
components.config: Requires clients that tolerate a partial failure — retry against the other members of the shard, or the isolation does nothing. Assign deterministically by hash of tenant id so the mapping is reproducible without a lookup. For queues, mirror Lambda: fixed queue pool, hash tenant to k queues, enqueue to the shortest. Consider recursive shuffle sharding to isolate your customer's customers.

components.service: Read path and write path as separate, separately scaled services
components.role: Writes go to the system of record; reads go to purpose-built read stores fed asynchronously.
components.why: Rather than one service doing both against one database. Read and write traffic diverge by an order of magnitude and have opposite requirements: reads want fan-out, caching and stale tolerance; writes want a single authority and durability. Keeping them fused means your write path is sized by your read traffic. Materialise reads into the right store: OpenSearch for text and faceting rather than Postgres LIKE/tsvector (which forces you to size the writer for search), DynamoDB for high-cardinality key lookups (40,000 RCU/WCU per table by default and adjustable, with no practical table size limit), S3 + Athena for anything analytical rather than analytics queries on a replica.
components.config: The read stores are fed from the outbox/CDC stream, never dual-written. Every read store is rebuildable from the system of record and you have actually rebuilt one — measure how long a full rebuild takes, because that is your recovery time. Publish read-store staleness as a metric and put an SLO on it; product decisions depend on whether 2s stale is acceptable, and that should be a written answer, not a shrug.

components.service: EventBridge for routing, Kinesis Data Streams for volume, SQS for work
components.role: The asynchronous spine. Outbox writes to the spine; consumers do the work.
components.why: EventBridge rather than Kinesis when you have many event types and many independent consumers and you want content-based filtering with no consumer coordination — you pay per event and add subscribers without touching the producer. Kinesis rather than EventBridge when you need ordering per key, replay, or sustained high volume: a Kinesis shard is a known 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write and 2 MB/s read, and at 1 GB/s of events EventBridge's per-event pricing is the wrong shape. The crossover is roughly: above a few thousand events/s with ordering or replay requirements, go Kinesis. SQS for units of work with retries and a DLQ.
components.config: Kinesis: partition key = the same tenant/entity key as the cell, so ordering and isolation agree. Watch for hot shards — one key doing 40% of traffic pins one shard at 1 MB/s while the others idle. Enhanced fan-out (max 20 registered consumers, 50 on On-demand Advantage) when more than two consumers need the same shard; a shard only supports 5 GetRecords/s shared otherwise. EventBridge: DLQ on every target, archive + replay enabled before you need it.

components.service: Load shedding and backpressure at the front door, backed by fairness quotas
components.role: Protects goodput when offered load exceeds capacity.
components.why: Rather than queuing everything and hoping. The Builders' Library is explicit: throughput is what arrives, goodput is what completes usefully, and past the knee an overloaded server's goodput COLLAPSES rather than plateauing — you serve fewer real requests than if you had rejected some. Reject fast and cheaply at the edge instead. Also: do not let long queues do the shedding for you; a server that finally dequeues a request the client abandoned 30 seconds ago is doing pure waste. That is the brownout.
components.config: Per-tenant rate limits as guardrails with burst allowance, raised deliberately as tenants grow. Shed by priority: reject bulk/batch before interactive, and always admit health checks. Load test past the point where goodput plateaus — the correct result is a flat goodput line as offered load rises, not a peak and a cliff. Retries: token-bucket limited locally and retried at ONE layer only. A 5-deep call stack each retrying 3 times multiplies load on the bottom database by 243×, which is how a blip becomes an outage that cannot recover. Jitter every timer, retry and cron; do not schedule anything on the hour.

components.service: Sampled tracing + aggregate metrics + full logs only on error
components.role: Observability that does not cost more than the service.
components.why: Rather than 100% tracing and full request logging. At 50,000 req/s, storing every trace and every request body will genuinely become one of your largest AWS line items and you will read 0.001% of it. Sample head-based at 1–5% for the normal path, but ALWAYS keep 100% of errors, 100% of slow requests over your p99 threshold, and 100% of a named tenant when you turn on a debug flag for them.
components.config: Trace id propagated through the async spine — a trace that stops at the queue boundary is useless for exactly the problems queues create. Emit metrics via EMF so you are not paying to grep logs for counts. Per-cell dashboards plus one aggregate; without per-cell views a single sick cell hides inside the average. Keep a live cost-per-user and cost-per-request metric on the same dashboard as latency.

blueprints.ceiling: Set by the cell contract you enforce, not by AWS. A practical cell built this way tops out around 10,000–25,000 req/s and tens of thousands of tenants before it hits the same Aurora writer wall as tier 1. The architecture itself scales to hundreds of cells; what actually stops you is the control plane and your ops automation. Per-cell numbers to hold in your head: 15 Aurora read replicas per cluster (non-adjustable), 128–256 TiB Aurora cluster volume, 40,000 RCU/WCU default per DynamoDB table, 1 MB/s per Kinesis shard, and a default 20,000-shard-per-account Kinesis quota in the big regions.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The cell router, or the tenant that outgrows a cell. Router: it is the one unsharded component, so a bug or a deploy there is a 100% event and you have spent a year of engineering to still have one. Second: a single tenant grows past a full cell and now needs splitting across cells, which your partition key does not support — this is the design mistake to catch on day one, because fixing the grain later is a migration, not a config change. Third and most insidious: a quiet cross-cell dependency creeps in (a shared config service, a shared cache, a shared feature-flag provider), and the first correlated incident is how you find out your cells were never independent.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: (1) A tenant's traffic alone approaches your stated per-cell maximum. (2) Cell count exceeds what your automation can deploy in one working day — you need the control plane before you need more cells. (3) You cannot load test a cell to 100% of its contract any more because the test costs too much; that means the cell is too big. (4) Latency for a geographic segment is structurally bad — physics, not capacity — which is a multi-region ARGUMENT, though usually one answered by read-local replicas rather than a full active-active. (5) A regulator or a signed contract names a specific RTO/RPO that a single region cannot meet.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build multi-region because you now have cells and it looks like the next box. Multi-AZ already survives a data centre. Cells already survive bad code. Multi-region survives a regional event — rare, and usually less likely than the outage your own failover automation will cause during a test. Do not shard the database if purpose-built read stores would do it: moving search to OpenSearch and sessions to DynamoDB frequently removes the pressure that looked like it needed sharding, and costs a sprint instead of three quarters. Do not put a service mesh in to get mTLS and retries — you can get both with less. Do not sub-divide into 60 microservices; at this tier the honest shape is roughly one service per team that can be on call for it, and a still-modular monolith inside each cell is a completely respectable answer. Do not build custom autoscaling on predicted load; you will chase a model instead of fixing the quota that actually caps you.

plain.plainName: Many identical copies so one bad customer cannot sink everyone
plain.problem: 1,000,000 to 10,000,000 users, or a platform with many customers where one bad release or one heavy customer takes down every other customer. 40 to 150 engineers with a platform team. The trigger is not traffic, it is that a single failure hits 100 percent of your customers and the board has noticed.
plain.answer: Run several complete independent copies of the stack, called cells, spread customers across them, and split the reading side from the writing side so each scales on its own.
plain.money: About $80,000 to $400,000 a month. The cells dominate, because four cells each with their own database, cache and servers cost about four times the fixed floor of one cell, so that floor is the number to attack.
plain.holdsUpTo: 1,000,000 to 10,000,000 users, 200,000 to 2,000,000 daily actives and 20,000 to 150,000 requests a second in total. One cell tops out around 10,000 to 25,000 requests a second and tens of thousands of customers before it hits the same database wall as the tier below.
plain.whatBreaks: The small piece that decides which cell a customer belongs to. It is the one part that is not duplicated, so a bug or a bad release there hits everyone, and you spent a year of work to still have one of those. The other one is a single customer growing bigger than a whole cell, which your design may not allow you to split.
plain.timeToMove: When one customer's traffic alone approaches the stated limit of a cell, or you have more cells than your automation can deploy in one working day, or a full load test of a cell has become too expensive to run, which means the cell is too big.
plain.dontYet: Do not add multi region because cells worked and it looks like the next box. Multiple data centres already survive a data centre failure and cells already survive bad code. Multi region only survives a whole region failing, which is rarer than the outage your own failover practice will cause. Do not shard the database if moving search to OpenSearch and sessions to DynamoDB would take the pressure off instead, which it often does and for less money.
plain.pitch: One bad deploy or one heavy customer takes down every customer I have.

blueprints.name: Multi-region, cells per region, and the honest ledger of what it costs you
blueprints.forWho: Only three situations genuinely buy this: (1) a contract or regulator names an RTO/RPO a single region cannot meet; (2) data residency law requires data to stay in a jurisdiction; (3) your users are genuinely global and the speed of light, not your capacity, is your latency problem. If none of those is written down somewhere signed, you are buying insurance against an event rarer than your own deploys, with a failover path you will not exercise often enough to trust. Say that out loud before you start.
blueprints.scale: 5M–10M+ users spread across continents, or any size with a hard regulatory driver. 50,000–500,000 req/s aggregate. Availability target 99.99%+ with penalties attached.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: 1.8×–2.5× the single-region build, so realistically $200k–$900k+. The line items people forget: cross-region data transfer on every replication stream, full duplicate non-production environments (you must test failover somewhere), duplicated observability, and the single biggest one — two senior engineers for two-plus quarters, plus permanent ongoing drill time. Budget the drills explicitly or the whole thing is theatre.

components.service: Route 53 (latency or geoproximity records) + Application Recovery Controller routing controls
components.role: Sends users to a region and, critically, lets a human take a region out of rotation with one deliberate action.
components.why: ARC routing controls rather than health-check-driven automatic failover. Automatic failover on health checks is how a partial dependency failure becomes a full evacuation in both directions, twice. ARC gives you a highly available, data-plane-simple switch with safety rules (for example: never allow both regions off at once) that keeps working even when the region you are failing away from is on fire. Route 53 latency records rather than plain weighted records because the whole justification for a second region, in the global-users case, is latency.
components.config: Readiness checks per region comparing actual capacity, quotas and config parity — a standby that is under-provisioned or has a different quota is not a standby, it is a surprise. Safety rule: minimum one cell/region on. Rehearse the switch on a schedule, in production, on a Tuesday morning, and treat the drill failing as an incident.

components.service: Active-active with per-region ownership of the write key, not global writes
components.role: Each partition key has one home region that owns its writes; other regions read locally and forward writes.
components.why: Rather than accepting writes anywhere into an eventually consistent store and resolving conflicts later. Last-writer-wins silently loses money in a financial system, and CRDTs only work for data shaped for them. Pinning write ownership per key keeps your transactional invariants inside one region, where a normal database can enforce them, and you still get local reads everywhere. This composes naturally with the cell model: a cell lives in a region, and the router already knows the key.
components.config: Ownership recorded in the same mapping the cell router reads. Failover transfers ownership explicitly as a control-plane operation with a fence token; never let two regions believe they own a key. Design and test the split-brain case before launch, not after.

components.service: DynamoDB global tables, or Aurora Global Database, depending on the consistency you can defend
components.role: Cross-region data replication.
components.why: DynamoDB global tables rather than Aurora Global Database when you can express the access pattern as key lookups and you want multi-region writes — it now offers a multi-Region strong consistency mode (MRSC) as well as the eventual mode, so you can choose per table instead of pretending. Aurora Global Database rather than global tables when you genuinely need SQL, joins and transactions: typical cross-region lag around a second, with a managed unplanned failover. Know both sets of quotas in advance — 40,000 RCU/WCU per table by default on either consistency mode, and a 10 TB/account/region/day backfill cap when you add a replica, which is what makes 'just add a region' take a week instead of an afternoon. Also note: raise a table's write quota in one region and you must raise it in every replica region or replica creation fails outright.
components.config: Replication lag alarmed and on the on-call dashboard, not buried. Rehearse an unplanned failover and measure real RPO — the measured number is the only one you may put in a contract. Keep a rebuild-from-source path for every derived store.

components.service: Region-scoped cells, and a global control plane that can fail regionally
components.role: Cells do not span regions. The control plane is regional with a designated leader.
components.why: Rather than letting anything span regions. A cross-region cell has a cross-region dependency, which is the one thing multi-region exists to eliminate. Static stability is the goal: a region under stress should keep serving with what it already has, using cached config and pre-provisioned capacity, and should not need a control-plane call to survive. Control-plane calls are exactly what fail during a regional event.
components.config: Pre-provision standby capacity — do not plan to autoscale into a failover, because everyone else is autoscaling at the same moment and you will meet the account quota. Verify quota parity across regions on a schedule, automatically; quota drift is the single most common cause of a failover that fails. Deploy region-by-region, never simultaneously, with a full bake between.

components.service: Idempotency and exactly-once-effect discipline, enforced globally
components.role: Makes retries, replays and failovers safe.
components.why: Rather than hoping FIFO queues give you exactly-once. Across regions, during a failover, you WILL replay. Every mutating API takes a client-supplied idempotency key; the handler records the key with the result and returns the stored result on a repeat. That is the only thing that makes a failover-triggered replay a non-event rather than a duplicate charge.
components.config: Idempotency key stored with the outcome, TTL of at least 24 hours (longer than your longest plausible replay window). Key must cover the business operation, not the HTTP request. Test it by deliberately replaying a day of production events into a staging region and diffing the resulting state — that diff is your proof, and if you have not run it, you do not have idempotency, you have an intention.

blueprints.ceiling: You have essentially removed the architectural ceiling and replaced it with an organisational one. What now limits you is the rate at which you can safely change the system: deploys must be region-by-region and cell-by-cell, schema migrations must be backward and forward compatible across regions simultaneously, and every feature has to be correct under replication lag. Teams routinely see change velocity drop 30–50% on entering this tier. That is the real price, and it is not on any bill.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The failover path itself, because it is the only part of the system that is not exercised by normal traffic. The classic sequence: quota drift in the standby region, a config value that was never parity-checked, or an IAM role that exists in one region only — discovered at 3am mid-incident. Second: a hidden global singleton (one identity provider, one licensing service, one Route 53 hosted zone edited by hand, one CI system) that makes your two regions one system wearing a costume. Third: cross-region replication lag during the incident, when write volume spikes exactly as bandwidth degrades, so your measured RPO in the calm drill is not the RPO you get in the event.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: There is no next tier. From here you subtract: fewer moving parts, smaller cells, fewer bespoke services, more managed ones. The remaining work is to make cost per user fall while user count rises, and to make the failover drill boring. If a quarterly production failover drill is not boring, you do not have multi-region — you have a second region and a hope.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add a third region because two worked. Each region adds a full replication edge and, in active-active, an n-squared consistency conversation. Do not build automatic cross-region failover without a human in the loop until you have run at least four successful manual drills; automated failover on partial signals is a well-documented way to turn a brownout into an outage. Do not write your own replication or your own consensus layer; it is a multi-year project with a long tail of correctness bugs that surface only under partition. Do not let 'we're multi-region' justify skipping cells and shuffle sharding inside each region — regions protect you from AWS's bad day, cells protect you from yours, and yours is far more frequent.

plain.plainName: Running in more than one part of the world, and what it really costs
plain.problem: Only three things genuinely buy this. A contract or regulator names a recovery target one region cannot meet. A law says the data must stay in a country. Or your users are truly global and the speed of light, not your capacity, is the slowness. If none of that is written down and signed, you are buying insurance against something rarer than your own releases.
plain.answer: Run cells in each region, route people with Route 53, and replicate data with DynamoDB global tables or Aurora Global Database, with each region owning its own writes.
plain.money: 1.8 to 2.5 times the single region build, so realistically $200,000 to $900,000 a month or more. The forgotten lines are cross region transfer on every replication stream, a full duplicate test environment, duplicate monitoring, and the biggest one, two senior engineers for more than two quarters.
plain.holdsUpTo: 5,000,000 to 10,000,000 plus users across continents, or any size with a hard legal driver, at 50,000 to 500,000 requests a second in total, aiming at 99.99 percent uptime with penalties attached. You have removed the technical ceiling and replaced it with how fast you can safely change anything. Teams routinely see their pace of change drop 30 to 50 percent.
plain.whatBreaks: The switchover itself, because it is the only part normal traffic never exercises. The classic story is a limit, a setting or a permission that exists in one region and not the other, found at 3am in the middle of an incident. The other one is a hidden single thing everywhere depends on, like one login provider or one hand edited DNS zone.
plain.timeToMove: There is no next step up. From here you subtract things, and the job is to make cost per user fall while users rise. If a quarterly real failover drill is not boring, you do not have multi region, you have a second region and a hope.
plain.dontYet: Do not add a third region because two worked. Each one adds another replication link and, when all regions accept writes, a conversation about consistency that grows with every pair. Do not build automatic cross region failover without a human in the loop until you have run at least four successful manual drills, because automatic failover on partial signals is a known way to turn a slowdown into an outage. Do not write your own replication layer.
plain.pitch: A signed contract or a data residency law says one region is not enough.

blueprints.name: Pre-warmed single-region live event plane with panic-mode degradation
blueprints.forWho: A live streaming or ticketing product where traffic is scheduled and known in advance — a cricket match toss, a show dropping at 09:00, a sale opening. Concurrency goes from 2M to 25M in the minutes around a wicket falling. You know the minute; you do not know the multiple.
blueprints.scale: Hotstar published 25.3M concurrent viewers on the 2019 India vs New Zealand World Cup semi-final, up from 18.6M at the IPL 2019 final and 10.3M at the IPL 2018 final (AWS re:Invent 2019 CMY302, Gaurav Kamboj, Hotstar). Ramps of several million concurrent in under a minute after a wicket or a restart. Later JioHotstar figures quoted in secondary press (60M+) are not in a first-party deck I could open — treat as unsourced.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Baseline day is small; the event is the bill. Expect a 10–40x cost multiple on event days versus a normal day, because you hold provisioned capacity for the peak you forecast, not the peak you get. Drivers, in order: (1) CDN egress, which dominates everything else for video — at tens of millions of concurrent 2–5 Mbps streams the egress is the single largest line item and is negotiated per-Gbps, not on-list; (2) pre-warmed EC2 you paid for and did not use; (3) the load-generation fleet for game days, which is real money spent on a test. A rehearsal simulating tens of millions of sessions is itself a large multi-region EC2 run — Hotstar's load generator ran out of four regions (us-east-1, us-west-1, eu-west-1, eu-west-2) per the re:Invent deck.

components.service: Multi-CDN for the video data plane (CloudFront plus at least one non-AWS CDN)
components.role: Carries essentially all bytes. Origin sees manifest and segment misses only.
components.why: Not one CDN. At this scale a single CDN's regional POPs are a correlated failure and a negotiating weakness — you need per-ISP, per-region steering to shift share live when one CDN's India edge degrades. The obvious alternative, CloudFront alone, is right up to roughly single-digit millions of concurrent streams; past that you want to move 30% of traffic to another provider in minutes without a DNS TTL fight. Netflix went the furthest version of this and built its own CDN, Open Connect, with appliances in 1000+ locations, because at their volume buying transit is worse than embedding hardware in ISPs.
components.config: Segment duration 4–6s (shorter = lower latency but linearly more requests and more manifest churn), manifest TTL 1–2s, segment TTL long (immutable names). Client-side CDN selection driven by a config the app polls, so share can be shifted without a client release.

components.service: EC2 Auto Scaling groups, pre-warmed on a manual ladder
components.role: API plane: playback authorization, subscription checks, metadata, social/engagement.
components.why: NOT reactive auto scaling. Hotstar's stated reason, in their own re:Invent slide titled 'Why we don't use auto scaling': a newly provisioned instance takes about 90 seconds to become healthy, and their traffic adds millions of concurrent users inside that window. Reactive scaling is always one step behind a step function. You pre-scale on a ladder keyed to forecast concurrency from historical match data, and you step it up before the toss, not after. Auto scaling stays configured — as a safety net above the forecast, never as the primary mechanism.
components.config: Pre-baked AMIs (no bootstrap-time package installs; that is where 90s becomes 5 minutes). Spot fleet plus a secondary on-demand ASG as fallback when spot is reclaimed. Ladder steps sized to forecast concurrency bands, stepped manually or by scheduled action tied to the event calendar. Warm pools where the workload allows.

components.service: Application Load Balancer, pre-warmed and over-provisioned by count
components.role: Ingress for the API plane.
components.why: ALBs scale, but on the same reactive logic as everything else — an ALB serving 5k rps does not instantly serve 500k. The alternative people reach for is 'it's managed, it'll be fine.' At a scheduled 10x it will not be, in the first 60–90 seconds.
components.config: Shard across multiple ALBs so no single one is asked for a 100x step; route a fixed hash slice of clients to each. Warm every ALB with real game-day traffic at forecast peak before the event. Deregistration delay low (5–30s) so scaling steps do not hold dead targets; cross-zone balancing on.

components.service: A purpose-built load generator and a scheduled game day
components.role: Rehearsal. Face the real game before the actual game.
components.why: Not a SaaS load tool at list price. Hotstar built their own ('Hulk') and ran it from four AWS regions because tools like Flood.io/Gatling as-a-service become economically absurd at tens of millions of simulated sessions, and because the generator has to replay a real user journey (open app, auth, subscription check, playback token, manifest, segments) rather than hammer one endpoint. The failure you are hunting is almost never the web tier; it is the fourth dependency down the auth path.
components.config: Run the full journey, not endpoints. Run it against production or a production-identical stack. Run it before every major event, not once. Drive from multiple regions so you are not testing one NAT path.

components.service: Panic mode: a runtime feature-flag plane with tiered service classes
components.role: Designed degradation. P0 services stay up; everything else is switched off by an operator or a trigger.
components.why: This is the component people skip, and the one that saves the event. Hotstar's deck names it directly: 'Panic mode — P0 services must be always up' and 'Graceful degradation — turn off non-critical services.' The alternative is letting every service compete for the same saturated dependency, at which point playback (P0) dies alongside comments and leaderboards (P3). You decide the tiering when calm, in a config, and flip it when hot.
components.config: Explicit P0/P1/P2 classification per service, written down. Flags served from a store with an aggressively cached client-side copy so the flag plane cannot itself be the failure. Client honours a server-sent 'degraded' signal and stops polling optional endpoints. Retries with jitter and exponential backoff everywhere on the client, because a synchronised client retry after a blip is a second, self-inflicted thundering herd.

blueprints.ceiling: The API plane ceiling is not a request rate, it is a step size. A pre-warmed fleet handles the peak you forecast; it fails when the actual peak exceeds forecast by more than your headroom, and that gap cannot be closed in under ~90 seconds. Practically: you absorb the ladder step you pre-provisioned plus your spare headroom, and nothing more, for a minute and a half. On the data plane, a single CDN relationship starts to constrain you in the low millions of concurrent streams — not technically, but in POP capacity in one country and in commercial terms.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The narrowest synchronous dependency on the playback authorization path — subscription/entitlement lookup. Every viewer hits it at the same instant, it is usually a database or a third-party billing system, and it was sized for steady state. It saturates, playback tokens stop being issued, and the client retries, doubling the load. Second: the client retry storm itself, which is why jitter and backoff are architecture and not politeness. Third: spot reclamation arriving exactly when you cannot replace instances in 90 seconds.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Peak concurrency forecast error exceeds your pre-warm headroom more than once. Instance-ready time (launch → healthy in target group) exceeds 120s at p50. CDN egress in one country exceeds what one provider will commit to in writing. Entitlement-check p99 above ~200ms at 50% of forecast peak during a game day. Any event where panic mode had to be flipped to keep P0 alive — that is the ceiling announcing itself.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not go multi-region for this. A live event for one country is a single-region problem plus a global CDN, and a second active region buys nothing against the failure you actually have (your own dependency saturating) while adding cross-region consistency to your incident surface. Do not add a service mesh before the event — the sidecar adds a hop and a novel failure mode on the exact path you cannot afford to be novel. Do not move to Kubernetes for the pre-warm story; ASGs with pre-baked AMIs pre-warm more predictably than cluster autoscaler plus pod scheduling, and you are optimising for the 90-second window, not developer ergonomics. Do not build panic mode as a dynamic rules engine; a static tier list in a config file is the version that works when everything else is on fire.

plain.plainName: A known big moment, like a match or a ticket drop
plain.problem: You run live streaming or ticketing. The rush is on the calendar, like a match starting or a sale opening at 09:00. People watching can go from 2 million to 25 million in the minutes around a wicket. You know the minute. You do not know the multiple.
plain.answer: Turn on the servers before the crowd arrives using pre warmed auto scaling groups, send the video through more than one CDN, and keep a panic switch that turns off the nice to have features.
plain.money: A normal day is small. The event is the bill. Expect 10 to 40 times a normal day's cost on event days, because you hold capacity for the peak you forecast, not the peak you get. Video delivery dominates everything else.
plain.holdsUpTo: Hotstar published 25.3 million people watching at once during the 2019 India versus New Zealand World Cup semi final, up from 18.6 million at the IPL 2019 final and 10.3 million at the IPL 2018 final. The real limit is not a request rate, it is one step of growth. You absorb the peak you pre booked plus your spare, and nothing more, for about 90 seconds, because you cannot add machines faster than that.
plain.whatBreaks: The check that says whether a viewer is allowed to watch. Everyone hits it at the same instant, it usually talks to a database or a billing company, and it was sized for a normal day. It stalls, playback stops being allowed, and every app retries, which doubles the load on the thing that is already stuck.
plain.timeToMove: When your peak forecast is wrong by more than your spare capacity more than once, or a new machine takes longer than 120 seconds to be ready to serve, or one country's video traffic passes what a single CDN will commit to in writing, or the entitlement check is slower than about 200 milliseconds at only half your forecast peak, or you had to flip panic mode to stay alive.
plain.dontYet: Do not go multi region for this. A live event for one country is a single region problem plus a global CDN, and a second live region buys nothing against the failure you actually have, which is your own dependency stalling, while adding cross region consistency to your incident list. Do not add a service mesh before the event, because it adds a hop and a brand new failure mode on the exact path you cannot afford surprises on. Do not move to Kubernetes for the pre warming story.
plain.pitch: I know the exact minute millions of people will arrive at once.

blueprints.name: Three-region active-active with control-plane-free evacuation
blueprints.forWho: A global service where an entire AWS region becoming unavailable is a business-ending event, and where you have enough traffic that the standby capacity is not pure waste. This is the Netflix shape: any one of three regions can absorb the whole world.
blueprints.scale: Netflix runs active-active in us-east-1, us-west-2 and eu-west-1 (Netflix Tech Blog, 'Global Cloud — Active-Active and Beyond'), sized so that losing two regions still leaves one able to serve global traffic. Region evacuation went from close to an hour to under 10 minutes with Project Nimble, and Netflix has published a 7-minute failover figure. Hundreds of millions of subscribers; edge traffic in millions of requests per second.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: The honest number is the one nobody quotes. Three-region active-active where any one region can serve 100% means each region runs at roughly 33% utilisation in steady state — you pay about 3x the compute you use. Add cross-region data transfer for continuous replication (a real line item at petabyte scale, charged per GB out of each region), 3x the storage, 3x the observability ingest, plus headcount for traffic-steering tooling and failover drills. Defensible planning figure: 2.5–3.5x the single-region bill for compute and data, before the engineering org that makes it work. If that multiple is not obviously worth it against your revenue-per-minute-of-downtime, you do not need this architecture.

components.service: Route 53 latency-based or geolocation routing, plus Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls
components.role: Steers users to a region; the ARC routing control is the on/off switch that evacuates one.
components.why: The routing control rather than 'change the DNS record during the incident'. ARC routing controls run on a dedicated five-region data plane on a quorum model — the cluster keeps working with up to two regional endpoints unavailable, and flipping a control needs no Route 53 control plane call. This matters because during a large regional event the control plane is the most likely thing to be impaired. AWS's own guidance (REL11-BP04) is explicit: rely on the data plane, not the control plane, during recovery. The obvious alternative — an operator editing a DNS record in the console — depends on the console, on the Route 53 control plane, and on a human under pressure.
components.config: Hard-code or bookmark all five regional cluster endpoints so you never need DescribeCluster (a control plane call) during failover. Drive failover from CLI/SDK against the cluster API, never the console. Define safety rules on the control panel — e.g. 'at most one region may be evacuated at a time' — so the cluster refuses an unsafe state change rather than trusting the operator. Record TTLs short (30–60s) on the steered names.

components.service: A cross-region-capable edge proxy (Netflix's is Zuul; AWS-native equivalent is ALB plus a proxy tier you own)
components.role: Progressive traffic shifting during evacuation, and load shedding at the edge.
components.why: DNS alone cannot evacuate gracefully. DNS gives a blunt, TTL-delayed, client-cache-poisoned switch. A cross-region proxy lets you move a trickle of traffic out of the suffering region, watch the receiving regions absorb it, then ramp to 100% — Netflix's published description of exactly this. It also gives you the place to shed load to protect downstream services, which DNS can never do. Global Accelerator is the managed alternative for the anycast-IP half and removes client DNS caching from the equation, but gives you neither ramping nor shedding.
components.config: Routing changeable at runtime without deploy, held in a config the proxy polls. Split evacuated traffic across both surviving regions proportional to available capacity, not 100% to one — dumping a region's full load onto a single neighbour turns one regional failure into two. Ramp in steps (1% → 5% → 25% → 100%) with a hold at each step long enough to see the receiving region's metrics move.

components.service: Asynchronously replicated, multi-master data (Cassandra-style, or DynamoDB global tables in MREC mode)
components.role: The same data readable and writable in every region.
components.why: Async multi-master, not synchronous. DynamoDB global tables in the default multi-Region eventual consistency mode replicate in about a second, resolve conflicts last-writer-wins at item level (not attribute level), do not support cross-region transactions, and accept local writes even when a peer region is offline — that last property is the entire point, because it is what makes the surviving region independent. The obvious alternative, a single global primary with regional read replicas, is active-passive wearing an active-active costume: a write during a primary-region failure is a write you lose.
components.config: Alarm on the per-Region-pair ReplicationLatency CloudWatch metric; there is no SLA on it. If you genuinely need cross-region strong consistency, DynamoDB offers MRSC, but read the constraints first: exactly three Regions (three replicas, or two replicas plus a witness), no transaction APIs, higher write and strongly-consistent-read latency proportional to inter-region round trip, ReplicatedWriteConflictException on concurrent cross-region item writes, and a limited Region list. Model data so item-granularity last-writer-wins is survivable — narrow items, no cross-region read-modify-write of wide records.

components.service: Statically stable regional capacity
components.role: Each region carries enough standing capacity to absorb its share of an evacuation without launching anything.
components.why: Because recovery must not depend on the control plane, and launching instances IS the control plane. AWS's static stability guidance uses the same arithmetic one level down: run three AZs at 66% so any two carry full load, requiring no action during an outage. Apply it at region level. The obvious alternative — 'we'll auto-scale the surviving regions when we fail over' — asks EC2's control plane for a large capacity step in a region simultaneously absorbing everyone else's, at the exact moment AWS is under most stress. It is the least reliable moment to ask.
components.config: Size each region for (global peak / (N-1)) plus headroom. For N=3 that is 50% of global peak per region as the floor; most run higher. On-Demand Capacity Reservations or Savings Plans for the standing capacity, since it is permanent. Never let the evacuation runbook contain a scale-up step as a prerequisite.

components.service: Chaos Kong-style scheduled regional failure
components.role: Proof that the evacuation works, run regularly, in production.
components.why: Netflix runs Chaos Kong — killing an entire region — on a regular basis. Not for fun: a failover path exercised once a year is a failover path that does not work. The alternative, a documented runbook, is a claim rather than a fact. An untested evacuation is not an evacuation.
components.config: Scheduled on a calendar, business hours, full team present. Measure time-to-full-evacuation as a tracked metric and treat regressions as bugs with named owners. Run the drill using the same tooling and the same five hard-coded endpoints the real incident would use — never a special drill path.

blueprints.ceiling: This architecture does not run out of scale; it runs out of consistency. It stops working the moment a feature genuinely requires read-your-writes across regions — money balances, inventory decrement, entitlement grants, anything where a ~1-second replication window and last-writer-wins produce a wrong answer a user can see. At that point you either pin those operations to one region (accepting they are unavailable during that region's failure) or pay MRSC latency, which is a real cross-region round trip on every write.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The data layer, specifically your data model's tolerance of last-writer-wins. Second: asymmetric capacity — evacuation succeeds on the traffic tier then saturates one shared dependency in the receiving region that was sized for its own traffic (a cache tier, a third-party API with a per-account rate limit, a Kafka cluster). Third: the failover tooling itself having a hidden dependency on something in the region being evacuated. That is a real and common bug, and only a real drill finds it.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Revenue-per-minute of a regional outage exceeds the annual cost of the extra region. Regulatory data residency forces a regional split anyway (the shape then becomes residency-partitioned rather than active-active). Evacuation drill time exceeds your stated RTO. Cross-region replication lag p99 rises past your product's tolerance.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not go active-active before exhausting multi-AZ. Multi-AZ in one region, statically stable, gets you through the overwhelming majority of real AWS failures at roughly 1.5x cost instead of 3x — and AZ failures are far more common than region failures. Do not attempt active-active with a single writable primary; that is active-passive, and pretending otherwise means discovering it during the incident. Do not build a bespoke global traffic manager before using Route 53 ARC and Global Accelerator — the failure mode of homegrown steering is that it is itself unavailable when needed. And do not go multi-region for latency: put a CDN and regional read caches in front of a single-region write tier first. That gets most of the latency win for a fraction of the complexity, and it keeps the word 'conflict' out of your data model.

plain.plainName: Running your whole service in three places at once
plain.problem: If one whole AWS region goes dark, our business is over. We are big enough that spare capacity in other places would not sit idle for nothing.
plain.answer: Run a full live copy in three regions, send users to the nearest one with Route 53, and copy data between them all the time so any one region can serve the whole world.
plain.money: Each region runs at about 33% use, so you pay roughly 3 times the compute you actually use, plus cross region data transfer charged per gigabyte.
plain.holdsUpTo: Netflix runs this in three regions and can lose two and still serve everyone. Region evacuation dropped from close to an hour to under 10 minutes.
plain.whatBreaks: A user updates something in one region and sees the old value, because copies are about a second behind and the last write wins. Money balances, stock counts and entitlements come out wrong in a way people notice.
plain.timeToMove: When the revenue lost in one minute of a regional outage is more than a year of the extra region. Or when your evacuation drill takes longer than the recovery time you promised.
plain.dontYet: Do not do this before you have squeezed multi AZ. Multi AZ in one region costs about 1.5 times instead of 3 times, and AZ failures are far more common than region failures. Also do not call it active active if only one place can accept writes, that is active passive and you will find out during the incident.
plain.pitch: One AWS region going down would end my company, and I have the traffic to justify paying three times over.

blueprints.name: Cell-partitioned persistent-connection fabric with a thin router
blueprints.forWho: A messaging, presence or realtime product holding tens to hundreds of millions of simultaneous long-lived connections, where any single shared component failing takes down everyone at once and that is unacceptable. The WhatsApp/Instagram shape.
blueprints.scale: WhatsApp published (Rick Reed, Erlang Factory) 147M peak concurrent connections, 230K peak logins/sec, 342K messages inbound and 712K outbound per second, 19B messages in and 40B out per day, on roughly 550 servers — 150 chat, 250 multimedia — >11,000 cores, 2x10-core Ivy Bridge per box, 512GB RAM on DB nodes, ~10 people on the Erlang system. Stated plainly: that was bare-metal FreeBSD, not AWS, and it is a 2014 figure. It is the right shape to reason from, not a design to copy onto EC2 line for line.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Dominated by two things: the connection tier (memory and file descriptors, not CPU) and cross-AZ/cross-region data transfer for fan-out. Cell replication multiplies fixed overhead — each cell needs its own cache, queue and data tier, so N cells cost meaningfully more than one monolith of equal total capacity, and that premium IS the product you are buying. Planning heuristic: 15–30% over a flat architecture of equivalent capacity, plus the engineering cost of a pipeline that can roll N cells independently. The connection tier itself is cheap per user if you get memory-per-connection right and disastrous if you do not.

components.service: A thin cell router (Route 53, API Gateway, or a small EC2/ECS proxy tier reading a cell map from S3)
components.role: Maps a partition key — user ID — to a cell, and does nothing else.
components.why: Thin, deliberately. AWS's cell-based architecture guidance is blunt: the router is the one shared component across cells, so it must be as simple and horizontally scalable as possible, must avoid business logic, must abstract cell placement from clients, and must keep serving other cells when one cell is unreachable. Use a cryptographic hash plus modular arithmetic on the partition key. The obvious alternative — a smart gateway doing auth, rate limiting and enrichment — reintroduces exactly the global blast radius cells exist to remove: one bug in the smart router is a 100% outage, and you have paid for cells and got nothing.
components.config: Cell map held in memory on the router, refreshed from S3 by a listener process; the control plane writes the map, the router never queries a control plane on the request path. Constant-work design — the router does the same work whether one cell or all cells are healthy. No per-request database lookup, no dynamic rule evaluation.

components.service: Independent cells, each a complete self-contained copy of the stack
components.role: App tier, cache, queues and data — no state shared across cells.
components.why: A cell is the blast-radius boundary. AWS's arithmetic: 10 cells cap worst-case impact at 10% of customers, 100 cells at 1%. Cell sizing is a genuine three-way trade — big enough to hold the largest single tenant, small enough to load-test one cell at full scale and stay under account/region quotas, big enough for economies of scale. Start with a small number of large cells and shrink over time. The alternative, one horizontally-scaled fleet, has excellent economics and a 100% blast radius; the first time a poison message or bad config reaches every node simultaneously you learn what the cell premium was buying.
components.config: No cross-cell calls, by rule, enforced in CI where possible. Shuffle-sharding may be used WITHIN a cell; never across cells — that breaks isolation by definition. Test a cell at its declared maximum size so the scaling cliff is found in rehearsal. Deploy cell-by-cell with the same soak between cells you would give a region.

components.service: Connection-tier instances tuned for concurrent sockets, not CPU
components.role: Holds the long-lived TCP/WebSocket connections.
components.why: Sized by memory and file descriptors. WhatsApp's whole published optimisation story is a socket-concurrency story — 1M established sessions on a single machine in 2011, 2M+ in 2012, then deliberately running at ~1M per server in production to halve the blast radius of losing a box. That last decision is the lesson, not the 2M record: the maximum a machine CAN hold and the number you SHOULD put on it are different, and the gap is your failure domain. The obvious alternative — treating connection servers as stateless web servers behind an ALB — fails because dropping a node does not drop requests, it drops connections, and every one reconnects at the same instant.
components.config: Memory-optimised instances; budget memory-per-connection explicitly and multiply. Raise file-descriptor and ephemeral-port limits, and tune TCP keepalive so dead peers are reaped without a heartbeat storm. Run each node at roughly half its tested maximum connections. Network Load Balancer, not ALB, for raw long-lived TCP; long idle timeout. Drain a node by refusing new connections and migrating existing ones in batches with jittered server-initiated reconnect, never all at once.

components.service: Regional write-locality with queued asynchronous cross-region writes
components.role: Keeps a user's writes in their own region; propagates asynchronously.
components.why: Instagram's published multi-region approach did exactly this: restrict EU writes to the local region and queue them locally rather than synchronously blocking on a remote master. Synchronous cross-region writes put a 100ms+ round trip on the critical path of every message send, which at hundreds of thousands of sends per second is not a latency problem but a concurrency problem — in-flight requests pile up until the connection pool dies. Instagram also published the corresponding cost: reducing the EU Cassandra replication factor from five to three saved storage but meant they needed more front-end Django capacity to absorb traffic from a failing region. That trade is the honest shape of multi-region — you do not skip paying, you only choose the line item.
components.config: Instagram's published split: Cassandra_US at replication factor 5, Cassandra_EU at replication factor 3. Local durable queue in front of cross-region propagation so a peer-region outage backs up rather than fails the user's write. Pin a user's writes to their home region for the life of a session, so read-your-writes holds locally. Size the front-end tier for the absorbed load of a failing peer, not for its own steady state.

components.service: Load shedding as designed behaviour, at the edge of every cell
components.role: Protects goodput when demand exceeds capacity.
components.why: The alternative to shedding is not 'serving everyone' — it is serving nobody, slowly. When a tier is overloaded, queued requests age out, clients time out and retry, and the server burns 100% CPU producing responses nobody is still waiting for. Shedding cheap and early, at the front door, keeps throughput of useful work high. AWS's Builders' Library covers this directly in 'Using load shedding to avoid overload'.
components.config: Reject fast with a retryable status plus a server-specified backoff, so the client does not choose the retry interval. Prioritise explicitly: a message send outranks a presence update outranks a read receipt. Cap the inbound queue by TIME, not depth — a request older than the client's timeout is dead work; drop it. Jitter every client retry. Shed at the cell edge so one hot cell cannot push load onto its neighbours.

blueprints.ceiling: Per connection-tier node: bounded by memory per connection and by descriptors, not CPU — practically hundreds of thousands to ~1M connections per node on a modern instance, and you should run well below the max so losing one node is survivable. Per cell: bounded by whichever regional or account quota the cell hits first — this is why the guidance says a cell must be small enough to test at full scale. Overall: the fabric scales by adding cells almost linearly, and the real ceiling is the router and the repartitioning story.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Reconnection storms. Lose a connection-tier node holding a million sockets and you get a million simultaneous reconnects, each carrying an authentication handshake — WhatsApp's published 230K logins/sec peak hints at how expensive that path is. The auth/session-establishment tier saturates long before the socket tier does. Second: cell rebalancing — moving a user between cells means moving their state, and the first time you need to split a hot cell you discover whether you designed for it. Third: the router's cell map going stale and black-holing a slice of users.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Any single incident affects more than your stated maximum customer percentage — that is the cell count telling you it is too low. A single cell approaches a regional service quota. One cell can no longer be load-tested at full scale in reasonable time. Reconnect-storm recovery after losing one node exceeds your SLO. Data residency law requires per-jurisdiction placement — cells map onto that cleanly, which is one of the quieter reasons to have them.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build cells at the start. Cells are a blast-radius tool, and blast radius only matters once 100% of your customers is a number that frightens you. Below roughly a few million users, a well-run multi-AZ single-region deployment beats a cellular one on every axis that matters to a small team — one deploy, one dashboard, one on-call runbook. The cost of premature cells is not money, it is that you now have N of everything to deploy, observe, migrate and debug with the same headcount, and your deploy pipeline becomes the thing that breaks. Equally: do not put business logic in the router 'just this once'. Do not build cross-cell features — the first one silently deletes the isolation you paid for, and nobody notices until the outage. And do not build your own connection-tier protocol before exhausting managed options; at low tens of thousands of connections, API Gateway WebSockets or AppSync is correct and you should feel no shame about it.

plain.plainName: Splitting users into separate self contained copies
plain.problem: Millions of people stay connected to my app all the time. Right now one shared piece breaking knocks out every single user at once, and I cannot live with that.
plain.answer: Split the whole stack into independent cells, each a full copy, and put a thin router in front that decides which cell a user belongs to.
plain.money: Mostly memory and connection slots on the connection servers, plus data transfer for fan out. Each cell needs its own cache, queue and database, so N cells cost noticeably more than one big system of the same total size.
plain.holdsUpTo: WhatsApp reported 147 million connections at once, 342,000 messages in and 712,000 out per second, on about 550 servers with roughly 10 people. Each node holds hundreds of thousands up to about 1 million connections.
plain.whatBreaks: One server dies and a million people all try to log back in at the same second. The sign in path chokes and people stare at a reconnecting spinner long after the original server is gone.
plain.timeToMove: When one incident hits more than the share of customers you said was acceptable, or one cell is close to an AWS account limit, or a cell is too big to load test properly.
plain.dontYet: Do not build cells at the start. Below roughly a few million users, a well run single region multi AZ setup wins on everything that matters to a small team, one deploy, one dashboard, one runbook. The cost is not money, it is that you now have N of everything to deploy, watch and debug with the same people.
plain.pitch: I hold tens of millions of live connections and one shared component failing for everyone is unacceptable.

blueprints.name: On-demand video: S3 upload, MediaConvert ABR ladder, CloudFront with signed cookies
blueprints.forWho: A course platform, media library, training or creator product with 500 to 50,000 hours of catalog and up to roughly 50,000 monthly viewers. Content is uploaded, not live. You need paywalled playback, not broadcast DRM, for most of it.
blueprints.scale: Tens of TB of source in S3, a few hundred TB/month egress at the top of this range. Playback concurrency of a few thousand simultaneous streams is fine because CloudFront absorbs it; the origin sees almost nothing. Transcode throughput is bounded only by MediaConvert queue concurrency, not by your own compute.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Small (2 TB/month egress, 50 h/month new content): roughly $200-400. Medium (100 TB/month egress, 500 h/month new content): roughly $9,000-12,000. The bill is 85-95% CloudFront egress in every real case. At $0.085/GB for the first 10 TB in US/Canada/Europe, stepping to $0.080/GB at 10-50 TB, 100 TB/month is about $8,500 before any commitment discount. India delivery is $0.109/GB and Japan/Singapore/Australia $0.114/GB, so an India-heavy audience costs ~30% more per GB than a US one. MediaConvert at the basic tier is $0.0075/normalized minute for the first 100,000 minutes, and an HD output carries roughly a 2x multiplier, so a 6-rendition HD ladder on a 60-minute video lands around $5-6 — transcoding 500 hours/month is a few thousand dollars and is the only non-egress line that matters. S3 Standard storage at $0.023/GB is noise until you hold tens of TB of mezzanine.

components.service: Amazon S3 (two buckets: source and output)
components.role: Ingest of the mezzanine file and storage of the packaged HLS/DASH renditions.
components.why: Rather than uploading through your API server (the obvious alternative, and what almost everyone builds first), issue a presigned POST or a multipart presigned URL and let the browser put bytes into S3 directly. An API server in the upload path means a 4 GB source file streams through your app, holds a request open for minutes, and forces you to size instances for upload concurrency rather than API concurrency.
