It also gives you an upload that cannot resume. Presigned multipart resumes, costs nothing in compute, and the S3 event is your trigger.
components.config: Two separate buckets, never one with prefixes — the output bucket is the CloudFront origin and must not be able to serve a raw mezzanine. Multipart with 8-16 MB parts; a lifecycle rule aborting incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days (skipping this quietly bills you for orphaned parts forever). Transition source to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval at 30 days, keep outputs in Standard. S3 Transfer Acceleration only if your uploaders are far from the bucket region; test it first, it is often not worth $0.04/GB.

components.service: AWS Elemental MediaConvert
components.role: Transcode the mezzanine into an adaptive bitrate ladder and package it as CMAF/HLS plus DASH.
components.why: The obvious alternative is FFmpeg on EC2 or in a container, and it genuinely is cheaper per minute at sustained high volume. It is the wrong choice below roughly 2,000 hours a month because you then own: the queue, the retry logic, spot interruption handling, codec licensing, and the ladder correctness. MediaConvert is per-minute with no idle cost, handles the whole ladder in one job, and emits a completion event. The crossover is real — if you are transcoding more than a few thousand hours a month and have an engineer to own it, self-hosted FFmpeg on Spot c7i/c7a instances is several times cheaper. Below that, the salary cost dominates the compute cost.
components.config: Use QVBR, not CBR — QVBR spends bits only where the picture needs them and typically cuts the top rendition's size 20-40% on talking-head content at the same perceived quality. Set QVBR quality level 7-8 for general content, 9 for high-motion. Ladder: 1920x1080 at ~5 Mbps max, 1280x720 at ~3 Mbps, 960x540 at ~1.8 Mbps, 640x360 at ~800 kbps, 480x270 at ~400 kbps, plus an audio-only rendition. Two-second GOP, closed GOP, aligned segments across renditions — misaligned keyframes are the single most common cause of a player that will not switch bitrates. Output CMAF with a single fMP4 set and both HLS and DASH manifests over it, rather than duplicating TS for HLS and fMP4 for DASH, which doubles storage and doubles CDN cache entries. Use a dedicated queue only if you need guaranteed throughput; on-demand queues are the default and are fine.

components.service: Amazon CloudFront with signed cookies and OAC
components.role: Delivery to players, and the authorization boundary for paid content.
components.why: Serving segments from S3 directly, or from an ALB, is the obvious alternative and it is wrong for two separate reasons. First cost: S3 direct egress is $0.09/GB versus CloudFront's $0.085/GB, and S3-to-CloudFront origin fetch is free, so the CDN is cheaper on the very first byte, not at some crossover. Second behaviour: one viewer watching a 1-hour HLS stream issues roughly 600-900 segment requests; a thousand concurrent viewers is close to 250 requests/second against your origin, and an ALB plus app tier in that path saturates its connection pool long before the video is the problem. With a CDN the origin sees the first request per segment and nothing after. Use signed COOKIES rather than signed URLs for HLS: a signed URL has to be minted per segment or you must rewrite the manifest, whereas one cookie set covers every segment under a path prefix.
components.config: Origin Access Control (not the legacy OAI) so the S3 bucket denies everything except the distribution. Signed cookies with a CloudFront key group, policy scoped to the title's path prefix, expiry 4-8 hours — long enough for a film plus pauses, short enough that a leaked cookie dies. Cache policy: manifests get a short TTL (VOD manifests are immutable, so actually give them a long TTL and version the path instead); segments get max TTL of a year because they never change. Do NOT forward cookies or query strings in the cache key for segments — that is the classic mistake that fragments the cache and drops the hit rate from 95% to near zero. Enable Origin Shield in the region of the output bucket to collapse fetches across edge locations. Price Class All unless you have no viewers outside North America and Europe, in which case Price Class 100 cuts the per-GB rate.

components.service: AWS Lambda plus EventBridge
components.role: Orchestration: S3 upload event starts the job, MediaConvert completion event writes the record and notifies the app.
components.why: The obvious alternative is Step Functions, which the AWS Video on Demand solution uses and which is correct once you have conditional ladders, QC steps and human approval. For a single linear path — upload lands, submit job, job finishes, mark ready — two Lambdas on EventBridge rules is less machinery to reason about. Move to Step Functions when you add a second branch, not before.
components.config: An S3 ObjectCreated rule filtered to the source prefix and to your accepted extensions, a MediaConvert job-state-change rule matching COMPLETE and ERROR. Handle ERROR explicitly and alarm on it; a transcode that silently fails leaves a catalog entry pointing at nothing. Lambda 512 MB, 30 s timeout — it only submits a job. Idempotency key on the S3 object version so a replayed event does not double-transcode.

components.service: DRM via SPEKE (only where required)
components.role: Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay key delivery for content whose licence demands it.
components.why: AES-128 or SAMPLE-AES with signed cookies is what most platforms actually need, and it is free. Studio DRM is a contractual requirement, not a security upgrade you choose — it costs a per-stream or per-device fee to a key vendor, forces FairPlay for Safari and Widevine for Chrome and so doubles your packaging and player test matrix, and breaks casual debugging. Add it when a rights holder's contract says the words, and not one day earlier.
components.config: MediaConvert or MediaPackage calling a SPEKE-compliant key provider over an API Gateway endpoint. Package CENC (Widevine + PlayReady) on the DASH/CMAF set and FairPlay on the HLS set. Budget a month of player integration work per platform you support.

blueprints.ceiling: This design runs comfortably to roughly 200-300 TB/month of egress and thousands of concurrent viewers without architectural change, because nothing in the hot path is yours. What actually ends the design is economics, not capacity: past roughly 150-200 TB/month the CloudFront list rate is the single largest line on your AWS bill and you are paying retail for a commodity. The second ceiling is transcode volume — past roughly 2,000 hours/month MediaConvert's per-minute pricing exceeds what Spot FFmpeg would cost by a wide enough margin to fund an engineer.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Not the video path. The first thing to break is your own entitlement API: every player start calls it to mint signed cookies, and a burst of viewers on a new release hits it all at once. On a single small instance with a synchronous database call per request that saturates somewhere around 300-600 requests/second and manifests as players spinning forever at 0:00 while the CDN sits idle. The second failure is cache-key fragmentation — someone adds a tracking query string to segment URLs, the CloudFront hit rate collapses, and the S3 GET bill and origin latency both jump overnight with no code change to the video pipeline at all.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: CloudFront egress exceeds 150 TB/month (start a CloudFront private pricing / committed-use negotiation, and price a second CDN). MediaConvert spend exceeds roughly $3,000/month or 2,000 source hours/month (price Spot FFmpeg). CloudFront cache hit ratio for segment requests drops below 90% (your cache key is wrong). Entitlement endpoint p99 exceeds 300 ms at peak, or its error rate exceeds 0.5% during a release. Time-to-first-frame p95 above 2 seconds.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build multi-CDN. It costs a CDN selection service, a second contract, duplicated cache warm-up and a whole class of bugs where two CDNs serve different manifest versions — and below 100 TB/month it saves nothing, because you are not on a committed rate with anyone yet. Do not build your own transcode farm on day one: teams routinely spend six weeks on a Spot FFmpeg pipeline to save $400/month. Do not add studio DRM before a contract requires it — it is roughly a month of engineering per platform plus a recurring vendor fee, in exchange for zero additional revenue. Do not add per-title encoding or ML-driven ladder optimisation; it is a real technique that saves real bandwidth, and it is worth nothing until egress is a five-figure monthly line. Do not put a Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Function on segment requests to do auth — it runs on every one of the ~700 requests per viewer-hour, and signed cookies already did the job for free. And do not store both TS and fMP4 packagings 'for compatibility'; it doubles storage and halves cache efficiency to support devices you probably do not have.

plain.plainName: Paid video library that people watch on demand
plain.problem: I have a course or media library people pay to watch. Videos get uploaded, not streamed live, and only paying members should be able to play them.
plain.answer: Store the files in S3, convert them into multiple quality versions with MediaConvert, and deliver them through CloudFront using signed cookies so only paying members can play.
plain.money: About 200 to 400 dollars a month for 2 TB of viewing. About 9,000 to 12,000 dollars at 100 TB a month. Delivery is 85 to 95 percent of the bill, roughly 8,500 dollars for 100 TB.
plain.holdsUpTo: Comfortable to roughly 200 to 300 TB a month and thousands of people watching at once, because the heavy work is not on your servers.
plain.whatBreaks: Not the video. Your own members only check breaks first. Everyone hits play on a new release, that check dies somewhere around 300 to 600 requests a second, and players spin forever at 0:00 while the delivery network sits idle.
plain.timeToMove: When delivery passes 150 TB a month, or conversion costs more than about 3,000 dollars a month, or fewer than 90 percent of video chunks are served from cache.
plain.dontYet: Do not build a second delivery network. Below 100 TB a month it saves nothing because you have no committed rate yet. Do not build your own conversion farm on day one, teams spend six weeks on it to save 400 dollars a month. Do not add studio grade copy protection until a contract demands it, that is about a month of work per platform.
plain.pitch: I sell access to recorded videos and I need people who did not pay to be unable to watch.

blueprints.name: Live streaming: contribution to MediaLive, MediaPackage origin, CloudFront, with a chosen latency tier
blueprints.forWho: A single live channel or a handful of them — a conference stream, a sports league below the national-event tier, a shopping or auction channel, a 24/7 linear feed. Audience from a few hundred to a few hundred thousand concurrent. You need it to stay up for the whole event, and the event does not move.
blueprints.scale: One STANDARD MediaLive channel handles one input and its full ABR ladder; concurrency is a CDN problem, not a MediaLive problem, so a single channel serves 500,000 viewers as easily as 500. Practical range for this shape is up to a few hundred thousand concurrent on a single CDN. Bandwidth at 100,000 concurrent viewers averaging 3 Mbps is 300 Gbps, which is about 135 TB per hour of egress.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: The encoder is a fixed hourly cost and the delivery is variable, and the second one is the one that hurts. A 1080p AVC STANDARD (dual-pipeline) MediaLive channel with a 5-6 rendition ladder runs roughly $1.50-3.00/hour on demand, so a 24/7 linear channel is roughly $1,100-2,200/month for encoding alone before a single viewer watches. A 12-month reserved commitment saves up to 75% on inputs and outputs and is the obvious move for anything always-on. MediaPackage charges both ingest GB and origination GB for live, and CloudFront in front of it collapses origination to near the number of unique segments, which is the whole reason it is there. Delivery dominates: at India's $0.109/GB, a 3-hour event with 100,000 average concurrent viewers at 3 Mbps is about 405 TB and roughly $44,000 of CloudFront egress for one evening. At the small end — a 2-hour webinar with 1,000 concurrent — it is about 2.7 TB, roughly $230 of egress plus $5 of encoder. Amazon IVS is the alternative cost model: $0.20-2.00/hour input and an hourly per-viewer output rate rather than per-GB, which for small bursty channels is often both cheaper and far less work.

components.service: AWS Elemental MediaConnect or a MediaLive RTP/SRT push input
components.role: Get the contribution feed from the venue or encoder into AWS reliably.
components.why: The obvious alternative is RTMP straight into MediaLive from OBS or a hardware encoder, and for a webinar that is genuinely the right answer — it is simple and it works. It is wrong for anything you cannot re-run, because RTMP over the public internet has no forward error correction and no retransmission window: a 2% packet loss event becomes a visible glitch or a dropped connection with no recovery. SRT and Zixi are ARQ protocols that buy back losses inside a configurable latency budget. Choose SRT (free, open) over Zixi (licensed) unless a broadcaster counterparty mandates Zixi. For a venue with a real production truck and a Direct Connect link, JPEG-XS over ST-2110 into MediaConnect is visually lossless and shaves latency versus compressed contribution, but it needs bandwidth most people do not have.
components.config: Two contribution paths from two different network providers into two Availability Zones — this is the single highest-value redundancy decision in live, because contribution is where events actually die. SRT latency setting at roughly 4x the measured RTT to the ingest region, minimum 200 ms; setting it too low is the common error and produces intermittent artefacting that looks like an encoder bug. Match the ingest region to the venue, not to your audience.

components.service: AWS Elemental MediaLive, channel class STANDARD
components.role: Decode the contribution feed and produce the adaptive bitrate ladder in real time.
components.why: SINGLE_PIPELINE is the obvious cheaper alternative and it is roughly half the price. It runs one pipeline in one Availability Zone, so an AZ event or a pipeline fault takes your event off air with no recovery. STANDARD runs two independent pipelines in two AZs feeding two MediaPackage ingest endpoints, and the packager picks whichever is healthy — the failover is invisible to viewers. Use SINGLE_PIPELINE only for an internal stream nobody is paying for. Against self-hosted FFmpeg on EC2: live is not VOD, there is no retry. A transcode that falls behind real time on a live channel never catches up, and you own the input-loss behaviour, the slate, the failover and the 3am page. The managed service earns its margin here in a way it does not for VOD.
components.config: Input loss behaviour set to a slate image plus silence with a defined timeout, never black — a black screen is indistinguishable from a client-side failure and generates a support storm. GOP of 2 seconds for standard latency, 1 second if you are going low latency. Set the ladder's top rendition to what your audience can actually receive rather than what your source is: shipping a 4K rendition to a mobile-heavy audience burns egress on bits almost nobody selects. Use a 5-6 step ladder and include a low rendition near 400 kbps — on a mobile network that rendition is the difference between a degraded picture and no picture. Enable CloudWatch alarms on input video freeze, input loss and pipeline state; MediaLive will keep emitting a stream long after the picture has gone wrong.

components.service: AWS Elemental MediaPackage v2
components.role: Just-in-time packaging into HLS/DASH, origin endpoints, DVR window, and the SPEKE integration point.
components.why: The obvious alternative is having MediaLive write HLS segments straight to S3 and serving from there. That works and is cheaper, and it locks you into one packaging format, one segment duration, and no DVR window — changing any of them means reconfiguring and restarting the encoder, which during a live event you cannot do. MediaPackage repackages from a single ingest into HLS and DASH with independent settings, gives you a rolling start-over window, handles the dual-pipeline input redundancy, and is where you attach DRM. It also decouples the encoder from the delivery format, so a player bug on one platform is a packager change rather than an encode change.
components.config: Two ingest endpoints, one per MediaLive pipeline. Segment duration 4-6 seconds for standard latency, 1-2 seconds with partial segments for low latency. Manifest window sized to the DVR you actually offer — a long window means large manifests refetched every segment by every viewer, and at 100,000 concurrent a bloated manifest is a real and surprising bandwidth line. Set a startover window only if you use it.

components.service: Amazon CloudFront, tuned for live
components.role: Fan-out. One segment is fetched from the origin once and delivered to every viewer from the edge.
components.why: There is no alternative to a CDN here; the alternative is failure. The knowledge is in the tuning, because the caching rules that are correct for VOD are wrong for live. The manifest changes every segment period, so it needs a TTL of roughly one segment duration — set it to VOD's long TTL and viewers freeze at the segment where they joined; set it to zero and every viewer's manifest poll goes to the origin, which at 100,000 concurrent and a 6-second segment is roughly 16,000 origin requests per second and will take the packager down. Segments themselves are immutable once written and should be cached for hours.
components.config: Two cache behaviours split by path or extension: manifests (.m3u8/.mpd) at TTL equal to one segment duration, segments (.ts/.m4s/.cmf*) at TTL of hours. Enable Origin Shield in the MediaPackage region — without it every edge location independently fetches each new segment from the packager, and the origin request rate scales with the number of active edges instead of being collapsed to one. Do not forward query strings or cookies on segments. Set an origin failover group across both MediaPackage endpoints.

blueprints.ceiling: A single MediaLive STANDARD channel plus MediaPackage behind CloudFront holds to roughly a few hundred thousand concurrent viewers. Beyond that you are contending for edge capacity in a specific country with everyone else on that CDN at the same instant, and the constraint stops being anything you configured and becomes physical CDN footprint in the viewers' metros. At that point you need a second CDN, which is the next blueprint. Low-latency mode lowers this ceiling: at 2-second parts the manifest and part request rate per viewer roughly triples, so the origin and edge request rates that were comfortable at standard latency are no longer comfortable.
blueprints.breaksFirst: In order of what actually kills live events: (1) contribution — the venue's uplink, which is why two paths from two providers is not optional; (2) the origin request rate, when manifest TTL is misconfigured or Origin Shield is off, and it presents as the packager 503ing while the encoder looks perfectly healthy; (3) the player's own retry behaviour, because a brief origin blip causes every client to retry simultaneously and the retry storm is larger than the original load; (4) only then bandwidth. Note what is NOT on the list: MediaLive itself. The encoder is rarely the thing that fails.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Peak concurrency exceeds roughly 200,000, or you are consistently above 100,000 in a single country. Origin (MediaPackage) request rate exceeds a few thousand per second, or CloudFront segment cache hit ratio falls below 95%. Egress for a single event exceeds roughly 200 TB. Rebuffer ratio above 1% or join time p95 above 3 seconds at peak. Any event where losing it costs more than the cost of a second CDN contract.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not reach for low latency by default. Standard HLS at 6-second segments with a 3-segment buffer gives roughly 20-30 seconds glass-to-glass and is extremely robust. LL-HLS with 1-2 second parts and chunked CMAF transfer gets you to roughly 5 seconds, which AWS's own reference architecture confirms, but you pay for it three times: the request rate per viewer roughly triples, the client buffer shrinks so every network hiccup becomes a visible rebuffer instead of being absorbed, and your CDN and player configuration both become far more fragile. Take low latency only when the product genuinely requires it — live betting, auctions, interactive chat where the delay is embarrassing, or simulcast against broadcast. If you need sub-second, HLS is the wrong family entirely: WebRTC (Amazon IVS Real-Time) does roughly 300 ms but AWS documents it as topping out around 25,000 concurrent viewers, so it is a different product, not a tier. Do not build multi-CDN for a channel under 100,000 concurrent. Do not build your own packager. Do not add SSAI before you have an ad contract — server-side ad insertion changes the manifest per cohort and is a large, separate system. And do not run 24/7 on-demand MediaLive pricing for more than a month or two without buying the 12-month reservation; on an always-on channel that is a straightforward saving of up to 75% on inputs and outputs that teams forget to take.

plain.plainName: Streaming a live event to a big audience
plain.problem: I am streaming something live, a conference, a match, a shopping channel. It has to stay up for the whole event and the event will not wait for me.
plain.answer: Send the camera feed into MediaLive, package it with MediaPackage, and deliver it through CloudFront at a latency setting you pick on purpose.
plain.money: A 1080p dual pipeline MediaLive channel is about 1.50 to 3.00 dollars an hour, so a 24/7 channel is roughly 1,100 to 2,200 dollars a month before any viewer watches. Delivery is the variable part and it is the one that hurts.
plain.holdsUpTo: One channel serves 500,000 viewers as easily as 500, and this shape holds to a few hundred thousand watching at once on a single delivery network.
plain.whatBreaks: The internet line at the venue goes first, which is why you run two from two providers. After that, viewers get errors while the encoder dashboard looks perfectly fine, and one small hiccup makes every player retry at the same moment.
plain.timeToMove: When you pass about 200,000 viewers at once, or over 100,000 in one country, or under 95 percent of video chunks come from cache, or more than 1 percent of viewing time is buffering.
plain.dontYet: Do not chase low latency by default. Normal streaming gives about 20 to 30 seconds delay and is very hard to break. Getting to about 5 seconds triples the requests per viewer, shrinks the player buffer so every network hiccup becomes a visible freeze, and costs you more in delivery and support.
plain.pitch: I have one live channel and losing it mid event would be a disaster.

blueprints.name: The mega live event: pre-scaled multi-CDN delivery with tiered graceful degradation
blueprints.forWho: A national-scale live event — a cricket final, an election night, a major product launch — where concurrency is measured in millions to tens of millions, the peak arrives in minutes, and the date is known months in advance. This is a planning and degradation problem, not an autoscaling problem.
blueprints.scale: Publicly reported by Hotstar/JioHotstar: 10M+ concurrent at the 2018 Vivo IPL final at 5.7 Tbps and ~1M requests/second; 25.3M concurrent at the 2019 World Cup semi-final; over 61M concurrent during the 2023 Cricket World Cup. Their published slides cite a concurrency growth rate of about +500,000 viewers per minute, roughly 36,000 CPUs and 72 TB of RAM in a single event footprint, and around 10 billion clickstream messages. JioCinema has published a comparable design for 20M concurrent.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: There is no meaningful per-month figure; this is priced per event and it is enormous. Arithmetic you can check: 20M concurrent viewers averaging 2.5 Mbps is 50 Tbps, which is 22.5 PB of egress for one 3.5-hour match. At CloudFront's India list rate of $0.109/GB that is roughly $2.4M for a single evening, which is exactly why nobody at this scale pays list — delivery at this tier runs on multi-year committed contracts with several CDNs at rates far below published pricing, and on ISP-embedded caches. The knowledge here is the shape, not the number: encoding is a rounding error, compute for the app tier is a large but bounded fixed cost planned weeks ahead, and delivery is essentially the entire bill and is negotiated, not metered. Note also that the bitrate ladder is a cost lever with a multi-million-dollar arm — cutting the average delivered bitrate from 2.5 to 2.0 Mbps removes 20% of the largest line item.

components.service: Multi-CDN with a real-time steering layer
components.role: Deliver the video, and route each viewer cohort to whichever CDN is healthiest right now.
components.why: Single-CDN is the obvious alternative and it is not viable, for a reason that is about physics rather than vendor quality: at tens of millions of concurrent viewers in one country you exceed any single CDN's edge capacity in specific metros, and you have no recourse when one provider's regional POP degrades. JioCinema has published a three-tier approach with a 'Multi-CDN Optimizer' that continuously evaluates edge health, latency and regional congestion and shifts a geographic cohort to an alternate CDN when a cluster shows packet loss or hits capacity. The second published insight is workload segregation: video, API and static assets each get separate CDN stacks so that a failure in one cannot cascade into the others. Hotstar published a related move — a dedicated CDN domain for cacheable APIs such as scorecards and summaries, with lighter security rules and faster routing, separated from the personalised APIs that must be computed fresh.
components.config: Three or more CDN vendors under committed contracts, plus ISP-embedded caches in the target country. Steering at the manifest or client level with per-cohort switching rather than global DNS, because DNS TTLs are too slow for a failure that unfolds in seconds. Separate hostnames and separate cache configurations per workload class. Bake the CDN choice into the client so it can be changed without a redeploy.

components.service: Pre-provisioned compute with reactive autoscaling explicitly disabled
components.role: Serve the app, entitlement, metadata and playback-start APIs during a load curve that is nearly vertical.
components.why: Autoscaling is the obvious answer and it is straightforwardly wrong here, and both companies have published why. Hotstar measured roughly 90 seconds for a new instance to become healthy and about 4 minutes of application boot time, against concurrency growing at about 500,000 viewers per minute — the scaling group is still booting while the event is already over its peak. They moved to fully baked AMIs and baked container images, deliberately avoiding configuration-management tools that add provisioning delay, and kept secondary autoscaling groups and diversified Spot Fleets as pre-warmed standby capacity. JioCinema published the same conclusion with the arithmetic: Total Origin Load = (Target Concurrency x Expected RPS per Client) x (1 - CDN Cache Hit Ratio), benchmark a single pod, run it at 60% CPU/memory with 40% headroom, and provision the resulting count weeks ahead. Reactive scaling is a cost optimisation that only works when load rises slower than instances boot.
components.config: Capacity provisioned to the modelled peak weeks in advance, validated by load tests at that level rather than extrapolated. Fully baked images, no config management in the boot path. Pods targeted at 60% utilisation with 40% headroom. A published operational cadence: JioCinema describe assembling a war room at T-2 hours, pre-scaling compute and databases with a metrics greenlight, then a 'Touch-Me-Not' policy of zero configuration changes from kickoff to T+3.5 hours, and a controlled ladder scale-down afterwards (20M to 15M to 10M to 5M) with graceful HTTP connection draining rather than a single step.

components.service: Panic mode and tiered graceful degradation
components.role: Decide in advance, in code, what gets sacrificed when saturation arrives — so that the video keeps playing.
components.why: The alternative is uniform degradation, where everything gets slower together and the video fails alongside the chat widget. That is the failure teams actually experience. Hotstar's published approach is a server-side panic mode: when the backend detects saturation it signals overload to clients, which back off exponentially with jitter, while the platform sheds non-essential services — recommendations first — to reclaim their CPU and database capacity for the critical path. JioCinema publish an explicit priority tiering: P0 is video playback plus ad insertion and never fails; P1 is personalised recommendations, which falls back silently to a static catalog; P2 is chat, stickers and reactions, which are suppressed entirely with no error dialog shown. They also describe a static fallback where, at 100% database CPU, pre-warmed JSON snapshots in object storage replace live API calls and CDN routes flip to serve static manifests — personalisation is sacrificed, playback survives. Note the detail that makes it work: degradation is silent. An error dialog turns a degraded experience into a support event and a retry storm.
components.config: Every endpoint labelled P0/P1/P2 at design time, with the P1 and P2 fallbacks built and tested, not planned. A server-signalled overload state the client understands. Client-side exponential backoff WITH jitter — jitter is the load-bearing word, since synchronised retries are themselves the outage. Pre-warmed static JSON snapshots for anything that can be stale. Chaos testing that injects over 2000 ms of latency plus DNS failure to prove the fallbacks actually fire.

components.service: Network and cluster plumbing sized for the event
components.role: The unglamorous layer that is usually the real ceiling.
components.why: Hotstar's published post-mortem work on scaling past 25M is almost entirely here, and it is the most transferable part. They found one cluster consuming 50% of NAT gateway bandwidth at only 10% of projected peak — a constraint invisible at normal load and fatal at peak. Fixes: moving from one NAT gateway per Availability Zone to one per subnet to spread the load, adopting nodes capable of 10+ Gbps with Kubernetes topology constraints limiting gateway pods to one per node, replacing 200+ individual load balancers with a centralised Envoy gateway, moving from NodePort to ClusterIP services to eliminate port exhaustion, and migrating from self-managed KOPS clusters (which they state were limited to around 25M users) to managed Amazon EKS. They also introduced a 'Datacenter Abstraction' grouping multiple clusters as one logical unit, and ran across 8 regions.
components.config: Load-test at true peak and measure NAT throughput, ephemeral port usage, load balancer counts and per-node network limits — not just CPU. Multi-region and multi-AZ. Centralised gateway rather than per-service load balancers. Instance types chosen for network bandwidth rather than for CPU price.

blueprints.ceiling: The published ceiling is the current record rather than an architectural one: 61M+ concurrent for JioHotstar in 2023. What genuinely bounds it is CDN and ISP capacity inside one country at one instant, plus the accuracy of your concurrency forecast — because capacity is bought in advance, forecasting low IS the outage. Hotstar's own account puts a hard number on a component ceiling: self-managed KOPS clusters capped them around 25M users until they moved to EKS.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The traffic shape is the thing general guidance gets wrong. Load is not smooth and does not track the clock — it tracks the drama. A wicket, a last-over finish or a push notification produces a near-vertical step, and Hotstar cite a 90-second reaction window on push notifications and about +500K concurrency per minute. What breaks first is almost never the video pipeline: it is the app tier's non-cacheable, personalised APIs at playback start, and the retry storm that follows any brief failure there. After that, NAT gateway and per-node network throughput — the limits nobody load-tests. Then database CPU on the personalisation path, which is exactly what the static-snapshot fallback exists to survive. The video itself, being cached and fanned out, is the most robust thing in the system.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: This is the top tier; there is no next one, only more of it. The signals that you have arrived here from the previous blueprint: peak concurrency above roughly 500,000, or the business consequence of a single failed event exceeding the annual cost of a second and third CDN. Concrete triggers to act on within the tier: forecast concurrency within 20% of contracted CDN capacity in any single country; NAT or per-node network utilisation above 40% at 10% of projected peak (Hotstar's actual warning sign); app-tier instance boot time exceeding the time in which concurrency doubles; any P1 or P2 fallback that has not been fired in a chaos test in the last event cycle.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Nothing in this blueprint belongs in a product that has not yet run a million-concurrent event, and copying it early is expensive in a specific way. Multi-CDN steering costs three contracts with minimum commitments, a steering service and a whole failure class where two CDNs disagree about which manifest is current — for a 50,000-concurrent product it buys nothing a single CDN was not already doing. Pre-provisioning instead of autoscaling means paying for peak capacity continuously; at normal scale that is a multiple of your compute bill in exchange for solving a problem you do not have, since autoscaling is only too slow when load outruns boot time. Panic mode and P0/P1/P2 tiering is real engineering effort across every endpoint plus a chaos-testing practice to keep it honest, and it is only worth it when you cannot simply add capacity. And do not skip the boring part in order to build the exciting part: the published record is that NAT gateways, port exhaustion, load balancer counts and node network bandwidth are what actually stopped these teams, not their CDN strategy. If you are going to take one thing from this tier early, take load-testing at true peak and measuring the network layer, not the architecture diagram.

plain.plainName: A national live event with millions watching at once
plain.problem: A cricket final or election night. Millions of people arrive within minutes, the date has been known for months, and I get exactly one chance.
plain.answer: Buy capacity across several delivery networks in advance, steer traffic between them live, and build in a panic mode that switches off nice to have features under load.
plain.money: Priced per event and it is huge. 20 million viewers at 2.5 Mbps is 22.5 petabytes for one 3.5 hour match, about 2.4 million dollars at India list rates for a single evening.
plain.holdsUpTo: JioHotstar reached over 61 million watching at once in 2023, after 10 million in 2018 at 5.7 Tbps and about 1 million requests a second. Growth runs at roughly 500,000 extra viewers per minute.
plain.whatBreaks: Load follows the drama, not the clock. A wicket or a push notification sends it near vertical within 90 seconds. The video usually survives, the personalised parts of the app do not, so the stream plays while the rest of the app stops responding.
plain.timeToMove: This is the top tier. You arrive here when you pass roughly 500,000 viewers at once, or when one failed event costs more than a year of extra delivery contracts. Inside it, act when the forecast comes within 20 percent of the capacity you bought in any one country.
plain.dontYet: None of this belongs in a product that has never run a million viewer event. Three delivery contracts with minimum commitments and a steering service buy nothing at 50,000 viewers. Pre buying peak capacity instead of scaling up on demand means paying for the peak all the time.
plain.pitch: My event will pull millions of people in the same five minutes and the date is already on the calendar.

blueprints.name: Serverless chat on API Gateway WebSockets (or AppSync Events) with DynamoDB as the log
blueprints.forWho: A team of one to five shipping 1:1 and small-group chat, a support inbox, collaborative cursors, or in-app notifications inside an existing product. Nobody wants to be paged at 3am for a connection server. Traffic is bursty and mostly idle — a few thousand people connected, most of them typing nothing.
blueprints.scale: 5,000-50,000 concurrent connections, 50-500 messages/sec steady, bursts to ~2,000/sec. Rooms up to ~500 members. History in the tens of millions of rows. Comfortably serves a product with 200k-1M registered users, because concurrency is usually 2-5% of MAU.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $150-$900 at 10k concurrent connections and 5M messages/day. Drivers in order: (1) connection-minutes — 10k connections held 24/7 is 432M connection-minutes/month = ~$108 on API Gateway at $0.25/M, but only ~$35 on AppSync Events at $0.08/M; (2) messages — API Gateway bills $1.00 per million messages and fan-out multiplies it: one message into a 50-person room is 50 billed outbound messages, so 5M sends into 50-member rooms is 250M messages = $250; (3) Lambda invocations on $connect/$disconnect/$default; (4) DynamoDB on-demand writes. The trap is (2): your bill scales with room size, not send rate.

components.service: Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API
components.role: Terminates every client WebSocket. Routes $connect, $disconnect, $default and custom routes (sendMessage, markRead, typing) to Lambda. Server-to-client delivery is the separate @connections POST endpoint, called with the stored connectionId.
components.why: Beats running your own Node/Go WebSocket server on ECS behind an NLB because at this size operational cost dominates dollar cost: no connection draining on deploy, no sticky-session problem, no per-host connection ceiling to tune (file descriptors, conntrack, TLS termination). Why NOT: it bills per connection-minute AND per message, and fan-out is billed per recipient, so the crossover against a self-run fleet arrives around 50k-100k steady connections or when average room size exceeds ~50. Versus AppSync Events: AppSync is cheaper on connection-minutes ($0.08/M vs $0.25/M), does server-side channel fan-out so you do not write a fan-out loop, and allows 200 subscriptions per connection — but its channel model is namespace/segment-shaped (max 5 segments, 50 chars each) and you get less control over per-message authorization. Pick AppSync Events when the shape is broadcast-to-channel; pick API Gateway when every message needs custom server logic and per-recipient auth.
components.config: Route selection expression $request.body.action. Lambda authorizer on $connect only — there is no per-message authorizer, so authorize once and stash the claims. Quotas that matter: 500 new connections/sec and 500,000 concurrent connections per account per region (both soft — raise them before launch; the connect-rate one bites during a mass reconnect); 128 KB message payload; 32 KB frame size, so larger payloads must be fragmented; 10-minute idle timeout; 2-hour hard maximum connection duration, so the client MUST have reconnect-with-jitter logic because AWS closes every connection at the 2-hour mark. Also: the account-wide 10,000 RPS API Gateway throttle is shared across REST, HTTP, WebSocket and the WebSocket callback API — your @connections fan-out posts eat the same budget as your REST API.

components.service: DynamoDB — connections table
components.role: Maps connectionId to userId, and userId to the set of connectionIds (a user has three devices). Written on $connect, deleted on $disconnect.
components.why: Beats ElastiCache/Redis here only because you are already serverless: no VPC, no subnet plumbing for Lambda (which adds ENI cold-start cost and a NAT Gateway bill). Redis is genuinely better once you need sub-millisecond membership reads at high fan-out rates — but at 500 msg/sec against a table with adaptive capacity, DynamoDB is not the bottleneck and costs near-nothing.
components.config: PK=connectionId, GSI on userId. TTL attribute set to now + 3 hours on every connect — not optional. $disconnect is best-effort and DOES get dropped (network partition, Lambda throttle), so without TTL you accumulate ghost connections and pay to POST to dead ids. Handle GoneException (410) from @connections by deleting the row inline; that is your real garbage collector.

components.service: DynamoDB — messages table
components.role: The durable ordered message log. Source of truth for history, offline delivery and read receipts.
components.why: Beats Aurora/RDS because the access pattern is exactly one shape — 'messages in conversation X after sequence N' — which is a partition-key plus sort-key range query, the thing DynamoDB is unambiguously best at, and because there is no connection pool for Lambda to saturate. Aurora wins the moment you need cross-conversation search or analytics; add OpenSearch rather than switching databases.
components.config: PK=CONV#<conversationId>, SK=<zero-padded sequence or ULID>. Do NOT use client wall-clock timestamps as the sort key — clock skew reorders messages and two devices collide. Get ordering from a per-conversation counter: a conditional UpdateItem on a CONV#<id> METADATA item incrementing lastSeq and returning the new value, then write at that seq. Two writes per message, worth it. Per-partition hard limits are 1,000 WCU and 3,000 RCU/sec, so one conversation tops out around 1,000 messages/sec — fine for chat, fatal for a 'general' channel firehose. Read state is one item per user: SK=READ#<userId> holding lastReadSeq — one small write per read receipt instead of one per message.

components.service: DynamoDB Streams + Lambda fan-out worker
components.role: Reads new message rows off the stream and does delivery: look up room members, look up live connections, POST via @connections, and for members with no live connection enqueue a push.
components.why: Beats fanning out inline in the $default handler because it decouples 'durably stored' from 'delivered'. The sender's ack returns as soon as the write lands, delivery retries independently, and a fan-out failure never loses the message. The obvious alternative — all in one Lambda — turns a 20ms write into a 3-second invocation the sender waits on for a 300-person room, with no retry story for partial failure.
components.config: Stream view NEW_IMAGE, batch size 10, ParallelizationFactor 10, bisectOnFunctionError true, maximumRetryAttempts ~5 with an on-failure SQS destination. Ordering is guaranteed per shard and shards key off the partition key — since PK is the conversation, messages within a conversation stay ordered, which is exactly why the PK choice above matters. Fan out with Promise.all in batches of ~25 @connections calls; sequential loops are what make this architecture feel slow.

components.service: SQS FIFO + Amazon SNS mobile push (APNs/FCM)
components.role: Anything not delivered over a live socket becomes a push notification; SQS holds the retry and the dedupe.
components.why: SNS mobile push beats calling APNs and FCM directly because it owns the platform-endpoint lifecycle — token rotation and the 'endpoint disabled' feedback when a user uninstalls — which is the part teams always get wrong and which silently degrades delivery over months. Direct APNs/FCM wins only when you need HTTP/2 per-message control, collapse-id or Live Activities; many teams then keep SNS for the token store and bypass it for the send. SQS FIFO over standard because a duplicate push is a user-visible bug.
components.config: MessageGroupId = userId so one user's notifications stay ordered and a slow device cannot head-of-line-block anyone else. MessageDeduplicationId = <conversationId>#<seq>. Set a 5-15 second delivery delay and on dequeue check whether the user's lastReadSeq has passed this message — if they read it on web meanwhile, drop the push. That one check removes the most common complaint about chat apps. Subscribe an SNS delivery-status Lambda to prune disabled endpoints; a token store nobody prunes is why delivery rate quietly falls to 60%.

blueprints.ceiling: Three walls in order. (1) Cost, around 50,000-100,000 steady connections or average room size above ~50 — 100k connections all month is 4.3B connection-minutes ≈ $1,080 plus per-recipient message billing, where two c7g.2xlarge instances running your own socket server cost ~$400 and do the same job. (2) The account-wide 10,000 RPS API Gateway throttle, shared with every other API in the region: at average room size 20, ~500 sends/sec becomes 10,000 @connections calls/sec and you are at the wall — one broadcast to a 10,000-member room exceeds the entire account budget in a single message. (3) The 1,000 WCU per-partition limit, i.e. ~1,000 messages/sec into one conversation; a 500-person 'general' during an incident brushes it.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The @connections fan-out path, as 429 TooManyRequestsException inside the stream Lambda — not as an error users see. What they see is messages arriving 8, then 30, then 90 seconds late for some people and instantly for others, because the stream Lambda retries, DynamoDB stream IteratorAge climbs, and delivery falls behind per shard while writes keep succeeding. The alarm that catches it early is IteratorAge over 10 seconds, not any API Gateway metric. Secondary: every 410 GoneException against a ghost connection still consumed a request against the throttle, so stale rows make the wall arrive sooner.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: (a) Stream Lambda IteratorAge p99 > 10s for 5 consecutive minutes; (b) API Gateway 5XXError or ThrottledCount on the callback API > 0.1% of calls; (c) monthly API Gateway WebSocket line item over ~$800; (d) p99 connect-to-first-message > 1s, usually Lambda cold starts under a reconnect storm; (e) sustained ConsumedWriteCapacity on a single conversation partition above 800 WCU; (f) you need a message delivered to more than ~200 recipients at once.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add Kafka/MSK — ~$500/month in broker hours before it moves a byte, plus a mental model the team must carry; DynamoDB Streams gives the same ordered-per-key log for effectively free at this volume. Do not add ElastiCache: it puts Lambda in a VPC, adding ENI cold-start latency and NAT Gateway charges (~$33/month/AZ plus $0.045/GB) to solve a read-latency problem you do not have. Do not build end-to-end encryption yet — E2EE means the server cannot read bodies, which kills server-side search, kills push previews (you need silent push plus local decryption, which iOS heavily rate-limits), kills moderation, and forces key distribution, multi-device key sync and a safety-number UI: a 3-6 month project touching every screen, so decide before launch or accept a hard migration. Do not store read receipts per (message, user) — a 200-message backlog read by 50 people is 10,000 writes; store one lastReadSeq per user per conversation. Do not pre-shard conversations: sharding forfeits the per-conversation stream ordering doing real work for you. Do not go multi-region — it doubles connection-minutes and forces you to solve cross-region ordering, and users do not notice 150ms on a chat message.

plain.plainName: Chat or live updates without running a server
plain.problem: I want chat, a support inbox or live notifications inside my product. We are a small team and nobody wants a 3am page about a connection server.
plain.answer: Use API Gateway WebSockets for the live connections, store messages in DynamoDB, and let DynamoDB Streams with Lambda push them out.
plain.money: About 150 to 900 dollars a month at 10,000 people connected and 5 million messages a day. Holding 10,000 connections all month is about 108 dollars on API Gateway, or about 35 dollars on AppSync Events.
plain.holdsUpTo: 5,000 to 50,000 people connected at once, 50 to 500 messages a second with bursts near 2,000, rooms up to about 500 people. That fits a product with 200,000 to 1,000,000 registered users.
plain.whatBreaks: Messages start arriving 8, then 30, then 90 seconds late for some people and instantly for others. Nobody sees an error, sending still works, delivery just falls behind.
plain.timeToMove: When delivery lag stays over 10 seconds for 5 minutes, or the WebSocket bill passes about 800 dollars a month, or one conversation needs more than 800 write units, or time to first message goes over 1 second.
plain.dontYet: Do not add Kafka, it costs about 500 dollars a month before it moves a single byte, and DynamoDB Streams already gives you the same ordered log for almost nothing here. Do not add a cache, it drags Lambda into a VPC and adds NAT charges of about 33 dollars per month per AZ to fix a speed problem you do not have. Do not build end to end encryption yet, it kills server side search.
plain.pitch: I need chat inside my app and we are too small to babysit servers.

blueprints.name: Your own connection layer: stateful gateway fleet on ECS, a pub/sub spine, and cheap presence, typing and live counters
blueprints.forWho: You outgrew per-message billing, or you need something managed services do not expose: rooms with tens of thousands of members, presence and typing indicators, live counters on a stream, binary protocols, custom backpressure, connection-level state that must survive a message. Typically 4-15 engineers with at least one person comfortable being paged.
blueprints.scale: 200,000 to 2,000,000 concurrent connections across 20-100 gateway nodes. 10,000-100,000 inbound messages/sec with outbound fan-out one to two orders of magnitude higher. Presence for millions of users. Rooms up to ~1M members if you adopt the relay pattern.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $4,000-$25,000 at ~500k concurrent connections. Drivers: (1) gateway compute — budget 40,000-80,000 idle connections per c7g.2xlarge-class node, so ~10 nodes for 500k but you run 2-3x for headroom and deploys: $1,500-$4,000; (2) the pub/sub spine — ElastiCache for Valkey at cache.r7g.large x 6 is ~$1,100, three-broker MSK m7g.large ~$800 plus storage; (3) NLB — ~$16 base plus LCUs, where one LCU covers 800 new flows/sec or 100,000 active flows, so 500k connections is ~5 active-flow LCUs, cheap; (4) cross-AZ transfer at $0.01/GB each way, which on a fan-out-heavy workload is the line item that surprises people.

components.service: ECS on EC2 (not Fargate) behind a Network Load Balancer
components.role: The connection tier: long-lived stateful nodes terminating TLS and WebSocket, holding per-connection state (subscriptions, auth claims, last-ack sequence, send buffer).
components.why: ECS on EC2 beats Fargate because connections are long-lived and memory-heavy per task: you want to choose the instance family (Graviton, network-optimised), you want placement control, and you want kernel tuning (net.core.somaxconn, nf_conntrack_max, fd limits) that Fargate does not expose — and connection-heavy workloads are cheaper on Savings-Plan EC2 than on Fargate per-vCPU-second. NLB rather than ALB: ALB does per-request HTTP processing you do not need after the upgrade and caps connection idle handling at 4,000 seconds, while NLB is layer 4, preserves client IP, scales flows without pre-warming and costs less per connection — and critically it does not interfere with your own heartbeat and backpressure protocol. Reject raw EC2 with a hand-rolled ASG: ECS gives you the rolling deploy and health-check plumbing you would otherwise write badly.
components.config: NLB deregistration delay 300s with draining: on deploy a node stops accepting new connections, pushes a 'reconnect after a jittered 0-120s' frame to its own clients, and lets them leave gradually. Without that, rolling 10 nodes produces a 500k-connection thundering herd that takes the fleet down — the most common self-inflicted outage in this architecture. Application-layer ping/pong every 30-45s, never TCP keepalive. Per-connection send buffer with a hard cap (~1MB or 500 frames) and a policy: on overflow drop the connection rather than grow the buffer, so one slow mobile client on a train cannot OOM the node. Expect 40k-80k idle connections/node at 4-8 KB heap each, falling fast as subscription state grows. Go, Rust or Elixir rather than Node: LinkedIn published holding hundreds of thousands of persistent connections on one machine with Play plus one Akka actor per connection, precisely because per-connection cost is a few KB rather than a thread.

components.service: ElastiCache for Valkey (cluster mode) as pub/sub spine and presence store
components.role: Routes a message from the gateway node that received it to the gateway nodes holding recipients; also holds presence, typing state and live counters.
components.why: Beats 'every gateway subscribes to every room', which turns the fleet into a full mesh. Beats Kafka for this hop because Kafka is a durable ordered log with consumer-group rebalancing — wrong for ephemeral, fire-and-forget, latency-sensitive routing where you do not want the message if the recipient is absent. Use both: Valkey pub/sub for the live hop and Kafka/Kinesis beside it for durability, search indexing and push workers. The non-obvious detail is sharded pub/sub (SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE, Redis 7+/Valkey) rather than classic PUBLISH: classic broadcasts every message to every node in the cluster, so a 12-node cluster does 12x the work and the cluster bus saturates long before CPU does.
components.config: Cluster mode enabled, cache.r7g.large or larger, at least 3 shards each with a replica across AZs. SSUBSCRIBE/SPUBLISH keyed by room id. Presence as presence:<userId> holding the node id with EX 60, refreshed by heartbeat — this is LinkedIn's published design: the client heartbeats every d seconds, the server checks the K/V store and publishes 'online' only when no unexpired entry existed, and arms a delayed trigger (an actor per online member) firing at d + 2ε to publish 'offline' if the heartbeat expired, with best-effort sticky routing of a member's heartbeats to one node. They reported status-change delivery under 200ms at p99 and ~1.8K QPS of incoming requests per node. The point: presence is derived from expiry, not from disconnect events, because disconnect events are unreliable and jittery mobile networks would otherwise flap a user online/offline every few seconds.

components.service: Presence, typing indicators and live counters — the ephemeral tier
components.role: The state nobody wants to pay for but everyone expects: who is online, who is typing, how many are watching.
components.why: These are expensive because their cost is O(viewers x subjects), not O(events). In a 1,000-person room where everyone is online, naive presence fan-out is 1,000 x 1,000 = 1,000,000 notifications for one round. Discord stated it directly: if a server has 1000 people online and they all say one thing, that is 1 million notifications, and at 100,000 concurrent users it becomes 10 billion. Their fix is the one to copy — lazy/passive sessions: a client only receives full member and presence updates for the guild it is actually looking at. Discord reported ~90% of user-guild connections in large servers were passive, making fan-out ~90% cheaper, which roughly tripled supportable community size. So subscribe on view, not on membership. The obvious alternative — pushing every presence change to every member — is exactly what not to do.
components.config: Four rules. (1) Subscribe on view: presence and typing are delivered only for the room on screen, torn down on blur/background. (2) Coalesce: never push per event — batch presence deltas into one frame every 3-5 seconds and typing into one frame per second; users cannot perceive the difference and you cut frames 10-50x. (3) Typing is a TTL, not an event pair: the client sends 'typing' at most once per 3 seconds while keys are pressed, the server stores it with a 5-second TTL, and 'stopped typing' is simply expiry — never send a stop event, because the stop event is the one that gets lost and leaves a permanent ellipsis on someone's screen. (4) Live counters are sampled: keep them in Redis INCR or HyperLogLog and broadcast on a 2-5 second tick, not per increment; above ~1,000 viewers switch to an approximate display ('12.4k watching') and a longer tick. At the top end add Discord-style relays — intermediary nodes between the room process and sessions, each handling up to ~15,000 sessions, spreading fan-out across machines instead of concentrating it in one process. Slack's Flannel is the same idea from another angle: an application-level edge cache that terminates the WebSocket and holds pre-warmed team metadata kept fresh from the event stream, reported serving roughly 4-5 million simultaneous connections at peak and 600K client queries/sec, cutting bootstrap payload for a 32K-user team by about 44x. The Flannel lesson: most of what a connection costs is not the socket, it is the metadata you push down it at boot.

components.service: MSK (Kafka) or Kinesis Data Streams as the durable spine
components.role: Every message that matters is appended here alongside the live hop. Consumers: persistence writer, push worker, search indexer, analytics, moderation.
components.why: Kafka over SQS because many independent consumers read the same stream at their own offsets, and partition-level ordering gives per-conversation ordering for free. Kinesis over MSK below ~10 MB/sec if you would rather not run brokers — on-demand removes shard math and has no idle broker cost; MSK wins above that on unit economics and when you need long retention, compaction or transactional semantics. Partition by conversationId, never round-robin: ordering is per-partition and round-robin will reorder your chat.
components.config: Kafka: partitions at least 2x peak consumer count, replication factor 3 across 3 AZs, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all for anything user-visible, retention 7 days so a broken consumer is replayed rather than losing a day of pushes. Kinesis: on-demand, partition key = conversationId, enhanced fan-out ($0.015/consumer-shard-hour) only for consumers that genuinely need sub-200ms.

components.service: Message ordering and delivery guarantees (protocol, not a service)
components.role: What makes this feel correct rather than merely fast.
components.why: WebSockets give ordered delivery within one connection and nothing across reconnects — and reconnects happen to every user many times a day. Everything else you build. The obvious alternative, trusting client timestamps, produces the bug where a reply appears above the message it replies to; Twitter's writeups note exactly this race, replies arriving before the original tweet, as a consequence of fan-out timing.
components.config: Server-assigned monotonic per-conversation sequence numbers, never client clocks. The client tracks its highest contiguous seq and sends it on reconnect; the server replays the gap from the durable store. That converts at-most-once socket delivery into at-least-once end to end, with client-side dedupe by seq. Each delivered frame carries a seq, the client acks periodically, and the server trims its send buffer to the ack — which also gives you backpressure. Every send carries a client-generated idempotency key so a retry after a flaky network does not duplicate. For E2EE the architectural consequence is that the server can no longer help: fan-out becomes per-recipient-device (a 5-device user is 5 ciphertexts), the server cannot dedupe or compress bodies, push must be silent-with-local-decryption, and you need prekey-bundle distribution plus multi-device key sync — budget it as its own subsystem, not a feature flag.

blueprints.ceiling: Roughly 1-2 million concurrent connections in one region before the pub/sub spine, not the gateway fleet, becomes the problem. A single Valkey/Redis shard handles on the order of 100k-200k pub/sub messages/sec before the cluster bus and single-threaded event loop saturate — and classic non-sharded pub/sub hits that far earlier because every message is replicated to every node. Room size ceiling without relays is ~50,000-100,000 members, beyond which one room's fan-out concentrates on whichever node owns it. Per-node ceiling is 40k-100k connections: you hit memory before CPU on idle connections and CPU before memory on chatty ones.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The pub/sub spine, and it looks like latency, not errors. Delivery p99 walks from 40ms to 400ms to 4s over about twenty minutes while the Redis dashboard shows one shard pinned at 100% on a single core and the rest idle — one hot room hashed to one shard. Nothing throws. The more violent failure is the deploy thundering herd: rolling 30 nodes drops 500k connections that all reconnect within seconds, and the $connect path (auth, session bootstrap, presence write, subscription restore) is 50-100x more expensive than steady state — so the fleet that comfortably held 500k connections cannot re-establish them and you get a sustained outage that looks like a DDoS you did to yourself. Third: slow consumers — one node's send buffers grow, GC pauses lengthen, heartbeats are missed, the NLB health check fails, connections move to surviving nodes, and the failure walks around the fleet.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: (a) Any Valkey shard sustaining >70% EngineCPUUtilization, or cluster-bus traffic growing faster than message volume — the sign you are still on classic pub/sub and need SSUBSCRIBE plus more shards; (b) end-to-end delivery p99 (publish to client receipt, not measured at the gateway) above 250ms; (c) reconnect-storm recovery taking more than 2 minutes in a game-day test — if you have not run that test you do not know your ceiling; (d) a single room above ~50,000 members, which is when the relay tier goes in; (e) connections per node falling below 30k as per-connection state grows, meaning subscription state must move off the node; (f) users concentrated in a second geography seeing >150ms RTT.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not go multi-region active-active for chat before you have real users in a second geography. It forces you to answer 'what is the order of messages written in two regions at once', and the honest answers are either a home region per conversation (so cross-region writes are slow anyway) or CRDTs/vector clocks (so you rewrite the client). Teams spend two quarters here and end up pinning conversations to a home region, which they could have done on day one. Do not put Kafka on the live delivery path: consumer-group rebalance takes seconds, and seconds of nobody receiving messages during a routine deploy is worse than the durability gained — keep Kafka beside the path. Do not build your own presence gossip protocol between gateway nodes; it is a research project that fails in netsplits, while a Redis TTL plus a heartbeat gets 95% of the value, which is what LinkedIn shipped. Do not implement exact live counters at high fan-out — broadcasting a counter per event to 50,000 viewers is 50,000 frames for an integer nobody verifies; a 2-second tick is 1/100th the cost and indistinguishable. Do not adopt Fargate for the connection tier to 'simplify ops': you lose kernel tuning and instance selection and pay more per connection. And do not skip the deploy-drain protocol because you are small — it costs a day and it is the difference between a routine deploy and an outage the first time you hold 200k connections.

plain.plainName: Running your own live connection servers
plain.problem: Paying per message stopped making sense, or I need things the managed services will not give me, like rooms with tens of thousands of people, presence and typing indicators, or live counters.
plain.answer: Run your own connection servers on ECS behind a Network Load Balancer, with ElastiCache for Valkey as the pub sub spine and Kafka or Kinesis as the durable log.
plain.money: About 4,000 to 25,000 dollars a month at 500,000 connections. Budget 40,000 to 80,000 idle connections per node, so about 10 nodes for 500,000, but run 2 to 3 times that for headroom, roughly 1,500 to 4,000 dollars, plus about 1,100 dollars for the pub sub spine.
plain.holdsUpTo: 200,000 to 2,000,000 connections across 20 to 100 nodes, 10,000 to 100,000 incoming messages a second. Roughly 1 to 2 million connections in one region before the pub sub spine, not the servers, becomes the limit.
plain.whatBreaks: Messages get slower, not broken. Delivery creeps from 40 milliseconds to 400 to 4 seconds over about twenty minutes, while one busy room pins a single shard and everything else looks idle. Nothing throws an error.
plain.timeToMove: When any Valkey shard sits above 70 percent CPU, or delivery time measured at the client passes 250 milliseconds, or reconnecting everyone after a test failure takes more than 2 minutes.
plain.dontYet: Do not go multi region active active for chat before you actually have users in a second country. It forces you to answer what order two simultaneous messages happened in, and teams spend two quarters on it only to pin each conversation to a home region, which they could have done on day one. Do not put Kafka in the live delivery path.
plain.pitch: My message bill is out of hand and I need presence, typing and huge rooms that managed services will not give me.

blueprints.name: A social feed that survives celebrities: hybrid fan-out with a Redis-materialized timeline and a read-time merge
blueprints.forWho: Anyone building a following-based feed — social app, creator platform, marketplace activity stream, internal company feed. The moment your follower distribution stops being uniform (and it always does) the naive design stops working, so this is worth understanding at 10,000 users rather than 10 million.
blueprints.scale: The pattern spans three orders of magnitude. Small: 100k users, 500 posts/hour, ~150 average followers — one Redis node and Postgres. Large: the published reference is Twitter at ~150M active users, ~300K QPS against timelines versus only ~6K writes/sec, ~400M tweets/day peaking above 12K/sec, with the materialized home timeline capped at ~800 tweet IDs per user, replicated 3x, on a Redis cluster holding a couple of terabytes of RAM.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $300-$1,200 at 100k users (one ElastiCache cache.r7g.large replication group ~$220, Aurora Serverless v2 at 0.5-4 ACU ~$100-$400, SQS and Lambda in the tens). At 10M users with 1M daily actives expect $15,000-$60,000, dominated by Redis memory for materialized timelines. The napkin math: 800 post ids x 8 bytes x 3 replicas ≈ 20 KB per active user before overhead, so 10M active users is roughly 200 GB of RAM — which is why the cap is 800 and why it covers only users active in the last 30 days.

components.service: ElastiCache for Valkey/Redis — the materialized timeline
components.role: One capped list per active user holding post IDs (not bodies). Reading a feed is one LRANGE.
components.why: Beats querying 'posts from everyone I follow ordered by time' against Postgres because that is a fan-in join over a set that grows with following count, and it degrades exactly when the user is most engaged. Twitter's design is the reference: LPUSH plus LTRIM on a capped list is precisely the shape the fan-out path needs and the read becomes a single cache hit. Store IDs not bodies — bodies are hydrated in one batched multi-get, so editing or deleting a post does not require rewriting millions of timelines. The obvious alternative, materializing full post objects into each timeline, multiplies memory 50-100x and makes deletes a nightmare.
components.config: LPUSH then LTRIM 0 799 — cap it, always. Materialize only for users active in the last 30 days; everyone else gets an on-demand build at next login with a slow first load. TTL the key at 30 days so churned users free memory automatically. Cluster mode on, key = user id so timelines shard evenly.

components.service: Fan-out-on-write worker (SQS + Lambda, or ECS consumers on Kafka)
components.role: On a post from a normal account, page the follower list and LPUSH the post id onto each follower's timeline.
components.why: Fan-out on write is chosen for the ~99.9% of accounts below the celebrity threshold because the read path runs far more often than the write path — Twitter's published split is ~300K reads/sec against ~6K writes/sec — so you want the expensive work on the rare side. The obvious alternative, fan-out on read for everyone, is cheap to write and always fresh, and it is what you should actually run below ~10k users, because maintaining materialized timelines is not yet worth its complexity.
components.config: Batch the LPUSHes: pipeline 500-1,000 followers per round trip — a per-follower round trip is what makes people think fan-out is slow. Target completion under 5 seconds for the whole follower set, the figure Twitter published as their goal. Make it idempotent so a replayed message does not double-insert (check the list head, or a per-(post,user) marker with a short TTL). Fan out only to active users; dormant accounts are often half your follower table and pure waste.

components.service: The celebrity path — read-time merge
components.role: Accounts above a follower threshold are NOT fanned out; their posts stay in their own author timeline and are pulled and merged when a follower loads their feed.
components.why: This is the whole point. Fan-out on write is O(followers) per post, so 10M followers is 10M writes — Twitter described exactly this as the painful case for Lady Gaga (31M followers then) and Barack Obama, tens of millions of inserts across the Redis cluster, and their documented fix was to stop fanning out high-value users and merge their timelines in at read time. Instagram is widely described as using the same follower-count-threshold hybrid, but I could not find a first-party Instagram or Meta post stating it, so treat that attribution as unsourced. What IS attributable is that Facebook's News Feed has been described as fan-out-on-read over the TAO graph with a Multifeed aggregator — the opposite default from Twitter, which is the more useful lesson: the choice follows your read/write ratio and your ranking needs, not fashion.
components.config: Threshold around 10,000-100,000 followers, tuned so a typical user follows fewer than ~50 celebrity accounts, because that count is the cost of the merge. At read time, in parallel: LRANGE the materialized timeline AND fetch recent posts of the celebrity accounts this user follows — cached once per celebrity and read by millions, which is why this is cheap — then merge and rank. Use hysteresis so an account crossing the line does not flip back and forth: promote above the threshold, demote below half of it, and on promotion leave already-fanned-out posts in place rather than retracting them. The seam that leaks: a user who follows only celebrities has an empty materialized timeline, so the merge path must work standalone.

components.service: Aurora PostgreSQL (or DynamoDB) — post store and follow graph
components.role: Source of truth for posts and edges; hydrates post IDs into bodies.
components.why: Postgres beats DynamoDB for the follow graph because graph queries are genuinely relational and you will want 'followers of X who also follow Y' sooner than you think; DynamoDB beats Postgres for the post store if reads are strictly by id, which after the timeline indirection they are. A reasonable split is Postgres for the graph, either for posts, and never the graph in Redis. What you must not do is make a follower list a single row or item — a 10M-follower list is not a value, it is a paginated query.
components.config: followers(followee_id, follower_id) with a covering index on followee_id, paginated by follower_id so the fan-out worker streams it in pages of 10,000. Keep a denormalized follower_count on the account row, updated asynchronously, because the celebrity-threshold check runs on every post and must not be a COUNT(*). Hydration: one batched multi-get of 50-100 ids per feed load behind a 60-300s cache; bodies are near-immutable and cache well.

components.service: Ranking and caching layer
components.role: Turns a chronological merge into a ranked feed and caches the result briefly.
components.why: Rank at read time, not at fan-out time. Ranking at write time bakes a score into every follower's timeline and makes it un-updatable without rewriting millions of rows — and engagement signals (likes in the last hour) change far faster than the timeline does. The obvious alternative, a fully personalized ML re-rank on every load, is fine at scale but the wrong first move: start with a scored chronological merge (recency decay x author affinity x early engagement) because it is debuggable and captures most of the value.
components.config: Over-fetch then rank: pull ~500 candidates from the merged set, score, return the top 50. Cache the ranked result per user for 30-120 seconds keyed by (userId, feedVersion) — short enough that pull-to-refresh feels live, long enough to absorb the double-taps and back-navigations that are most of your read traffic. Serve by opaque cursor encoding last-seen score plus id, never OFFSET, or infinite scroll will duplicate and skip posts as new items arrive. Budget: Twitter's published Timeline Service was ~5ms p50 and ~100ms p99 — treat 100ms p99 for the assembled feed as the bar.

blueprints.ceiling: Two. Pure fan-out on write breaks at the first account above ~1M followers: at 10M followers and 1,000 per pipeline that is 10,000 Redis round trips for one post, several seconds of sustained cluster write load, and everyone else's posts queue behind it. The hybrid's ceiling is the read-time merge: it holds until a typical user follows more than ~100 celebrity accounts, at which point each feed load fetches 100 cached lists and p99 walks past 300ms. Memory is the third wall — ~20 KB per active user at an 800-entry 3x-replicated timeline, so 50M active users is about a terabyte of RAM and you will be told to shorten the cap.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The fan-out queue, as head-of-line blocking rather than an error. One celebrity post enters the queue, the worker on that partition spends 40 seconds on it, and every ordinary user whose post landed behind it sees their post appear in friends' feeds two minutes late — support tickets say 'posting is broken' while every dashboard is green. The fix that is not obvious until you have lived it: a separate queue (or separate Kafka partitions with their own consumer group) for high-follower accounts, so a slow fan-out can never delay a fast one. Second failure: the read-path merge silently slowing as the threshold stays fixed while following behaviour changes — watch the distribution of 'celebrity accounts followed per user', not just p99.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: (a) Fan-out p99 completion above 5 seconds or queue age above 30 seconds — split the celebrity queue; (b) any account above ~100k followers — turn on the read-time merge before you need it; (c) feed assembly p99 above 200ms — the merge is fetching too many celebrity lists, raise the threshold or cache the merged celebrity set per user; (d) Redis memory above 70% with eviction enabled — shorten the cap from 800 to 400 or tighten the active-user window; (e) more than 20% of feed loads served from an empty materialized timeline — your active-user definition is wrong; (f) you are under ~10,000 users — stay on fan-out on read, you need none of this yet.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build fan-out on write at all below roughly 10,000 users or 100 posts/hour. A single indexed query — posts where author in (my followees) order by created_at desc limit 50 — served by Postgres with a covering index runs in single-digit milliseconds and gives you correctness, instant deletes, instant unfollows and zero cache-invalidation bugs for free. Teams routinely spend six weeks building fan-out for a feed two hundred people read, and the real cost is not the six weeks: every later product change (mute, block, unfollow, edit, delete, 'show me only X') must now be reflected across millions of materialized lists instead of being one WHERE clause. Do not add an ML ranking service before you have engagement data to train on — a scored chronological merge beats a badly trained model and you can explain it to a user who complains. Do not add Neptune for the follow graph: a two-column Postgres table with two indexes serves follower lookups at hundreds of thousands of rows/sec, while Neptune adds a query language nobody knows plus ~$200/month minimum. Do not precompute feeds for inactive users — typically half your fan-out cost for zero reads. Do not retract a celebrity's already-fanned-out posts on promotion; leave them and suppress duplicates at merge time, rather than inventing a distributed deletion problem. And do not store post bodies in the timeline — the day you ship 'edit post' you will have to rewrite ten million list entries.

plain.plainName: A follow based feed that survives famous accounts
plain.problem: People follow each other and see a feed of posts. It works fine until someone with a huge following posts, and then everything crawls.
plain.answer: Write most posts straight into each follower's ready made timeline in Redis, but leave famous accounts out and merge their posts in when the feed is read.
plain.money: About 300 to 1,200 dollars a month at 100,000 users, roughly 220 dollars for one Redis group and 100 to 400 dollars for the database. At 10 million users with 1 million daily actives, 15,000 to 60,000 dollars, mostly Redis memory.
plain.holdsUpTo: Works from 100,000 users on one Redis node up to the published Twitter scale of about 150 million active users, 300,000 feed reads a second against only about 6,000 writes a second.
plain.whatBreaks: One famous person posts, the worker spends 40 seconds on it, and everyone whose post landed behind theirs shows up in friends' feeds two minutes late. Support says posting is broken while every dashboard stays green.
plain.timeToMove: When fan out takes more than 5 seconds, or any account crosses about 100,000 followers, or building a feed takes more than 200 milliseconds, or Redis memory passes 70 percent.
plain.dontYet: Do not build fan out at all below roughly 10,000 users or 100 posts an hour. One indexed database query for the latest 50 posts from people you follow runs in single digit milliseconds and gives you correct deletes and unfollows with no cache bugs. Teams routinely spend six weeks building fan out for a feed two hundred people read.
plain.pitch: I am building a follow based feed and I know one popular account will eventually break it.

blueprints.name: One database, Multi-AZ, and nothing else
blueprints.forWho: A product with real users but one team. You have a web/API tier and you need durable storage that you will not be paged about at 3am.
