blueprints.scale: 0 to roughly 200-500 req/s of mixed read/write on a normalised schema; low tens of GB; a few hundred concurrent app connections at most.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $120-$450. Driver: Multi-AZ doubles instance cost, and gp3 storage plus 7-35 days of automated backup is the rest. A db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ sits near the bottom; db.m7g.large Multi-AZ near the top.

components.service: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
components.role: The single source of truth for all operational data.
components.why: Rather than Aurora, which is the obvious 'AWS-native' pick. At this size Aurora's storage architecture buys you almost nothing you can measure, and Aurora's I/O-per-request billing is genuinely unpredictable for a workload you have not profiled. RDS gp3 gives you a fixed, boring bill. Move to Aurora when you have a specific reason (see the Aurora blueprint), not on day one. Rather than self-managed Postgres on EC2: you would be buying yourself backup, patching and failover work that costs more than the managed premium.
components.config: db.m7g.large (2 vCPU / 8 GiB) or db.t4g.medium if traffic is spiky and you can live with burst credits. Multi-AZ instance deployment ON from day one. gp3 storage, 100 GiB baseline (3000 IOPS / 125 MB/s included), storage autoscaling enabled with a hard max so a runaway job cannot bankrupt you. Backup retention 7 days minimum, 35 if you have any compliance story. Deletion protection ON. Performance Insights ON (free tier, 7 days) - you will need the baseline later.

components.service: Private subnets + security group
components.role: The database is not on the internet.
components.why: Rather than publicly_accessible with an IP allowlist, which is what every tutorial does. An allowlist is one console mistake from exposure; a private subnet is structural. Pay the small cost of a bastion or SSM Session Manager port-forward for admin access.
components.config: DB subnet group across 3 AZs, publicly_accessible = false, SG ingress only from the app tier's SG (not a CIDR). Admin access via SSM Session Manager port forwarding, no bastion host to patch.

components.service: AWS Secrets Manager with rotation
components.role: Database credentials.
components.why: Rather than an environment variable set at deploy time, which means the password is in your CI logs, your task definition, and someone's laptop forever. Rather than SSM Parameter Store SecureString: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation Lambda for RDS.
components.config: Managed rotation, 30 days. App reads the secret at startup AND on auth failure - if it only reads at startup, rotation becomes an outage.

components.service: CloudWatch alarms
components.role: The three alarms that actually matter at this stage.
components.why: Rather than a dashboard nobody looks at. Rather than alarming on CPUUtilization alone, which is the metric that will NOT be the one that kills you.
components.config: DatabaseConnections > 70% of max_connections (this is what breaks first). FreeStorageSpace < 20%. FreeableMemory < 10%. Plus ReadLatency/WriteLatency p99 as a canary. Route to a phone, not an inbox.

blueprints.ceiling: You are done when connections, not CPU, run out. A db.m7g.large's default max_connections under the RDS formula lands near 850 (LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392}, 5000)); with 8 GiB that is roughly 800-900. A Node or Python app with 10 workers x 20-connection pools x 4 tasks is already 800. Separately: a single writer on gp3 at 3000 provisioned IOPS saturates I/O long before it saturates 2 vCPU on a write-heavy workload.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The connection pool, and it looks like a total outage, not a slowdown. PostgreSQL forks an OS process per connection and has no internal pooler, so when slots run out every new request gets 'FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections' - including your health checks, so your load balancer starts killing healthy tasks, which restart, which each open a fresh pool, which makes it worse. It is a cascade, and it typically arrives during your first traffic spike, not gradually.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: DatabaseConnections sustained above 70% of max_connections for 5 minutes. OR p99 write latency above 20ms while CPU is under 50% (that is I/O, not compute). OR FreeableMemory trending down across a week with no deploy. OR your largest table's index no longer fits in shared_buffers (check pg_statio_user_tables hit ratio dropping below ~0.99).
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No read replica. No cache. No RDS Proxy. No separate analytics store. Each of these is a real answer to a problem you do not have, and each costs you a failure mode you now have to understand: a replica gives you stale reads in your application, a cache gives you the invalidation problem, a proxy gives you session pinning. Teams that add all three in month one spend roughly $600/month extra and, more expensively, debug three distributed-systems problems instead of shipping. The one thing you SHOULD add early and almost nobody does: a restore drill. Restore a snapshot to a throwaway instance and diff row counts. A backup nobody restored is not a backup.

plain.plainName: One database, with an automatic spare copy
plain.problem: I have real users and one team. I need somewhere safe to keep the data that will not wake me up at 3am.
plain.answer: Run one Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database with Multi AZ on, keep it in private subnets, and put the password in Secrets Manager.
plain.money: About 120 to 450 dollars a month. The standby copy doubles the instance cost, storage and backups are the rest.
plain.holdsUpTo: Roughly 200 to 500 requests a second and low tens of gigabytes. A db.m7g.large allows around 800 to 900 connections at once.
plain.whatBreaks: It looks like a complete outage, not a slowdown. Once connection slots run out even your health checks are refused, so the load balancer kills healthy app tasks, they restart, each opens fresh connections, and it gets worse.
plain.timeToMove: When connections stay above 70 percent of the limit for 5 minutes, or write time passes 20 milliseconds while CPU is under 50 percent, or free memory keeps falling all week with no deploy.
plain.dontYet: No read copy, no cache, no connection proxy, no separate analytics database. Each one answers a problem you do not have and hands you a new one, stale reads, cache invalidation, session pinning. Teams that add all three in month one spend about 600 dollars a month extra and debug three distributed systems problems instead of shipping.
plain.pitch: I have paying users, one team, and I just need storage that will not page me at night.

blueprints.name: Buy a bigger box, and know exactly where that stops
blueprints.forWho: You hit a ceiling and you have a week, not a quarter. Vertical scaling is the correct, unglamorous answer far longer than architecture blogs admit.
blueprints.scale: Up to roughly 5,000-15,000 read req/s and 1,000-3,000 write req/s on a well-indexed schema; single-digit TB.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $450 to $12,000+. Driver: instance class, near-linear. Multi-AZ doubles it. Above db.r7g.4xlarge, a 1-year Reserved Instance or Savings Plan cuts 30-40% and you should buy one, because you will be on this size for at least a year.

components.service: RDS instance class change, memory-optimised family
components.role: More RAM so the working set stays in shared_buffers; more vCPU for connections.
components.why: Rather than compute-optimised (c-family) or general purpose (m-family). Databases are memory machines: the thing that makes queries fast is the index and hot rows living in RAM, not clock speed. r7g gives you 8 GiB per vCPU against m7g's 4. Rather than jumping straight to a read replica, which is the instinct: a replica adds application complexity and a lag problem, while a resize is a 60-second failover and zero code change. Exhaust the box first.
components.config: Step r7g.large -> r7g.xlarge -> r7g.2xlarge -> r7g.4xlarge -> r7g.8xlarge. Graviton (g-suffix) rather than Intel for roughly 20% better price/performance on Postgres. Resize during a maintenance window: Multi-AZ resize modifies the standby, fails over, then modifies the old primary - about 60-120 seconds of write unavailability.

components.service: gp3 with provisioned IOPS, or io2 Block Express
components.role: Storage that is not the bottleneck.
components.why: gp3 rather than gp2, always: gp2 ties IOPS to volume size (3 IOPS/GiB), so with gp2 you buy 10 TiB of disk you do not need in order to get 30,000 IOPS. gp3 decouples them. io2 Block Express rather than gp3 only above ~64,000 IOPS or when you need sub-millisecond consistency - the crossover is around 80,000 IOPS where io2's price stops being punitive relative to the gp3 provisioning you would need.
components.config: gp3 with IOPS provisioned to observed peak ReadIOPS+WriteIOPS x 1.5, throughput to peak x 1.5. Watch EBSIOBalance% - if it is not pinned at 100%, you are throttled.

components.service: Parameter group tuning
components.role: The settings that actually move the needle after a resize.
components.why: Rather than accepting RDS defaults, which are conservative and sized for the smallest instance in the class. Rather than tuning fifty parameters from a blog post: four of them do 90% of the work.
components.config: shared_buffers = 25% of RAM (RDS default is already {DBInstanceClassMemory/32768} which is ~25%, verify it followed the resize). effective_cache_size = 70-75% of RAM. work_mem sized deliberately: it is PER SORT PER CONNECTION, so 64MB x 500 connections x 2 sorts is 64 GB of potential allocation - this is how people OOM a database by 'tuning' it. max_connections left at the formula default; raising it is the wrong fix. random_page_cost = 1.1 on SSD (default 4.0 assumes spinning disks and makes the planner avoid indexes it should use).

components.service: pg_stat_statements + Performance Insights
components.role: Find the three queries causing 80% of load before buying hardware to hide them.
components.why: Rather than resizing first. Most teams that 'need a bigger instance' need one missing index. An index build is free; a class jump is $400/month forever.
components.config: shared_preload_libraries = pg_stat_statements. Weekly: ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 20. Performance Insights with 'Top SQL' by wait event - if the top wait is IO:DataFileRead you need indexes or RAM; if it is Lock:transactionid you have a contention problem no instance size fixes.

blueprints.ceiling: Two hard walls. (1) You run out of instance classes: db.r7g.16xlarge / 24xlarge is the practical top of the memory-optimised line, and there is no 33rd doubling. (2) Long before that, single-writer physics: one primary, one WAL stream, one set of locks. Figma reached 'AWS's largest physical instance' on a single Postgres and then still had tables 'several terabytes and billions of rows' where VACUUM caused reliability problems and write-heavy tables approached the maximum IOPS supported by RDS. That is the real ceiling and it arrives as table-level pain, not instance-level pain.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Autovacuum. On a multi-TB, high-churn table, vacuum cannot keep up with dead tuple generation; bloat grows, the planner's estimates drift, queries that took 5ms take 500ms, and the fix (VACUUM FULL) needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock you cannot take in production. Notion's trigger was precisely this: VACUUM began to stall consistently, and behind it the transaction ID wraparound threat, which forces the database to stop accepting writes entirely. That is not a performance problem, it is an outage with a countdown.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: You are two instance classes from the top of the family. OR age(datfrozenxid) on any database exceeds ~1 billion and is climbing (wraparound runway). OR n_dead_tup on your largest table exceeds n_live_tup and autovacuum has been running continuously for hours. OR EBSIOBalance% / WriteIOPS pinned at the provisioned ceiling during normal traffic. OR a resize now costs more per month than an engineer-week, which is the economic signal to go architectural.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not shard. Not yet, not even a little. Sharding at this stage costs you 6-9 months (Figma: nine months to the first sharded table) and is nearly irreversible. Do not introduce a second database engine 'for the write-heavy table' before you have tried table partitioning (declarative RANGE/LIST partitioning), which gets you per-partition vacuum and cheap data expiry for days of work instead of quarters. Do not add a cache to hide a missing index - you will cache a wrong answer and then have two bugs.

plain.plainName: Rent a bigger database machine
plain.problem: Your app is slow and the database is the thing struggling. You have about a week to fix it, not three months.
plain.answer: Move the database to a bigger machine size, and watch the few numbers that tell you when bigger stops working.
plain.money: About 450 dollars a month at the small end, and over 12,000 dollars at the big end. Cost goes up almost in line with size. Keeping a standby copy in a second data centre doubles it. Above the db.r7g.4xlarge size, paying for one year up front cuts 30 to 40 percent, and you should, because you will sit at that size for at least a year.
plain.holdsUpTo: Roughly 5,000 to 15,000 reads a second and 1,000 to 3,000 writes a second, if your data is well organised, with a few thousand gigabytes of data.
plain.whatBreaks: Pages that used to open instantly start taking half a second, then longer. The database has an internal clean up job that falls behind on very large tables, and the proper fix needs a lock that freezes the table, which you cannot do while customers are using it. Notion hit exactly this.
plain.timeToMove: When you are two sizes from the biggest machine on offer. Or when the database's internal clean up has been running for hours and the dead rows on your biggest table outnumber the live ones. Or when the disk is at its speed limit during normal traffic. Or when the next size up costs more per month than a week of an engineer's time.
plain.dontYet: Do not split your data across many databases yet. That takes 6 to 9 months, Figma needed nine months just for the first table, and it is close to impossible to undo. Do not add a second kind of database for one busy table before you have tried splitting that table into date ranges inside the same database, which takes days instead of months. Do not add a cache to hide a missing index, you will store a wrong answer and then have two problems.
plain.pitch: My database is the bottleneck and I need breathing room this week, not a rebuild.

blueprints.name: Read replicas, and the lag that ambushes you
blueprints.forWho: Read:write is 10:1 or worse, the writer is CPU/IO bound on SELECTs, and you have a place in the app where you can route reads.
blueprints.scale: Adds roughly 2-5x read capacity per replica; realistically 2-5 replicas before the fan-out itself costs the writer.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: +100% of the primary's instance cost per replica (replicas are single-AZ and billed as full instances), plus cross-AZ data transfer on replication traffic. Two replicas on r7g.2xlarge: roughly +$1,400/month.

components.service: RDS read replicas (async physical/streaming replication)
components.role: Serve SELECTs that tolerate staleness.
components.why: Rather than a bigger primary, once you are near the top of the family - a replica is horizontal read capacity you can add in 20 minutes. Rather than Multi-AZ standby: on an RDS Multi-AZ DB *instance* deployment the standby is NOT readable, it is a failover target only. People confuse these constantly and 'I have Multi-AZ so I have a read replica' is a wrong and expensive belief. Rather than Multi-AZ DB *cluster* (primary + two readable standbys, semi-sync): that IS readable and has lower lag, but caps at two readers and fewer engine versions - it is the right pick if you need low-lag reads and only need 2x.
components.config: 2-3 replicas, same instance class as the primary (a smaller replica falls behind under replay load - replay is single-threaded-ish and a weak replica is a lag generator). Spread across AZs. Reader endpoint via Route 53 or the application's own list; RDS for PostgreSQL has no built-in load-balanced reader endpoint the way Aurora does.

components.service: Replica lag monitoring and fencing
components.role: Know how stale each replica is, and stop serving from it when it is too stale.
components.why: Rather than assuming lag is small. This is the stage's whole lesson. On RDS Postgres the replica replays WAL on its own local storage, so lag is a real, workload-dependent number: single-digit milliseconds at idle, and tens of seconds to minutes during a bulk backfill, a large index build, or a long-running query on the replica holding back replay (hot_standby_feedback). On Aurora the same metric means something different: replicas share the storage volume, so ReplicaLag measures page-cache lag and is typically well under 100ms, often single-digit ms.
components.config: Alarm on ReplicaLag > 5s (warn) / 30s (page). Application-side: SELECT pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() as a health check; route reads away from any replica whose lag exceeds your freshness budget. Decide hot_standby_feedback consciously: ON prevents replica query cancellation but lets replica queries cause bloat on the PRIMARY; OFF keeps the primary clean but kills long replica queries with 'canceling statement due to conflict with recovery'. There is no free option.

components.service: Explicit read-after-write handling in the application
components.role: Stop the class of bug where a user saves and the next page shows the old value.
components.why: Rather than hoping lag is small enough. This bug is 100% reproducible for the one user who is fast, is reported as 'the save button doesn't work', and is invisible in your metrics. Rather than routing everything to the primary 'to be safe', which defeats the replicas entirely.
components.config: Pattern: after a write, pin that user's session to the primary for N seconds (N = your p99 lag x 3), or capture the primary's LSN on write (pg_current_wal_lsn()) and require the replica's pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() to have caught up before reading. Simplest workable rule: writes and any read in the same request as a write go to the primary; list/search/report reads go to replicas.

blueprints.ceiling: Replication is one stream from one writer, so replicas multiply reads and do nothing for writes. Beyond roughly 5 replicas the primary spends measurable CPU and network on WAL shipping. And every replica is a full copy of your storage bill.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Replica lag, at the worst possible moment: during a migration or backfill, which is exactly when you are already stressed. WAL generation spikes, the single replay stream cannot keep up, lag goes to minutes, your read-routed app starts serving data that is visibly old, and if you have no fencing you find out from users. Second failure mode: a long analytics query on a replica with hot_standby_feedback=on quietly bloats the PRIMARY.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: ReplicaLag p99 above your freshness budget during normal (not backfill) traffic. OR you are adding a 4th replica to buy read capacity. OR total connections across primary + replicas is approaching the aggregate connection ceiling (each replica has its own max_connections, and your app now opens pools to all of them - this is how the next stage arrives).
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not route reads to replicas globally via a config flag. Route them per-query-site, deliberately, starting with the ones you can prove tolerate staleness (search, listings, dashboards). A global flag turns every read-after-write in your codebase into a latent bug at once. Do not put reporting queries on a replica and call it 'analytics separation' - a replica is still a row-store with your OLTP indexes, and a 30-second report will still cause replay conflicts.

plain.plainName: Extra copies of the database for reading
plain.problem: People read from your app far more than they write to it, and the one database is worn out just answering read requests.
plain.answer: Run extra read only copies of the database, and send some reads to them.
plain.money: Each copy costs the same as the main database, so plus 100 percent each, plus a small charge for shipping the data between data centres. Two copies of an r7g.2xlarge is about 1,400 dollars a month extra.
plain.holdsUpTo: Each copy adds roughly 2 to 5 times more read capacity. In practice 2 to 5 copies before the copying itself starts costing the main database.
plain.whatBreaks: The copies fall behind the main database, usually right in the middle of a big data change when you are already stressed. Users start seeing old information, a price or a post that is minutes stale, and if you are not watching for it, a customer tells you first.
plain.timeToMove: When the lag on the copies goes past what your users can tolerate during normal traffic. Or when you are about to add a fourth copy just to get more reading power. Or when the total number of open connections across the main database and all copies is nearing the limit.
plain.dontYet: Do not flip one setting that sends all reads to the copies. Choose them one place at a time, starting with pages that can safely show slightly old data, like search, listings and dashboards. A global switch turns every save then read in your code into a hidden bug on the same day. Do not put reports on a copy and call it analytics, a 30 second report still causes trouble there.
plain.pitch: Reads are ten times my writes and the database is drowning in them.

blueprints.name: Connection exhaustion, and the pooler that fixes it
blueprints.forWho: Any team whose app tier autoscales, or that runs Lambda, or that has more than a handful of containers. This arrives earlier than you expect and is the most common self-inflicted database outage.
blueprints.scale: Lets one database serve thousands of application connections on hundreds of real backend connections. Typical: 5,000 client connections collapsed onto 200-400 database connections.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: RDS Proxy: roughly $0.015 per vCPU-hour of the target instance, so about $22/month per vCPU - on an r7g.2xlarge (8 vCPU) roughly $175/month. PgBouncer on ECS Fargate: roughly $30-60/month for two small tasks, plus your operational time.

components.service: Amazon RDS Proxy
components.role: Connection pool and multiplexer between the app and the database; also preserves application connections across failover.
components.why: Rather than raising max_connections, which is the instinctive fix and makes things worse: PostgreSQL forks an OS process per connection, so more connections consume RAM that would otherwise be shared_buffers and work_mem - you buy connection slots by making every query slower. Rather than self-hosted PgBouncer: PgBouncer is faster and cheaper and gives you transaction pooling with full control, but you now own an HA pair, its failover, its version upgrades and its own connection limits. Choose RDS Proxy when you want it to be someone else's problem and when failover resilience matters (it holds client connections open and reconnects to the new writer); choose PgBouncer when you need aggressive transaction-mode pooling ratios or are cost-sensitive at scale. Rather than fixing it in the app's pool config alone - correct pool sizing is necessary but does not survive autoscaling.
components.config: MaxConnectionsPercent 80-90 (leave headroom for admin and for your own psql session during the incident). MaxIdleConnectionsPercent well below that so idle connections are reaped. IdleClientTimeout matched to your app. Credentials via Secrets Manager; IAM auth from clients. One proxy per workload class (API vs batch vs admin), each with its own slice of the connection budget, so a runaway batch job cannot starve the API. Constraints: a proxy attaches to the WRITER only, not a read replica; it must be in the same VPC and cannot be publicly accessible; 20 proxies per account by default.

components.service: Application-side pool sizing, deliberately computed
components.role: Stop the app from asking for connections it cannot use.
components.why: Rather than the framework default (often 10 per process), which silently multiplies by worker count and task count. The arithmetic is the whole problem and almost nobody does it.
components.config: Write it down: pool_size x workers_per_task x max_tasks_at_autoscale_ceiling <= MaxConnectionsPercent x max_connections. A pool of 5 with 4 workers and 50 tasks is 1000 connections. Use the autoscaling MAX, not the current task count, as the multiplier. Enforce with a test that fails CI if the product exceeds budget.

components.service: Session pinning awareness
components.role: Know what silently turns multiplexing back off.
components.why: This is the RDS Proxy footgun: pinning drops you back to one-connection-per-client and your pool ratio evaporates without an error message. Rather than discovering it under load, instrument it.
components.config: Watch the DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned CloudWatch metric - if it is a meaningful fraction of your connections, multiplexing is not happening. Known pinners include any statement with text over 16 KB. For Postgres specifically: RDS Proxy does not support session pinning filters, does not support CancelRequest (so Ctrl-C on a long psql query does nothing), lastval() results are unreliable (use INSERT ... RETURNING), and streaming replication mode is unsupported.

components.service: Lambda + RDS Proxy, or Aurora Data API
components.role: Serverless compute against a connection-oriented database.
components.why: A Lambda concurrency of 1,000 means up to 1,000 database connections with no pooling, which will take down the database. RDS Proxy rather than a per-invocation connection. Aurora's Data API rather than a proxy when the workload is low-throughput and HTTP-shaped, since it removes connections entirely - but it adds per-request overhead and is not a fit for chatty transactions.
components.config: Reserved concurrency set below what the proxy connection budget supports. Create the connection/pool OUTSIDE the handler so it is reused across warm invocations. IAM auth so there is no secret in the function environment.

blueprints.ceiling: A pooler fixes connection count, not database capacity. Once backend connections are efficiently multiplexed, the next wall is genuine: CPU, IOPS, or lock contention on the writer. Also: transaction-mode pooling breaks anything that relies on session state - advisory locks, prepared statements outside a transaction, temp tables, SET session parameters, LISTEN/NOTIFY.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Pinning, quietly. Everything works in staging at 10 connections, then in production one code path uses a session-level feature, every client that touches it pins, the multiplexing ratio collapses from 20:1 to 1:1, and you are back to connection exhaustion - but now with an extra component in the path that you trust and therefore do not suspect.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Backend DatabaseConnections is now stable and low, and CPUUtilization or ReadIOPS is the new pinned metric. That is the signal that pooling worked and the next stage is real capacity, not plumbing.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add a pooler and simultaneously raise max_connections - you will not know which one helped, and the raised max_connections permanently costs you memory. Do not put a pooler in front of a database whose actual problem is one unindexed query; you will have spent $175/month to make a bad query queue more politely. Do not run PgBouncer as a single task 'for now': a non-HA pooler in the hot path is a new single point of failure in front of your Multi-AZ database, which is a strictly worse availability posture than no pooler at all.

plain.plainName: A traffic controller in front of the database
plain.problem: Your app runs on many copies of itself, or on Lambda, and the database keeps refusing new connections and falling over.
plain.answer: Put a connection pooler like RDS Proxy in front, so thousands of app connections share a few hundred real database ones.
plain.money: RDS Proxy is about 22 dollars a month per processor core of your database, so roughly 175 dollars a month on an 8 core r7g.2xlarge. Running PgBouncer yourself on Fargate is about 30 to 60 dollars a month for two small tasks, plus your time.
plain.holdsUpTo: One database can serve thousands of app connections. A common result is 5,000 app connections collapsed onto 200 to 400 real database connections.
plain.whatBreaks: Something called pinning. It all works in testing. Then one piece of code uses a feature that needs its own private connection, the sharing collapses from 20 to 1 down to 1 to 1, and you are out of connections again, with an extra piece in the path that you trust and so do not suspect.
plain.timeToMove: When connection counts are finally low and steady, and processor use or disk speed becomes the new pinned number. That means the plumbing is fixed and the next problem is real capacity.
plain.dontYet: Do not add the pooler and raise the connection limit at the same time, you will not know which helped, and the raised limit costs you memory forever. Do not put a pooler in front of a database whose real problem is one query missing an index, you will have spent 175 dollars a month to make a bad query wait more politely. Do not run PgBouncer as a single task for now, a pooler with no backup in front of a two data centre database makes your uptime worse, not better.
plain.pitch: My database keeps running out of connections whenever traffic scales up.

blueprints.name: A cache in front, and owning the invalidation problem before you create it
blueprints.forWho: Read-heavy workload where the same rows are read thousands of times between writes: sessions, feature flags, product catalogues, user profiles, permission checks, rendered fragments.
blueprints.scale: Removes 60-95% of read queries from the database. A cache hit is roughly 0.5-1ms against 5-50ms for a database read, so it also flattens your p99.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $50-$800. ElastiCache Valkey/Redis cache.r7g.large x2 (primary + replica, Multi-AZ) is roughly $250/month. Serverless pricing is usage-based and better below ~1 GB and spiky. Driver: memory size and node count, not throughput.

components.service: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey (or Redis OSS)
components.role: Low-latency key/value in front of the database.
components.why: Rather than Memcached: you will eventually want sorted sets, TTL-per-key semantics, persistence for warm restarts, and pub/sub for invalidation fan-out. Memcached is simpler and multi-threaded but you outgrow it. Valkey rather than Redis OSS at this point for licensing and cost reasons on ElastiCache; API-compatible. Rather than DAX - that is DynamoDB-specific. Rather than caching in application process memory: with N autoscaled tasks you get N inconsistent caches and an invalidation problem you cannot solve, though a small in-process L1 in FRONT of the shared cache is legitimate for the very hottest keys.
components.config: Cluster mode disabled at first (one shard, primary + one replica across AZs) - cluster mode adds client-side constraints (CROSSSLOT restrictions on multi-key ops) you do not need yet. maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for a pure cache. Encryption in transit and at rest ON. Automatic failover ON.

components.service: Cache-aside (lazy loading) as the default pattern
components.role: Read: check cache, miss -> read DB -> write cache with TTL. Write: write DB, then DELETE the key.
components.why: Rather than write-through, which keeps the cache warm but writes data nobody will read and couples write latency to cache availability. Rather than updating the cache on write (write-behind or write-update): under concurrency, two writers can interleave DB-write and cache-write so the cache ends up holding the older value permanently. DELETE-on-write is strictly safer than SET-on-write for exactly this reason, and this is the single most valuable sentence in this blueprint.
components.config: Every key gets a TTL - the TTL is your bound on how wrong you can be, and your safety net for every invalidation you forget. Short TTL (30-300s) for anything user-visible; hours for reference data with explicit invalidation. Key naming with a version prefix (v3:user:123:profile) so a schema change is a prefix bump, not a flush.

components.service: Invalidation strategy, written down
components.role: The part everyone skips and then pays for.
components.why: The real problem is not 'the cache is stale', it is 'the cache is stale and nobody can tell which code path wrote the row'. A cached row updated by an admin tool, a background job and a webhook needs invalidation at three sites; you will remember two.
components.config: Centralise writes through a repository layer that invalidates as part of the write, so there is exactly one place. For rows written outside the app (DBA scripts, other services), drive invalidation from the database's change stream instead of trusting callers - Aurora/RDS logical replication into a small consumer that deletes keys. Track CacheHitRate; a sudden drop means an invalidation storm, a sudden rise to 100% often means you stopped writing.

components.service: Stampede protection
components.role: Stop a cold key from becoming a thundering herd.
components.why: Rather than nothing, which is the default. When a hot key expires under load, every concurrent request misses simultaneously and hits the database at once - the classic pattern where adding a cache makes your outage WORSE than having no cache, because the database now gets 5,000 identical queries in one millisecond instead of a steady 500/s.
components.config: Per-key mutex: first miss acquires a short lock (SET NX with a few-second TTL) and repopulates, others wait briefly or serve stale. Plus TTL jitter (TTL x random 0.8-1.2) so keys populated together do not expire together. Both are ten lines of code and prevent a real outage.

blueprints.ceiling: Cache memory, and the consistency budget. When the working set exceeds node memory, hit rate falls off a cliff and you are paying for a cache that mostly misses. Cluster mode (sharding across shards) extends this to hundreds of GB. The harder ceiling is semantic: there is a class of data - balances, inventory, entitlements, permissions during revocation - where any staleness is a correctness bug, and no TTL is short enough.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Correctness, and it breaks in a way metrics do not show. The database is fine, latency is great, and a user sees a deleted document or an old price. Second: cache-dependency, where the database can no longer survive a cold cache. Test this deliberately - fail over the cache during a load test and see whether the database survives. If it does not, your cache is not a cache, it is an undeclared tier of your database.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Cache hit rate below 80% with the working set exceeding node memory (scale the cache, not the database). OR the writer is still CPU-bound after caching - that means writes, not reads, are the load, and caching cannot help; go to read/write splitting and then Aurora. OR you are adding cache entries for data that must never be stale, which means you are using the wrong tool for that path.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not cache before you have indexed. A cache over an unindexed query hides the problem until the cache misses, and then the outage is worse. Do not use the cache as a database (no durable-only-in-Redis state, no sessions without a fallback) unless you have consciously chosen persistence and tested restore. Do not adopt cluster mode on day one - the client-side constraints (hash tags, no cross-slot multi-key operations, pipeline rewrites) will cost you a week for capacity you do not need.

plain.plainName: Keep popular answers in fast memory
plain.problem: The same information gets read thousands of times before it ever changes: sessions, product listings, user profiles, permission checks.
plain.answer: Put ElastiCache in front of the database and keep hot answers in memory, with a written plan for clearing them when things change.
plain.money: 50 to 800 dollars a month. Two cache.r7g.large nodes across two data centres is about 250 dollars a month. The serverless option is cheaper below about one gigabyte and spiky traffic. What drives the price is memory size and node count, not how much traffic it handles.
plain.holdsUpTo: Takes 60 to 95 percent of reads off the database. A cache answer takes about 0.5 to 1 millisecond against 5 to 50 milliseconds from the database, so slow pages get faster too.
plain.whatBreaks: Correctness, and your dashboards will look fine while it happens. Everything is fast, and a user sees a deleted document or an old price. The other trap is that the database can no longer survive the cache going away. Turn the cache off during a load test on purpose. If the database falls over, it was never a cache, it was a hidden part of your database.
plain.timeToMove: When the hit rate drops below 80 percent because the data no longer fits in memory, then grow the cache, not the database. Or when the database is still busy after caching, which means writes are the load and caching cannot help. Or when you find yourself caching things that must never be out of date.
plain.dontYet: Do not cache before you have added the right indexes. A cache over a slow query hides it until the cache misses, and then the outage is worse. Do not use the cache as your only copy of anything unless you deliberately chose that and tested getting it back. Do not turn on cluster mode on day one, the code changes it forces will cost you a week for capacity you do not need.
plain.pitch: The same few thousand things get read over and over and my database is doing it all again each time.

blueprints.name: Splitting reads from writes in the application, on purpose
blueprints.forWho: You have replicas and a cache and the writer is still the constraint. Now the application has to become explicitly aware that there is more than one database.
blueprints.scale: Unlocks the full read capacity of your replica fleet; typically 3-8x total read throughput versus naive single-endpoint usage.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: No new AWS spend. This stage is engineering time: realistically 2-6 weeks for a mature codebase, because the work is auditing every query site.

components.service: Two connection pools in the application (writer pool, reader pool)
components.role: Make the destination of every query an explicit decision.
components.why: Rather than a middleware proxy that parses SQL and routes automatically (ProxySQL, pgpool-II, or a homegrown one). Automatic routing looks like it saves you the audit, but it guesses wrong on exactly the cases that matter: a SELECT inside a write transaction, a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, a function call with a side effect. Figma eventually did build a routing proxy (DBProxy) - but as part of a nine-month sharding project with a dedicated team, which is the honest cost of that choice. For one team, two explicit pools and a code audit is cheaper and safer.
components.config: writer_pool -> primary endpoint. reader_pool -> reader endpoint / replica list with lag-aware health checks. Default the ORM to the WRITER and opt INTO the reader per call site. Defaulting to the reader means every unaudited query is a potential staleness bug; defaulting to the writer means the worst case is 'no improvement yet', which is a safe failure.

components.service: Transaction-aware routing rule
components.role: One rule that prevents most of the bugs.
components.why: Rather than per-query heuristics. The rule: any read inside an open write transaction goes to the writer, full stop. Rather than trusting 'it's a SELECT so it's safe' - a SELECT that feeds a subsequent UPDATE must see the writer's view or you have a lost-update bug.
components.config: Enforce in the data-access layer, not by convention. If a reader-pool query is attempted while a writer transaction is open, raise in dev/CI and fall back to the writer in production. Make the violation loud where it is cheap and safe where it is expensive.

components.service: Per-request freshness contract
components.role: Every endpoint declares how stale it may be.
components.why: Rather than one global staleness policy. 'The dashboard may be 30s stale, the checkout page may not be stale at all' is a product decision, and writing it down turns an invisible distributed-systems problem into a reviewable annotation.
components.config: Annotate handlers: FRESH (writer), BOUNDED(5s) (reader, fenced on lag), ANY (reader). Reject deploys of unannotated handlers in CI. Pair BOUNDED with the LSN catch-up check from the replica blueprint.

components.service: Dark-read verification during rollout
components.role: Prove the reader path returns the same answers before you trust it.
components.why: Rather than flipping traffic and watching error rates - a staleness bug produces no errors. Notion used exactly this technique (sampling and 'dark reads' comparing old and new data) to verify their far riskier migration.
components.config: For a sampled percentage of requests, run the query against both writer and reader, compare, log mismatches with the query text and the measured lag at that moment, and return the writer's result. Ramp the reader percentage only once the mismatch rate is at the floor explained by lag alone. Keep the harness in the codebase at low sample rate permanently.

blueprints.ceiling: Reads are now horizontally scalable; writes are exactly where they were. Every subsequent stage in this track exists because of that sentence. You are also now carrying permanent complexity: every new feature needs a routing decision, and every new engineer needs to learn the rule.
blueprints.breaksFirst: A routing mistake in a new feature, discovered by a user. The failure is a correctness bug with no error signal - which is why the dark-read harness should stay in the codebase after the migration, sampled at a low rate, forever.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Writer CPU or IOPS sustained above 70% with reads already offloaded. OR write latency p99 degrading while read latency is flat. OR you need more than ~5 replicas, or replica provisioning time (a full storage copy - hours on multi-TB) is now an operational problem. Those three together are the case for Aurora.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build a query-parsing routing proxy. It is a service you must now operate in the hot path of every query, and it will be the cause of an outage before it is the cure for one. Do not shard to solve a read problem - sharding is a WRITE scaling technique and a cripplingly expensive way to get reads. Do not split reads and writes into separate SERVICES at this point; that is a different and worse change dressed up as the same one.

plain.plainName: Teach your app which database to talk to
plain.problem: You already have read copies and a cache, and the main database is still the thing holding you back.
plain.answer: Change the app so each query knowingly goes to the writer or to a reader, with a rule for what may be slightly old.
plain.money: No new AWS bill. The cost is engineering time, realistically 2 to 6 weeks on an established codebase, because the work is checking every single query.
plain.holdsUpTo: Gives you the full reading power of all your copies, usually 3 to 8 times more total reads than using one address for everything.
plain.whatBreaks: Someone builds a new feature, points a query at the wrong place, and a user finds it. Nothing errors. That is why the shadow checking you build for the rollout should stay in the code forever, running on a small sample.
plain.timeToMove: When the main database sits above 70 percent busy even with reads moved off. Or when write times get worse while read times stay flat. Or when you need more than about 5 copies, or making a new copy takes hours because the data is so large. Those three together are the case for Aurora.
plain.dontYet: Do not build a smart proxy that reads your queries and routes them. It becomes a service you have to keep alive in the path of every single query, and it will cause an outage before it prevents one. Do not split the data across many databases to fix a reading problem, that technique is for writes and is a painfully expensive way to get reads. Do not split reads and writes into separate services now, that is a bigger and worse change wearing the same clothes.
plain.pitch: I have replicas and a cache and the main database is still the wall.

blueprints.name: Moving to Aurora, and what it actually buys you
blueprints.forWho: Replica provisioning time, failover time, or the storage ceiling has become an operational constraint. Not for 'it's faster' - that is not reliably true for your workload until you measure it.
blueprints.scale: Up to 15 Aurora Replicas per cluster; cluster volume up to 128 TiB, and 256 TiB on current Aurora PostgreSQL versions. Single writer still.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Typically 20-40% more than equivalent RDS for a steady workload, and unpredictably more for I/O-heavy ones on the standard (per-I/O-billed) configuration. Aurora I/O-Optimized removes I/O charges for a ~30% higher instance/storage rate and is the better deal once I/O exceeds roughly 25% of your Aurora bill - check the bill, do not guess.

components.service: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster
components.role: Same engine, different storage architecture: compute separated from a distributed cluster volume spanning multiple AZs.
components.why: Rather than staying on RDS, which is the right answer until one of four things bites: (1) replicas share the storage volume so ReplicaLag is typically under 100ms and often single-digit ms, against seconds-to-minutes on RDS under load; (2) adding a replica takes minutes because there is no storage copy, against hours on RDS for multi-TB; (3) failover promotes an existing replica in roughly 30 seconds or less rather than the ~60-120s of an RDS Multi-AZ failover; (4) storage autogrows with no provisioning decision. Rather than Aurora Serverless v2 as the default: excellent for spiky/dev/multi-tenant-with-idle-tenants, but for a steady production workload provisioned instances are cheaper, and ACU scaling has its own latency and floor cost.
components.config: Writer + at least 2 readers across AZs. Use the cluster WRITER endpoint and READER endpoint (Aurora load-balances the reader endpoint across replicas - a real convenience RDS does not give you). Set failover priority tiers so the beefiest replica is promoted. Note Backtrack exists only on Aurora MySQL, not Aurora PostgreSQL - people plan around it and are wrong. Choose I/O-Optimized vs Standard from your actual I/O bill.

components.service: RDS Blue/Green Deployments for the cut-over
components.role: Near-zero-downtime migration and, afterwards, near-zero-downtime major version upgrades forever.
components.why: Rather than snapshot-restore-and-cut-over, which costs hours of downtime on a multi-TB database. Rather than hand-rolled DMS replication, which you would need for a cross-engine move but is unnecessary overhead for RDS Postgres -> Aurora Postgres. Blue/green creates a full topology copy, keeps it in sync, lets you test against it, and switches over typically in under a minute with no data loss and no application changes - and it works with RDS Proxy and smart drivers, which detect the topology change and redirect connections without waiting for DNS propagation.
components.config: Create the green environment, keep it READ ONLY during testing (writes there cause replication conflicts and unintended data after switchover), run your dark-read harness against it, then switch over in a low-traffic window. Budget the switchover as 'under a minute, plan for five'. The old blue environment is retained (renamed -old1) - do not delete it for a week, it is your rollback and your regression-test target.

components.service: Aurora Global Database (only if you need it)
components.role: Cross-region read scaling and disaster recovery.
components.why: Rather than cross-region read replicas on RDS: storage-level replication with typically sub-second cross-region lag and an RPO measured in seconds. Rather than adding it by default - it roughly doubles your database spend and adds a promotion runbook you must actually rehearse.
components.config: Only adopt with a regulatory RTO/RPO or a genuine global read-latency requirement. Secondary region with at least one reader. Rehearse the promotion quarterly and record the measured RTO - otherwise you do not have DR, you have a diagram.

blueprints.ceiling: One writer. That is the whole point. Aurora buys you a better single writer, faster replicas, easier operations and a much higher storage ceiling - it does not buy you write scaling. Even Aurora's largest instance classes bottom out at one node accepting writes, and at that point the next stages (purpose-built stores, then sharding) are the only remaining moves.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The bill, for the unprepared. Aurora Standard bills per I/O request, and a workload with poor cache locality or heavy sequential scans can produce an I/O charge that dwarfs the instance charge. Teams migrate for the operational benefits, never switch to I/O-Optimized, and get a surprise. Second: people assume Aurora removed the write ceiling and stop planning, which is how you arrive at the sharding decision with no runway.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Writer instance at the top of its family with sustained high CPU on WRITE workload. OR one table's write pattern is clearly not relational (append-only event log, time series, blobs, full-text search) - go to purpose-built stores before sharding, it is an order of magnitude cheaper. OR the single-writer ceiling is now the explicit blocker with a forecast date.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not adopt Aurora Serverless v2 for the main production cluster without measuring: scaling is not instantaneous, and a workload with fast, sharp spikes gets throttled at the bottom of the ramp. Do not enable Global Database 'for DR' without a rehearsed promotion runbook and a named owner. Do not assume Aurora makes your queries faster - it makes your OPERATIONS faster; a bad query is equally bad on both, and migrating is not a substitute for reading pg_stat_statements.

plain.plainName: Switch to Amazon's own database engine
plain.problem: Making a new database copy takes hours, failovers are slow, and you are close to the storage limit. Operations, not speed, is the pain.
plain.answer: Move to Aurora PostgreSQL, using Blue/Green Deployments for the switch over.
plain.money: Usually 20 to 40 percent more than the same setup on RDS for steady traffic, and unpredictably more if your work is heavy on disk activity, because the standard plan charges per disk request. The I/O-Optimized plan removes those charges for about 30 percent higher base rate, and is the better deal once disk charges pass roughly 25 percent of your Aurora bill.
plain.holdsUpTo: Up to 15 read copies per cluster, and storage up to 128 TiB, or 256 TiB on current versions. Still only one machine accepting writes.
plain.whatBreaks: The bill, if you did not plan for it. On the standard plan a workload that scans a lot of data can run up a disk charge bigger than the machine charge. The other failure is people assuming Aurora removed the write limit, so they stop planning, and arrive at the hard decision with no runway.
plain.timeToMove: When the writer is on the biggest machine in its family and stays busy on writes. Or when one table clearly is not a normal table, an append only log, time series, files, full text search. Move those to fitting tools before splitting the database, it is ten times cheaper. Or when the one writer limit is now the named blocker with a date on it.
plain.dontYet: Do not put Aurora Serverless v2 under your main production cluster without measuring it. It does not grow instantly, and sharp spikes get throttled while it ramps. Do not turn on Global Database for disaster recovery without a rehearsed plan and a named owner. Do not expect Aurora to make your queries faster, it makes your operations faster. A bad query is just as bad on Aurora, and moving is not a replacement for reading your slow query stats.
plain.pitch: My database is fine, but making copies and doing failovers has become an operations problem.

blueprints.name: The moment a relational database is the wrong tool for ONE part of the workload
blueprints.forWho: One table or one access pattern is generating a disproportionate share of load, and it does not look relational when you describe it out loud. This is the highest-leverage stage in the whole track and the most commonly skipped.
blueprints.scale: Typically removes 30-70% of write volume or storage from the primary, buying 1-3 years of runway for weeks of work.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Varies by store; the point is that each is far cheaper per unit of its own workload than forcing it into Postgres. DynamoDB on-demand for a high-write table is often a fifth of the RDS capacity it displaces. Budget $200-$2,000/month per store plus the migration.

components.service: Amazon DynamoDB
components.role: High-volume, key-access, append-or-overwrite workloads: sessions, idempotency keys, feature flags, device state, audit/event logs, per-user timelines, rate-limit counters.
components.why: Rather than a Postgres table, when the access pattern is 'get by key' or 'get a range under a key' and never 'join'. The specific wins: no connection model at all (HTTP + IAM, so Lambda concurrency stops being a database problem - this alone solves the connection-exhaustion stage for that workload), single-digit millisecond latency at any size, and no vacuum. Rather than DynamoDB for everything: the moment you need an ad-hoc query you did not design for, you are stuck, because the access patterns ARE the schema. Choose it only where you can enumerate every query up front.
components.config: On-demand capacity to start (you do not know your pattern yet); switch to provisioned + autoscaling once the shape is stable, typically 40-70% cheaper. Partition key with high cardinality - a low-cardinality key is the hot-partition failure, the same failure that eventually broke Discord's Cassandra deployment. TTL attribute on anything expiring, which gives you free, load-free data lifecycle. Point-in-time recovery ON.

components.service: Amazon OpenSearch Service (after Postgres tsvector/pg_trgm, not before)
components.role: Full-text search, faceting, fuzzy matching, relevance ranking.
components.why: Rather than LIKE '%term%' on Postgres, which cannot use a b-tree index and table-scans. Important honest ordering: try Postgres tsvector + GIN, or pg_trgm, FIRST - it is free, transactional, and good to surprisingly large scale. Move to OpenSearch only when you need relevance tuning, faceted aggregation, typo tolerance or multi-field scoring, which is where Postgres genuinely stops. Rather than OpenSearch as system of record: it is a derived index and must be rebuildable.
components.config: 3 dedicated master nodes + data nodes across 3 AZs (a single-node domain is a toy). Index from the database's change stream or an outbox, never by dual-writing from application code. Write and schedule the full reindex job on day one, and run it once before go-live so you know how long it takes - that number is your recovery time.

components.service: Amazon S3 (+ a pointer column)
components.role: Blobs, attachments, exports, generated documents, anything over ~100 KB.
components.why: Rather than a bytea column, which is the most common and most damaging schema mistake at this stage. Large values in Postgres go to TOAST, bloat the table, make every backup and restore slower, make replica provisioning slower, and consume the RAM you wanted for indexes. Rather than EFS: S3 is cheaper, has lifecycle policies, and gives you presigned URLs so blobs never transit your app tier.
components.config: Store s3://bucket/key plus size, checksum and content-type in the database row. Presigned URLs for upload and download so bytes never touch your servers. Versioning ON. Lifecycle policy per the retention blueprint.

components.service: Time-series store: Postgres declarative RANGE partitioning, or Amazon Timestream
components.role: Metrics, IoT readings, high-frequency append-only series.
components.why: Rather than a wide Postgres table with a timestamp index, where the index grows without bound and DELETE-based expiry generates dead tuples faster than autovacuum can reclaim them. Stay in Postgres with native RANGE partitioning if you want one engine - expiry becomes DETACH/DROP PARTITION, an instant metadata operation with zero vacuum cost. Move to a dedicated time-series store only when ingest rate or retention volume makes even partitioned Postgres uneconomic.
components.config: If staying in Postgres: PARTITION BY RANGE (recorded_at), monthly or daily partitions, pg_partman (or a cron job) to pre-create partitions ahead of time and drop expired ones. Pre-create at least 3 partitions ahead - a missing future partition means inserts fail at midnight.

components.service: Amazon ElastiCache / Valkey for ephemeral counters and locks
components.role: Rate limits, distributed locks, leaderboards, presence.
components.why: Rather than a Postgres table being UPDATEd thousands of times a second, which is a dead-tuple factory: every UPDATE in Postgres writes a new row version. A counter table is the single fastest way to bloat a database.
components.config: INCR/EXPIRE for counters, SET NX PX for locks with a TTL shorter than your worst-case processing time. Accept that this data is losable on failover - if it is not losable, you have chosen the wrong store.

blueprints.ceiling: Each store has its own, but the meta-ceiling is operational: every store added is a new backup story, a new access-control story, a new on-call runbook, a new consistency boundary and a new 'which is the source of truth' argument. Three stores is manageable for a small team; six is a platform team.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Dual-write consistency. The moment a fact lives in both Postgres and DynamoDB/OpenSearch and the app writes both, you will get divergence - a crash between the two writes, a retry, an ordering inversion. Fix the pattern, not the instance: write to ONE store of record and derive the other from its change stream (DynamoDB Streams, Aurora logical replication, or an outbox table drained by a worker). A dual-write in application code is a data-corruption bug on a timer.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: You have moved the obvious workloads out and the remaining relational core is STILL write-bound at the top of the instance family. Only then is sharding the next step. Most teams never get here, which is the point of this stage.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not move everything. Move ONE workload, prove the pattern (including the rebuild path), then move the next. Do not adopt a store you cannot back up and restore on demand - run the restore drill before it holds production data. Do not build a generic 'data platform' abstraction over multiple stores; it will leak, and it will make each store worse than using it directly.

plain.plainName: Move one odd workload to a tool built for it
plain.problem: One table or one thing your app does is creating most of the load, and when you describe it out loud it does not sound like a normal table at all.
plain.answer: Move that one workload to the tool that fits it, DynamoDB, OpenSearch, S3, or date range partitioning, and keep the rest where it is.
plain.money: Depends on the tool, but each is far cheaper for its own kind of work than forcing it into Postgres. DynamoDB on demand for a write heavy table is often a fifth of the database capacity it replaces. Budget 200 to 2,000 dollars a month per tool plus the move itself.
plain.holdsUpTo: Usually takes 30 to 70 percent of writes or storage off the main database, buying 1 to 3 years of room for a few weeks of work.
plain.whatBreaks: The two copies stop agreeing. Once a fact lives in both places and your app writes to both, a crash between the two writes, a retry or an out of order update makes them differ. Fix the pattern everywhere, not the one case: write to one place and let the other be built from its change feed, using DynamoDB Streams, Aurora logical replication or an outbox table drained by a worker.
plain.timeToMove: When you have moved the obvious things out and what is left is still hitting the write limit on the biggest machine. Only then does splitting the database make sense. Most teams never get here, which is the whole point of this step.
plain.dontYet: Do not move everything. Move one workload, prove the whole pattern including how you rebuild it, then move the next. Do not adopt a tool you cannot back up and restore on demand, run the restore drill before real data goes in. Do not build a general purpose wrapper over several tools, it will leak and it makes each tool worse than using it directly.
plain.pitch: One table is eating my database and it does not really behave like a table.

blueprints.name: Sharding, and the key choice you cannot take back
blueprints.forWho: You have exhausted vertical scaling, offloaded reads, cached, split read/write, moved to Aurora, and extracted every non-relational workload - and a single writer is still the wall. This is a multi-quarter project with a dedicated team.
blueprints.scale: Notion: 480 logical shards across 32 physical Postgres hosts (15 logical shards per host). Figma: multiple sharding keys across a dozen vertically partitioned databases, having grown roughly 100x since 2020.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Roughly N x your current database cost, plus the routing layer, plus - dominating everything - 6-12 months of a team. Figma's first sharded table took nine months. Treat engineering cost as the real number.

components.service: Vertical partitioning FIRST (split tables by domain onto separate clusters)
components.role: Buy years before you shard horizontally.
components.why: Rather than going straight to horizontal sharding, which is what the word makes people imagine. Figma moved groups of related tables - 'Figma files', 'Organizations' - into their own vertical partitions and ran a dozen of them before they had to shard anything horizontally. Vertical partitioning is dramatically cheaper: no routing layer, no cross-shard joins, no resharding, and each partition gets its own write capacity, vacuum and IOPS budget. You lose cross-domain foreign keys and cross-domain transactions - that is the real cost, and it is usually acceptable.
components.config: Split on the seams where you already have few joins. Move one domain at a time using logical replication, verify with dark reads, cut over per domain with a brief writer freeze.

components.service: The shard key
components.role: The irreversible decision.
components.why: Pick the entity that CONTAINS the data and matches how users query. Notion chose workspace ID because each block belongs to exactly one workspace and users query within one workspace, so cross-shard joins essentially vanish. Figma could not find one good candidate and ended up sharding different tables on UserID, FileID and OrgID. That difference - one natural containment boundary versus three - is most of the difference in project difficulty. Hash the key rather than using it raw: Figma explicitly hashed to avoid hotspots from auto-incrementing IDs, since a monotonic key concentrates all new writes on one shard. Discord's Cassandra pain was the same failure through a different door: partitioning by channel meant a 200,000-member server and a five-friend server got identical partition treatment, and one hot partition degraded the whole cluster through quorum.
components.config: Test the key before committing: run your top 50 queries against a simulated shard map and count how many require scatter-gather. If more than ~5% of query VOLUME is cross-shard, the key is wrong - and you will not get to change it later.

components.service: Many logical shards on few physical hosts
components.role: Make future rebalancing a data move, not a rewrite.
components.why: Rather than one logical shard per host, which means growing from 32 to 40 hosts requires rehashing every row. Notion created 480 logical shards on 32 physical machines precisely because 480 divides evenly by 32, 40, 48 and 64 - so they can add capacity without doubling. This is the cheapest good decision in the entire project and costs nothing to make correctly on day one.
components.config: Pick a logical shard count with many divisors (480, 1024, 4096). Store the logical-shard -> physical-host map in a small, highly available config store, not in application constants, so a rebalance is a config change plus a data copy.

components.service: A routing layer
components.role: Turn a shard key into a connection.
components.why: Rather than sprinkling routing logic through the application. Figma built DBProxy, a service that parses and routes queries across shards - that is the mature answer, and it is a service you must operate in the hot path. The cheaper starting point is a library in the data-access layer that REQUIRES a shard key on every call and refuses queries that do not carry one, which forces you to discover every un-shardable query at test time rather than in production.
components.config: Start as a library, not a service. Every repository method takes the shard key as an explicit argument; a call without one fails to compile or fails in CI. Maintain an explicit allowlist of scatter-gather queries, with a latency budget, reviewed like a schema change. Promote to a proxy service only when multiple languages or multiple services need routing.

components.service: Double-write, backfill, verify, cut over
components.role: The migration, without downtime.
components.why: Rather than a maintenance-window dump and load, impossible at this size. Notion's sequence: double-write via an audit log into both the monolith and the new sharded databases; backfill historical data (~3 days on a 96-CPU instance); verify by sampling and dark reads comparing old and new; then a 5-minute scheduled maintenance switch - and they noted afterwards that with more script optimisation, a hot-swap at the load balancer with no downtime was probably achievable. Figma's failover produced only ten seconds of partial availability impact on primaries, none on replicas, with no latency or availability regression.
components.config: Budget the backfill as the long pole and run it at CONTROLLED concurrency - an uncontrolled backfill blows out replica lag on the source and causes an incident while you are mid-migration. Keep the double-write running until verification is clean for days, not hours. Keep the old path live and revertible behind a flag for a full week after cut-over.

blueprints.ceiling: Cross-shard operations. Anything needing a global transaction, a global unique constraint, a global join or a global ORDER BY is now either a scatter-gather (whose latency is the SLOWEST shard's) or impossible. Global aggregates move to the analytics store. Resharding, if the key is wrong, is another project of the same size.
blueprints.breaksFirst: A hot shard, caused by skewed key cardinality. One tenant is 100x bigger than the median, lands on one shard, and that shard is at capacity while the other 31 idle. You cannot fix it by adding hosts. Hashing is necessary but not sufficient - it spreads many keys evenly, it does not split one huge key. Plan tenant-level splitting for your largest tenants before you need it.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Sharding is near the end of the path. What follows is not 'more sharding' but specialisation: CQRS/event sourcing where read and write models have genuinely diverged, and a purpose-built engine where the workload has outgrown the general-purpose one entirely. Discord's move off Cassandra to ScyllaDB is the reference point: 177 nodes to 72, 9 TB per node against 4 TB, historical-fetch p99 from 40-125ms to 15ms, inserts to a consistent 5ms p99, migrated in nine days by a Rust migrator running at 3.2 million messages per second.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not shard to solve a read problem, a storage-size problem, or a vacuum problem - replicas, purpose-built stores and declarative partitioning each solve one of those for a fraction of the cost. Do not adopt a distributed SQL engine (CockroachDB, Vitess, Spanner-likes) without a hard look at migration cost: Figma considered exactly this and built in-house instead, citing complex data migration and having to rebuild domain expertise from scratch with only months of runway. That reasoning may or may not apply to you - but make the decision explicitly, in writing, because it is the other irreversible choice in this stage.

plain.plainName: Split the data across many databases
plain.problem: You have tried everything else, bigger machines, read copies, caching, routing, Aurora, moving odd workloads out, and one machine taking all the writes is still the wall.
plain.answer: Split the data across many databases by a chosen key, with a routing layer, after first splitting tables by area onto separate clusters.
plain.money: Roughly your current database cost times the number of pieces, plus the routing layer, plus the thing that dominates everything, 6 to 12 months of a dedicated team. Figma's first split table took nine months. Treat the engineering time as the real number.
plain.holdsUpTo: Notion runs 480 logical pieces across 32 physical Postgres machines. Figma uses several keys across about a dozen databases and has grown roughly 100 times since 2020.
plain.whatBreaks: One piece gets far more traffic than the rest. A single customer is 100 times bigger than the average, lands on one piece, and that piece is maxed out while the other 31 sit idle. Adding machines does not fix it. Spreading keys evenly helps but it cannot split one huge key, so plan how to split your biggest customers before you need to.
plain.timeToMove: This is near the end of the path. What comes next is not more splitting but specialisation, separating read and write models where they have truly diverged, or a purpose built engine. Discord moving from Cassandra to ScyllaDB is the reference: 177 machines down to 72, 9 TB per machine instead of 4 TB, and slow historical reads dropping from 40 to 125 milliseconds down to 15.
plain.dontYet: Do not split the database to fix a reading problem, a storage size problem or a clean up problem. Read copies, fitting tools and date range partitioning each solve one of those for a fraction of the cost. Do not adopt a distributed SQL engine like CockroachDB, Vitess or a Spanner style system without honestly costing the move. Figma looked at exactly that and built their own instead, because the data migration was complex and they would have had to learn a whole new system from scratch with only months of runway.
plain.pitch: One machine takes all my writes and I have genuinely run out of other options.

blueprints.name: CQRS and event sourcing, and the narrow case where the complexity pays
blueprints.forWho: A domain where the write model and the read model have genuinely diverged: one write produces many different views, or you have a regulatory or product need to know not just the current state but every state it passed through.
blueprints.scale: Applied to ONE bounded context, not the whole system. Typical: 1,000-100,000 events/sec into a log, with several independently scaled projections.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $300-$3,000 for the infrastructure (stream + projection consumers + projection stores), plus a permanent tax on every feature in that domain - new engineers need weeks to become productive in an event-sourced codebase.

components.service: The transactional outbox (start here, and often stop here)
components.role: Reliably publish events derived from database writes, without a dual write.
components.why: Rather than publishing to a queue and writing to the database as two operations, which is the dual-write bug: crash between them and the two diverge permanently. Rather than full event sourcing, which is what people jump to. Roughly 80% of the benefit people actually want from CQRS - reliable async projections, search indexes that stay in sync, downstream notification - comes from an outbox table written in the SAME transaction as the business write and drained by a poller. Days of work, not quarters, and reversible.
components.config: outbox(id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload jsonb, created_at, published_at). Write inside the business transaction. Drain with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Partition the outbox by day and DROP published partitions - an unbounded outbox becomes your next vacuum problem.

components.service: Change Data Capture instead of an outbox, where the writes are not all yours
components.role: Derive the event stream from the database's own WAL.
components.why: Rather than an outbox, when writes come from places you do not control (admin tools, other services, migrations). Aurora/RDS logical replication or AWS DMS reading the WAL captures everything by construction. Rather than CDC by default: CDC events are row-shaped, not domain-shaped, so consumers end up reimplementing your domain logic - an outbox lets you publish meaningful events.
components.config: Logical replication slot with wal_level=logical, and MONITOR ITS LAG with an alarm: an abandoned or stalled replication slot prevents WAL recycling, fills the disk and takes the database down. This is a genuine, common, self-inflicted outage. Drop unused slots as part of the runbook.

components.service: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK as the log
components.role: The ordered, replayable event stream.
components.why: Kinesis rather than SQS when you need ordering, replay and multiple independent consumers - SQS deletes on consume and cannot replay, which defeats the point. Kinesis rather than MSK for most teams: no cluster to operate, and ordering is per-partition-key, which is what you actually need. MSK rather than Kinesis when you need the Kafka ecosystem (Connect, Streams), longer retention, or you already have Kafka expertise. EventBridge rather than either when volume is low and the value is routing and filtering rather than an ordered log.
components.config: Partition key = aggregate ID, so all events for one entity are ordered. Retention long enough to rebuild the slowest projection (24h default; extend to 7-365 days). If the log is your system of record, also archive it to S3 via Firehose - a stream is not a durable system of record at multi-year horizons.

components.service: Projections into purpose-fit read stores
components.role: One write model, many read models, each shaped for its queries.
components.why: This is the actual payoff and the only reason to accept the complexity. The same event stream populates a normalised Postgres view for the app, an OpenSearch index for search, a DynamoDB table for a per-user timeline, and Redshift for analytics - each scaled and optimised independently, each rebuildable from the log. Rather than one relational schema trying to serve all four, which is what forced this stage in the first place.
components.config: Every projection must be rebuildable from zero, and you must have REHEARSED the rebuild and recorded how long it takes. Version projections (orders_v2 built alongside orders_v1, then cut over) so a schema change is never an in-place migration. Store each projection's last-processed sequence number so it can resume.

components.service: Full event sourcing (the log IS the system of record)
components.role: Reserved for domains where history is the product.
components.why: Rather than CQRS-with-a-normal-database, which is the far more common correct answer. Take this only for ledgers, financial transactions, regulated audit trails, collaborative document editing, or anything where 'what was the state on 3 March and who changed it' is a first-class requirement. The cost is permanent: eventual consistency becomes user-visible, every event schema change needs an upcaster because you can never rewrite history, and debugging requires replay tooling.
components.config: Append-only store: DynamoDB with a composite key (aggregate_id + sequence) and a condition expression on sequence for optimistic concurrency, or a dedicated event store. Snapshot every N events or rehydrating a long-lived aggregate becomes O(history). Event schema versioning and upcasters from day one. Per-subject encryption keys if the domain holds personal data - see the lifecycle blueprint on crypto-shredding.

blueprints.ceiling: Human, not technical. Eventual consistency becomes a product constraint: the user clicks save and the list does not update, and 'it will be there in 200ms' is not always acceptable. Projection lag becomes an SLO you must monitor and page on. Team onboarding time roughly doubles for that domain.
blueprints.breaksFirst: A projection silently falls behind or dies on a poison event, and the read model quietly diverges from the write model. Nothing errors. Users see stale or missing data, and because the write model is correct, every investigation starts in the wrong place. Instrument projection lag per projection and alarm on it as hard as you alarm on the database itself, and build a dead-letter path with an alert - a silently skipped event is a permanent data bug.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Do not 'move on' from this. CQRS is a tool applied per bounded context, not a rung on a ladder. The signal that you applied it correctly: exactly one or two domains use it, and the rest of the system is boring CRUD.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not apply CQRS system-wide. This is the single most expensive architectural mistake available to a small team: you get eventual consistency everywhere, debugging becomes archaeology, and you pay it on every feature forever, typically for zero measured benefit. Do not event-source a domain whose events you cannot name in a meeting - if the team cannot list the domain events on a whiteboard, the model is not ready. Do not use event sourcing as an audit-log substitute: an append-only audit TABLE gives you 90% of that for 2% of the cost.

plain.plainName: Store every change, build views from it
plain.problem: In one part of your product, one save has to update many different views, or you must be able to show not just how things are now but every step they passed through.
plain.answer: Record changes to a log, using an outbox table to start, and build separate read views from that log.
plain.money: 300 to 3,000 dollars a month for the stream and the view builders and their stores, plus a permanent tax on every feature in that area, because new engineers need weeks to become useful in it.
plain.holdsUpTo: Apply it to one area of the product, not the whole system. Typically 1,000 to 100,000 changes a second into the log, with several views that scale on their own.
plain.whatBreaks: A view quietly falls behind, or chokes on one bad record and stops. Nothing shows an error. Users see stale or missing data, and because the saved data is correct, everyone investigates the wrong place first. Track how far behind each view is and alarm on it as hard as you alarm on the database, and send bad records to a side queue with an alert.
