plain.timeToMove: You do not move on from this one. It is a tool for one area, not a rung on a ladder. The sign you did it right is that one or two areas use it and everything else stays boring.
plain.dontYet: Do not apply this across the whole system. It is the most expensive mistake available to a small team: everything becomes slightly out of date, debugging turns into digging, and you pay for it on every feature forever, usually for no measured gain. Do not use it for an area whose events your team cannot list on a whiteboard in a meeting. Do not use it as a stand in for an audit log, an append only audit table is the simpler answer.
plain.pitch: One save in my product has to feed many different views, and I need the full history too.

blueprints.name: Analytics off the operational store, because reports on production are a self-inflicted outage
blueprints.forWho: Anyone whose team runs a query with GROUP BY over months of data against the production database. Which, at some point, is everyone.
blueprints.scale: Handles TB-to-PB scans that would be impossible on the OLTP store, while removing an entire category of production incident.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $150-$3,000+. S3 + Athena is usage-based and can be under $100/month at modest volumes. Redshift Serverless starts around $0.36/RPU-hour with a minimum; a small provisioned cluster is roughly $200-900/month. Zero-ETL itself carries no separate charge beyond the Aurora and Redshift resources.

components.service: Aurora zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift
components.role: Continuously replicate operational tables into a warehouse with no pipeline to maintain.
components.why: Rather than a nightly ETL job you build and maintain, which is a scheduled job that fails silently, is a day stale, and becomes someone's second job. Rather than a read replica for reporting: a replica is still a row-store with OLTP indexes, so a 100M-row aggregation is still a 100M-row aggregation - and worse, a long analytics query on a replica causes replication conflicts (queries cancelled with 'conflict with recovery') or, with hot_standby_feedback on, causes bloat on the PRIMARY. A replica moves the CPU off the writer but does not make the query appropriate. Zero-ETL: data written to Aurora is available in Redshift within seconds - AWS states the Aurora MySQL integration processes over 1 million transactions per minute with p50 latency under 15 seconds - and Redshift's columnar storage makes the aggregation itself orders of magnitude faster. Rather than DMS: DMS is the right tool for cross-engine and one-time migrations, and unnecessary operational surface here.
components.config: Select only the tables analysts actually need - replicating everything doubles Redshift storage for tables nobody queries. Redshift Serverless rather than provisioned unless query volume is steady; the crossover is roughly 8-10 hours/day of sustained compute. Alarm on integration lag AND on an end-to-end freshness check (max(updated_at) in Redshift versus now), because the integration's own status field can look healthy while data is stale.

components.service: S3 + Glue Catalog + Athena (the cheap tier, and often the right one)
components.role: Query exported and archived data with SQL, paying only per scan.
components.why: Rather than a warehouse, when analytics is ad hoc and infrequent - a warehouse you query twice a week is an expensive idle cluster. Athena has no cluster at all. The crossover to Redshift is roughly when the same tables are scanned many times a day, or when query latency needs to be interactive for a dashboard, because Athena re-scans S3 each time while Redshift keeps data in an optimised columnar store.
components.config: Parquet, not JSON or CSV - typically 5-10x less data scanned and therefore 5-10x cheaper per query. Partition by date (s3://bucket/table/dt=2026-09-30/) so a one-day query scans one day. Compress with Snappy or ZSTD. Glue crawler or explicit partition projection to keep the catalogue current.

components.service: A hard boundary: no BI tool credentials on the operational database
components.role: The control that actually prevents the outage.
components.why: Rather than a policy and good intentions. The incident is always the same: an analyst or a scheduled dashboard runs an unbounded query, it takes a long-lived transaction or saturates I/O, and either it blocks a DDL migration behind it or it simply starves the OLTP workload. On Postgres a long-running transaction also stops autovacuum reclaiming anything newer than its snapshot, so a single forgotten query can bloat production for hours.
components.config: Revoke direct access; analysts get Redshift or Athena only. If someone MUST query production, give them a dedicated read replica with statement_timeout (30s), idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (60s), and a role with a low CONNECTION LIMIT so they cannot exhaust slots. Set a statement_timeout on the production application role too - an unbounded query should be impossible by configuration, not by discipline.

components.service: Amazon QuickSight (or your existing BI tool), pointed only at the warehouse
components.role: Where the humans actually go, with exactly one permitted data source.
components.why: Rather than letting each tool and each analyst connect wherever is convenient, which is what makes the boundary above unenforceable. One documented destination is what turns 'please do not query production' from a request into a fact.
components.config: QuickSight SPICE for dashboards that many people open (it caches, so the warehouse is not re-queried per viewer) and direct query only for genuinely live views. Its VPC connection and credentials scoped to the warehouse only, with no network path to the operational database. Row-level security in QuickSight if dashboards are multi-tenant.

blueprints.ceiling: Freshness. Zero-ETL gives you seconds, which covers almost every business question; a sub-second operational dashboard is still an operational-store concern and should be served by a materialised counter or cache, not by the warehouse. Cost ceiling: Redshift storage for replicated tables nobody queries.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Before you do this: the production database, during month-end close, when finance runs the big report. After you do this: the integration, silently - it pauses on a DDL change it cannot handle, nobody notices, and analysts spend a week making decisions on stale data. That is why the end-to-end freshness alarm above matters more than the integration's status field.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: This is a terminal stage, not a rung. The signal that you did it too late is a postmortem whose root cause is 'a report'. Do it before that postmortem.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build a lakehouse, a medallion architecture, dbt, Airflow and a data team before you have three analysts and a question they cannot answer. The minimum viable version is zero-ETL (or a nightly Parquet export to S3) plus Athena, and it is a day of work. Do not replicate every table by default. Do not let 'we need real-time analytics' justify querying production - real-time means a materialised counter in the operational store, not an ad-hoc GROUP BY.

plain.plainName: Reports that do not slow down the live app
plain.problem: Someone on my team runs a big report over months of data, and the live app slows down or falls over. It always seems to happen at month end.
plain.answer: Keep a second copy of the data just for reports, either in Redshift fed automatically from Aurora, or as files in S3 that you query with Athena.
plain.money: About $150 to $3,000 a month. S3 plus Athena can be under $100 a month at modest volumes. A small Redshift cluster is roughly $200 to $900 a month. The automatic Aurora to Redshift copy has no charge of its own.
plain.holdsUpTo: It can scan terabytes to petabytes, amounts the live database could never handle, and it removes a whole class of outage.
plain.whatBreaks: Before you do this, the live database dies during month end close when finance runs the big report. After you do this, the copying quietly stops after a schema change, nobody notices, and analysts spend a week making decisions on old numbers.
plain.timeToMove: This is the end of the road, not a step. The sign you left it too late is a postmortem where the cause was a report. Do it before that.
plain.dontYet: Do not build a data lake, dbt, Airflow and hire a data team before you have three analysts and a question they cannot answer. The smallest useful version is the automatic copy, or a nightly file export to S3, plus Athena, and it is a day of work. Do not copy every table by default. Do not let the words real time analytics become an excuse to query the live database. Real time means a running counter kept in the live database, not a big ad hoc query.
plain.pitch: Our reports keep hurting the live app, and I want them somewhere else.

blueprints.name: Data lifecycle, retention, archival, and the compliance that quietly forces your architecture
blueprints.forWho: Every stage above. This is not a late-stage concern - the decisions here are cheap on day one and brutally expensive to retrofit once you have 5 TB and a customer asking to be deleted.
blueprints.scale: Determines whether your operational store is 200 GB or 5 TB at the same user count. Directly sets your vacuum pain, backup duration, replica provisioning time and restore RTO.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Usually NEGATIVE - this stage saves money. Moving cold rows from RDS gp3 (~$0.115/GiB-month plus backup) to S3 Standard (~$0.023) to Glacier Instant Retrieval (~$0.004) to Deep Archive (~$0.00099) is a 20-100x reduction on the archived portion.

components.service: Declarative time-based partitioning on every append-heavy table
components.role: Make expiry a metadata operation instead of a vacuum problem.
components.why: Rather than DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days', which is the default approach and is actively harmful at scale: every deleted row becomes a dead tuple, autovacuum must reclaim it, the table does not shrink, and the DELETE itself generates WAL that blows out replica lag. With RANGE partitioning, expiry is DETACH PARTITION + DROP - instant, no dead tuples, no WAL flood, no vacuum debt. This one decision prevents the failure mode that eventually forced Notion to shard: VACUUM stalling consistently, with transaction ID wraparound behind it.
components.config: PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at), monthly partitions, pg_partman or a scheduled job creating partitions at least 3 months ahead and detaching expired ones. Retrofitting partitioning onto a 2 TB table requires a full rewrite or a logical-replication migration - which is exactly why this belongs in the FIRST blueprint, not this one.

components.service: S3 Lifecycle policies + Glacier tiers
components.role: Tiered archive for detached partitions, blobs, logs and exports.
components.why: Rather than keeping everything in the operational store 'in case'. Rather than deleting outright, which compliance often forbids. The trade: Glacier Deep Archive is roughly a twentieth of S3 Standard but retrieval takes hours and costs per GB - correct for legal-hold data nobody reads, wrong for anything a support agent might need this week. Glacier Instant Retrieval is the middle ground: millisecond access, roughly a fifth of Standard, with a 90-day minimum storage duration and a per-GB retrieval fee.
components.config: Standard -> Standard-IA at 30 days -> Glacier Instant Retrieval at 90 -> Deep Archive at 365, tuned to your real access pattern. Watch minimum-duration charges: objects deleted before the tier minimum are still billed for it, so lifecycle-ing small short-lived objects into IA can cost MORE than leaving them in Standard.

components.service: S3 Object Lock, where a regulator requires immutability
components.role: WORM storage that even the root account cannot delete.
components.why: Rather than an IAM or bucket policy, which a sufficiently privileged principal can change and which therefore does not satisfy regulations requiring immutability. This is the architectural point of the whole blueprint: a sentence in a regulation ('records must be immutable for seven years') dictates a specific service configuration, and the two are not negotiable against each other. Governance mode rather than compliance mode when you need a privileged escape hatch - choose consciously, because compliance mode is genuinely irreversible for the retention period.
components.config: Object Lock must be enabled AT BUCKET CREATION - it cannot be turned on later for an existing bucket, so this is another day-one decision. Default retention period taken from legal, in writing, with the regulation cited in the ticket.

components.service: Deletion machinery for data-subject erasure requests
components.role: Actually erase a person's data, everywhere it went.
components.why: This is where lifecycle stops being a cost exercise and becomes an architecture constraint. GDPR Article 17 and India's DPDP Act both give individuals erasure rights, and the obligation follows the data into every store you added in this track: the primary, every replica, the cache, OpenSearch, DynamoDB, S3 blobs, the Redshift warehouse, the event log and every backup. An append-only event log is in direct tension with an erasure obligation - the standard resolution is crypto-shredding (encrypt each subject's data under a per-subject key, then delete the key), which must be decided BEFORE you event-source, not after.
components.config: Maintain a written data inventory: every store, what personal data it holds, its retention period, its deletion mechanism. Implement erasure as a fan-out job with per-store confirmation and an audit record, not a DELETE on one table. Per-subject KMS keys for any append-only store. Be honest about backups: automated RDS snapshots cannot be selectively edited, so the policy must state that erasure completes for backups when they age out - which means your retention window must be defensibly short.

components.service: Restore rehearsal, on a schedule
components.role: Prove the backup is a backup.
components.why: Rather than trusting that snapshots exist. A snapshot that has never been restored is an untested assumption in the one position where assumptions are fatal. Restore time on a multi-TB database is also not a number you want to discover during an incident - Aurora restores from its cluster volume far faster than RDS restores from a snapshot, and that difference IS your RTO.
components.config: Quarterly, monthly if regulated: restore the latest snapshot to a throwaway instance, run row-count and checksum diffs against production for a sample of tables, record wall-clock restore time, delete the instance. Write the measured RTO into the runbook. Repeat per region if you claim cross-region DR.

components.service: Data residency as an architecture input
components.role: Where the bytes are legally allowed to live.
components.why: Residency requirements (GDPR transfer rules, India's sectoral localisation mandates, sector-specific rules) can force a region-per-jurisdiction topology - which changes your sharding key, your DR design and your analytics pipeline all at once. Discovering this after you have sharded is the expensive version.
components.config: Ask the residency question during customer-onboarding design, not during the enterprise deal. If any answer is 'data must stay in region X', that constraint belongs in the shard-key conversation before the shard key is chosen. Tag every bucket, table and cluster with its jurisdiction and audit with AWS Config.

blueprints.ceiling: None technically - this is a discipline, not a tier. The practical ceiling is the inventory: once data lives in six stores, keeping the inventory accurate needs automation (AWS Config rules, Macie for discovery, tag-driven policy) rather than a spreadsheet.
blueprints.breaksFirst: An erasure request you cannot fully honour, discovered during an audit or a customer security review - because the data was copied into a store added after the deletion job was written. Fix the class: make the deletion fan-out list the SAME artefact as the data inventory, and make adding a new store require updating both, enforced in code review.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Not applicable - this runs continuously alongside every other blueprint. The review trigger is: any new data store, any new region, any new customer category with a different regulatory profile.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not buy a data-governance platform before you have a one-page written inventory - the platform will just inventory your confusion faster. Do not set retention to 'forever' because deciding is hard: forever IS a decision, it is usually the wrong one, and it is the one that makes every other blueprint in this track arrive sooner and hurt more. Do not implement crypto-shredding across the whole system 'for safety' - it makes key management a hot path and a new single point of failure; apply it only to the append-only stores where ordinary deletion genuinely cannot work.

plain.plainName: Deciding how long you keep data, and where
plain.problem: Our database keeps growing and nothing is ever deleted. A customer has asked us to delete their data and I am not sure we can actually find all of it.
plain.answer: Split big tables by date, move old rows out to S3 and down into Glacier storage tiers, and keep one written list of every place data lives so deletion can reach all of them.
plain.money: This usually saves money. Moving cold rows from RDS storage at about $0.115 per GB a month, to S3 at $0.023, to Glacier Instant at $0.004, to Deep Archive at $0.00099, is a 20 to 100 times cut on the archived part.
plain.holdsUpTo: It decides whether your live database is 200 GB or 5 TB at the same number of users, which sets your backup time, replica setup time and how long a restore takes.
plain.whatBreaks: A customer asks to be deleted and you cannot fully do it, and you find out in an audit or a security review, because the data had been copied into a store that was added after the deletion job was written.
plain.timeToMove: It never ends. Review it whenever you add a data store, add a region, or take on a customer with different rules.
plain.dontYet: Do not buy a data governance product before you have a one page written list of where data lives. The product will only catalogue your confusion faster. Do not set retention to forever because deciding is hard. Forever is a decision, it is usually the wrong one, and it makes every other problem here arrive sooner and hurt more. Do not encrypt everything so you can delete by throwing away keys, across the whole system, for safety. It turns key management into a new single point of failure.
plain.pitch: Data goes into our system and never leaves, and that is starting to scare me.

blueprints.name: One EC2 box to an ALB in front of two boxes in two AZs
blueprints.forWho: A live app on a single EC2 instance with an Elastic IP in DNS, where a reboot or an AZ event is a full outage, and where you now need to deploy without downtime.
blueprints.scale: Typically 50-800 req/s of dynamic traffic, one app process group, a few hundred GB of state, single-digit-thousand daily users.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Adds roughly $18-25/mo for the ALB itself (~$16 fixed plus LCU) plus the cost of the second instance (a second m7g.large is ~$60/mo on-demand, ~$35 on a 1-year Compute Savings Plan). Cost is driven by instance duplication, not the ALB. Cross-AZ data transfer between ALB and targets is free for ALB, but app-to-DB cross-AZ is $0.01/GB each way.

components.service: Application Load Balancer
components.role: The new stable front door and the thing DNS points at from now on
components.why: Rather than keeping the Elastic IP on an instance and re-associating it during failover: EIP re-association is a manual, minutes-long, human-triggered action with no health checking, and clients that cached the ARP/route see resets. Rather than NLB: you want HTTP health checks, host/path routing and TLS termination with ACM certs you never rotate by hand. NLB wins only if you need static IPs, non-HTTP protocols, or sub-millisecond added latency.
components.config: Two subnets in two AZs (this is a hard ALB requirement), deletion protection on, idle timeout set ABOVE your app's keep-alive timeout (app 75s > ALB 60s, or you get random 502s), access logs to S3 from day one, target group health check on a real /health that touches the DB, healthy threshold 2, interval 10s, deregistration delay 30s.

components.service: EC2 Auto Scaling group (min 2, max 2 at first)
components.role: Holds the instances so replacement is automatic and identical
components.why: Rather than two hand-built instances registered manually: the whole point of the move is that a dead instance is replaced without you. Set max=min=2 initially — you are buying availability now, elasticity later. Adding scaling policies in the same change doubles the number of things that can go wrong on cutover night.
components.config: Launch template with a baked AMI (Packer or EC2 Image Builder) or user-data that pulls a versioned artifact; ASG health check type ELB with a 300s grace period; instance refresh with MinHealthyPercentage 50 as your deploy mechanism.

components.service: Route 53 weighted A/ALIAS records
components.role: The gradual traffic move from the old EIP to the ALB
components.why: Rather than flipping the A record in one edit: a single flip is an all-or-nothing bet with a TTL-shaped rollback window. Weighted records let you send 1%, then 10%, then 50%, and the rollback is setting one weight to 0 — which propagates within the TTL rather than requiring a new record to propagate.
components.config: Drop the record TTL to 60s at least 24h (one old-TTL period) BEFORE the migration day. Two weighted records, same name: old EIP weight 255, ALB ALIAS weight 0. Then 250/5, 200/55, 128/128, 0/255.

components.service: ElastiCache for Redis (or DynamoDB) for session state
components.role: Removes the one thing that actually blocks two instances: local session/file state
components.why: Rather than turning on ALB sticky sessions and calling it done: stickiness hides the statefulness instead of removing it, and then every deploy and every instance replacement logs users out, and load skews badly. Use stickiness only as a temporary bridge with a dated ticket to remove it. cache.t4g.micro is ~$12/mo.
components.config: cache.t4g.small, one replica in the second AZ, Multi-AZ with automatic failover on. Move sessions first, as its own release, with both code paths live (read from Redis, fall back to local) before the ALB exists.

components.service: EFS or S3 for user uploads
components.role: The second hidden blocker: files written to local disk
components.why: Rather than rsync between the two instances: rsync is eventually-inconsistent-by-cron and a user who uploads then immediately views hits the other box and gets a 404. S3 for anything served to users (add CloudFront later); EFS only if the code genuinely needs a POSIX path and you cannot change it — EFS adds ~1-3ms per operation and metadata-heavy workloads feel it.
components.config: S3 bucket, versioning on, presigned URLs for upload. Migration: dual-write to disk AND S3 for a week, backfill old files with `aws s3 sync`, then read from S3 with disk fallback, then drop disk.

blueprints.ceiling: This shape comfortably serves roughly 2,000-5,000 req/s of typical dynamic requests across two m7g.large instances before you are DB-bound rather than app-bound. The ALB itself is effectively not the limit — but it scales its own capacity in steps and takes about 5-15 minutes to warm, so a flash from 100 to 20,000 req/s gets 503s at the ALB.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The database connection pool, essentially always. Two app instances each holding a 20-connection pool is 40 connections; a db.t3.medium PostgreSQL has max_connections around 410 but starts thrashing on memory well before that, and every autoscaling event multiplies the pool. It looks like 'the site is slow and the DB CPU is fine' — the queue is in the pool, not the DB. The second failure is anything that assumed one process: an in-process cron now runs twice, an in-memory rate limiter now allows double, a local lock no longer locks.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: p99 latency at the ALB (TargetResponseTime) exceeds 500ms for 5 minutes while target CPU is under 50%; or DatabaseConnections is above 70% of max_connections; or RejectedConnectionCount on the DB is non-zero; or you have had to add a third instance manually more than once in a month.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add autoscaling policies, CloudFront, a read replica, containers or a service mesh in this same move. A team that bundles ECS into the 'add a load balancer' project turns a two-week change into a two-month one and loses the ability to say which change caused the regression. Specifically: no autoscaling until you have run min=max=2 for a month and know your per-instance capacity number; no CloudFront until static assets are actually on S3. The cost of adding it early is not dollars, it is that your rollback is no longer a single weight change.

plain.plainName: Two servers instead of one, so a reboot is not an outage
plain.problem: My whole app runs on one server. If it reboots, the site is down. I also cannot deploy without taking the site off for a minute.
plain.answer: Put an Application Load Balancer, which is a traffic splitter, in front of two servers in two different data centres, and keep login sessions in Redis instead of on the server.
plain.money: About $18 to $25 a month for the load balancer, plus the second server. A second m7g.large is about $60 a month, or about $35 on a one year Savings Plan. The duplicate server is the real cost, not the balancer.
plain.holdsUpTo: Roughly 2,000 to 5,000 requests a second across two m7g.large servers before the database, not the app, is the limit. Typical starting point is 50 to 800 requests a second and a few thousand users a day.
plain.whatBreaks: The database connection pool, nearly always. Two servers each holding 20 connections is 40, and a small database starts struggling long before its stated limit. It looks like the site is slow while the database CPU looks fine.
plain.timeToMove: When p99 response time at the balancer is over 500ms for 5 minutes while the servers are under 50% busy, or database connections are over 70% of the maximum, or you have had to add a third server by hand more than once in a month.
plain.dontYet: Do not add auto scaling, CloudFront, a read replica, containers or a service mesh in this same move. A team that bundles containers into the add a load balancer project turns a two week change into a two month one and can no longer tell which change caused a problem. No auto scaling until you have run with exactly two servers for a month and know what one server can take. No CloudFront until your images and files are actually on S3.
plain.pitch: One server runs everything, and a reboot takes my business offline.

blueprints.name: EC2 Auto Scaling group to ECS on Fargate, one service at a time
blueprints.forWho: A team with working AMI-based deploys that now takes 12+ minutes per deploy, cannot reproduce prod locally, and has drift between instances.
blueprints.scale: 10-60 instances, 5-40 deployable units, 500-10,000 req/s.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Fargate typically runs 20-50% more per vCPU-hour than equivalent on-demand EC2 (and far more versus Spot/Savings Plans), but usually removes 1-2 FTE-weeks/month of AMI and patching work. A 1 vCPU / 2GB Fargate task is about $36/mo running 24/7; Fargate Spot cuts that ~70% for interruption-tolerant work. Budget an extra $50-200/mo for ECR storage, NAT Gateway data and extra CloudWatch Logs.

components.service: ECS on Fargate
components.role: Runs the containerized service without you owning hosts
components.why: Rather than EKS: if you have fewer than ~30 services and no team member who wants Kubernetes as their job, EKS adds a $73/mo control plane, a cluster upgrade every ~14 months whether you want one or not, and a CNI whose IP exhaustion will eventually become your outage. Rather than ECS on EC2: Fargate removes the AMI/patching loop, which is the reason you are migrating. Go EC2-backed only when you need GPUs, very large memory, or your bill is dominated by steady 24/7 compute where Savings Plans on EC2 win.
components.config: awsvpc networking, a task role per service (never one shared role), 1 vCPU/2GB as your starting size, awslogs driver to a per-service log group with 30-day retention, ECS Exec enabled for debugging, `enableExecuteCommand: true`, circuit breaker with rollback enabled on the service deployment config.

components.service: The SAME Application Load Balancer, with a second target group
components.role: The seam that lets EC2 and Fargate serve the same hostname simultaneously
components.why: Rather than a second ALB and a Route 53 weighted split: one ALB with weighted target groups shifts traffic in seconds with no DNS TTL involved, so your rollback is instant instead of TTL-bounded. A second ALB is only worth it if the new stack needs different TLS or WAF settings.
components.config: Listener rule with forward to two target groups: ip-type target group (Fargate) and instance-type target group (existing ASG), weights 0/100 to start. Move 5 / 25 / 50 / 100 with at least one full business cycle at each step. Turn on target-group-level 5xx and TargetResponseTime metrics and alarm on the DIFFERENCE between the two groups, not the aggregate — the aggregate hides a broken canary at 5%.

components.service: ECR with immutable tags and a lifecycle policy
components.role: Image storage
components.why: Rather than Docker Hub: rate limits will take down a scale-out event at exactly the wrong time, and pulls from ECR over a VPC endpoint never leave AWS. Immutable tags rather than `latest`: with `latest` you cannot tell what is running, and rollback becomes a rebuild.
components.config: imageTagMutability IMMUTABLE, scan on push, lifecycle rule keeping the last 30 images, VPC endpoints for ecr.api, ecr.dkr, S3 (gateway) and logs — without the S3 gateway endpoint your image layer pulls go through NAT Gateway at $0.045/GB and a big image pulled 200 times a day is a real line item.

components.service: AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store via task definition secrets
components.role: Config that no longer lives in a file baked into the AMI
components.why: Rather than environment variables in the task definition: those are visible in the console and in every DescribeTaskDefinition call and get copied into CI logs. `secrets` blocks inject at task start and never appear in the definition. Parameter Store SecureString is free-tier-ish and fine for most; Secrets Manager ($0.40/secret/mo) earns it only when you need rotation.
components.config: `secrets: [{name: DB_PASSWORD, valueFrom: <ssm arn>}]`, execution role granted ssm:GetParameters and kms:Decrypt on just those paths.

blueprints.ceiling: ECS Fargate handles hundreds of services and low thousands of tasks per cluster fine. The practical friction points: Fargate task launch takes roughly 30-60 seconds (image pull dominates), so scale-out is not instant and a spiky workload needs headroom or a warm pool pattern; and the default RunTask/rate quotas plus ENI attachment rate will throttle a scale-out of hundreds of tasks at once.
blueprints.breaksFirst: VPC IP address exhaustion. awvpc gives every task its own ENI and therefore its own IP: a /24 private subnet holds 251 tasks, and a deployment that doubles task count during rollout needs double. You discover this as tasks stuck in PROVISIONING with 'unable to attach ENI'. Second: anything that was on the instance and not in the container — the log shipper, the monitoring agent, the cron entries, the /etc/hosts entry someone added in 2022.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Deploy time consistently over 10 minutes on the EC2 path; more than two config-drift incidents in a quarter; you cannot reproduce a production bug locally; or you are running more than about 8 deployable units on shared instances.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not introduce a service mesh (App Mesh is EOL; Istio on EKS is not your problem today), do not split the monolith while containerizing it, and do not move the database. Containerize the thing you have, unchanged, first — same process, same config, same ports. Teams that rewrite while containerizing cannot answer 'is the new latency from the container or the rewrite', and that question costs weeks. Also skip Service Connect / service discovery until you have more than one service that actually needs to find another.

plain.plainName: Packaging the app so deploys are fast and identical
plain.problem: Every deploy takes over 12 minutes, I cannot run production properly on my laptop, and our servers have slowly drifted apart from each other.
plain.answer: Move each service, one at a time, into ECS on Fargate, keep the same load balancer, and store the packaged images in ECR.
plain.money: Fargate costs about 20 to 50% more per CPU hour than equivalent EC2, but usually removes 1 to 2 person weeks a month of server patching. A 1 vCPU, 2GB task running all day is about $36 a month. Fargate Spot cuts that by about 70% for work that can be interrupted.
plain.holdsUpTo: Hundreds of services and low thousands of tasks per cluster. Typical range is 10 to 60 servers, 5 to 40 deployable pieces, 500 to 10,000 requests a second.
plain.whatBreaks: You run out of private IP addresses. Each task takes its own IP, a /24 subnet holds 251, and a deploy briefly doubles the count. You see it as tasks stuck starting with an error about not being able to attach a network card. Next, anything that lived on the old server and not in the container, like the log shipper or the cron jobs, just stops happening.
plain.timeToMove: When deploys are consistently over 10 minutes, or you have had more than two drift incidents in a quarter, or you cannot reproduce a production bug locally, or you are running more than about 8 deployable pieces on shared servers.
plain.dontYet: Do not add a service mesh, do not split the monolith while you containerise it, and do not move the database. Package what you already have, unchanged, with the same process, config and ports. Teams that rewrite while containerising cannot answer whether new slowness came from the container or the rewrite, and that question costs weeks. Skip service discovery until you have more than one service that actually needs it.
plain.pitch: Deploys take too long and our servers are no longer identical.

blueprints.name: Containers to Lambda, and the honest path back when it does not fit
blueprints.forWho: A team with spiky or low-duty-cycle traffic paying for idle Fargate tasks, or a team that went all-Lambda and is now fighting cold starts, 15-minute timeouts and a bill that grew faster than traffic.
blueprints.scale: Going in: under ~200 req/s sustained per endpoint, or bursty traffic with long idle periods. Coming back: over roughly 300-500 req/s sustained on one function, or per-request work over ~5 seconds.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: The crossover: a 1 vCPU/2GB Fargate task at ~$36/mo equals roughly 36M Lambda invocations at 128MB/100ms, or about 300,000 at 1GB/1s. Concretely, a 1GB function running 200ms costs about $3.50 per million requests. Above roughly 1.5-2 million GB-seconds/month for a single always-busy path, containers win on raw compute; below that, Lambda usually wins once you price in the idle.

components.service: AWS Lambda behind API Gateway HTTP API (or a Lambda Function URL)
components.role: The new execution path for one route at a time
components.why: HTTP API rather than REST API: about 1/3 the price ($1.00 vs $3.50 per million) and lower latency; take REST API only if you need request validation, API keys/usage plans, WAF, or private endpoints. Lambda rather than keeping Fargate: you stop paying for idle and you stop patching a base image. Function URL rather than API Gateway when the ALB or CloudFront is already doing auth and routing.
components.config: arm64 (about 20% cheaper per GB-second and usually faster for interpreted runtimes), memory tuned with Lambda Power Tuning rather than guessed — 1769MB is one full vCPU and often cheaper end-to-end than 512MB for CPU-bound work. Reserved concurrency on every function so one runaway path cannot eat the account's 1,000-concurrency default and take down every other function.

components.service: ALB with a Lambda target group, OR API Gateway stage weighting
components.role: The per-route seam for shifting traffic
components.why: ALB Lambda targets rather than a full API Gateway front door when you are migrating INTO Lambda: the ALB already fronts your containers, so a single listener rule can send /reports to Lambda and everything else to Fargate, and the rollback is deleting one rule. No DNS, no client change. Note the ALB-to-Lambda 1MB response limit — a report download will fail here and must go via S3 presigned URL.
components.config: Listener rule priority above the catch-all, path-pattern scoped to exactly one route. Keep the container path deployed and warm for at least two weeks after the route moves.

components.service: RDS Proxy (or Data API) if the function touches a relational DB
components.role: Stops Lambda concurrency from becoming database connections
components.why: This is THE reason serverless migrations fail. Rather than connecting directly from the function: 500 concurrent Lambdas means 500 connection attempts, and a db.r6g.large tops out around 1,000 max_connections but degrades long before. RDS Proxy multiplexes to a small pool and costs about $0.015/vCPU-hour of the DB instance (~$22/mo on a 2-vCPU instance). Pin transactions matter: long transactions and session state defeat multiplexing.
components.config: IAM auth, connection borrow timeout 120s, MaxConnectionsPercent 75. Alarm on DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency.

components.service: Provisioned Concurrency or SnapStart — only where measured
components.role: The cold start fix, applied surgically
components.why: Rather than turning provisioned concurrency on everywhere: it reverts you to paying for idle, which is why you left containers. Buy it only for the specific user-facing function whose p99 you can show is cold-start-dominated. SnapStart (Java, .NET, Python) is free and often the better first move; it cuts init from seconds to ~200ms but you must handle the snapshot-resume hazards — cached connections, seeded RNGs and cached clock values are all restored identical across every resumed environment.
components.config: Measure first: CloudWatch Logs Insights over the `Init Duration` field, and the `INIT_START` phase. If under 5% of invocations are cold and init is under 400ms, do nothing.

components.service: The return path: the same container image, run as both
components.role: The escape hatch that makes the experiment reversible
components.why: Package the handler so the same code runs as a Lambda (container image support, up to 10GB) and as a Fargate task with a thin HTTP shim. Rather than rewriting for Lambda's event shape: keep your framework and put the adapter at the edge (Lambda Web Adapter, Mangum, serverless-express). A team that rewrites into a Lambda-native shape has no way back and finds that out at 400 req/s.
components.config: Keep the Dockerfile as the single build artifact. Keep the Fargate service definition in IaC with desiredCount 0 rather than deleting it — going back is then a count change and an ALB rule, roughly 10 minutes.

blueprints.ceiling: Lambda's default 1,000 concurrent executions per region (raisable to tens of thousands) with a burst of 500-3,000 depending on region, then 1,000 more per 10 seconds. Hard 15-minute timeout, 10GB memory, 6MB synchronous payload, 512MB-10GB ephemeral /tmp. Sustained high-throughput CPU work is where the economics invert: one busy function at 500 req/s x 1GB x 200ms is ~$43/mo in duration alone plus requests, against maybe two Fargate tasks.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Coming in: database connections, then per-request cost on the hottest endpoint. Going in with heavy work: the 15-minute timeout on a batch job nobody measured. Coming back: nothing breaks technically — what breaks is the team's assumption that the rewrite was reversible, because the code now depends on the event object shape everywhere.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: To Lambda: average Fargate task CPU under 15% over a month, or a path that is called fewer than ~50,000 times/day. Back to containers: a single function's monthly duration cost exceeds two Fargate tasks; or p99 is over 1s and over 20% of that is init; or you are buying provisioned concurrency on more than two functions.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not move everything. Move ONE route with a clear shape (async, spiky, or cron) and live with it for a month. Do not adopt Step Functions in the same change — teams reach for it to work around the 15-minute timeout and end up with the business logic split across a state machine definition that no one can test locally. Do not go event-driven (EventBridge everywhere) at the same time: you will lose your stack traces and your ability to answer 'what happened to this request', and rebuilding that observability costs more than the compute you saved.

plain.plainName: Paying per request instead of per hour, and how to undo it
plain.problem: Our traffic comes in bursts and sits idle in between, so we pay all day for servers doing nothing. Or we went all in on Lambda and now the bill grows faster than our traffic.
plain.answer: Move one route to Lambda behind API Gateway, add RDS Proxy if it touches a relational database, and keep the same container image so you can go back.
plain.money: A 1 vCPU, 2GB Fargate task at about $36 a month equals roughly 36 million Lambda calls at 128MB and 100ms, or about 300,000 at 1GB and 1 second. A 1GB function running 200ms is about $3.50 per million requests. Above roughly 1.5 to 2 million GB seconds a month on one busy path, containers are cheaper.
plain.holdsUpTo: Good under about 200 requests a second per endpoint, or bursty traffic with long quiet gaps. Default limit is 1,000 running at once per region, raisable, with a hard 15 minute timeout and 10GB memory.
plain.whatBreaks: Going in, database connections run out, then the cost on your busiest endpoint. With heavy work, a batch job nobody timed hits the 15 minute cutoff. Coming back, nothing breaks technically. What breaks is the belief that the move was reversible, because the code now depends on the Lambda event shape everywhere.
plain.timeToMove: To Lambda when average Fargate CPU is under 15% for a month, or a path is called fewer than about 50,000 times a day. Back to containers when one function's monthly run cost exceeds two Fargate tasks, or p99 is over 1 second with over 20% of it startup, or you are paying for warm capacity on more than two functions.
plain.dontYet: Do not move everything. Move one route with a clear shape, background, bursty or scheduled, and live with it for a month. Do not adopt Step Functions in the same change. Teams reach for it to dodge the 15 minute limit and end up with business logic split across a state machine nobody can test locally. Do not go event driven at the same time either. You lose your stack traces and your ability to answer what happened to this one request.
plain.pitch: We pay all day for servers that are busy for an hour.

blueprints.name: One RDS writer to a writer plus read replicas, with a routing layer the app can actually use
blueprints.forWho: A single RDS/Aurora instance where read CPU is the bottleneck, reporting queries hurt the checkout path, and vertical scaling is out of runway or out of budget.
blueprints.scale: Read:write ratio above about 5:1, 2,000-50,000 reads/s, DB CPU above 70% during business hours.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Each Aurora replica costs the same as the writer (a db.r6g.large is ~$210/mo in us-east-1 on-demand) with no extra storage cost since Aurora shares one volume. RDS Multi-AZ read replicas each duplicate storage AND its IOPS. Aurora Serverless v2 replicas scale to 0.5 ACU (~$43/mo) when idle, which makes a replica you only need at peak cheap.

components.service: Aurora reader endpoint (or RDS read replica endpoints)
components.role: Where read traffic goes
components.why: Aurora's reader endpoint DNS-round-robins across replicas, with sub-100ms typical replica lag because replicas read the same storage volume rather than replaying a log. RDS read replicas use asynchronous engine replication with lag that can be seconds to minutes under write load, and a single-threaded apply on older MySQL versions means lag grows non-linearly. If you are on RDS and adding replicas for load, this is the moment to evaluate Aurora — but do not do both moves at once.
components.config: Aurora: two replicas minimum (one is a single point of failure for reads AND your failover target), spread across AZs, promotion tiers set so the largest replica is tier-0. Alarm on AuroraReplicaLag over 1s and on ReplicaLagMaximum.

components.service: Application-level read/write splitting behind a feature flag
components.role: Deciding, per query, which endpoint to use
components.why: Rather than a proxy that auto-splits (RDS Proxy does NOT do read/write splitting for you in the general case): only your code knows whether a read can tolerate replica lag. An automatic splitter will route a SELECT that immediately follows an INSERT in the same user action to a replica and show the user stale data — the classic 'I saved it and it is not there' bug. Explicit is correct here.
components.config: Start with a per-call-site opt-in: `with_replica():` wrapping specific, known-tolerant queries (dashboards, search, lists, exports). Never route reads-inside-a-transaction or read-after-write-in-the-same-request. Feature-flag the routing so a lag incident is one flag flip back to the writer, not a deploy.

components.service: A lag-aware guard in the routing helper
components.role: Automatic fallback to the writer when replicas fall behind
components.why: Rather than trusting the replica unconditionally: during a big migration, bulk delete or a vacuum, lag spikes to minutes and every replica-routed page shows wrong data silently — a rule-2 silent failure. The guard reads the lag metric (cheap, cached for a few seconds) and falls back.
components.config: Threshold set from your product's actual tolerance, not a round number: e.g. fall back to writer if lag > 2s. Emit a metric every time the fallback fires; a fallback rate above a few percent means you have a write-volume problem, not a read problem.

components.service: Performance Insights + a slow query baseline, captured BEFORE the change
components.role: The way you prove the replicas helped
components.why: Rather than declaring victory because writer CPU dropped: you need the per-query top-N from before, so that after the move you can show which queries left the writer and that p99 on the remaining ones improved. Without the baseline you cannot tell replica benefit from a traffic dip.
components.config: Performance Insights with 7-day free retention at minimum, `log_min_duration_statement` at 500ms, and a saved Top-SQL snapshot exported before the first read is routed away.

blueprints.ceiling: Aurora supports up to 15 replicas per cluster; in practice read scaling is linear to roughly 5-8 replicas before the writer's own replication and the connection count across all readers becomes the constraint. This shape does nothing for write throughput — a single Aurora writer on a db.r6g.8xlarge peaks in the low tens of thousands of writes/second depending on row size and index count.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Read-after-write consistency bugs in exactly the paths nobody flagged, appearing as intermittent support tickets rather than errors. Then: connection count, because each replica has its own max_connections and your pool config usually gets copy-pasted, so three replicas silently triples total connections. Then: the writer, unchanged, when your problem was actually writes all along.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Add replicas when: reader-eligible queries are over 60% of DB time in Performance Insights AND writer CPU is over 70%. Move past this tier (to sharding, CQRS, a cache tier, or a different store) when: writer CPU is over 70% with reads already offloaded; or you are at 5+ replicas; or WriteIOPS/commit latency is the top wait event.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add replicas before you have added a cache. A single ElastiCache node in front of the 10 hottest read queries frequently removes 60-80% of read load for $15-40/mo against $210/mo per replica, and takes a day. Do not add replicas before you have run the top-5 slow queries through EXPLAIN — a missing index has taken more DB instances offline than a lack of replicas. And do not enable auto-splitting at the driver or proxy layer as the first step; the stale-read bugs it creates are the expensive kind, because they are silent and land as lost user data.

plain.plainName: Extra copies of the database for reading
plain.problem: Our database is pegged during business hours, reporting queries slow down checkout, and buying a bigger machine is no longer an option.
plain.answer: Add Aurora read replicas, send read only queries to them through a feature flag in the app, and check replica lag before trusting a read.
plain.money: Each Aurora replica costs the same as the main database, about $210 a month for a db.r6g.large on demand, with no extra storage charge. RDS replicas duplicate storage too. Aurora Serverless v2 replicas drop to about $43 a month when idle.
plain.holdsUpTo: Good when reads outnumber writes by about 5 to 1, at 2,000 to 50,000 reads a second. Aurora allows up to 15 replicas, but reading scales well only to about 5 to 8. It does nothing at all for writes.
plain.whatBreaks: You save something, then immediately read it back and get the old value, in the exact paths nobody flagged. It shows up as odd support tickets, not errors. Then connections run out, because each replica has its own limit and the pool settings get copy pasted, so three replicas quietly triples the total.
plain.timeToMove: Add replicas when read queries are over 60% of database time and the writer is over 70% busy. Move past this when the writer is still over 70% busy with reads already moved off, or you are at 5 or more replicas, or write speed is your top wait.
plain.dontYet: Do not add replicas before you add a cache. One ElastiCache node in front of the 10 hottest read queries often removes 60 to 80% of read load for $15 to $40 a month, against $210 a month per replica, and takes a day. Do not add replicas before you run your five slowest queries through EXPLAIN. A missing index has taken down more databases than a lack of replicas. And do not let a driver or proxy split reads automatically as your first step. The stale read bugs it creates are expensive.
plain.pitch: Our database is maxed out on reading and reports are hurting checkout.

blueprints.name: Changing the database engine or major version under a live system (DMS + blue/green)
blueprints.forWho: Moving off self-managed MySQL/PostgreSQL to Aurora, off Oracle/SQL Server to PostgreSQL, or doing a major version upgrade you cannot take an hour of downtime for.
blueprints.scale: 50GB to 20TB. Below ~50GB with a tolerable maintenance window, a dump-and-restore at 3am is genuinely the better engineering decision and takes a night rather than a quarter.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: DMS replication instance: a dms.r5.large is about $180/mo, run for the 2-8 weeks of the migration. Double database cost for the overlap period. Budget the real cost as engineering time: a same-engine major upgrade is 2-6 weeks; a heterogeneous engine change (Oracle to PostgreSQL) is 6-18 months for a system of any size, dominated by stored procedures, and no tool changes that.

components.service: RDS/Aurora Blue/Green Deployments — for SAME-engine version upgrades
components.role: Managed staging copy plus a guarded switchover
components.why: Rather than an in-place `ModifyDBInstance` upgrade: in-place is a one-way door with an outage measured in tens of minutes for a large instance and a rollback that means restoring a snapshot and losing writes. Blue/green keeps the old cluster intact, runs logical replication into the green one, runs guardrail checks, and switches over typically in under a minute — AWS documents cutovers under five minutes. Critically, it renames endpoints so the app needs no config change. Know the limits: it does not replicate DDL, sequences, large-object changes, or DML on tables without a primary key — find your PK-less tables BEFORE you start, because they will silently not replicate.
components.config: Create green, apply the version change and any parameter-group changes there, let replication catch up to zero lag, run your read-only test suite against the green endpoint, then switch over with a timeout set. Keep blue for at least 48 hours. Rollback after switchover is NOT automatic — plan the reverse replication if you need one.

components.service: AWS DMS full load + CDC — for engine CHANGES and anything blue/green cannot cover
components.role: Continuous replication from old engine to new while both are live
components.why: Rather than a one-shot dump/restore: the dump of a 2TB database plus index rebuild is many hours of write-frozen downtime. DMS does a full load, then streams changes, so your cutover window is 'stop writes, wait for CDC lag to hit zero, flip'. Rather than native logical replication: use native where both sides are the same engine (it is faster and cheaper); DMS earns its keep across engines and where you need the built-in row-level validation.
components.config: Drop secondary indexes and FK constraints for the full load, then rebuild them during the paused phase before CDC — AWS's own best-practice guidance, and it can be the difference between 6 hours and 3 days. Enable ValidationSettings on the task for row-by-row comparison. Alarm on CDCLatencySource and CDCLatencyTarget; a rising target latency means your new DB cannot keep up with production write volume and your cutover would have failed anyway.

components.service: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) + DMS Schema Conversion
components.role: Converts DDL and tells you what it cannot convert
components.why: For heterogeneous moves only. Its real value is the assessment report, which is the honest number for the project: it lists every object it cannot auto-convert. That count, not the data volume, is your schedule. Rather than starting the migration and discovering the 400 Oracle packages: run the assessment in week one and make the go/no-go on it.
components.config: Run the assessment report before committing to the project at all. Treat anything over ~20% manual conversion as a rewrite, not a migration.

components.service: A read-only shadow comparison harness
components.role: Verifying correctness DURING the move, not after
components.why: Rather than comparing row counts at cutover: counts match while values differ (timezone handling, numeric precision, collation and sort order, empty-string-vs-NULL in Oracle). Run production read queries against BOTH databases for a week and diff the results, logging mismatches. This is the single highest-value thing in the whole blueprint and the step most often skipped. Oracle-to-PostgreSQL collation differences alone will reorder every paginated list you have.
components.config: Sample 1-5% of read requests, execute against both, compare serialized results, emit a mismatch metric with the query fingerprint. Require zero unexplained mismatches for 7 consecutive days as the cutover gate.

blueprints.ceiling: DMS full load throughput is roughly 30-100 GB/hour per task depending on row width and target write capacity; parallel-load by partition to go faster. CDC apply is the harder limit — DMS applies changes with much less parallelism than the source generated them, so a source doing sustained heavy writes can have CDC that never catches up. Test this early with a production-rate write replay, not at 2am on cutover night.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Tables without a primary key (DMS CDC cannot reliably apply updates/deletes to them; blue/green does not replicate DML on them at all), then LOB columns (DMS handles them separately and slowly, and truncates past your configured LobMaxSize — silently), then sequences/auto-increment counters that do not carry over and collide on the first write after cutover. Set every sequence to max(id)+buffer as an explicit cutover step.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: This is a one-time move, but the gate to actually cut over is machine-checkable and should be: DMS CDC latency under 5 seconds sustained for 24h; DMS validation task reporting zero failed rows; shadow-read mismatch rate zero for 7 days; every sequence reset step scripted and dry-run; and the reverse-replication path tested at least once.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not change schema, engine and application version in the same cutover. Move the data with the schema identical (even keeping the ugly column names), then refactor afterwards — otherwise when something is wrong you have no way to isolate which change caused it and your rollback is not a rollback. Do not turn on new engine features (partitioning, new index types, different isolation defaults) in the green database before cutover. And do not delete the old database for at least 30 days, regardless of how well it went; the bug you find in week 3 is the one you need it for.

plain.plainName: Switching database software without going offline
plain.problem: We need to move off our old database, or do a big version upgrade, and we cannot take an hour of downtime to do it.
plain.answer: Use RDS Blue/Green for same engine upgrades, or DMS full load plus ongoing change capture for an actual engine change, with a read only comparison harness checking both sides.
plain.money: A DMS replication instance, dms.r5.large, is about $180 a month for the 2 to 8 weeks of the move, plus double database cost during overlap. The real cost is people time. A same engine major upgrade is 2 to 6 weeks. An engine change like Oracle to PostgreSQL is 6 to 18 months.
plain.holdsUpTo: 50GB to 20TB. Below about 50GB, if you can take a maintenance window, a dump and restore at 3am is genuinely the better call and takes a night instead of a quarter. DMS loads roughly 30 to 100 GB an hour.
plain.whatBreaks: Tables with no primary key, which cannot be copied reliably. Then large text or file columns, which get cut off past your configured limit without telling you. Then auto numbering counters that do not carry over and collide on the first write after the switch.
plain.timeToMove: You may cut over when change capture lag stays under 5 seconds for 24 hours, the validation task reports zero failed rows, shadow reads match exactly for 7 days, every counter reset step is scripted and rehearsed, and you have tested replicating backwards at least once.
plain.dontYet: Do not change the schema, the engine and the application version in the same cutover. Move the data with the schema identical, ugly column names and all, then clean up afterwards. Otherwise when something is wrong you cannot tell which change did it, and your rollback is not really a rollback. Do not switch on new engine features before cutover. And do not delete the old database for at least 30 days.
plain.pitch: We have to change databases under a system that cannot go down.

blueprints.name: Single region to multi region: warm standby first, active-active only if the data model allows it
blueprints.forWho: A team with a contractual RTO/RPO they cannot meet in one region, or real users on another continent whose latency is dominated by round trips.
blueprints.scale: Any scale, but the honest threshold is: revenue impact per hour of downtime exceeds roughly $50-100k, or a regulator requires it. Below that, multi-AZ plus a tested restore is the better spend.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Warm standby realistically costs 30-60% of primary region spend (scaled-down compute, full-size data). Active-active costs 100-130%. Plus cross-region data transfer at $0.02/GB and the engineering cost, which is the real one: budget 3-9 months of a team's attention, and a permanent ongoing tax on every future change because every change now ships twice.

components.service: Aurora Global Database (single writer) OR DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-active)
components.role: The data layer, and the decision that determines everything else
components.why: This one choice decides whether active-active is even possible. DynamoDB global tables are multi-active — every region accepts writes, with last-writer-wins conflict resolution (and a newer strong-consistency mode giving zero RPO). Aurora Global Database is single-writer: secondaries are read-only, replication lag is typically under a second, cross-region failover is documented on the order of a minute with RPO in seconds. So: with Aurora you get active-ACTIVE-READS, not active-active writes, and every write in the secondary region takes a cross-region round trip (70-150ms US east-west). Teams that promise the business active-active on a relational database have promised something the database does not do.
components.config: Aurora Global: managed planned failover for drills, unplanned failover (detach-and-promote) understood and scripted. DynamoDB: global tables with PITR in every region, and a conflict strategy written down — last-writer-wins silently destroys data in a counter or a balance.

components.service: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls
components.role: The failover switch, and the thing that makes failover a decision rather than an inference
components.why: Rather than Route 53 health checks alone: health-check-driven failover is an inference from an endpoint's behaviour, and it will flip you mid-partition when you did not want it to, or fail to flip when the app is up but broken. ARC routing controls are an explicit on/off you operate, with a data plane spread across five regions specifically so it works when a region is impaired. Rather than editing DNS during an incident: editing DNS requires the console and your credentials in the region you are failing away from. ARC costs about $3/hr per cluster, which is the single biggest reason teams skip it — a shared cluster across applications is the usual answer.
components.config: Routing controls per region per tier, safety rules that prevent turning both off at once (or, where appropriate, prevent turning both ON). Readiness checks on capacity in the standby region — a standby that cannot hold the load is not a standby.

components.service: Pre-provisioned capacity in the standby region (warm, not pilot-light)
components.role: Making sure the standby can actually take the traffic
components.why: Rather than pilot light (data replicating, compute off): when you fail over, you need EC2/Fargate capacity NOW, in a region that is currently absorbing everyone else's failover too. Capacity is not guaranteed on demand during a regional event. Warm standby at 20-30% of primary, scaled up by the same autoscaling policies, is the pragmatic shape; use On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the critical tier if the RTO is tight.
components.config: Standby running at min capacity continuously and serving synthetic canary traffic — a standby that has never served a real request will fail on a config difference you did not know about. Run at least 5% of real production traffic through it permanently. This is the whole trick: continuous low-volume real traffic converts an untested DR plan into a tested one.

components.service: Region-scoped deployment pipeline with a mandatory bake
components.role: Preventing your own deploy from being the correlated failure
components.why: Rather than deploying to all regions at once: a bad deploy that lands everywhere simultaneously removes the entire point of multi-region. Deploy to the standby region first, bake, then primary — or the reverse, but always sequenced with time between.
components.config: Minimum 1-hour bake between regions with automated rollback on the canary's error rate. No exceptions for urgent fixes; urgency is when the sequencing matters most.

blueprints.ceiling: Aurora Global Database supports up to 5 secondary regions. The real ceiling is organizational: every stateful component you add must have a cross-region story, and the list is longer than anyone estimates — object storage (S3 CRR is async, minutes), caches, search indexes, queues (SQS is regional, in-flight messages do not replicate), secrets, feature flags, certificates, and anything in someone's laptop-run script.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The things you forgot were regional. In a real failover: SQS messages in flight are stranded in the failed region; S3 objects written in the last few minutes have not replicated; the ElastiCache in the standby is cold and the thundering herd takes down the database; and the standby's IAM roles were never used, so an unnoticed permission gap surfaces as 403s under load. Second: split-brain, if your failover is health-check-automatic and the partition was in the network, not the region.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Signals that you genuinely need this: a documented RTO under 1 hour that a restore cannot meet; measured p50 latency over 150ms for a material user population; or a regulator. Signals you are NOT ready: you have not restored a backup in the last quarter, you do not have a single-region runbook, or your deploy is manual.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not go multi-region until multi-AZ is genuinely correct and you have proven a restore (a backup nobody restored is not a backup). Far more outages come from a bad deploy, a full disk, an expired certificate and a bad migration than from a region failing — and multi-region makes each of those harder to fix, not easier. Specifically do not: add a global accelerator, a global cache, or cross-region service calls in this phase. Cross-region synchronous calls turn two regions into one system with two failure domains and worse availability than either alone.

plain.plainName: A second copy of everything in another part of the world
plain.problem: We have promised a customer we can recover fast from a disaster, or our users on another continent wait too long for every page.
plain.answer: Run a warm standby in a second region using Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables, with Route 53 recovery controls to switch traffic.
plain.money: A warm standby realistically costs 30 to 60% of your main region spend. Active in both regions costs 100 to 130%. Add cross region transfer at $0.02 per GB. The real cost is 3 to 9 months of a team's attention plus a permanent tax on every future change.
plain.holdsUpTo: Aurora Global Database allows up to 5 secondary regions. The honest threshold is money, about $50,000 to $100,000 of lost revenue per hour of downtime, or a regulator saying so. Below that, multi AZ plus a tested restore is the better spend.
plain.whatBreaks: The things you forgot were tied to one region. Queued messages are stranded, the last few minutes of uploaded files never copied over, the standby's cache is empty so the sudden rush knocks the database over, and permissions nobody ever used show up as access errors under load.
plain.timeToMove: You need this when you have a written recovery target under 1 hour that a restore cannot meet, or measured page load over 150ms for a large group of users, or a regulator. You are not ready if you have not restored a backup this quarter, have no runbook for one region, or deploy by hand.
plain.dontYet: Do not go multi region until multi AZ is genuinely right and you have proven a restore. A backup nobody restored is not a backup. Far more outages come from a bad deploy, a full disk, an expired certificate or a bad migration than from a region failing, and multi region makes each of those harder to fix. Do not add a global accelerator, a global cache, or calls between regions in this phase. Synchronous cross region calls turn two regions into one system.
plain.pitch: We have a contract or regulator that says one region is not enough.

blueprints.name: Monolith to services with the strangler fig: a proxy, one capability at a time, over 18 months
blueprints.forWho: A monolith where deploys are coordinated across teams, where one team's change breaks another's, and where the merge queue is the bottleneck. Not a monolith that is merely large.
blueprints.scale: Any. The honest trigger is team count (above about 4 teams sharing one deploy) rather than lines of code or traffic.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Infrastructure barely moves; the proxy tier adds ~$20-50/mo. The real cost is duplicated effort during coexistence — plan for 15-25% ongoing capacity drag for the whole migration, and a migration that runs 12-24 months for a real system. Anyone quoting a quarter has not done one.

components.service: Amazon API Gateway or the existing ALB as the interception facade
components.role: The seam: everything enters here, and this is where a route stops going to the monolith
components.why: AWS's own prescriptive guidance names exactly this — API Gateway or an ALB at the perimeter of the monolith, transform / coexist / eliminate. ALB rather than API Gateway when the traffic is already HTTP inside your VPC and you want path-based rules with near-zero added latency and no per-request fee. API Gateway when you need per-route auth, throttling, request validation or usage plans as part of the seam. Rather than putting routing logic inside the monolith: then your rollback requires a monolith deploy, which is the thing you are trying to escape.
components.config: Introduce the facade FIRST, with 100% of routes forwarding to the monolith unchanged, and run it for a month. If the facade alone causes no incident, it is trustworthy. Path-based rules, one rule per extracted capability, weights for gradual shift.

components.service: Branch-by-abstraction inside the monolith
components.role: The seam INSIDE the code, for logic that is not reachable as an HTTP route
components.why: Most of a monolith's interesting logic is called internally, not over HTTP, so a perimeter proxy cannot reach it. AWS documents branch-by-abstraction as the companion pattern: introduce an interface, implement it twice (in-process and remote-call), pick with a flag. Rather than extracting directly: direct extraction means a big-bang swap with no gradual shift and no per-request rollback.
components.config: The flag is per-request and runtime-changeable (AppConfig or a flag service), never a deploy-time constant. Default off. Percentage rollout on a stable hash of user id, so a user's experience is consistent.

components.service: Shadow / parallel-run comparison
components.role: Proving the new service is correct BEFORE it serves anyone
components.why: Rather than testing the new service and then switching: call BOTH, return the monolith's answer, and log the diff. AWS publishes a reference architecture for exactly this (replaying parallel requests to break a monolith). This is how you find the undocumented behaviour — the rounding, the special case for one customer, the bug that downstream code now depends on. Rather than a test suite: the test suite encodes what you think the monolith does.
components.config: Run the new path asynchronously so it cannot add latency or fail the request. Normalize before diffing (ordering, timestamps, float precision) or you will drown in false positives. Gate: diff rate under 0.01% for two weeks before the flag moves off 0.

components.service: The database boundary: keep it shared, then split it LAST
components.role: The decision that determines whether this succeeds
components.why: Rather than splitting the database with the service: a new service reading the monolith's tables is not 'wrong' — it is the correct intermediate state, and it lets you move logic without a dual-write problem at all. The dual-write problem (writing the same fact to two stores with no transaction across them, so a crash between writes leaves them permanently inconsistent) is avoided entirely by not dual-writing: ONE store owns each fact. When you finally do split, use the outbox pattern — the service writes its business change and an outbox row in one local transaction, and a relay (DynamoDB Streams, or Debezium/DMS reading the WAL) publishes it. Rather than 'write to DB then publish to SNS': that is a dual write and it will lose events.
components.config: Rule: exactly one service writes each table. Others read (via a view or a replica) until they are ready to own it. Split storage only after the service has owned the writes for months.

components.service: Per-capability ownership and an explicit kill list
components.role: Making 'eliminate' actually happen
components.why: The failure mode of strangler fig is not technical — it is stopping halfway and running both forever, which is strictly worse than either end state. Every extraction gets a dated commitment to delete the monolith code, and the deletion is part of the same epic, not a follow-up ticket.
components.config: Instrument the old code path with a counter. When it reads zero for 30 days, delete it that sprint. An extraction is not done until the old code is gone.

blueprints.ceiling: Not a throughput ceiling. The limit is how many simultaneous extractions a team can hold: roughly one capability in flight per team, two or three total for an organization of 30 engineers. Beyond that, the coexistence complexity — every extraction adding a flag, a diff harness, a routing rule and a deprecation — exceeds the benefit.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Shared mutable state that both sides touch, discovered after the flag hits 50%. Then distributed transactions you did not know you had: an operation that was one DB transaction now spans two services, and partial failures create states your code has never seen. Then latency — an in-process call at 0.1ms becomes a network call at 2-10ms, and a loop that made 200 of them is now a 2-second page.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Extract the next capability when the current one's old code path has been deleted and the service has run a month without an incident. Stop extracting when deploy independence is achieved for the teams that needed it — not when the monolith is gone. A small durable monolith core is a fine end state.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not add Kubernetes, a service mesh, gRPC, event sourcing, CQRS or a new language in the same programme. Each of those is a separate multi-month learning curve and together they guarantee that when something is slow nobody can say why. Extract services onto the SAME runtime the monolith uses. Do not build a shared internal platform team's golden path before you have three services — you will build it for a shape you have not learned yet. And do not split the database first: teams that start with 'database per service' create the dual-write problem on day one and spend a year on eventual-consistency bugs before delivering any deploy independence.

plain.plainName: Slicing one big app into parts, slowly
plain.problem: Every deploy has to be coordinated across teams, one team's change breaks another's, and the merge queue is where work goes to wait.
plain.answer: Put API Gateway or your existing load balancer in front, move out one capability at a time behind a feature flag, run both sides side by side and compare, and split the database last.
plain.money: Infrastructure barely changes. The routing layer adds about $20 to $50 a month. The real cost is duplicated work while both versions exist. Plan for 15 to 25% ongoing drag on capacity, over 12 to 24 months. Anyone promising a quarter has not done one.
plain.holdsUpTo: The trigger is team count, above about 4 teams sharing one deploy, not code size. A 30 engineer organisation can hold about one extraction per team in flight, two or three in total.
plain.whatBreaks: Shared data that both sides write to, found after the flag reaches 50%. Then operations that used to be one safe database transaction now span two services, so a half finished state appears that your code has never seen. Then speed, because a call that took 0.1ms inside the app now takes 2 to 10ms over the network, and a loop doing 200 of them becomes a 2 second page.
plain.timeToMove: Extract the next piece when the old code path is deleted and the new service has run a month without an incident. Stop when the teams that needed independent deploys have them, not when the monolith is gone. A small stable core is a fine end state.
plain.dontYet: Do not add Kubernetes, a service mesh, gRPC, event sourcing or a new language in the same programme. Each is a separate multi month learning curve, and together they guarantee that when something is slow nobody can say why. Put new services on the same runtime the monolith already uses. Do not build a shared internal platform before you have three services, because you will build it for a shape you have not learned yet. And do not split the database first.
plain.pitch: Four teams share one deploy and we are always waiting on each other.

blueprints.name: Moving off another provider onto AWS without a big-bang weekend
blueprints.forWho: A working system on Heroku, DigitalOcean, a colo, or another cloud, where the move is driven by a real constraint (cost, compliance, a service you need) rather than fashion.
blueprints.scale: Whatever you have. The variable that matters is data volume and how chatty the app is with its database.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Expect to pay for both environments for 1-3 months. Direct Connect for a serious colo move is $300+/mo for a 1Gbps hosted connection plus port hours; Site-to-Site VPN is ~$36/mo plus data and is enough for most application migrations. Snowball is worth it above roughly 10-20TB, or wherever transfer over your link would take more than a week.

components.service: Site-to-Site VPN (or Direct Connect) between old and new
components.role: Makes the two environments one network so a service can move without its callers changing
components.why: Rather than moving everything at once because the pieces cannot reach each other: with a tunnel, the app can stay put while the database moves, or vice versa. This single decision converts a big-bang weekend into an incremental move. Direct Connect rather than VPN when you need consistent latency for a chatty app-to-DB path or are moving many TB — VPN throughput is ~1.25Gbps per tunnel and latency over the public internet is variable.
components.config: Measure the round-trip latency across the tunnel FIRST. If app-to-DB RTT goes from 0.5ms to 30ms and a page makes 80 queries, that page just went from 40ms to 2.4s. Find your N+1 queries before the move, not during.

components.service: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) for lift-and-shift servers
components.role: Block-level continuous replication of existing VMs/servers into EC2
components.why: Rather than rebuilding each server from a runbook: MGN replicates continuously, so you can boot a test instance from current data any time, validate, and throw it away — as many rehearsals as you want. Rather than a rebuild-first (replatform) approach for everything: rebuild is better long-term but couples the migration risk to the rewrite risk.
