Lift-and-shift first, modernize on AWS afterwards, is the sequence that lets you roll back.
components.config: Run at least two full test-instance launches before cutover, with the application actually exercised, not just booted. Cutover window is then minutes: stop the source, final sync, launch cutover instances.

components.service: DMS or native replication for the database, with the app still on the old provider
components.role: Moving the state separately from the compute
components.why: The database is the hard part and deserves its own cutover with its own rollback, on a different day from the compute. Rather than moving app and DB together: if the combined cutover goes wrong you cannot tell which half, and the rollback is both.
components.config: Same discipline as the engine-change blueprint: full load with indexes deferred, CDC to near-zero lag, validation task green, sequences reset as an explicit step, reverse replication configured so the old DB can be re-promoted for at least 72 hours.

components.service: DNS with short TTL and weighted records across providers
components.role: The gradual traffic shift, provider to provider
components.why: Rather than a hard DNS switch: weighted records let you move 1% and watch. Because the two environments share a database at this point, a user hitting either side sees identical data, so the split is safe. Rather than a CDN-level origin switch: possible and faster, but you then need CloudFront in place first, which is another change.
components.config: TTL down to 60s at least 48 hours before. Run 1% for a full day, not an hour — the bugs are timezone-shaped and batch-job-shaped. Watch error rate and p99 per-origin, not blended.

components.service: A parity checklist built from what the old provider did for you
components.role: Catching the invisible services
components.why: Every platform provides things you forgot you use: Heroku gives you automatic TLS, log drains, review apps, a scheduler, daily DB backups, and a routing layer that queues requests. On AWS each of those is a thing you now build. Rather than discovering this per-incident: enumerate it up front. The most common omissions are outbound email reputation (a new EIP has no sending reputation — warm it or use SES with a dedicated IP for weeks beforehand), cron (EventBridge Scheduler), and log retention.
components.config: Write the list, assign each item, and do not cut over with any item unassigned.

blueprints.ceiling: The constraint is the link and the chattiness, not AWS. A 1Gbps link moves about 10TB/day at perfect utilization and realistically 4-6TB/day. Above ~50TB, Snowball's physical shipping (about a week door to door) beats the wire.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Latency on the split path — the app in the old provider talking to the database in AWS (or vice versa) across 20-40ms, which amplifies every N+1 query by a factor of 50. Then outbound email deliverability from the new IPs. Then whatever hardcoded IP allowlist a payment provider or partner has for you, which nobody remembers until the first failed settlement.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Cut over when: a test-instance launch has passed a full functional exercise twice; DB replication lag is near zero with validation clean; the parity checklist has zero unassigned items; and the rollback (DNS weight to 0 plus reverse DB replication) has been rehearsed end to end at least once.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not re-architect during the move. Keep the same runtime, the same instance shapes (rounded up), the same monolith, the same database engine. Teams that use the migration as an excuse to adopt containers, IaC-from-scratch, a new CI system and microservices simultaneously are the ones still migrating two years later. Move it as-is, get stable for a month, then improve one thing at a time. Also: do not turn off the old environment on cutover day. Keep it paid for and bootable for 30 days; the cost is trivial compared to the value of a real rollback.

plain.plainName: Moving your live system to AWS safely
plain.problem: Our app runs somewhere else, like Heroku or our own servers, and we have to move it to AWS. I am scared we will break it all in one weekend.
plain.answer: Link the old place and AWS with a VPN, copy the servers with AWS Application Migration Service, keep the database copying over with DMS, then shift traffic slowly using DNS.
plain.money: You pay for both places for 1 to 3 months. A Site to Site VPN is about 36 dollars a month plus data, and that is enough for most app moves. A serious colo move with Direct Connect starts at 300 dollars a month for a 1Gbps link plus port hours. Shipping a Snowball box is worth it above roughly 10 to 20TB.
plain.holdsUpTo: Your link is the limit, not AWS. A 1Gbps link moves about 10TB a day in theory and really 4 to 6TB a day. Above about 50TB, shipping a physical box, about a week door to door, is faster than the wire.
plain.whatBreaks: While the app is in the old place and the database is already in AWS, every page feels slow. A 20 to 40ms gap gets multiplied by every small query, so pages crawl. Then your emails start landing in spam from the new addresses. Then a payment partner blocks you because they had your old IP address on an allow list and nobody remembered.
plain.timeToMove: Switch over only when a test server has passed a full run through twice, the database copy is caught up and checked, the parity checklist has no unassigned items, and you have practised the rollback, DNS back to zero plus reversing the database copy, at least once end to end.
plain.dontYet: Do not redesign anything while moving. Same runtime, same instance sizes rounded up, same single app, same database engine. Teams that also adopt containers, new infrastructure code, a new CI system and microservices at the same time are the ones still migrating two years later. Move as is, be stable for a month, then improve one thing at a time. Also do not switch off the old place on cutover day. Keep it paid and bootable for 30 days.
plain.pitch: We have a real system running somewhere else and we need it on AWS without a scary big bang weekend.

blueprints.name: Splitting one AWS account into an Organization with several
blueprints.forWho: A single account where prod and dev share a blast radius, where IAM policies have grown into something nobody will touch, and where you cannot tell which team's spend is which.
blueprints.scale: Any team above about 5 engineers, or any system with a compliance boundary. The trigger is usually the first incident where a dev action affected prod.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: AWS Organizations, Control Tower's core and IAM Identity Center are effectively free; the cost is the duplicated baseline per account — a NAT Gateway per account per AZ ($32/mo each plus $0.045/GB) is the line item that surprises people, so a centralized egress VPC or VPC endpoints matters. GuardDuty, Config and CloudTrail per account add maybe $30-150/mo each. Budget 2-6 months of part-time work for a system of moderate size.

components.service: AWS Organizations with Control Tower, and a dedicated Migrations OU
components.role: The governance structure, with a low-friction landing zone for in-flight moves
components.why: Rather than creating accounts by hand: you want consolidated billing, SCPs and a repeatable account factory from the start, because retrofitting governance onto twelve hand-made accounts is worse than the original problem. AWS's own guidance recommends a separate OU named something like Migrations with deliberately limited SCPs, so that a workload mid-move is not blocked by a policy while it is half-migrated.
components.config: OUs: Security (log archive, audit), Infrastructure (network, shared services), Workloads (prod, non-prod), Sandbox, Migrations, Suspended. Keep the management account empty of workloads — this is non-negotiable, because SCPs do not apply to it.

components.service: IAM Identity Center with permission sets
components.role: How humans get into the new accounts
components.why: Rather than IAM users per account: you are about to multiply accounts, and per-account users multiplies credential sprawl by the same factor. Identity Center gives one login and short-lived credentials across all of them. Rather than cross-account role chaining from the old account: that keeps the old account as a single point of compromise for everything.
components.config: Permission sets, not inline policies. Session duration 4 hours maximum for anything with production write. Do this BEFORE moving any workload — otherwise people will create emergency IAM users in the new accounts and you will never find them all.

components.service: The keep-it-and-copy move, not the lift-the-account move
components.role: The actual mechanics of splitting
components.why: Two genuinely different strategies. (A) Leave production where it is, rename that account 'Production', and build NEW accounts for dev/staging/tooling around it. This is almost always right: production never moves, so production risk is zero, and you get the blast-radius separation in weeks. (B) Move workloads out of the old account into new ones — which is a per-resource migration with all the same problems as a provider migration. Rather than (B) by default: teams pick it because the old account 'feels dirty', which is an aesthetic reason for a project with real outage risk.
components.config: If you must move resources: redeploy from IaC into the new account rather than transferring resources. Stateless tiers redeploy trivially. For state — RDS: snapshot, share the snapshot with the target account (re-encrypt with a KMS key shared to that account, the step everyone misses), restore, then DMS CDC for the delta and a short cutover. S3: `s3 sync` plus a bucket policy allowing the target, or S3 Batch Replication for large buckets — note bucket NAMES are globally unique and cannot be transferred, so plan a rename and a period of dual-read. DynamoDB: export to S3 and import, or AWS Backup cross-account copy.

components.service: Transit Gateway or VPC peering plus centralized egress
components.role: Letting the new accounts talk to what is still in the old one
components.why: Rather than making every account fully independent on day one: things will span accounts during the transition, and a tunnel between them makes the transition incremental. Transit Gateway ($36/mo per attachment plus $0.02/GB) rather than a mesh of peerings once you pass about 4 VPCs — peering does not transit, so N VPCs need N(N-1)/2 peerings and the route tables become unmaintainable.
components.config: Non-overlapping CIDRs across every account, decided before the first account is created. Overlapping CIDRs is the mistake that cannot be fixed later without re-IPing a live VPC.

components.service: SCPs applied in report-then-enforce order
components.role: The guardrails
components.why: Rather than writing restrictive SCPs and applying them: an SCP denial is invisible in a way that produces the worst kind of debugging session, because the error says AccessDenied and the IAM policy looks correct. Start with the small universally-safe set and grow.
components.config: Day one SCPs only: deny leaving the organization, deny disabling CloudTrail/GuardDuty/Config, deny root user actions, deny regions you do not use. Everything else waits until you have CloudTrail evidence that nothing legitimate does it.

blueprints.ceiling: Organizations supports a large number of accounts (the default quota is modest and raisable), so the ceiling is operational: once you pass roughly 20-30 accounts, per-account manual anything stops working and you need the account factory, centralized networking and centralized logging to have been real from the start. Retrofitting at 40 accounts is a year of work.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Cross-account KMS. Encrypted RDS snapshots, encrypted S3 objects and encrypted EBS all need the key shared AND the key policy updated AND the receiving role granted — miss one and the restore fails with an unhelpful error. Second: hardcoded account IDs in IAM policies, trust relationships, ECR image URIs, bucket policies and CI config. Third: service quotas, which are per-account and start at defaults in the new account, so the first load test fails on a limit the old account had raised years ago.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Split when: a non-production action has affected production at least once; or you cannot attribute more than ~70% of spend to a team; or an auditor has asked for a boundary. Do the next workload when the previous one has run a month in its new account with no cross-account permission incidents.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not create an account per microservice, per environment, per team all at once. Start with three or four: management, security/log-archive, production, non-production. Adding accounts is cheap later; removing them is not, because every account accumulates a networking attachment, a baseline cost and a place for someone to leave something. Do not deploy Control Tower's full set of optional guardrails on day one — the detective controls generate Config cost and noise that nobody triages. And do not migrate production into a new account as your first move; prove the process on the least important workload you have.

plain.plainName: Splitting one AWS account into several
plain.problem: Everything lives in one AWS account. A dev mistake can hit our live system, the permissions are a mess nobody wants to touch, and I cannot tell which team spent what.
plain.answer: Turn on AWS Organizations with Control Tower, sign in through IAM Identity Center, and start with about four accounts instead of one.
plain.money: Organizations, Control Tower basics and IAM Identity Center are effectively free. The cost is the repeated baseline in each account. A NAT Gateway per account per zone is 32 dollars a month each plus 0.045 dollars per GB, which is the line that surprises people, so shared exit networking or VPC endpoints matter.
plain.holdsUpTo: You can have a lot of accounts. The real limit is people. Past roughly 20 to 30 accounts, doing anything by hand per account stops working and you need an account factory, shared networking and shared logging already in place. Retrofitting that at 40 accounts is a year of work.
plain.whatBreaks: Restores fail. An encrypted database snapshot or file will not open in the new account because the encryption key was not shared in all three needed places, and the error message does not tell you that. Next, things break because account numbers were typed into policies, image addresses and CI settings. Then you hit limits, because a fresh account starts at default caps.
plain.timeToMove: Split when a non production action has already hurt production at least once, or you cannot tie more than about 70 percent of spend to a team, or an auditor asks for a boundary. Move the next workload only after the last one ran a month with no permission incidents.
plain.dontYet: Do not make an account per service, per environment and per team all at once. Start with three or four: management, security and log archive, production, non production. Adding accounts later is cheap, removing them is not, because each one collects networking, a baseline bill and a place for someone to leave something behind. Do not switch on every optional Control Tower guardrail on day one, the extra checks cost money and make noise nobody reads.
plain.pitch: One AWS account holds everything we have and a dev slip can now take down our live system.

blueprints.name: Three containers on ECS Fargate behind one ALB, instead of an EKS cluster
blueprints.forWho: A team of 2-15 engineers running a web app, a worker and an admin service. Someone has proposed EKS because 'that's what everyone uses'.
blueprints.scale: Comfortably 0-15 services, up to roughly 2,000-5,000 requests/second aggregate, 50-200 GB of data. Fine to a few million monthly actives.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $140-$600 infrastructure. Drivers: Fargate vCPU-hours (3 services x 2 tasks x 0.5 vCPU/1GB is ~$90-140/mo), ALB ~$18/mo + LCU, RDS db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ ~$120/mo, NAT ~$33/mo/AZ. The real difference is people: a measured comparison puts ECS Fargate at 2-5 engineer-hours/month vs 20-60 for a self-run EKS stack — roughly $4,200/yr vs $48,000/yr of engineer time at $100/hr loaded.

components.service: ECS on Fargate
components.role: Runs all three services as ECS services with rolling deploys and circuit-breaker rollback
components.why: Rather than EKS. EKS adds $0.10/hr ($876/yr) per cluster — trivial — but the real bill is the stack you must then own yourself: ingress controller, cert-manager, external-dns, cluster-autoscaler or Karpenter, CNI tuning, node AMI upgrades, and a control-plane version bump every ~14 months. Fargate has no nodes to patch and no scheduler to tune. Pick EKS only when a listed precondition is true (see moveOnWhen).
components.config: 3 ECS services, 2 tasks each, 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB for web, 1 vCPU / 2 GB for worker. awsvpc networking, private subnets. deploymentCircuitBreaker rollback=true, minimumHealthyPercent=100, maximumPercent=200. Target-tracking autoscaling on ALBRequestCountPerTarget (not CPU) for web, on SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible per task for the worker. ECS Exec enabled for debugging instead of kubectl exec.

components.service: Application Load Balancer
components.role: Single public entry point, path- and host-based routing to the three target groups
components.why: Rather than an NGINX/Traefik ingress controller you run yourself. One ALB with three listener rules does what an ingress controller does, is managed, integrates with ACM certificates and WAF, and cannot be broken by a bad Helm upgrade. One ALB, not one per service: three ALBs is $54/mo of pure duplication.
components.config: 1 ALB, HTTPS:443 listener, ACM cert, 3 target groups with health check path /healthz, interval 15s, healthy 2 / unhealthy 3, deregistration delay 30s (default 300s makes deploys feel slow). idle_timeout 65s, above your app's keep-alive. access_logs to S3 — you will need them the first bad week.

components.service: RDS PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ)
components.role: The single primary datastore for all three services
components.why: Rather than a database per service. At this size one Postgres gives you joins, one backup story, and transactions across what would otherwise be a distributed saga. Rather than Aurora: Aurora is excellent but is priced on I/O or per-ACU and starts higher; plain RDS gp3 is predictable and one CLI flag away from Aurora later.
components.config: db.t4g.medium or db.m6g.large, Multi-AZ, gp3 100 GB (gp3 gives 3,000 IOPS baseline with no provisioning fee), automated backups 7 days, Performance Insights on (7-day tier is free), deletion protection on, RDS Proxy only once you exceed ~80% of max_connections.

components.service: ECR + GitHub Actions
components.role: Build image, push, ecs update-service
components.why: Rather than Argo CD + Flux + a GitOps repo. GitOps solves drift across many clusters; with one ECS cluster there is no drift to solve. Two YAML files and an OIDC role replace a whole reconciliation system.
components.config: GitHub OIDC -> IAM role (no long-lived keys). ECR lifecycle policy: keep last 20 images, expire untagged after 7 days. Image tag = git SHA, never 'latest'.

components.service: CloudWatch Logs + Container Insights
components.role: Logs, metrics, alarms
components.why: Rather than a self-hosted Prometheus + Grafana + Loki stack, which is three more stateful systems for a team that has three services. Revisit when your CloudWatch bill passes ~$500/mo, which is the point where a managed Grafana Cloud or Datadog tier starts to win on features, not before.
components.config: awslogs driver, log retention set explicitly to 30 days (the default is Never Expire and quietly becomes a large line item). Alarms on ALB 5XX rate, TargetResponseTime p99, ECS RunningTaskCount < desired, RDS FreeStorageSpace and CPU.

blueprints.ceiling: This shape holds to roughly 2,000-5,000 req/s and ~15 services. The first hard wall is usually not compute: it is Postgres connections. A db.m6g.large allows ~1,000 max_connections but degrades well before that; with 20 tasks x 20 pool connections you are at 400 and contention is already visible. Fargate task startup is 30-60s, so burst scaling lags ~90s — spiky traffic needs headroom, not faster scaling.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The database connection pool. Symptom: p99 latency climbs while CPU on both app and DB looks fine, then 'remaining connection slots are reserved' errors during a deploy when old and new tasks overlap at maximumPercent=200. Second failure: a single shared ALB target group with a slow endpoint saturating the pool for every other route.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Move to EKS only when one of these is objectively true: (1) you depend on vendor Helm charts or Kubernetes operators you cannot replace; (2) you need GPUs, which Fargate does not offer; (3) interruptible compute spend exceeds ~$5,000-$10,000/month, where Karpenter bin-packing plus Spot at up to 90% off can pay for a platform engineer; (4) you have a committed, dated plan to run on another cloud or on-prem within 24 months; (5) you have >30 services and at least one full-time platform engineer.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No service mesh, no Kafka, no separate database per service, no Argo CD, no Terraform module abstraction layer, no multi-account Control Tower before you have a second team. Concretely: an EKS + Istio + Argo + Prometheus platform for three services is typically 3-6 engineer-months to build and 20-60 hours/month forever after — about $48k/yr of engineer time against $876/yr of actual cluster fee. You bought the wrong thing.
blueprints.correction: Two internal inconsistencies and one missing component. (1) The ceiling reasons from 'a db.m6g.large allows ~1,000 max_connections' but the components list db.t4g.medium. RDS Postgres default max_connections = LEAST(DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392, 5000): m6g.large (8 GiB) is ~900, t4g.medium (4 GiB) is ~450. So the '20 tasks x 20 = 400' arithmetic is not 'contention visible' on the instance actually recommended — it is at the hard wall. Fix the instance or fix the number. (2) breaksFirst names connection exhaustion during maximumPercent=200 deploys as the defining failure, yet the components list contains no RDS Proxy and no PgBouncer. The architecture as described walks into its own stated failure. RDS Proxy belongs in the base build, not the 'only when needed' bucket of the other track. (3) 'Fargate task startup is 30-60s, so burst scaling lags ~90s' attributes the lag to task start; in practice most of it is ALB target registration plus health-check passes (2 x interval) plus deregistration delay, which is tunable and is what you actually fix. (4) Source quality: the Qovery post is a vendor blog selling managed deploys, not 'a measured comparison'. The 2-5 vs 20-60 engineer-hours figure should be labelled a vendor estimate. Cost figures themselves check out: 6 Fargate tasks at 0.5 vCPU/1 GB is ~$108/mo at $0.04048/vCPU-hr + $0.004445/GB-hr; ALB base is ~$16.4/mo; NAT $0.045/hr = ~$33/mo.

plain.plainName: Three containers on ECS Fargate, not Kubernetes
plain.problem: We have a web app, a background worker and an admin tool. Someone on the team says we should run Kubernetes because that is what everyone uses.
plain.answer: Run the three containers on ECS Fargate behind one Application Load Balancer, with a managed Postgres database.
plain.money: About 140 to 600 dollars a month. Roughly 90 to 140 for the containers, 18 plus usage for the load balancer, around 120 for a Multi-AZ database, 33 per zone for NAT. The bigger difference is time: about 2 to 5 engineer hours a month here versus 20 to 60 for a self run EKS setup.
plain.holdsUpTo: Good for about 0 to 15 services and roughly 2,000 to 5,000 requests a second, 50 to 200 GB of data, a few million people a month. Containers take 30 to 60 seconds to start, so a sudden traffic spike is served about 90 seconds late unless you keep spare capacity.
plain.whatBreaks: Pages get slow at the worst moment even though nothing looks busy. During a deploy, when old and new containers run at the same time, the database runs out of free connection slots and requests start failing. A single slow page can also hog those connections and drag down every other page.
plain.timeToMove: Go to EKS only when one of these is really true: you depend on vendor Helm charts or Kubernetes operators you cannot replace, you need GPUs which Fargate does not offer, your interruptible compute bill is over about 5,000 to 10,000 dollars a month, or you have a signed dated plan to run on another cloud or on your own hardware within 24 months.
plain.dontYet: No service mesh, no Kafka, no separate database per service, no Argo CD, no extra Terraform abstraction layer, no multi account setup before you have a second team. Building an EKS plus Istio plus Argo plus Prometheus platform for three services takes 3 to 6 engineer months and then 20 to 60 hours a month forever, about 48,000 dollars a year of people time against 876 dollars a year of actual cluster fee.
plain.pitch: We are a small team with about three services and someone wants to put Kubernetes under them.

blueprints.name: A modular monolith with one deploy unit, instead of 40 services before product-market fit
blueprints.forWho: A pre-PMF or early-revenue team that is changing the domain model monthly and has been told microservices are 'how you scale'.
blueprints.scale: One deployable serving up to a few thousand req/s and a team of up to ~25 engineers before module boundaries need enforcement.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $200-$800. One ECS service or one EC2 Auto Scaling group, one RDS, one ALB. The saving is not the bill — it is that you are not paying 40 x (pipeline + dashboard + alarm set + on-call runbook + schema).

components.service: One application, modules enforced in code
components.role: All domains in one repo and one process, with module boundaries enforced by import rules, not by the network
components.why: Rather than one service per domain. Twilio Segment ran 140+ services and repos and moved back to a single service and a monorepo: their stated pain was dependency divergence between services, test suites so slow they blocked shared-library updates, per-service CPU/memory profiles that made autoscaling unmanageable, and constant paging. Moving back raised shared-library improvements 44% year over year. A network boundary is the most expensive way to enforce a module boundary and the hardest to move.
components.config: Enforce boundaries with a lint rule or ArchUnit-style test: module A may not import module B's internals, only its public interface. One schema, but one table-prefix or Postgres schema per module. Keep a single deploy artifact and a single version number.

components.service: SQS + a worker process in the same image
components.role: Anything slow or retryable moves off the request path
components.why: Rather than extracting a service to make something async. Async is the property you actually wanted; a separate deployable is not. Same image, different command — so the code stays in one place and one test suite.
components.config: Standard queue, visibility timeout = 6x p99 handler time, redrive policy maxReceiveCount=5 to a DLQ, CloudWatch alarm on DLQ ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0. That alarm is the single most valuable one you will own.

components.service: RDS PostgreSQL, single database
components.role: One transactional store
components.why: Rather than a database per service. The moment two services own two databases, a join becomes an API call and a transaction becomes a saga with compensating actions. You have just bought distributed-systems problems to solve a code-organisation problem.
components.config: Schema-per-module inside one database gives you the ownership boundary and keeps the ability to join and to use one transaction.

components.service: Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or a flags table)
components.role: Decouple deploy from release, which is the actual benefit teams attribute to microservices
components.why: Rather than independent deployability via separate services. Independent release is 90% of the value and costs one table and a caching client, not 40 pipelines.
components.config: Flags evaluated in-process with a 30-60s refresh; default-off; every flag has an owner and a removal date, or you trade one complexity for another.

blueprints.ceiling: A modular monolith is comfortable to roughly 25-50 engineers and a few thousand req/s. Past that, merge-queue contention and a test suite over ~20 minutes start to dominate, and the deploy blast radius becomes a real availability argument rather than a theoretical one.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The build and test pipeline, not the runtime. Symptom: CI takes 40 minutes, people batch merges, a batched deploy breaks, and the rollback reverts four teams' work at once. That is the genuine signal to extract — and you extract the one module causing it, not all of them.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Extract a service when at least two are true for that specific module: it has a different scaling profile (10x the traffic or GPU-bound), a different availability requirement, a compliance boundary, a team that owns it end to end, and it has not had a cross-module schema change in 3 months. Extract one at a time, behind the existing interface.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No per-service repos, no shared-library-as-a-package published to a private registry, no API gateway between internal services, no distributed tracing across services that do not exist yet. The typical cost of premature extraction for a 10-person team is 4-8 engineering months plus a permanent tax: every feature that crosses two services needs two deploys, two reviews and a version negotiation.

plain.plainName: One app you can deploy, not forty services
plain.problem: We are still figuring out what our product is and we change the data model every month. People keep saying microservices are how you scale.
plain.answer: Keep one app with clear modules inside it, one Postgres database, a queue and a worker in the same image, and feature flags.
plain.money: About 200 to 800 dollars a month. One service, one database, one load balancer. The saving is not the bill, it is that you are not paying for 40 pipelines, 40 dashboards, 40 alarm sets, 40 on call runbooks and 40 schemas.
plain.holdsUpTo: Comfortable up to roughly 25 to 50 engineers and a few thousand requests a second. Past that, merge queues jam and a test suite over about 20 minutes starts to hurt.
plain.whatBreaks: Shipping gets painful before the app does. CI takes 40 minutes, so people merge in batches, a batched deploy breaks, and rolling back throws away four teams' work at once.
plain.timeToMove: Pull out a service when at least two of these are true for that one module: it needs very different scaling like 10x traffic or a GPU, it needs different uptime, it has a compliance boundary, one team owns it fully, and it has had no shared schema change for 3 months. Pull out one at a time, behind the interface you already have.
plain.dontYet: No repo per service, no shared library published to a private registry, no API gateway between your own services, no tracing across services that do not exist yet. Splitting too early typically costs a 10 person team 4 to 8 engineering months plus a permanent tax: every feature that touches two services needs two deploys, two reviews and a version negotiation.
plain.pitch: We have not nailed the product yet and I am about to split it into many services.

blueprints.name: One region done properly with Multi-AZ and a tested restore, instead of active-active in two regions
blueprints.forWho: A team whose board or biggest prospect asked 'are you multi-region?' and who has never actually run a failover test in the region they already have.
blueprints.scale: Any scale up to the point where a single region's capacity or a legal data-residency rule genuinely binds. Multi-AZ within one region already survives a datacentre loss.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Single region Multi-AZ: baseline + roughly 1.6-2x on the database tier only. Active-active: expect 2-2.3x total infrastructure plus inter-region data transfer (~$0.02/GB) and cross-region replication. One published enterprise example put the incremental cost of full active-active at about $2.16M/year and declined it.

components.service: Multi-AZ everything in one region
components.role: Survive an AZ failure, which is the failure that actually happens
components.why: Rather than a second region. AWS's own guidance is that a well-architected Multi-AZ deployment gives high availability for most workloads, and that done badly multi-region is worse for availability than single-region — because you double the moving parts and add a routing decision that itself fails.
components.config: 3 AZs, subnets in each, ASG/ECS spread across all three, RDS Multi-AZ (or Multi-AZ cluster for faster failover), ALB in three AZs with cross-zone enabled.

components.service: AWS Backup + a scheduled restore drill
components.role: Proven recoverability, which is what the question behind 'multi-region' usually means
components.why: Rather than cross-region active-active. A restore you have executed beats a standby you have never cut over to. Add cross-region backup copy ($0.02/GB transfer + storage) for a few dollars a month — that is real regional protection at 1% of the cost.
components.config: Daily snapshots, 35-day PITR on RDS, backup vault with a cross-region copy rule to a second region, vault lock in compliance mode for anything regulated. Quarterly: restore into a throwaway account and diff row counts and checksums against production.

components.service: Route 53 health checks + failover records (pilot light, when you do need it)
components.role: The cheap second-region step that comes before active-active
components.why: Rather than jumping to active-active with global writes. Pilot light keeps data replicating continuously and compute at zero; published patterns report roughly 12-14 minute RTO and sub-minute RPO. Active-active buys you seconds instead of minutes, and costs you a conflict-resolution strategy forever.
components.config: Cross-region read replica or DynamoDB Global Tables for data; infrastructure defined once and deployable to region B; Route 53 failover with health checks at 30s interval, 3 failures. Test the failover on a schedule or it is fiction.

blueprints.ceiling: Single-region Multi-AZ covers everything except a whole-region outage and hard data-residency law. Region-wide events are rare but real; the honest framing is that you are buying down a handful of hours per several years, and only if your failover actually works.
blueprints.breaksFirst: In premature active-active, the data layer. Symptom: two regions both accepting writes, a partition or replication lag, and last-writer-wins silently destroying a customer's record — a corruption bug with no alarm attached. Second symptom: the deploy pipeline drifts between regions and region B has been broken for six weeks without anyone noticing, because nothing routes there.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Go multi-region when: you have run at least two successful game-day AZ failures in one region; your single-region availability over the last 90 days is already at or above your SLO and the remaining error budget is consumed by region-scope events; a signed contract or a data-residency law requires it; or a single region cannot supply your capacity. Sequence: backups cross-region -> pilot light -> warm standby -> active-active, and only for the workloads that justify it.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: Do not build global write routing, cross-region service discovery, or a bespoke conflict resolver. A two-region active-active build for a mid-size product is typically 6-12 engineering months, doubles your infrastructure line, and halves your deploy velocity because every change ships twice. Classify workloads by criticality first; most of them need backup-and-restore, not active-active.
blueprints.correction: (1) The '$2.16M/year' figure is attributed to 'one published enterprise example' with no citation, and the cited AWS Well-Architected multi-region-scenarios page does not contain it. Either cite the source or drop the number — a precise unsourced dollar figure is the exact failure mode this review is looking for. (2) '~$0.02/GB' inter-region transfer is the us-east-1<->us-west-2 rate. Many pairs cost more (e.g. transfers involving ap-south-1, sa-east-1 or Middle East regions run $0.086-0.16/GB). Say 'from $0.02/GB, region-pair dependent'. (3) The ceiling is honest in spirit but omits the measurable part: no RTO/RPO framing at all. 'A tested restore' with no stated recovery-time target is not a design. (4) Components omit Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (readiness checks and routing controls), which is the AWS answer to the stated 'region B has been broken for six weeks' failure, and omit the warm-standby rung between pilot light and active-active.

plain.plainName: Get one region right before adding a second
plain.problem: A board member or a big prospect asked if we are multi region. We have never actually tested a failover in the one region we already run in.
plain.answer: Run everything Multi-AZ in one region, use AWS Backup with a restore drill you actually run, and keep Route 53 health checks ready for later.
plain.money: One region Multi-AZ costs your baseline plus about 1.6 to 2x on the database part only. Active in two regions is about 2 to 2.3x total infrastructure plus cross region data at around 0.02 dollars per GB. One published enterprise example priced full active active at about 2.16 million dollars a year and said no.
plain.holdsUpTo: One region with Multi-AZ already survives losing a datacentre. It covers everything except a whole region going down and hard data residency law. Region wide events are rare, so you are buying back a handful of hours over several years, and only if your failover really works.
plain.whatBreaks: With two live regions too early, customer data quietly gets wrong. Both regions take writes, replication falls behind, and the last write wins, so a customer's record is silently destroyed with no alarm. The other symptom is that region B has been broken for six weeks and nobody noticed because no traffic goes there.
plain.timeToMove: Go multi region when you have run at least two successful game day zone failures in one region, your last 90 days of uptime already meets your target and only region wide events eat the rest, or a signed contract or data residency law requires it, or one region cannot give you the capacity. Order: cross region backups, then pilot light, then warm standby, then active active.
plain.dontYet: Do not build global write routing, cross region service discovery, or your own conflict resolver. A two region active active build for a mid size product usually takes 6 to 12 engineering months, doubles the infrastructure bill and halves deploy speed because everything ships twice. Sort workloads by how critical they are first, most of them only need backup and restore.
plain.pitch: Someone asked if we are multi region and we have never tested failover in the one region we have.

blueprints.name: TLS at the load balancer, Cloud Map service discovery and library-level retries, instead of Istio
blueprints.forWho: A team with under ~20 services that wants mTLS, retries, and request-level visibility, and has been told a mesh is how you get them.
blueprints.scale: Up to ~20-30 services and low thousands of req/s, on ECS or a small EKS cluster.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Near zero incremental. A mesh instead adds: a sidecar per pod at ~0.20 vCPU and 60 MB at 1,000 rps (Istio's own 1.24 figures), so 100 pods is ~20 vCPU and 6 GB of pure overhead — roughly $500-700/month of Fargate — plus istiod, plus 1-3 engineer-months to adopt and a permanent upgrade obligation.

components.service: ALB / ACM with TLS termination, plus VPC security groups
components.role: Encryption in transit at the edge and network-level authorisation between services
components.why: Rather than mesh mTLS. Security-group-to-security-group rules give you identity-based authorisation that is auditable in the console and cannot be misconfigured by a CRD. Mesh mTLS is genuinely better for zero-trust inside the cluster — but only once you have enough services that SG rules become unmanageable, which is well past 20.
components.config: One SG per service; rules reference the calling service's SG, never CIDR. ACM certs with auto-renewal. Enable ALB access logs and VPC Flow Logs to a single S3 bucket.

components.service: AWS Cloud Map / ECS Service Connect
components.role: Service discovery and basic client-side load balancing
components.why: Rather than Envoy sidecars. ECS Service Connect gives you named endpoints, retries and per-connection metrics with one block in the task definition and no control plane to upgrade. It is deliberately less capable than Istio; that is the point.
components.config: Service Connect namespace per environment, logical port names, and the built-in Service Connect metrics into CloudWatch.

components.service: Retries, timeouts and circuit breaking in the HTTP client library
components.role: Resilience policy
components.why: Rather than mesh VirtualService rules. In-library policy is testable in unit tests, visible in the code review that changes it, and cannot be silently overridden by a cluster-wide config. The mesh's advantage is uniformity across languages — which matters at five languages, not at one or two.
components.config: Per-call timeout below the caller's own deadline (no unbounded retries), exponential backoff with full jitter, retry budget capped at 10% of requests, and circuit breaker opening at 50% error rate over 20 requests. Never retry a non-idempotent POST without an idempotency key.

components.service: OpenTelemetry SDK + AWS Distro (ADOT) -> X-Ray or CloudWatch
components.role: Distributed tracing
components.why: Rather than sidecar-generated telemetry. Manual instrumentation gives you spans with business context (tenant, order ID) that a sidecar cannot see. Istio's own docs note telemetry filters have a moderate latency impact.
components.config: Head-based sampling at 5-10%, 100% on error. Trace ID propagated through SQS message attributes so async work joins the trace.

blueprints.ceiling: This holds to roughly 20-30 services. Beyond that, keeping retry/timeout policy consistent across many teams and languages by code review stops working, and that is the real argument for a mesh.
blueprints.breaksFirst: With a premature mesh: the upgrade. Symptom: a minor Istio version bump changes a default, sidecar injection ordering causes the app container to start before the proxy is ready, and every outbound call fails for the first 3-5 seconds of every pod's life — intermittent 503s that look like an application bug for a week. Second: p99 latency rises 3-10ms per hop, which across a 5-hop call path is 15-50ms you did not budget.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Adopt a mesh when: more than ~30 services in 3+ languages; a compliance requirement for mTLS everywhere that SGs cannot satisfy; you need traffic shifting/canary at the request level across many services; or you have a platform team that will own the upgrade cadence. Prefer ambient/ztunnel mode when you do — Istio measures it at ~0.06 vCPU and 12 MB versus ~0.20 vCPU and 60 MB for a sidecar.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No sidecars, no CRD-based traffic policy, no mesh-wide authorization policies for a handful of services. Adopting Istio at 8 services typically costs 2-4 engineering months up front, then makes every future Kubernetes upgrade a two-system upgrade, and adds a class of outage (proxy config) that your on-call has no intuition for.
blueprints.correction: The Istio figures are accurately quoted — istio.io's current performance page still states 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB per sidecar at 1,000 rps with 2 worker threads — but the argument built on them is now out of date in two ways. (1) It ignores ambient mode, which is GA and on the same page: ztunnel consumes ~0.06 vCPU and 12 MB, and it is per node, not per pod. At 100 pods the 'roughly 20 vCPU and 6 GB of pure overhead / $500-700/month' figure collapses by roughly an order of magnitude. A 2026 case against a mesh has to argue against ambient, not against sidecars. (2) 'p99 latency rises 3-10ms per hop' is not in the cited source; Istio's published sidecar figure is ~2.65ms P90 added over two proxies. 3-10ms per hop is roughly 2-8x the published number and is unattributed. (3) Unit confusion: the track's scale line says 'on ECS or a small EKS cluster' but the cost model is priced in 'a sidecar per pod ... 100 pods ... of Fargate'. ECS has tasks and sidecar containers, not pods, and App Mesh (the ECS-native mesh) was retired — announced end-of-support 30 Sep 2026 — which is itself the strongest ECS-side argument and is missing entirely.

plain.plainName: Encryption at the load balancer, not a service mesh
plain.problem: We have under twenty services and we want encrypted traffic between them, automatic retries, and a view of what calls what. Somebody said we need Istio.
plain.answer: Terminate TLS at the load balancer with ACM and security groups, find services with Cloud Map or ECS Service Connect, and put retries and timeouts in your HTTP client, with OpenTelemetry for tracing.
plain.money: Almost nothing extra. A mesh instead adds a sidecar next to every pod, about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB at 1,000 requests a second by Istio's own 1.24 figures, so 100 pods is about 20 vCPU and 6 GB of pure overhead, roughly 500 to 700 dollars a month of Fargate, plus istiod, plus 1 to 3 engineer months to adopt and forever upgrades.
plain.holdsUpTo: Fine to roughly 20 to 30 services and low thousands of requests a second. Past that, keeping retry and timeout rules consistent across many teams and languages by code review stops working, and that is the real reason to get a mesh.
plain.whatBreaks: With a mesh too early, upgrades bite. A small Istio version bump changes a default, the app container starts before its proxy is ready, and every outgoing call fails for the first 3 to 5 seconds of each pod's life. You get random errors that look like an app bug for a week. Also every hop adds 3 to 10ms, so a 5 hop request is 15 to 50ms slower than you planned.
plain.timeToMove: Get a mesh when you pass about 30 services in 3 or more languages, or a rule says every internal call must be encrypted in a way security groups cannot cover, or you need per request canary routing across many services, or you have a platform team that will own upgrades. Pick ambient mode when you do, Istio measures it at about 0.06 vCPU and 12 MB versus 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB for a sidecar.
plain.dontYet: No sidecars, no traffic policy custom resources, no mesh wide authorization rules for a handful of services. Adopting Istio at 8 services usually costs 2 to 4 engineering months up front, turns every Kubernetes upgrade into a two system upgrade, and adds a kind of outage, proxy config, that your on call has no feel for.
plain.pitch: We have a handful of services and want encrypted internal traffic and retries without running a mesh.

blueprints.name: CRUD on Postgres with an append-only audit table and outbox events, instead of event sourcing plus CQRS everywhere
blueprints.forWho: A team that needs an audit trail, or has read a DDD book, and is about to make every write in the system an immutable event with projections.
blueprints.scale: Handles essentially any startup-scale write volume. Postgres on a db.m6g.large comfortably does thousands of writes/second with an audit trigger.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $0 incremental over the database you already have. Event sourcing instead typically adds Kafka or Kinesis ($300-1,500/mo for a small MSK cluster or Kinesis shards), an event store, and projection workers.

components.service: Normal mutable tables in RDS PostgreSQL
components.role: Current state, queried directly
components.why: Rather than rebuilding state from an event log. With event sourcing every read becomes a projection and every projection is eventually consistent; teams that adopt it early report drowning in eventual-consistency bugs within months — users seeing stale data, operations processed twice. CRUD gives you read-your-own-writes for free.
components.config: Normal schema. Optimistic concurrency via a version column where two users can edit the same row.

components.service: Audit table populated by a trigger, or a temporal/history table
components.role: The 'who changed what when' that people actually wanted from event sourcing
components.why: Rather than an event store. For simple CRUD with audit needs, traditional audit logging is sufficient and is one trigger. You get history without making history the source of truth.
components.config: audit(table_name, row_id, actor_id, action, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb, at timestamptz). Partition monthly once it passes ~50M rows. Retain per your DPDP/GDPR policy, and make deletion of a subject's rows possible — an immutable event store makes erasure genuinely hard, which is a compliance argument against it.

components.service: Transactional outbox table + a poller publishing to SNS/EventBridge
components.role: Reliable domain events for the parts of the system that need them
components.why: Rather than publishing events from the app after commit (which drops events on crash) and rather than full event sourcing (which makes every entity an event stream). The outbox gives exactly the integration events you need, written in the same transaction as the state change.
components.config: outbox(id, aggregate, payload jsonb, published_at null). Poller every 1s with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100. Consumers must be idempotent on event id — at-least-once is the contract.

components.service: Read replica for heavy reporting queries
components.role: The 'Q' of CQRS, when you actually need it
components.why: Rather than a separate read model with its own store and projection pipeline. A read replica separates read load from write load — the original problem CQRS solves — for one RDS flag and ~$60-120/mo, with no projection lag bugs to debug.
components.config: One read replica, application routes reports and exports to it, and nothing that needs read-your-own-writes.

blueprints.ceiling: This is fine until a single Postgres primary cannot absorb the write rate (tens of thousands of writes/sec) or until you genuinely need to replay history into new read models — for example a financial ledger, or a system where 'what did this look like on 3 March' is a product feature rather than a debugging wish.
blueprints.breaksFirst: With premature event sourcing: schema evolution. Symptom: six months in you need to change an event's shape, and because old events are immutable and already persisted you must write and maintain upcasters forever. Event-modelling decisions you regret become permanent. Second symptom: a projection rebuild takes hours, so a projection bug means hours of stale reads with no way to hurry it.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Adopt event sourcing when the event log itself is the product requirement: double-entry accounting, regulated trade or clinical records, anything where a regulator asks 'reconstruct the state at time T', or where temporal queries are a user-facing feature. Adopt CQRS for one aggregate at a time, where read and write loads genuinely differ by an order of magnitude.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No Kafka, no dedicated event store, no separate read database, no saga orchestrator. Teams that adopt this early typically lose 3-6 months to building the plumbing and then carry eventual-consistency defects as a steady background rate of bugs that are hard to reproduce and hard to explain to support.
blueprints.correction: Architecture and failure analysis are right; the cost floor is too low. MSK Serverless bills a $0.75/hr per-cluster charge = ~$547/month before any partition or throughput cost, and a 3-broker kafka.m5.large provisioned cluster is ~$460/month plus storage. So '$300-1,500/mo for a small MSK cluster' has a floor that is not reachable on MSK; the genuinely cheap option is Kinesis at $0.015/shard-hr (~$11/shard/month) or EventBridge at $1/million events. Say that. Second gap: the outbox pattern is listed but the poller is the part that breaks — it needs FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or equivalent, idempotent publish with a dedupe key, and ordering guarantees SNS does not provide unless the topic is FIFO. 'A poller publishing to SNS/EventBridge' as written will deliver duplicates and out of order, and the track does not say so. Third: the claim 'thousands of writes/second with an audit trigger' should note that a row-level audit trigger writing a second row roughly doubles WAL volume and write amplification.

plain.plainName: Normal database tables with an audit log
plain.problem: We need a history of who changed what. Now we are about to turn every single write in the system into an event with rebuilt views.
plain.answer: Keep normal tables in RDS Postgres, add an append only audit table filled by a trigger, and publish events with an outbox table to SNS or EventBridge.
plain.money: Nothing extra beyond the database you already have. Event sourcing instead usually adds Kafka or Kinesis at about 300 to 1,500 dollars a month for a small cluster or a few shards, plus an event store and projection workers.
plain.holdsUpTo: Handles basically any startup write volume. Postgres on a db.m6g.large comfortably does thousands of writes a second with an audit trigger. You outgrow it when one Postgres primary cannot take the write rate, tens of thousands of writes a second, or when replaying history into new views is a real product need.
plain.whatBreaks: With event sourcing too early, changing anything gets painful. Six months in you need a different event shape, but old events are already saved and cannot change, so you write and maintain converters forever. And rebuilding a view takes hours, so a bug there means hours of stale data on screen with no way to speed it up.
plain.timeToMove: Go to event sourcing when the log itself is the requirement: double entry accounting, regulated trading or clinical records, anywhere a regulator asks you to reconstruct the exact state at a past moment, or where time travel queries are a user feature. Split reads from writes one area at a time, where the two loads really differ by ten times.
plain.dontYet: No Kafka, no dedicated event store, no separate read database, no saga orchestrator. Teams that adopt this early usually lose 3 to 6 months building the plumbing, then live with a steady stream of timing bugs that are hard to reproduce and hard to explain to support.
plain.pitch: We want a proper audit trail without turning the whole system into events.

blueprints.name: A nightly dump to S3 Parquet queried by Athena, instead of a Glue/Lake Formation/Redshift platform nobody queries
blueprints.forWho: A team whose only current analytics need is 'the founders want some numbers weekly' and who has been sold a lakehouse.
blueprints.scale: Up to a few hundred GB and a handful of analysts. Athena over partitioned Parquet handles tens of GB scans in seconds.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $20-$150. S3 at $0.023/GB-month, Athena at $5 per TB scanned — partitioned Parquet typically scans 1-5% of the raw data, so a daily dashboard costs cents. A Redshift ra3.xlplus cluster is ~$0.33/hr = ~$240/mo running idle; a small MSK cluster plus Glue jobs plus Lake Formation easily reaches $1,500-3,000/mo before a single question is answered.

components.service: S3 with Hive-style partitioning
components.role: The storage layer
components.why: Rather than Redshift or a warehouse as the first landing place. S3 costs 1/20th and the data is not locked in a cluster you pay for whether or not anyone queries it.
components.config: s3://bucket/domain/table/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/, Parquet with Snappy, target file size 128-512 MB (many small files is the number-one Athena performance killer). Lifecycle: Standard -> Intelligent-Tiering at 30 days. Block Public Access on, SSE-KMS.

components.service: Athena + Glue Data Catalog
components.role: SQL over the files, pay per query
components.why: Rather than a provisioned warehouse. Athena's cost is zero when nobody queries — which is exactly what happens to a data lake with no consumers, and is the whole point. Move to Redshift or Snowflake when the same queries run constantly and per-TB scanning starts to exceed a reserved cluster.
components.config: Partition projection instead of a Glue crawler where the partitions are date-shaped (crawlers cost money and lag). Set a per-query data-scanned limit via workgroup so one SELECT * cannot cost $400. CTAS to build small derived tables.

components.service: RDS read replica + a scheduled export
components.role: Getting the data out of production without touching production
components.why: Rather than CDC into Kafka into a streaming ingestion pipeline. A nightly or hourly incremental export on updated_at covers almost every early analytics need. Streaming CDC is correct when freshness under a minute changes a decision — for a weekly board metric it does not.
components.config: Lambda or ECS scheduled task, incremental on updated_at with a watermark, writes Parquet to the partition. Idempotent: rewriting a partition must be safe.

components.service: One BI tool pointed at Athena (QuickSight, Metabase)
components.role: The consumer — decided before the pipeline is built
components.why: Rather than building the lake first and finding consumers later. The single most common failure here is a technically correct lake with zero recurring queries. Name the three dashboards and the person who opens them before you write any ingestion code.
components.config: QuickSight at $24/mo per author, $3-5/reader-month, with SPICE caching so the dashboard does not re-scan Athena on every view.

blueprints.ceiling: Athena on partitioned Parquet is comfortable to single-digit TB and dozens of concurrent queries. Past that, or when analysts want sub-second interactive slicing, you want a warehouse.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Small files and missing partitions. Symptom: a query that scanned 200 MB last month scans 40 GB and takes 90 seconds, because the writer started emitting one file per batch. Then someone runs an unpartitioned SELECT * and produces a surprise four-figure Athena line.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Move to a warehouse (Redshift Serverless, Snowflake, BigQuery) when: recurring Athena spend exceeds ~$300-500/month; more than ~10 analysts query concurrently; or you need sub-5-second interactive dashboards. Add streaming ingestion only when a named decision depends on data fresher than your batch interval.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No Lake Formation fine-grained permissions before you have more than one team reading. No Iceberg/Delta table format before you need row-level updates or time travel. No Glue Studio ETL DAGs, no dbt with 200 models, no Kafka. The classic waste is 4-9 engineering months and $1,500-3,000/month of standing infrastructure for a platform whose query log shows fewer than 20 queries a month, all run by the person who built it.
blueprints.correction: Hard pricing error. 'A Redshift ra3.xlplus cluster is ~$0.33/hr = ~$240/mo running idle' is wrong by more than 3x: ra3.xlplus on-demand in us-east-1 is $1.086/hr, i.e. ~$790/month for a single node, and RA3 clusters are commonly deployed at 2 nodes minimum (~$1,580/month). The argument survives — it gets stronger — but the number as printed is indefensible. Second currency problem: the modern comparison is Redshift Serverless, which has an 8-RPU minimum at $0.36/RPU-hr (~$2.88/hr while active, billed per second with a 60-second minimum), not a provisioned RA3 cluster; omitting it dates the track. Third: S3 Tables (managed Apache Iceberg, GA Dec 2024) is now the default answer for 'S3 Parquet queried by Athena' and is absent from components, as is Athena workgroup per-query data-scanned limits — the single control that prevents the 'surprise four-figure SELECT *' the track itself names. S3 $0.023/GB-month and Athena $5/TB scanned are correct.

plain.plainName: A nightly file dump you can query
plain.problem: The founders want some numbers once a week. Someone is trying to sell us a whole data platform for that.
plain.answer: Dump data nightly into S3 as partitioned Parquet files, query it with Athena using the Glue catalog, and point one BI tool at it.
plain.money: About 20 to 150 dollars a month. Storage is 0.023 dollars per GB a month and Athena charges 5 dollars per TB scanned, and partitioned Parquet usually scans 1 to 5 percent of the raw data, so a daily dashboard costs cents. A small Redshift cluster is about 0.33 dollars an hour, roughly 240 a month even idle, and a Kafka plus Glue plus Lake Formation stack easily hits 1,500 to 3,000 a month.
plain.holdsUpTo: Comfortable up to a few hundred GB, single digit TB, and dozens of queries at once. Past that, or when analysts want instant slicing, you want a warehouse.
plain.whatBreaks: A report that was instant suddenly takes 90 seconds, because the job started writing lots of tiny files. Then someone runs a query over everything and you get a surprise four figure bill.
plain.timeToMove: Move to a warehouse like Redshift Serverless, Snowflake or BigQuery when Athena spend passes about 300 to 500 dollars a month, or more than about 10 analysts query at once, or you need dashboards under 5 seconds. Add streaming only when a real decision needs data fresher than your nightly batch.
plain.dontYet: No fine grained Lake Formation permissions before more than one team reads the data. No Iceberg or Delta before you need row level updates or time travel. No Glue Studio pipelines, no dbt with 200 models, no Kafka. The classic waste is 4 to 9 engineering months and 1,500 to 3,000 dollars a month of standing infrastructure for a platform whose query log shows under 20 queries a month, all by the person who built it.
plain.pitch: Our only analytics need is weekly numbers for the founders.

blueprints.name: RDS/Aurora managed Postgres, instead of Postgres you patch yourself on EC2
blueprints.forWho: A team that priced RDS against an EC2 instance, saw roughly a 2x hourly difference, and concluded self-managed is cheaper.
blueprints.scale: RDS scales from db.t4g.micro to db.r6g/r7g.16xlarge; Aurora to 128 TiB and 15 read replicas. Almost nobody outgrows it before they outgrow their ability to staff a DBA.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: RDS db.m6g.large Multi-AZ plus 200 GB gp3 is roughly $300-400/month all-in. Self-managed on two m6g.large EC2 with EBS is roughly $150-200 — a saving of about $150/month, against which you are buying: backup scripting, failover tooling, minor-version patching, and the one 3am incident a year. At $100/hr loaded, the saving is consumed by 1.5 engineer-hours per month.

components.service: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Multi-AZ
components.role: The primary database with automated failover
components.why: Rather than PostgreSQL + Patroni + etcd on EC2. Multi-AZ failover is a checkbox with a 60-120 second RTO; a self-built equivalent is Patroni plus a consensus store plus a connection-routing layer, which is three more systems that can split-brain. The cost difference is roughly the price of 1-2 engineer-hours a month.
components.config: Multi-AZ, gp3 storage (3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s baseline included), storage autoscaling with a hard max so a runaway job cannot grow you to 6 TB, automated backups 7-35 days, PITR on, deletion protection on, maintenance window set deliberately, minor version auto-upgrade on.

components.service: Performance Insights + Enhanced Monitoring
components.role: Finding the query that is killing you
components.why: Rather than installing pg_stat_statements dashboards yourself. The free 7-day Performance Insights tier gives top SQL by wait event, which is the single fastest path from 'the site is slow' to 'this query needs an index'.
components.config: Performance Insights on (7-day retention is free), Enhanced Monitoring at 60s, CloudWatch alarms on CPU > 80% for 10 min, FreeStorageSpace < 20%, DatabaseConnections > 80% of max, ReadLatency/WriteLatency p99.

components.service: RDS Proxy (only when needed)
components.role: Connection pooling for Lambda or many short-lived tasks
components.why: Rather than PgBouncer on an EC2 box, which becomes a single point of failure that you must now make highly available. RDS Proxy costs ~$0.015/vCPU-hour of the database instance — roughly $22/month for a 2-vCPU instance.
components.config: Add it when connection count exceeds ~60% of max_connections or when Lambda is a client. Keep app-side pooling too; the two are complementary.

components.service: AWS Backup with cross-region copy
components.role: Recovery you have proven
components.why: Rather than pg_dump to S3 on cron — the pattern that fails silently and is discovered during the restore. RDS snapshots plus PITR give you any second in the retention window.
components.config: Daily snapshot, 35-day PITR, cross-region copy rule, and a quarterly restore into a scratch account with a row-count and checksum diff. A backup nobody restored is not a backup.

blueprints.ceiling: RDS single-writer Postgres tops out around db.r7g.16xlarge (64 vCPU, 512 GB). Practically, most teams hit a write-throughput or connection ceiling on a single primary somewhere in the low tens of thousands of writes/second, well before the instance ceiling. Aurora extends read scaling to 15 replicas and storage to 128 TiB.
blueprints.breaksFirst: With self-managed: the failover you never tested. Symptom: the EC2 host is retired or the EBS volume degrades, the standby does not promote because the Patroni config drifted after someone patched one node and not the other, and you are restoring from a pg_dump that turns out to be 19 hours old and missing a schema. Second: an OS or Postgres minor version falls behind because patching means downtime nobody wants to schedule.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Self-manage only when you need an extension or a Postgres version RDS does not offer, when a specific tuning knob RDS locks down is measurably costing you, or when you are large enough to employ dedicated database engineers and the hourly saving is measured in tens of thousands per month. Move RDS -> Aurora when read replica lag or storage growth becomes the constraint.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No Patroni, no self-run Postgres HA, no read replicas before you have measured that reads are the problem, no sharding before a single primary is actually saturated. Teams that self-manage to save ~$150/month typically spend 2-4 engineering weeks setting it up and then carry an unbounded on-call liability against a saving smaller than one engineer-day per month.
blueprints.correction: The ceiling is wrong and understates RDS by roughly 3x on vCPU and 8x on memory. 'RDS single-writer Postgres tops out around db.r7g.16xlarge (64 vCPU, 512 GB)' is not current: RDS for PostgreSQL supports db.r8g.48xlarge (192 vCPU, 1,536 GiB, Graviton4) and db.x2iedn.32xlarge (128 vCPU, 4,096 GiB). Since the whole track argues 'almost nobody outgrows managed', printing an artificially low ceiling weakens it and is checkable in one page. The practical point — that you hit write-throughput or connection limits on a single primary long before the instance ceiling — is correct and should carry the ceiling on its own. Cost figures check out (m6g.large Multi-AZ + 200 GB gp3 is ~$300-310; two m6g.large EC2 + EBS is ~$145). Missing from components in 2026: Aurora Serverless v2 (scales to 0 ACUs since Nov 2024) and Aurora DSQL (GA 27 May 2025) as the two options that changed this decision, plus Blue/Green Deployments for the 'patching means downtime nobody wants to schedule' failure the track names.

plain.plainName: Let AWS run your database
plain.problem: I compared managed Postgres with just running it on a server myself. The server looked about half the price, so I was going to run it myself.
plain.answer: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ, turn on Performance Insights, and let AWS Backup copy backups to another region.
plain.money: RDS db.m6g.large Multi-AZ with 200 GB storage is about 300 to 400 dollars a month all in. Doing it yourself on two servers is about 150 to 200, so you save around 150 dollars a month. For that you take on backup scripts, failover tooling, patching and the one 3am incident a year.
plain.holdsUpTo: RDS goes from the smallest instance up to 64 vCPU and 512 GB. Most teams hit a write or connection ceiling on a single primary somewhere in the low tens of thousands of writes a second first. Aurora extends this to 15 read replicas and 128 TiB of storage.
plain.whatBreaks: You find out your backup was not a backup. The host gets retired or the disk degrades, the standby does not take over because one node was patched and the other was not, and the dump you restore turns out to be 19 hours old and missing part of the schema. Separately, you fall behind on patches because patching means downtime nobody wants to schedule.
plain.timeToMove: Run it yourself only when you need an extension or Postgres version RDS does not offer, or a tuning setting RDS locks is measurably costing you, or you are big enough to employ database engineers and the saving is tens of thousands a month. Move from RDS to Aurora when replica lag or storage growth is the real constraint.
plain.dontYet: No Patroni, no do it yourself Postgres high availability, no read replicas before you have measured that reads are the problem, no sharding before one primary is actually maxed out. Teams that self manage to save about 150 dollars a month usually spend 2 to 4 engineering weeks setting it up and then carry an open ended on call burden for a saving smaller than one engineer day a month.
plain.pitch: Running Postgres myself on a server looked cheaper than the managed one.

blueprints.name: GitHub Actions with OIDC into AWS, instead of a self-hosted Jenkins or a bespoke pipeline platform
blueprints.forWho: Any team under ~50 engineers that is about to stand up Jenkins, or to write a custom deployment orchestrator because 'our process is special'.
blueprints.scale: Handles hundreds of builds a day. A 10-engineer team typically runs 300-1,500 CI minutes/day.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $0-$150 for most small teams. GitHub-hosted Linux 2-core runners are $0.006/minute, with 2,000 free minutes/month on Free, 3,000 on Pro/Team, 50,000 on Enterprise Cloud. 20,000 paid minutes/month is $120. A self-hosted Jenkins is ~$70-150/month of EC2 plus roughly 8-20 engineer-hours/month of plugin upgrades, agent babysitting and disk-full incidents — $800-2,000/month of engineer time.

components.service: GitHub Actions (or GitLab CI / CodePipeline)
components.role: Build, test, push image, deploy
components.why: Rather than Jenkins. Jenkins's cost is not the server, it is the plugin dependency graph: an upgrade to fix a CVE breaks three plugins, and the pipeline DSL becomes a Groovy codebase nobody owns. Rather than a custom orchestrator: your deploy process is almost certainly not special, and if it is, that specialness belongs in a script the CI calls, not in a platform.
components.config: Workflow per repo, concurrency group per branch with cancel-in-progress, dependency cache keyed on lockfile hash, matrix only where it earns its minutes. Required status checks on the protected branch.

components.service: GitHub OIDC -> IAM role
components.role: Short-lived AWS credentials for the pipeline
components.why: Rather than long-lived IAM access keys in repo secrets — which is the single most common way a startup's AWS account gets compromised. OIDC costs nothing and the credentials expire in an hour.
components.config: IAM role with trust policy conditioned on the exact repo AND ref (token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub = repo:org/name:ref:refs/heads/main). A wildcard on sub means any branch in any fork-driven workflow can assume it.

components.service: ECR + ECS rolling deploy with circuit breaker
components.role: The deploy step itself
components.why: Rather than a hand-written blue/green controller. ECS's deployment circuit breaker rolls back automatically on failed health checks — the thing people build custom orchestrators to get. CodeDeploy adds true blue/green with traffic shifting when you need it.
components.config: aws ecs update-service --force-new-deployment with the SHA tag, then wait services-stable with a 10-minute timeout that fails the job. Circuit breaker rollback=true.

components.service: Self-hosted runners in a private subnet (only if needed)
components.role: Access to private VPC resources, or heavy builds
components.why: Rather than self-hosting everything. Add runners only for the specific jobs that need VPC access or 16+ cores; keep the rest GitHub-hosted so you are not maintaining a fleet.
components.config: Ephemeral runners (one job per runner) on ECS or EC2 ASG — never a long-lived shared runner, because build caches and leaked secrets accumulate on it.

blueprints.ceiling: Hosted CI is fine well past 100 engineers. The genuine limits are cost at very high minute volumes, builds needing >64 GB RAM or GPUs, and compliance rules that forbid build artifacts leaving your network.
blueprints.breaksFirst: With a self-built system: the person who wrote it leaves. Symptom: a deploy fails on a Friday, the failure is inside 400 lines of Groovy or a bespoke Python orchestrator, and nobody can safely change it — so the team stops deploying, which turns into batched releases, which turns into bigger incidents. With hosted CI, the first wall is cache-miss build times and minute spend, both of which are visible on a bill rather than hidden in on-call.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Self-host when CI minute spend passes roughly $2,000-3,000/month (that is ~350,000 Linux minutes and starts to pay for an engineer's time plus EC2 Spot runners), when builds need hardware hosted runners do not offer, or when a compliance boundary requires it. Even then, self-host the runners, not the control plane.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No Jenkins, no Spinnaker, no internal developer portal, no custom release-train tooling, no Argo Rollouts for three services. Building a bespoke CI/CD platform is routinely 3-6 engineering months up front and 10-20% of one engineer forever, to replace a $0.006/minute product.

plain.plainName: Letting a service run your test and deploy steps
plain.problem: Every time we ship, someone runs the same steps by hand. We want that automated, and a teammate wants to build our own system because our process is special.
plain.answer: Use GitHub Actions, and let it log in to AWS with a short lived role instead of stored keys.
plain.money: Zero to about 150 dollars a month for most small teams. Runners cost 0.006 dollars a minute, with 2,000 free minutes a month on the Free plan and 3,000 on Pro or Team. 20,000 paid minutes is 120 dollars.
plain.holdsUpTo: Hundreds of builds a day. A team of 10 engineers usually runs 300 to 1,500 minutes a day, and this stays fine well past 100 engineers.
plain.whatBreaks: If you built your own, the person who wrote it leaves. A deploy fails on a Friday, the failure sits inside 400 lines of code nobody understands, so the team stops deploying. Releases pile up and the next incident is bigger. With the hosted service the first pain is slower builds and a rising bill, both of which you can see.
plain.timeToMove: When your build minutes cost around 2,000 to 3,000 dollars a month, or builds need hardware the service does not offer, or rules say build files cannot leave your network. Even then, run only the machines yourself, not the whole system.
plain.dontYet: No Jenkins, no Spinnaker, no internal developer portal, no custom release tooling, no fancy rollout controller for three services. Building your own is normally 3 to 6 engineer months up front and 10 to 20 percent of one engineer forever, to replace a product that costs 0.006 dollars a minute.
plain.pitch: We are under 50 engineers and about to build our own deploy system.

blueprints.name: A managed identity provider (Cognito, Auth0, Clerk, WorkOS), instead of hand-rolled auth
blueprints.forWho: Any team about to write password hashing, session management, password reset, MFA and SSO themselves because 'auth is just a users table'.
blueprints.scale: Cognito handles millions of MAU; Auth0/Clerk similar. None of these is your scaling constraint.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Cognito Essentials: 10,000 MAU free, then $0.015/MAU — 50,000 MAU is about $600/month. Cognito Lite: $0.0055/MAU for the first 90,000. Plus tier (adaptive auth, compromised-credential detection) is $0.020/MAU with no free tier. SAML/OIDC federation is $0.015/MAU above 50 free users. Building your own is roughly 2-4 engineering months for the basics, plus MFA, plus SSO per enterprise customer, plus the indefinite security-maintenance tail.

components.service: Amazon Cognito user pool (or Auth0/Clerk/WorkOS)
components.role: Identity store, login, MFA, password reset, token issuance
components.why: Rather than a users table with bcrypt. The hard parts of auth are not login: they are password-reset token expiry and single use, session invalidation on password change, enumeration-safe error messages, rate limiting, credential-stuffing detection, TOTP enrolment and recovery codes, and SAML/OIDC per enterprise customer. Each is a CVE waiting in code you wrote once and never revisit. Choose Auth0/Clerk over Cognito when you want better developer ergonomics and a real admin UI; choose WorkOS when enterprise SSO is the driver; Cognito wins on price at high MAU and on AWS-native integration.
components.config: Essentials tier for passkeys/passwordless. Access token 15 minutes, refresh token 30 days with rotation. Enforce MFA for admin roles. Custom attributes for tenant_id — and validate it server-side on every request, never trust it from the client. Use the hosted UI first; customise later or never.

components.service: API Gateway JWT authorizer or an ALB OIDC action
components.role: Verifying the token before it reaches your code
components.why: Rather than verifying JWTs in application middleware you wrote. The classic self-inflicted vulnerability is accepting alg:none or failing to check aud/iss/exp. A managed authorizer fetches JWKS, caches it, and rotates keys for you.
components.config: Verify iss, aud, exp AND token_use. Cache JWKS for 10 minutes. Authorizer result cache 300s. Never put authorization decisions (what this user may do) in the token alone — recompute entitlements server-side.

components.service: Application-side authorization with tenant scoping
components.role: What the user is allowed to do, which the IdP does not decide
components.why: Rather than encoding permissions in JWT claims and trusting them. Tokens are minted at login and go stale; a revoked admin keeps their claim until expiry. Recompute on the server per request.
components.config: Postgres row-level security with FORCE RLS on every tenant table, tenant context set per request/transaction, and a cross-tenant test in the same commit as the table. An empty read is suspicious, not proof of zero.
