blueprints.ceiling: Managed IdPs are not usually the ceiling. Cognito's real limits are customisation of the hosted UI, migration friction (passwords cannot be exported — you migrate lazily on next login), and per-MAU cost at very high consumer scale.
blueprints.breaksFirst: With hand-rolled auth: the password-reset flow. Symptom: reset tokens are guessable, or not single-use, or do not expire, and you find out from a security researcher or a customer. Second: session fixation after password change. Third, and most expensive commercially: an enterprise deal stalls for a quarter because you cannot deliver SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, which a managed provider ships as configuration.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Build your own only when you have a genuinely unusual identity model no provider supports, when per-MAU cost at your consumer scale exceeds an engineer's salary (millions of MAU), or when regulation requires credentials never leave your infrastructure. Even then, use a vetted library for the primitives; never write your own password hashing or token format.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No custom session store, no bespoke RBAC engine before you have more than three roles, no multi-tenant auth abstraction before your second tenant type exists, no self-hosted Keycloak (that is running your own auth system with extra steps and an upgrade cadence). Hand-rolled auth costs 2-4 months to build and then a permanent obligation to track every new attack class.

plain.plainName: Letting someone else handle logins and passwords
plain.problem: People need accounts on our app. Someone said it is just a users table with a password column, so we were going to write it ourselves.
plain.answer: Use a ready made login service like Cognito, Auth0, Clerk or WorkOS, and keep your own code only for who is allowed to do what.
plain.money: Cognito gives 10,000 monthly active users free, then 0.015 dollars per user, so 50,000 users is about 600 dollars a month. The cheaper Lite tier is 0.0055 per user for the first 90,000. Company logins cost 0.015 per user above 50 free users.
plain.holdsUpTo: Millions of monthly users. Logins will not be the thing that runs out.
plain.whatBreaks: With your own login code, password reset goes wrong first. Reset links turn out to be guessable, or reusable, or never expire, and you hear it from a stranger or a customer. Next, changing a password does not actually kick out the old session. The most costly one is a big customer deal stalling for three months because you cannot offer company sign in, which the ready made services turn on with a setting.
plain.timeToMove: Only when your identity model is truly unusual, or per user cost beats an engineer's salary at millions of users, or a regulator says passwords may never leave your systems. Even then use a trusted library and never write your own password hashing.
plain.dontYet: No custom session store, no home made permission engine before you have more than three roles, no multi customer login layer before the second kind of customer exists, no self hosted Keycloak, which is running your own login system with extra steps. Writing your own takes 2 to 4 months and then a permanent job of tracking every new attack.
plain.pitch: We need users to sign up and log in, and we were about to write that ourselves.

blueprints.name: One cloud, with portability kept where it is cheap, instead of multi-cloud as a strategy
blueprints.forWho: A team hedging against vendor lock-in, or a CTO answering a board question about concentration risk, by running on two clouds.
blueprints.scale: Irrelevant to scale. This is an organisational decision that costs at every scale.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: Egress is the visible cost: cross-cloud data transfer is typically $0.05-0.09/GB, so 10 TB/month between clouds is $500-900 of pure tax. The invisible cost is larger: every capability is built to the lowest common denominator, you need expertise in two IAM models, two networking models and two monitoring stacks, and you forfeit committed-use discounts (Savings Plans / RIs at 30-70%) by splitting spend across two vendors.

components.service: One primary cloud, chosen and committed to
components.role: Everything runs here
components.why: Rather than two. Multi-cloud as insurance against a provider failing is insurance against an event that has essentially never taken the whole provider down, purchased at a premium of roughly 1.3-2x engineering effort on every project. Concentrate and take the Savings Plan discount instead.
components.config: Commit to Savings Plans/RIs once usage is stable for 3 months. A 1-year no-upfront Compute Savings Plan is typically ~27% off on-demand for zero risk if your baseline is real.

components.service: Containers + Postgres + S3-compatible object storage
components.role: The portability that is actually cheap to keep
components.why: Rather than an abstraction layer over every cloud service. Containers, standard Postgres, and S3-API object storage are portable by default and cost nothing extra. That covers 80% of most systems. Going further — abstracting queues, identity, or managed AI services — is where the price climbs steeply for portability you will probably never exercise.
components.config: Keep vendor-specific code behind a thin interface only where the vendor API is already narrow (object storage, queue publish/subscribe). Do not abstract IAM, networking or observability; those abstractions leak immediately.

components.service: A written exit plan instead of a running second cloud
components.role: The deliverable the board actually wants
components.why: Rather than live dual deployment. A documented, costed migration plan (what would move, in what order, how long, what it would cost) satisfies concentration-risk governance at the price of a week of work, versus doubling your platform surface permanently.
components.config: Name the 5 hardest-to-move dependencies, estimate each, and re-cost annually. Keep infrastructure as code and data exports working — an export you have never run is not an exit.

blueprints.ceiling: A single cloud is not the constraint for almost anyone. Real constraints that force a second cloud: a customer contractually requiring their cloud, a regulator requiring provider diversity, a specific capability only one vendor offers (certain GPU capacity, certain models), or acquisition inheritance.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Feature velocity, silently. Symptom: every proposal now includes 'and how does that work on the other cloud', so the team picks the generic option every time and ends up self-managing databases, queues and secrets that were free and managed on either cloud individually. The second failure: the second cloud's environment rots because nothing real runs there, so it would not work if you needed it.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Run on a second cloud when a signed contract requires it, when a regulator mandates provider diversity, when a needed capability exists only there (run that one workload there, not everything), or after an acquisition. Then isolate it: one workload on the second cloud, not a portability layer across all workloads.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No cross-cloud abstraction layer, no Kubernetes adopted purely for portability (portability of the scheduler is not portability of your data, IAM, or networking), no dual-writing data to two clouds. Teams that adopt multi-cloud as a strategy typically add 30-50% to delivery time on every infrastructure project and forfeit six figures a year in committed-use discounts.
blueprints.correction: (1) '$0.05-0.09/GB' is presented as a cross-cloud transfer rate but it is really AWS internet egress, which is $0.09/GB for the first 10 TB/month in us-east-1 and tiers down to $0.05/GB above 150 TB — plus the other cloud's own ingress/egress. The framing understates a 10 TB/month bill by whatever GCP or Azure charges on their side. (2) It omits that since March 2024 AWS waives data-transfer-out charges for customers fully exiting AWS (EU Data Act driven), which is directly relevant to a track whose recommended component is 'a written exit plan'. Leaving it out makes the exit look more expensive than it is and weakens the recommendation. (3) Savings Plans are 'up to 72%', not 30-70%. Minor, but it is the one number AWS states precisely.

plain.plainName: Picking one cloud and staying there
plain.problem: Our board asked what happens if our cloud provider fails us, so we are thinking of running everything on two clouds at once.
plain.answer: Run on one cloud using plain containers, Postgres and object storage, and write an exit plan instead of running a second cloud.
plain.money: Moving data between clouds costs about 0.05 to 0.09 dollars a gigabyte, so 10 terabytes a month is 500 to 900 dollars of pure waste. Teams doing this add 30 to 50 percent to every infrastructure project and give up six figures a year in volume discounts.
plain.holdsUpTo: This has nothing to do with size. One cloud is not the limit for almost anyone.
plain.whatBreaks: Your speed, quietly. Every idea now gets the question, and how does that work on the other cloud, so the team always picks the plain option and ends up running its own databases, queues and secret storage that either cloud would have handled. Then the second cloud goes stale because nothing real runs there, so it would not work on the day you needed it.
plain.timeToMove: When a signed contract demands it, when a regulator demands two providers, when something you need exists only on the other cloud, or after buying a company that is already there. Then put one workload there, not everything.
plain.dontYet: No layer that hides the difference between clouds, no Kubernetes picked only for portability, since moving the scheduler is not moving your data, permissions or network, and no writing every record to both clouds.
plain.pitch: I am worried about being stuck with one cloud provider.

blueprints.name: One NAT gateway plus VPC endpoints, instead of three NAT gateways carrying all your AWS traffic
blueprints.forWho: Anyone who ran the standard three-AZ VPC template and has a four-figure 'EC2-Other' line on their bill they cannot explain.
blueprints.scale: A NAT gateway handles up to 100 Gbps and ~55,000 concurrent connections per destination. Capacity is rarely your problem; the bill is.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: NAT gateway is $0.045/hour (~$33/month) plus $0.045 per GB processed — in every direction, including to S3 and ECR in the same region if you route that way. Three AZs = ~$99/month standing. Add 5 TB/month of traffic and you are at ~$324 of data processing on top. A busy account pulling container images and writing to S3 through NAT routinely sees $1,000-3,000/month here. Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB have no hourly and no data-processing charge at all.

components.service: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB
components.role: Keep the highest-volume AWS traffic off the NAT entirely
components.why: Rather than routing S3 traffic through NAT. Gateway endpoints are free — no hourly charge, no per-GB charge. This is the single highest-return change on most AWS bills and takes ten minutes. Rather than interface endpoints for S3: the gateway type is free, the interface type is not.
components.config: Add the gateway endpoint to every private route table. Verify with VPC Flow Logs that S3 traffic no longer traverses the NAT ENI — do not assume the route took effect.

components.service: Interface VPC endpoints for ECR (api + dkr), CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, STS
components.role: The other chronic NAT consumers
components.why: Rather than leaving them on NAT. Interface endpoints cost ~$0.01/hour per AZ (~$7.30/month per endpoint per AZ) plus ~$0.01/GB — roughly a quarter of NAT's per-GB rate. Container image pulls are the usual hidden whale: every task launch pulling a 1 GB image through NAT is $0.045 a launch, which at 500 deploys-plus-scaling-events a day is real money.
components.config: ecr.api, ecr.dkr, logs, secretsmanager, sts, plus the S3 gateway endpoint (ECR stores layers in S3 — without the S3 gateway endpoint the image pull still goes out through NAT). Private DNS enabled. Only in the AZs you actually run in.

components.service: One NAT gateway in one AZ (for dev/staging), three for production
components.role: Outbound internet for the traffic that genuinely leaves AWS
components.why: Rather than three per environment everywhere. In dev and staging, one NAT saves ~$66/month per environment and the AZ-failure risk is acceptable. In production keep one per AZ — with a single NAT, an AZ failure takes out egress for all AZs and cross-AZ data transfer ($0.01/GB each way) quietly adds to the bill. Rather than a NAT instance: a t4g.nano NAT instance is ~$3/month but is now a box you patch, a single point of failure, and a bandwidth ceiling.
components.config: Production: one NAT per AZ, private route table per AZ pointing at its local NAT (the common misconfiguration is all three route tables pointing at one NAT, which pays for three and uses one while adding cross-AZ charges). Dev/staging: one NAT, all subnets routed to it. Alarm on BytesOutToDestination to catch a runaway job.

components.service: VPC Flow Logs into an Athena table
components.role: Finding out what is actually going through the NAT
components.why: Rather than guessing from the bill. The bill says 'NAT gateway data processing'; flow logs say which ENI and which destination. Almost every time it is ECR, S3, or a chatty third-party API.
components.config: Flow logs to S3 in Parquet, partitioned by date, queried by Athena. Run this once a quarter as a cost review.

blueprints.ceiling: A single NAT gateway scales to 100 Gbps and ~55,000 simultaneous connections per unique destination — exceeding that produces ErrorPortAllocation errors, usually from a job hammering one external endpoint.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Port allocation, not bandwidth. Symptom: intermittent connection failures to one third-party API under load, with the NAT's ErrorPortAllocation metric climbing, while overall throughput looks fine. Fix by spreading across multiple NATs or reducing connection churn with keep-alive. The more common failure is financial: a monthly bill with a four-figure line nobody owns.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Add NAT gateways per-AZ when production egress is on the critical path and an AZ loss would be an outage. Consider a NAT instance fleet or egress-only architecture when NAT data processing alone passes ~$2,000/month, since at that volume the per-GB rate dominates the hourly rate.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No Transit Gateway before you have more than about three VPCs to connect (TGW is ~$0.05/attachment-hour = ~$36/month per attachment plus $0.02/GB, on top of NAT). No centralised egress VPC, no third-party firewall appliance, and no NAT in every AZ of every non-production environment. The typical waste is $800-2,500/month, running for a year before anyone reads the bill line by line.
blueprints.correction: (1) The 55,000 figure is incomplete in a way that changes the advice: AWS documents ~55,000 simultaneous connections per assigned IP address per unique destination, and a NAT gateway supports one primary plus up to seven secondary IPv4 addresses, giving ~440,000 to a single destination IP and port. The track's prescribed fix ('spread across multiple NATs') is therefore the expensive version of the real fix (add secondary IPs to the existing NAT). (2) The cost model says interface endpoints are the cure but never prices them: interface (PrivateLink) endpoints are ~$0.01/hr per endpoint per AZ plus ~$0.01/GB processed. The five endpoint types listed (ECR api, ECR dkr, Logs, Secrets Manager, STS) across 3 AZs is ~$110/month standing before any traffic — a real number that must appear next to the $99 of NAT it replaces, or the recommendation looks free and is not. (3) ECR image pulls need the S3 gateway endpoint alongside ecr.dkr, because layers are served from S3; the track lists both but does not say why, and omitting the S3 gateway endpoint is the single most common reason this setup silently keeps billing NAT data processing. (4) 'One NAT gateway in one AZ for production... three for production' — a single-AZ NAT is a cross-AZ data-transfer charge and an AZ-failure blast radius; that tradeoff is unstated.

plain.plainName: Cutting the mystery network charge on your bill
plain.problem: We followed the standard setup guide and now there is a four figure line on our AWS bill called EC2-Other that nobody can explain.
plain.answer: Run one NAT gateway and add VPC endpoints, which are private doors to S3, ECR, logs and secrets so that traffic never pays the NAT fee.
plain.money: A NAT gateway is 0.045 dollars an hour, about 33 dollars a month, plus 0.045 dollars per gigabyte moved, in both directions. Three of them is about 99 dollars a month standing, and 5 terabytes of traffic adds about 324 dollars. Typical waste is 800 to 2,500 dollars a month, often running a full year before anyone reads the bill.
plain.holdsUpTo: One gateway carries up to 100 gigabits a second and about 55,000 open connections per destination. Capacity is rarely the problem, the bill is.
plain.whatBreaks: Not speed, connections. One outside service starts failing on and off when you are busy, even though overall traffic looks normal. The more common failure is money, a big bill line nobody owns.
plain.timeToMove: Add one gateway per zone once real customer traffic depends on it and losing a zone would mean an outage. Look at other options when the per gigabyte charge alone passes about 2,000 dollars a month.
plain.dontYet: No Transit Gateway until you have more than about three networks to join, since it adds about 36 dollars a month per connection plus 0.02 dollars a gigabyte on top of NAT. No central exit network, no third party firewall box, and no NAT in every zone of your test environments.
plain.pitch: There is a big line on my AWS bill and I have no idea what it is.

blueprints.name: Indexes, connection pooling and HTTP caching first, then one cache with TTL-only invalidation
blueprints.forWho: A team that has an endpoint responding in 800ms and is about to put Redis in front of it.
blueprints.scale: A correctly indexed Postgres on db.m6g.large serves thousands of point reads/second at single-digit milliseconds. Most 'we need a cache' problems are a missing index.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $0 for indexes. ElastiCache Serverless has a minimum of ~1 GB data stored (~$0.084/GB-hr in us-east-1 for data, plus ECPU charges) — realistically $70-120/month at a small scale; cache.t4g.micro node-based is ~$12/month but single-node means data loss on failover. CloudFront is $0.085/GB for the first 10 TB with 1 TB/month free.

components.service: Database indexes and query fixes
components.role: The actual fix in most cases
components.why: Rather than a cache. A cache in front of a slow query hides the query, so it grows worse unobserved, and the first cache miss storm after a deploy hits the database with the full unoptimised load at once. Find the query with Performance Insights or pg_stat_statements, EXPLAIN it, index it. This routinely turns 800ms into 8ms and adds no invalidation surface.
components.config: Index for the actual predicate order; partial indexes for status flags; covering indexes for hot read paths. Set statement_timeout so a pathological query cannot pin a connection indefinitely.

components.service: CloudFront in front of the ALB
components.role: Cache what is genuinely public and static or near-static
components.why: Rather than serving assets from the ALB, and rather than an application cache for public content. CloudFront caching is invalidated by changing the URL (content-hashed filenames), so there is no invalidation bug to write. The crossover: CloudFront egress is $0.085/GB versus $0.09/GB direct from EC2/ALB, so it is cheaper on bytes AND faster from the first GB — there is no volume threshold to wait for. Plus 1 TB/month free.
components.config: Content-hashed asset filenames with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. HTML with max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=86400. Origin Shield if you have many edge locations hitting a small origin. Never invalidate by path as a routine operation; change the URL.

components.service: HTTP caching headers and ETags on API responses
components.role: Free caching in the client and the CDN
components.why: Rather than a server-side cache store. A 304 Not Modified costs you a cheap request and no cache-coherence problem at all. This is the tier almost everyone skips.
components.config: ETag from a content hash or a row version; honour If-None-Match. Cache-Control: private, max-age=30 on per-user data is often enough to kill a traffic spike.

components.service: ElastiCache for Redis / Valkey — one cache, TTL-only
components.role: The cache you add last, for genuinely expensive computations
components.why: Rather than write-through or explicit invalidation on every write. Explicit invalidation is where the bugs live: a write path added six months later forgets to invalidate one key, and a user sees stale data intermittently in a way nobody can reproduce. TTL-only caching is boring, bounded and self-healing — you trade a known staleness window for an entire class of bug you never have.
components.config: TTL 30-300s chosen so staleness is acceptable to the product, not to the engineer. Cache-aside only. Jittered TTLs (base ± 20%) to prevent synchronised expiry stampedes. Single-flight / request coalescing on miss so one expiry does not send 500 identical queries. Multi-AZ with automatic failover if the app cannot tolerate a cold cache — and it must tolerate a cold cache, so test with the cache flushed.

blueprints.ceiling: TTL caching in front of a healthy database carries you a long way. The wall is data that must be strictly consistent and read very heavily — inventory counts, balances, entitlements — where a 60-second stale read is a business error rather than a cosmetic one.
blueprints.breaksFirst: The cold start. Symptom: the cache node fails over or is flushed, every request misses simultaneously, and the database — which has been sized for the cached load — saturates and takes the site down. This is the thundering herd, and it is why a cache is an availability dependency, not just a speed-up. The second failure is the missed invalidation: intermittent stale data reported by one customer, unreproducible, traced weeks later to one write path.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Add the cache when a profiled, indexed query is still too slow or too expensive at your read volume, when the same expensive computation is repeated for many users, or when database CPU is above ~60% at peak and the queries are already optimised. Move from TTL to explicit invalidation only when the staleness window is a product-level problem, and then centralise every write through one function that owns invalidation.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No Redis before you have read an EXPLAIN plan. No multi-tier cache (local + Redis + CDN) — each tier multiplies the invalidation matrix. No cache warming jobs, no write-through caching, no caching of per-user data before per-user data is measurably the bottleneck. A premature cache typically costs $70-120/month plus 2-4 weeks, and pays it back in a recurring category of stale-data bugs that are expensive to diagnose.
blueprints.correction: The ElastiCache Serverless figure conflates two different engines' pricing. $0.084/GB-hour is the Valkey Serverless rate, and Valkey Serverless meters a 100 MB minimum (~$6/month floor), not ~1 GB. The 1 GB minimum belongs to Redis OSS and Memcached Serverless, which are priced at $0.125/GB-hour (~$91/month floor). The track pairs Valkey's rate with Redis OSS's minimum and arrives at '$70-120/month at a small scale' — a number that matches neither product. Since the components line already says 'Redis / Valkey', pick one. This matters for the argument, not just the arithmetic: Valkey Serverless at ~$6/month materially weakens the case for deferring a cache on cost grounds; the case has to rest on the thundering-herd availability argument, which the track already makes well and should lead with. Also: cache.t4g.micro is ~$0.016/hr = ~$12/month, correct; CloudFront $0.085/GB first 10 TB with 1 TB/month always-free, correct.

plain.plainName: Making a slow page fast without adding a cache
plain.problem: One of our pages takes 800 milliseconds to load. Someone said put Redis in front of it.
plain.answer: Add the missing database indexes first, then CloudFront and normal browser caching headers, and only then one cache that expires on a timer.
plain.money: Indexes cost nothing. A small managed cache is realistically 70 to 120 dollars a month, or about 12 dollars a month for a single tiny node, which loses its data if it restarts. CloudFront is 0.085 dollars a gigabyte for the first 10 terabytes. A cache added too early usually costs 70 to 120 dollars a month plus 2 to 4 weeks of work.
plain.holdsUpTo: A properly indexed Postgres on a mid size machine answers thousands of simple reads a second in single digit milliseconds. Most we need a cache problems are a missing index.
plain.whatBreaks: The cache restarts and every request misses at the same moment. The database was sized for the easy cached load, so it chokes and the whole site goes down. The other failure is a customer seeing old numbers now and then, which you cannot reproduce and take days to trace.
plain.timeToMove: When a query you have actually measured and indexed is still too slow, when the same heavy calculation repeats for many users, or when the database is above about 60 percent busy at peak with the queries already tidy.
plain.dontYet: No Redis before you have looked at how the database runs your query. No stacking a local cache plus Redis plus a CDN, since each layer multiplies the ways old data sticks around. No cache warming jobs and no caching per user data before you have measured that it matters.
plain.pitch: My pages feel slow and I am about to bolt a cache onto them.

blueprints.name: Flat, explicit Terraform per environment, instead of a module hierarchy nobody can read
blueprints.forWho: A team whose infrastructure repo has modules calling modules calling modules, and where changing an instance size requires editing four files and nobody can answer 'what will this actually create'.
blueprints.scale: Flat, explicit IaC works well to 3-5 environments and a few hundred resources per state file.
blueprints.monthlyCostUSD: $0 direct. The cost is velocity: in over-abstracted estates a one-line change routinely takes half a day to trace, and terraform plan output becomes unreadable so people stop reading it — which is how a plan that destroys a database gets approved.

components.service: Terraform (or CDK/Pulumi) — one state file per environment per blast-radius boundary
components.role: The whole infrastructure definition
components.why: Rather than one giant state, and rather than a module per resource. One state for everything means a 20-minute plan and a change to a Lambda risking the VPC. A module per resource means every AWS resource is wrapped in a bespoke interface that exposes 10% of its arguments, so every new requirement is a module change plus a version bump plus a consumer update.
components.config: Split states: network (rarely changes), data (databases, very rarely changes), application (changes daily). S3 backend with native state locking, versioning on, and separate keys per environment.

components.service: Copy-paste between environments, deliberately
components.role: dev/staging/prod as three explicit directories
components.why: Rather than one parameterised module with per-environment tfvars and conditionals. Three near-identical files are readable and independently changeable; a module with 40 variables and count = var.enable_x ? 1 : 0 is a programming language written in HCL. The rule of three: do not abstract until the third real occurrence, and abstract only the part that is genuinely identical. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.
components.config: envs/dev, envs/staging, envs/prod as directories with their own main.tf. Accept that prod differs — that is information, not drift.

components.service: Public, well-maintained modules where they exist
components.role: VPC, EKS, ALB — the fiddly, standard pieces
components.why: Rather than writing your own VPC module. terraform-aws-modules/vpc encodes hundreds of edge cases and is maintained by people who are not you. Use it pinned to an exact version; write your own only for genuinely company-specific composition.
components.config: Pin exact versions (= 5.x.y, not ~>). Upgrade deliberately, reading the changelog, one module at a time.

components.service: Plan output in CI as a required review artifact
components.role: The safety mechanism
components.why: Rather than trusting the abstraction. If your plan output is not human-readable, your abstraction has failed regardless of how elegant it is. This is the objective test.
components.config: terraform plan posted to the PR, apply only from the protected branch via OIDC. Block any plan containing a destroy of a stateful resource unless a reviewer explicitly acknowledges it. prevent_destroy = true lifecycle on databases and state buckets.

blueprints.ceiling: Flat explicit IaC gets awkward past roughly 5 environments or 20 near-identical accounts, where genuine duplication becomes a maintenance problem rather than a readability benefit.
blueprints.breaksFirst: Reviewability. Symptom: someone changes a default deep in a shared module, and the plan for an unrelated service shows a replacement of an RDS instance — and because plans are 900 lines of noise, it is approved. The classic follow-on is an accidental resource replacement in production that nobody predicted because the abstraction hid the causal chain. Second symptom: a module version bump that must be rolled out to 12 consumers, so it never happens and versions fragment.
blueprints.moveOnWhen: Introduce shared modules when the same composition appears a third time and has stayed identical through at least one change cycle. Introduce a generator or Terragrunt-style DRY layer only at many-account scale (10+ accounts), where you have someone whose job is the platform. Prefer explicitness over cleverness until the duplication itself is demonstrably causing bugs.
blueprints.doNotAddYet: No internal module registry before you have three consumers, no custom Terraform provider, no policy-as-code framework beyond a few tflint/checkov rules, no multi-account Control Tower landing zone for a single-team product. The recurring cost of over-abstracted IaC is that infrastructure changes move from minutes to days, and the people who understand it become a bottleneck — which is 20-40% of an engineer's time indefinitely, with no line on the AWS bill to reveal it.

plain.plainName: Keeping your infrastructure files boring and readable
plain.problem: Changing one server size means editing four files, and nobody can tell me what the change will actually create before we run it.
plain.answer: Write plain Terraform per environment, copy and paste between them on purpose, and make the plan output a required part of review.
plain.money: No direct cost. The cost is time. A one line change often takes half a day to trace, and infrastructure work slips from minutes to days, which is 20 to 40 percent of an engineer forever with nothing on the AWS bill to show it.
plain.holdsUpTo: Works well up to about 3 to 5 environments and a few hundred resources in each file. It gets awkward past 5 environments or 20 near identical accounts.
plain.whatBreaks: Review stops meaning anything. Someone changes a default buried in a shared piece, and the preview for an unrelated service says it will replace a database. The preview is 900 lines of noise, so it gets approved, and production loses something nobody expected.
plain.timeToMove: Share a piece once the same combination shows up a third time and has stayed identical through at least one round of change. Add a DRY generator layer only at 10 or more accounts, when someone's actual job is the platform.
plain.dontYet: No internal module library before three things use it, no custom Terraform provider, no policy framework beyond a few basic lint rules, and no full multi account landing zone for a single team product.
plain.pitch: Our infrastructure code is so layered that nobody can read a change any more.

procedure.question: Who uses this, and from where on the map? Name the actual humans or systems, and the countries they sit in.
procedure.whyItMatters: Every latency number, every residency constraint, and the entire question of multi-region vs single-region falls out of this one answer, and it is cheap to answer on day one and ruinous to discover on month nine. A workload for 400 internal staff in one city and a workload for anonymous consumers across three continents share almost no design DNA, even when the feature list is identical. Physics does not negotiate: Mumbai to Virginia is roughly 190-200 ms round trip on a good day, so if the users are in India and the database is in us-east-1, you have already spent your entire latency budget before writing a line of code.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Region choice and region count; whether CloudFront sits in front at all (it earns its keep for a globally spread audience mostly through TLS termination and TCP offload at the edge, not caching, which is why it beats serving directly from an ALB even for a fully dynamic API); whether you need Route 53 latency or geolocation routing; whether auth is regional or global; whether you can get away with one VPC.
procedure.badAnswers: "Everyone, globally" on a product with 50 named pilot customers — that is aspiration leaking into requirements, and it will buy you a multi-region design you cannot operate. "Just us for now" from a founder whose sales deck names three continents — the roadmap and the architecture are already diverging. "Mostly the US, plus a few in Europe" — probe the few: if any of them is a regulated European entity, GDPR has just entered the room and question 6 moves up the list. Silence about internal admin users is common and dangerous; the admin console is very often the surface with the worst latency and the widest blast radius.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, Reliability and Performance Efficiency pillars — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/welcome.html ; AWS global infrastructure and region selection — https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/

procedure.question: How many users and how many requests today — actual numbers from a log, not an estimate — and honestly how many in twelve months?
procedure.whyItMatters: Almost all premature complexity traces to a number nobody measured. The gap between 50 requests per second and 5,000 is three architectural generations, and the gap between the two numbers a team gives you (today's real figure, and the one in the board deck) tells you how much of the design is being built for a fantasy. Ask for the number from an access log, a Stripe dashboard, or a CRM export. If the system does not exist yet, ask for the number of sales conversations in flight, which is a real number about a real pipeline.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Compute shape and the entire stateless-tier decision: single ALB plus two Auto Scaling t3.medium/m7g.large instances carries a well-behaved JSON API to roughly the low thousands of requests per second before anything interesting happens, and a Lambda-per-request design becomes more expensive than always-on Fargate somewhere around 25-40 percent sustained utilisation of an equivalent container. It also determines whether the database is a single Multi-AZ RDS instance, an instance plus read replicas, or a sharded or Aurora Limitless design (which you almost certainly do not need).
procedure.badAnswers: "We need to handle a million users" with no current users — this is the single most expensive sentence in small-team architecture; it buys Kubernetes, a service mesh, Kafka and a six-month runway burn to serve 200 people. "We don't know" when the system is already live — the logs exist and nobody has looked, which tells you observability is absent and question 11 just got worse. A twelve-month number more than 100x today's without a named distribution channel is a fantasy; a number less than 3x is usually honest and should be believed. Also watch for users counted instead of requests: 10,000 registered users might be 3 requests per second or 3,000, depending entirely on question 3.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, Cost Optimization pillar (COST 5, selecting the right resources) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/cost-optimization-pillar/welcome.html ; AWS Builders' Library, "Using load shedding to avoid overload" — https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/

procedure.question: What shape is the traffic — flat, diurnal, or spiky — and is any spike predictable? Show me a week of requests per minute.
procedure.whyItMatters: Peak-to-average ratio is the number that decides whether you buy capacity or rent it. A flat workload at ratio 1.5:1 should be on Savings Plans or Reserved Instances and can be sized once. A workload that sits at 20 requests per second and hits 4,000 for ninety seconds when a marketing email goes out is a completely different animal, and the ninety seconds is where it will break. Predictability matters as much as amplitude: a predictable spike can be pre-warmed on a schedule, which is trivially cheap; an unpredictable one has to be absorbed by a queue, a cache, or shed deliberately. Scale-out is never instant — EC2 Auto Scaling realistically takes 2-5 minutes to place and health-check a new instance, and Lambda concurrency scales in bursts (1,000 immediately in most regions, then +1,000 per 10 seconds), so any spike that arrives faster than that must be absorbed, not scaled into.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Whether writes go through an SQS queue and a worker fleet rather than straight to the database (the queue turns a 4,000/s spike into a 200/s sustained drain and is the single highest-leverage piece of small-team architecture); whether you use scheduled scaling ahead of a known event; whether Fargate or Lambda beats EC2 on cost; whether you need a provisioned-concurrency floor; and whether request-level load shedding with a 429 is part of the design rather than an afterthought.
procedure.badAnswers: "It's pretty steady" from someone who has only looked at a daily or monthly graph — minute-level resolution regularly reveals a 30x peak that hourly averaging erased entirely. "We'll just autoscale" — this is a statement of faith, not a design; it ignores the 2-5 minute lag and, far more often, ignores that the database does not autoscale with the web tier, so scaling out simply moves the failure into RDS. "We send a push notification to all users at once" delivered casually — that is a self-inflicted thundering herd and it needs jitter at the source before it needs any infrastructure at all.
procedure.source: AWS Builders' Library, "Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs" — https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ ; AWS Builders' Library, "Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter" — https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/ ; Lambda scaling behaviour — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/scaling.html

procedure.question: What does one hour of this being down cost, in money? Not in adjectives — in rupees or dollars.
procedure.whyItMatters: This is the question that converts an argument about architecture into an arithmetic problem. Multi-AZ RDS roughly doubles the database bill; a warm standby in a second region roughly doubles everything. Those are justifiable if an hour of downtime costs 400,000 rupees and unjustifiable if it costs 4,000. Without this number, availability decisions are made by whoever is most anxious in the room, which is how small teams end up with active-active multi-region designs protecting a workload whose users would not notice a two-hour outage on a Sunday. The number also has a shape: downtime at 3am on a Tuesday and downtime during the Friday billing run are not the same event, and the architecture should protect the expensive window.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: The target availability tier, and therefore: single-AZ vs Multi-AZ RDS; one Availability Zone vs three; whether you keep a pilot-light or warm standby in a second region or simply restore from backup; whether deployments are rolling or blue/green; whether you buy an AWS Business Support plan (roughly the greater of 100 dollars a month or 10 percent of spend, and worth it the first time you need a 1-hour-response case on a production outage).
procedure.badAnswers: "We haven't thought about it" is the real finding, and it should stop the conversation. It means nobody has asked the business what this system is worth, which means every subsequent availability decision will be a guess wearing a number. Do not move on: make them estimate on the spot, badly, out loud — revenue per hour, staff idled, contractual penalty, churned customers. A bad number beats no number because it can be argued with. "It can never go down" is the other bad answer and it means the same thing: no one has priced it. Push back with the real cost of the next nine and watch the requirement soften. Also treat "our SLA says 99.9%" as unverified until you see whether anything is actually owed on breach — an SLA with no penalty is marketing, not a constraint.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, Reliability pillar — availability and cost of nines — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/measuring-availability.html ; AWS Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS whitepaper — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws.html

procedure.question: What does losing one hour of data cost? And is there any data where losing five minutes is unacceptable?
procedure.whyItMatters: RTO and RPO are different questions and teams reliably conflate them. A system can be down for four hours with no lasting harm and still be destroyed by losing four minutes of financial transactions. RPO is usually not uniform across the data: the ledger, the audit trail and the uploaded documents have a different tolerance from the session cache and the derived analytics table. Sorting data by RPO before designing storage is what stops you paying for the strictest tier across everything.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Backup and replication design: whether RDS automated backups (daily snapshot plus transaction logs, giving roughly 5-minute point-in-time recovery within the retention window, up to 35 days) are sufficient, or whether you need cross-region automated backup replication, an Aurora global database with sub-second typical replica lag, or synchronous write confirmation to a second store. It also determines S3 versioning and Object Lock, DynamoDB point-in-time recovery, and whether deletes in the application are soft.
procedure.badAnswers: "We have backups" — a backup nobody has restored is not a backup. Ask when the last restore test ran and how long it took; if the honest answer is never, the real RPO is unknown and the real RTO is unbounded. "Everything is in the database, it's fine" — ask about the S3 bucket of user uploads, which very often has no versioning and no lifecycle policy and is the thing that actually cannot be reconstructed. "Zero data loss" for a workload with a 500-rupee-per-hour downtime cost is an unpriced demand; synchronous cross-region durability costs latency on every single write, and the team should be made to feel that cost before agreeing to it.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Reliability pillar, Disaster Recovery objectives — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/disaster-recovery-dr-objectives.html ; Amazon RDS point-in-time recovery — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PIT.html

procedure.question: Is any of this data regulated, and under which specific regime? Personal data, health data, cardholder data, financial records — and whose law applies?
procedure.whyItMatters: Regulation is a constraint, not a feature, which means it cannot be retrofitted cheaply and it silently invalidates otherwise good designs. India's DPDP Act, GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS each impose different and sometimes contradictory obligations — data residency, breach notification windows, the right to erasure, retention minimums that directly conflict with erasure, and audit trails that must themselves be tamper-evident. The right to erasure is the one that most often breaks an architecture built without it: it means personal data cannot live in an append-only event log, an unversioned analytics warehouse and four denormalised caches unless you have a way to reach all of them.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Region selection becomes a hard constraint rather than a latency optimisation; encryption at rest and in transit stops being optional; KMS customer-managed keys vs AWS-managed keys; whether logs can contain request bodies at all; VPC endpoints instead of NAT for service traffic; how tenancy is enforced (row-level security forced at the database, not filtering in application code); data retention lifecycle rules; and whether a third-party subprocessor can be used for anything.
procedure.badAnswers: "It's just email addresses and names" — that is personal data under both GDPR and DPDP and the obligations attach immediately. "We'll get compliant later" — later means re-architecting storage, rewriting the logging layer and re-signing every customer contract. "Our customers haven't asked" — enterprise procurement will ask, in a security questionnaire, at the exact moment a deal is closing. And be alert to the inverse failure: a team asserting HIPAA or PCI scope that they are not actually in, which buys enormous cost for nothing. Make them name the specific regime and the specific data element that triggers it.
procedure.source: AWS compliance programs and shared responsibility — https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/ ; AWS Well-Architected Security pillar, data classification — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/data-classification.html

procedure.question: Is there a hard latency requirement, and for which operation specifically? Name the endpoint and the percentile.
procedure.whyItMatters: "It must be fast" is not a requirement. "The search endpoint must return in under 300 ms at p99 for users in India" is a requirement, and it is testable. Percentile matters more than the number: a p50 target is nearly free, a p99 target constrains your garbage collector, your connection pool and your cold starts, and a p99.9 target constrains your retry policy and your dependency graph. Almost always only one or two operations have a genuine latency requirement — the checkout, the autocomplete, the login — and everything else can be slow without anyone caring. Finding the one or two is what lets you spend effort precisely.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Whether a cache tier exists at all and where (ElastiCache/Valkey in front of the database only beats a well-indexed query when the working set is hot and the query is genuinely expensive — a Postgres primary-key lookup on a warm buffer cache is already sub-millisecond, so a cache in front of it adds a network hop and a cache-invalidation bug for no gain); whether Lambda is disqualified by cold starts on that path (typically 200 ms to well over 1 s for a JVM or heavy Python function, which SnapStart or provisioned concurrency mitigates at a cost); whether the database must be in the same AZ as the compute; whether synchronous calls become asynchronous.
procedure.badAnswers: "As fast as possible" — no budget, so no design. "Under 100 ms" for users on the other side of the planet — physically impossible without edge compute, and the person saying it has not done the round-trip arithmetic. "We measure average response time" — averages hide exactly the tail that users experience and that pages the on-call; ask for p99 and if the tooling cannot produce it, that is a finding about observability, not latency. Be suspicious of a latency requirement attached to a batch or reporting endpoint; it is usually a UI problem that should be solved with an async job and a progress indicator rather than with infrastructure.
procedure.source: AWS Builders' Library, "Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter" — https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/ ; Lambda SnapStart and cold-start behaviour — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/snapstart.html

procedure.question: What is the read-to-write ratio, and is a read allowed to be a few seconds stale?
procedure.whyItMatters: This is the question that decides whether scaling is easy or hard. A 100:1 read-heavy workload is a solved problem — cache it, replicate it, put it behind a CDN, and it scales almost indefinitely on commodity parts. A write-heavy or write-contended workload cannot be scaled by adding replicas at all, because every replica makes the write path more expensive, and it pushes you towards partitioning, queueing or a different data store entirely. The staleness half of the question is what unlocks the cheap solutions: if a read may be 5 seconds old, read replicas and caches are available to you; if every read must observe the immediately preceding write, they are not, and a replica will produce bugs that surface once a month and take a week to diagnose.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Whether you add RDS read replicas (and whether the application has a routing layer capable of using them, which most do not until someone builds it); whether CloudFront or ElastiCache carries the read load; whether writes need a queue; whether DynamoDB's single-digit-millisecond reads and predictable partition behaviour beat relational, and whether you can live with eventually consistent reads at half the cost of strongly consistent ones.
procedure.badAnswers: "Roughly even" — usually wrong, and usually means nobody has instrumented it; real CRUD applications are frequently 20:1 or 50:1 read-heavy and the team is leaving free scaling on the table. "Everything must be immediately consistent" asserted without a case — ask for the specific operation where a 2-second-stale read causes a real problem. Often it is exactly one flow (read-after-write on the user's own profile, or a balance check before a payment) and that one flow can be pinned to the primary while everything else reads from replicas. "We'll just scale the database" — vertical scaling ends, and it ends abruptly; note that a db.t3.medium (4 GiB) allows only about 450 Postgres connections under the default LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392},5000) formula, and an unpooled application will exhaust that long before CPU becomes the limit.
procedure.source: Amazon RDS max_connections default formula and parameter groups — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithParamGroups.html ; RDS Proxy for connection pooling — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.html ; DynamoDB read consistency — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html

procedure.question: How big does the data get, how fast does it grow, and what fraction of it is ever read after thirty days?
procedure.whyItMatters: Data volume determines storage cost, backup duration, restore duration and — the one people forget — the feasibility of schema migrations. A table with 50 million rows can be altered in a maintenance window; the same alter on 5 billion rows is a project. Growth rate matters more than current size, because it tells you when you hit the wall, and the shape of access over age tells you whether the wall is avoidable: most operational data is written once, read hard for a week and then never touched again, which means the expensive hot store only ever needs to hold a small slice of it.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Storage class and tiering (S3 Intelligent-Tiering vs explicit lifecycle rules to Standard-IA and Glacier); whether you partition tables by time and detach old partitions; whether cold data moves to S3 and is queried with Athena rather than living in RDS storage that you pay for at roughly ten times the price; the provisioned IOPS decision (gp3 gives a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s baseline free of provisioning, which covers far more workloads than people assume, and io2 is usually a symptom of a missing index rather than a genuine IO requirement); and the realistic restore time, because restoring a 4 TB snapshot is not a 5-minute operation.
procedure.badAnswers: "It's not much" with no figure — get GB and GB per month. "We keep everything forever" — that is a cost curve with no ceiling and, if question 6 turned up a regulated regime, it may also be a compliance violation, since retention minimums are not retention permissions. "We'll archive it later" — later never arrives, and the lifecycle rule costs ten minutes to write today. Watch for logs and uploaded files being excluded from the estimate; they are routinely larger than the application database and growing faster.
procedure.source: Amazon S3 storage classes and lifecycle — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html ; Amazon EBS gp3 volume performance — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/general-purpose.html

procedure.question: Who gets woken at 3am when this breaks, and what do they actually know?
procedure.whyItMatters: An architecture is not a diagram, it is a thing that has to be operated by a specific tired human at a specific bad hour. A design that exceeds the operational capability of the people who will hold the pager is a design that will fail in production regardless of its technical merit. This is the single most common reason elegant architectures collapse at small companies: a five-person team with no Kubernetes experience inherits an EKS cluster from a contractor, and the first time a node group fails to roll, nobody can diagnose it. The honest version of this question is less about seniority than about specifics: has this person ever restored a database, read a CloudWatch Logs Insights query, or interpreted a 5xx spike on an ALB target group?
procedure.answerChangesWhat: The managed-versus-self-managed line across the whole stack, which is the biggest single cost-and-risk lever available: RDS over self-managed Postgres on EC2, Fargate or ECS over EKS, SQS over self-hosted RabbitMQ, ALB over nginx you maintain. It also determines how much of the budget goes to observability rather than compute, whether runbooks are a deliverable in the same sprint as the feature, and whether the design can contain any component that requires deep expertise to recover.
procedure.badAnswers: "We'll figure it out" — there is no on-call, which means the real RTO is "whenever someone notices," which contradicts whatever was answered at question 4. Go back and reconcile the two. "The developer who built it" — a single point of failure that takes holidays and resigns; ask what happens in the week after they leave. "We have alerts" — ask what fired last month and what was done about it; if the answer is that alerts fire constantly and are ignored, there is no monitoring, only noise, and adding more will not help. And if nobody on the team has ever performed a restore, the backup strategy is unproven and question 5's answer is fiction.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Operational Excellence pillar, OPS07 operational readiness and runbooks — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/ops_ready_to_support_use_runbooks.html ; AWS Builders' Library, "Instrumenting distributed systems for operational visibility" — https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/instrumenting-distributed-systems-for-operational-visibility/

procedure.question: What is the actual monthly infrastructure budget — the number someone has already agreed to pay — and what is the ceiling before it needs a new approval?
procedure.whyItMatters: Budget is a design constraint of exactly the same kind as latency, and treating it as a footnote is how teams produce architectures that get cancelled in month three. The number must be the approved one, not the aspirational one, and it must include the things people forget: NAT Gateway (roughly 32-45 dollars a month per gateway before data-processing charges, and three gateways for three-AZ high availability is over 100 dollars before a single byte moves), cross-AZ data transfer, CloudWatch Logs ingestion (which regularly becomes a top-three line item on a chatty application), and support plan. Knowing the ceiling matters as much as knowing the number, because it tells you where the design must degrade gracefully rather than fail an approval.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Nearly everything about the first version: single NAT gateway with the accepted AZ risk versus one per AZ; whether non-production environments run at all outside business hours; Graviton instance families as the default (typically 20 percent better price-performance for the same workload, and essentially free to adopt for interpreted languages); Fargate Spot for workers; log retention set to 14 or 30 days rather than never expiring; and whether Savings Plans are bought at all, which requires question 3's answer about how flat the load is.
procedure.badAnswers: "Cost is not a concern" — it becomes one, abruptly, usually at the first finance review, and the architecture will then be cut under pressure rather than designed to a number. "As cheap as possible" paired with a 99.99 percent availability answer at question 4 — those two are incompatible and the contradiction must be surfaced now rather than discovered later. "We have credits" — credits expire, and an architecture calibrated to free capacity becomes unaffordable on the day it converts to a real bill; ask what the post-credit run rate is. No AWS Budgets alarm configured is itself the finding: without one, the first signal of a cost problem is an invoice.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Cost Optimization pillar — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/cost-optimization-pillar/welcome.html ; VPC NAT Gateway pricing — https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/ ; AWS Graviton price-performance — https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/graviton/

procedure.question: How fast must the first version be in front of real users, and what specifically must it do on that date?
procedure.whyItMatters: Time is the constraint that determines how much architecture you are permitted to have. A six-week deadline forbids anything the team has to learn first; a six-month runway permits one, at most one, significant new technology. This question also separates the deadline from the scope: a date that cannot move with a scope that cannot move is not a plan, and forcing that conversation early is more valuable than any technical decision you will make. The right posture is to ask what must be true on launch day for the launch to count, and to design exactly that, plus the seams that let the rest arrive later.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: How much is managed versus built; whether infrastructure is CDK/CloudFormation from day one (it should be — the cost is a few days and the alternative is an environment nobody can reproduce) versus hand-built; whether the first version is a monolith behind one ALB with one database, which for almost every small team it should be; and which parts get a deliberate seam — an interface, a queue boundary, a separate schema — so they can be pulled out later without a rewrite.
procedure.badAnswers: "Yesterday" — means scope has not been negotiated and quality will be the silent variable that absorbs the pressure. "No fixed date" — surprisingly dangerous, because a project with no date accretes architecture indefinitely and ships nothing; ask what event or customer the launch is tied to. "Three months, and we're also going to move to microservices" — the deadline and the migration are competing for the same weeks and one of them is going to lose; say so now. And any answer that assumes no time for testing, deployment pipelines or monitoring is really an answer about what will be missing on launch day.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Operational Excellence pillar, evolve and organisational priorities — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/operational-excellence-pillar/welcome.html ; AWS Architecture Center, modern application patterns — https://aws.amazon.com/architecture/

procedure.question: How many engineers will build and own this, and what do they already know well enough to debug under pressure?
procedure.whyItMatters: Team size sets the maximum number of moving parts the system may have, and existing skill sets the shortest path to a working system. A three-person team can genuinely operate one application, one database, one queue and one cache. It cannot operate eleven services, a service mesh and a streaming platform, no matter how correct that design is in the abstract — the arithmetic of who is awake and who has context does not work. Existing knowledge is worth more than theoretical fit: a team fluent in Postgres will build a better system on RDS Postgres than on a document store that is a marginally better shape for the data, because they will index it correctly, read the query plans, and know what a lock wait looks like.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: The number of deployable units (the honest default for a team under about eight engineers is one); the language and runtime; whether to adopt Kubernetes at all (below roughly 15-20 engineers and a handful of services, ECS on Fargate delivers most of the benefit with a fraction of the operational surface); whether infrastructure-as-code is CDK in the team's own language or Terraform; and how much of the design budget must be spent on documentation and runbooks because the knowledge is concentrated in one head.
procedure.badAnswers: "We'll hire" — design for the team you have, because hiring takes months and the new people will inherit whatever you built before they arrived. "Everyone is full-stack" — often means nobody owns the database, which is where the incidents will come from. "We want to use this project to learn X" — a legitimate desire and a terrible reason to put X on the critical path of a production system with a deadline; find a lower-stakes place to learn it. Also note when the answer names a contractor or agency: the person building it and the person who will operate it are different people, and question 10 is the one that matters, not this one.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Operational Excellence pillar, OPS07-BP01 personnel capability — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/ops_ready_to_support_personnel_capability.html ; Amazon ECS vs EKS positioning — https://aws.amazon.com/containers/

procedure.question: If this fails commercially in twelve months, what happens to it — and if it succeeds beyond plan, what is the first thing that breaks?
procedure.whyItMatters: Both branches inform the design and both are routinely skipped. The failure branch asks how much unamortised commitment you are willing to make: three-year Reserved Instances, a proprietary managed service with no export path, a data model that only one vendor can read. The success branch is a forcing function for honesty — asking the team to name the first component that breaks at 10x is the fastest way to find out whether they understand their own system. If nobody can name it, nobody has thought about capacity, and the real answer is that it will be the database, because it almost always is.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: Commitment depth (on-demand and Savings Plans with a one-year term rather than three-year RIs when the future is uncertain); portability decisions (Postgres over a proprietary dialect, containers over a vendor-specific runtime, S3-compatible access patterns) — noting that portability has a real cost and is only worth buying where the exit risk is real; data export tooling built in from the start; and which single scaling seam gets designed now (usually: the write path can be moved behind a queue, or the read path can be moved to replicas) even though it is not built now.
procedure.badAnswers: "It won't fail" — everyone says this, and the architectures that survive are the ones built by people who nevertheless answered the question. "We'd just shut it down" without knowing what the contractual data-return obligations are, especially if question 6 found a regulated regime — customers may have a legal right to their data in a usable form, and that is a feature, built in advance. On the success side, "we'd add more servers" is the answer of someone who has not identified the stateful bottleneck; press until they name the component and the number at which it goes, and if they cannot, that measurement is the first piece of work.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Cost Optimization pillar, COST 4 decommissioning resources — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/cost-optimization-pillar/cost-effective-resources.html ; AWS Savings Plans — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/what-is-savings-plans.html

procedure.question: Now say it back: given all of the above, what is the smallest system that satisfies every stated constraint — and what did we deliberately leave out, and what would adding it have cost?
procedure.whyItMatters: This is the step that converts fourteen answers into a design, and it is the step that prevents premature complexity, which is the most expensive mistake small teams make. The deliverable is two lists of equal weight: what is being built, and what is explicitly not being built yet, each exclusion paired with the trigger that would change the decision. An exclusion without a trigger is procrastination; an exclusion with a trigger is architecture. Writing this down also makes the next architect's job possible, because they inherit the reasoning and not just the result.
procedure.answerChangesWhat: The actual build list, and — equally — the documented not-yet list with its triggers. Typical entries for a small team: no Kubernetes until there are more than about ten independently deployed services or a dedicated platform person (EKS is roughly 73 dollars a month for the control plane before a single node, and the real cost is the weeks of learning and the 3am unknowns); no microservices until team ownership boundaries genuinely conflict inside one repository (the distributed monolith costs you network failures between things that used to be function calls, and distributed transactions you did not have); no multi-region until question 4 produced a downtime cost that justifies roughly doubling the bill and permanently doubling the operational surface; no Kafka until SQS or Kinesis demonstrably cannot carry the ordering or replay requirement (MSK starts in the hundreds of dollars a month and requires someone who understands partitions, consumer groups and rebalancing at 3am); no service mesh below roughly 20 services; no separate caching tier until a specific measured query proves it is needed; no custom autoscaling logic until target-tracking has been observed to fail.
procedure.badAnswers: A design that contains a component nobody can trace back to a specific answer above is a design containing someone's resume. A not-yet list that is empty means the exercise was not done. And an answer that claims all fifteen constraints are satisfiable simultaneously deserves one more pass: usually budget and availability, or deadline and scope, are in genuine conflict, and the architect's job at this point is to name the conflict precisely and hand the trade-off back to whoever owns the money — not to quietly resolve it with optimism.
procedure.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework overview and trade-offs — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html ; Amazon EKS pricing — https://aws.amazon.com/eks/pricing/ ; AWS Architecture Center reference architectures — https://aws.amazon.com/architecture/

missing: tier-starter: Backup and restore that is actually proven: RDS automated backup retention defaults (7 days in console, 1 day via some API/CLI paths), a stated RPO/RTO, and a restore drill to a throwaway instance. The components list says 'Backups + a proven restore' but defines none of it.

tier-starter: Single-AZ consequences stated honestly: a single-AZ RDS instance is unavailable for several minutes during every maintenance window, minor-version auto-upgrade and storage-scaling event, and is unrecoverable if the AZ is lost. Writing 'SINGLE-AZ' without naming the downtime it buys is the hand-waving the track otherwise avoids.

tier-starter: Network posture: nothing says the database must be non-public (RDS 'Publicly accessible: No' plus a security group scoped to the app's SG) — the most common starter-tier breach. Nor that moving Fargate/EC2 into private subnets adds a NAT Gateway at ~$32/mo plus $0.045/GB, which breaks the stated budget.

tier-starter: IAM and deploy identity: GitHub Actions OIDC is named for the static site with no least-privilege scope (repo/branch-scoped trust policy, s3:PutObject limited to the bucket, cloudfront:CreateInvalidation only), and the dynamic tier has no deploy identity story at all.

tier-starter: Cost guardrails: no AWS Budgets alert, no Cost Anomaly Detection, and no explicit CloudWatch log-group retention setting — despite the entry naming 'Never Expire' log retention as its third-most-common failure. Naming a failure without prescribing the one-line fix is a gap.

tier-starter: DDoS and bot exposure: CloudFront bills traffic you did not want. No mention of AWS WAF (~$5/month per web ACL plus per-rule and per-request charges), rate-based rules, or what Shield Standard does and does not cover. For the brochure tier this is the realistic path to a surprise bill.

tier-starter: Static-site correctness details the architecture needs to actually work: CloudFront default root object, custom error responses mapping 403/404 to /index.html for client-side routing, and the split cache policy (immutable hashed assets on long max-age, index.html on no-cache) — which is the actual fix for the cache-busting failure the entry describes but never prescribes.
tier-starter: Security response headers: no HSTS, CSP or X-Content-Type-Options via a CloudFront response headers policy, and no minimum TLS protocol version on the viewer certificate.

tier-starter: Region and data residency: every number is us-east-1, with no guidance on choosing a region for latency or for Indian/EU residency obligations. ap-south-1 prices differ and carries a lower default RDS instance quota (20 vs 40).

tier-starter: The migration trigger: ceilings are defined but no named next step — which signal (CPUCreditBalance trending to zero, connection waits, deploy downtime) maps to which change (non-burstable instance, Multi-AZ, second instance behind the ALB, RDS Proxy) and at what cost. Without it the ceiling is a wall, not a ramp.

tier-starter: Environments: no staging/production separation, no schema-migration procedure, and no rollback story for a bad deploy (S3 versioning for the static site; ECS canary rollback, which Express Mode actually enables by default via its faulty-deployment alarm — an asset the track never mentions).

tier-starter: Observability specifics: '5 alarms' names a count, not the alarms. The five the entry's own failure analysis implies are DatabaseConnections against max, CPUCreditBalance, 5xx rate, FreeStorageSpace, and CloudFront CacheHitRate — plus a CloudWatch Synthetics canary at ~$0.0012/run.

tier-starter: Secrets handling beyond storage: Secrets Manager is priced but with no rotation, no note that SSM Parameter Store SecureString is free at standard tier, and no requirement that the app read the secret at runtime rather than baking it into an image or task-definition environment variable.

tier-starter: Aurora Serverless v2 as considered-and-rejected: its floor is now 0 ACUs with auto-pause, which changes the small-app calculus. The track should say why db.t4g still wins here rather than leaving readers to assume it was never considered.
tier-growing: HTTPS at all: ACM certificate, ALB HTTPS listener, HTTP->HTTPS redirect, Route 53 hosted zone and health checks. Not mentioned in any tier.
tier-growing: Security group topology (ALB SG -> app SG -> DB SG, no 0.0.0.0/0 on the DB), and IMDSv2 required on the launch template.

tier-growing: ASG health check type ELB + grace period, connection draining / deregistration delay, and lifecycle hooks. The track's own 'instances are not sick, they are blocked' story is unresolvable without these.

tier-growing: Database schema migration strategy in CI/CD: expand/contract, who runs migrations when N instances boot simultaneously, and how a rollback works when the schema moved forward. Completely absent, and it is the single most common cause of a failed deploy at these tiers.
tier-growing: RDS Blue/Green Deployments for engine upgrades and schema changes — the current AWS answer for the above, unmentioned.

tier-growing: Backup specifics: automated backup retention window, PITR, whether backups are copied to a second region or a separate account, and backup storage cost beyond 100% of allocated storage. 'Backups you have restored' is a slogan with no mechanism (AWS Backup, vault lock, restore-test plan).

tier-growing: RTO/RPO stated as numbers, and an explicit answer to 'what happens if the region goes away' — even if the answer is 'we accept multi-hour recovery from snapshot', it must be written down.

tier-growing: Parameter groups: the track leans on max_connections and buffer cache behaviour but never mentions that these live in a custom DB parameter group that must exist before you need it (changing some parameters requires a reboot).

tier-growing: Cross-AZ data transfer economics ($0.01/GB each direction) — affects the single-NAT design, app-to-DB traffic when the writer fails over to the other AZ, and ElastiCache replica reads in tier 2.

tier-growing: VPC endpoints beyond S3/DynamoDB: interface endpoints for Secrets Manager, SSM, ECR (api + dkr), CloudWatch Logs, STS. Tier 2 runs Fargate, which pulls every image through NAT unless ECR endpoints exist — this is the actual fix for the 'NAT is a surprise line item' complaint the track repeats twice.
tier-growing: WAF on the ALB/CloudFront, and a rate-limit rule. At 'the first enterprise customer' this becomes a contractual requirement, not an option.
tier-growing: GuardDuty, Security Hub and AWS Config enabled org-wide with a delegated admin account — tier 3 discusses account separation without any detective controls.
tier-growing: Secrets ROTATION, not just storage. Secrets Manager is listed; rotation lambdas, and how the app picks up a rotated credential without a restart, are not.

tier-growing: Autoscaling policy detail: tier 1 says 'auto scaling group' with no scaling metric. Request-count-per-target or ALB target response time, not CPU, is the right signal for this shape — and scaling on CPU is precisely what produces the 'scale the app tier, make it worse' failure the track describes.

tier-growing: SQS worker autoscaling on backlog-per-task (queue depth / tasks, targeting a latency budget) — tier 2 cites the Builders' Library queue-backlog article but never gives the metric math that article implies.

tier-growing: ECS Fargate specifics tier 2 assumes: deployment circuit breaker, minimumHealthyPercent/maximumPercent, task-level ephemeral storage, ECS Exec for debugging, awsvpc ENI limits and subnet IP exhaustion, and Fargate platform version pinning.
tier-growing: Session/state placement: where sessions, file uploads in progress, and sticky state live once instances are cattle. Implied by ElastiCache in tier 2, never stated in tier 1.
tier-growing: Idempotency and exactly-once semantics for the SQS path, visibility timeout vs worker runtime, DLQ redrive procedure and an alarm on DLQ depth > 0.

tier-growing: Cache correctness in tier 2 beyond stampede: invalidation strategy, what happens to the cache on ElastiCache failover (cold cache thundering herd onto the primary), and whether the system can serve at all with the cache down.

tier-growing: Read-replica routing discipline: which endpoints are safe to read-after-write from, and how a developer knows. The track names stale-replica reads as a failure mode but gives no mechanism to prevent it (no replica-lag-aware routing, no GTID/LSN wait).

tier-growing: Observability specifics: the actual alarm set with thresholds (ALB 5xx, TargetResponseTime p99, UnHealthyHostCount, DatabaseConnections vs max_connections, ReplicaLag, BurstBalance/credit balance, DLQ depth, NAT PacketsDropCount), plus structured logs, a trace ID propagated end to end, and CloudWatch Logs retention + Infrequent Access log class to control the cost the track flags.

tier-growing: Service Quotas as a per-account concern in tier 3 — splitting into accounts resets quotas per account, and a production account with default EC2/ENI/Fargate quotas is a launch-day outage.

tier-growing: Tier 3 account baseline as code: who provisions the VPC/NAT/endpoints/roles in each new account (Terraform/CDK/AFT), and tagging + cost allocation policy. 'Budget 1-2 weeks' is stated without naming the artifact produced.
tier-growing: Resource Control Policies (RCPs) and centralized root access management in tier 3 — see the verdict above.

tier-growing: Cost controls as mechanism, not estimate: AWS Budgets with actions, Cost Anomaly Detection, and the Savings Plan commitment review cadence. The track quotes Savings Plan prices in every tier without saying who owns the commitment or what happens when the fleet shrinks below it.

tier-growing: An explicit 'when do I leave this tier' trigger list per tier, expressed as observable metrics with thresholds rather than user counts — the track's scale bands are in registered users, which is the least predictive variable on the page.

tier-high: Savings Plans / Reserved Instances / Aurora Reserved Nodes — the single largest cost lever in every tier (30–50% off compute and DB) is never mentioned in any of the three cost sections. A cost ledger that lists NAT Gateway but not commitment discounts is not an honest ledger.
tier-high: Aurora I/O-Optimized as an explicit configuration decision, with the ~25%-of-bill crossover rule, rather than the parenthetical 'before I/O'.

tier-high: Backup, PITR and restore-proof. No tier states a backup retention, a PITR window, or — critically — that a backup nobody has restored is not a backup. Tier 3 budgets failover drills but no tier budgets restore drills.

tier-high: Schema migration discipline. Tier 3 mentions forward/backward compatibility in passing; tier 1 and 2 say nothing about online DDL, lock timeouts, or the fact that a single ALTER TABLE on a multi-TB Aurora table is the most common self-inflicted outage at tier 1. Aurora Blue/Green Deployments are the managed answer and appear nowhere.
