tier-high: Security baseline. No WAF, no Shield, no KMS/Secrets Manager, no IAM database authentication, no VPC endpoints, no multi-account boundary. For a multi-tenant cell architecture in tier 2, the absence of any tenant-isolation mechanism (row-level security, per-cell credentials, tenant context on background jobs) is a structural omission, not a detail.

tier-high: Autoscaling specifics. 'ECS Fargate or EC2 ASG' with no scaling signal. Target-tracking on what metric, what warm-up, what minimum capacity for AZ loss, and the crucial one: scaling the app tier multiplies connections into the database, so the app autoscaling policy and the DB connection ceiling are one coupled system. The track identifies pool exhaustion as failure #1 and then omits the control that causes it.

tier-high: Read-replica lag and read-after-write. Two readers are in the topology with no statement of how the application decides what is safe to read from them. This is the most common correctness bug in exactly this architecture.

tier-high: Deployment and rollback mechanics. No blue/green, canary, or rollback story at tier 1 or 2; tier 3 says deploys must be region-by-region and cell-by-cell but names no mechanism. The cell router is called the highest-risk component and then given no special deploy treatment.

tier-high: Infrastructure as code and environment parity. Tier 3's own 'quota drift in the standby region, a config value never parity-checked, an IAM role in one region only' is an argument for IaC plus automated quota/parity checking, and neither is listed as a component.

tier-high: VPC endpoints as the fix for the NAT Gateway line. The track flags NAT cost as 'almost always unbudgeted' and then does not name the mitigation (S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints are free; interface endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch).

tier-high: SLO and error-budget instrumentation. Tier 2 claims '99.95%+ with a real error budget' but lists no mechanism to measure availability — no synthetic canaries, no per-cell SLI, no burn-rate alerting.

tier-high: Idempotency at tier 1. It appears only in tier 3, but the moment SQS standard queues enter the design at tier 1 you need idempotency keys and a dedup store. It is required two tiers earlier than stated.

tier-high: Data residency and sticky-region routing. Tier 3 names regulatory drivers as a reason to go multi-region but never covers pinning a user's data to a region, which is the actual regulatory requirement (GDPR/DPDP), nor what happens to that pinning during failover.

tier-high: Cell lifecycle tooling at tier 2. Creating a cell, migrating a tenant between cells, draining and retiring a cell, and per-cell canary health — the control plane is named as the real limit and then never specified.

tier-high: The bridge between tiers. Nothing says how you get from tier 1 to tier 2 without a rewrite: what to decide on day one (tenant-id in every table, no cross-tenant queries, no shared sequences) so the cell migration is possible later. The track correctly calls partition grain a day-one decision at tier 2, then omits that warning from tier 1, where the decision is actually made.

tier-global: Capacity guarantees, not just pre-warming: On-Demand Capacity Reservations and EC2 Capacity Blocks are the only things that reserve the instances a forecast peak needs. The live-event track pre-warms but never reserves, so the last rungs of its ladder can fail with InsufficientInstanceCapacity on event day — the exact failure it claims to prevent.

tier-global: EC2 Auto Scaling warm pools (Stopped/Hibernated), predictive scaling, and scaling-policy warm-up settings. The track's '~90 seconds, unclosable' ceiling is a 2019 measurement presented as physics; warm pools materially change it and are the modern form of the 'manual ladder'.

tier-global: Service quotas as a pre-event checklist item. Nothing in three tracks names a single AWS quota by name or says to file increases weeks ahead: CloudFront per-distribution data-transfer-rate and requests-per-second limits (soft), Route 53 queries, ELB targets per LB, EC2 vCPU quotas per family per region, API Gateway account-level throttle. For a scheduled spike this is the #1 preventable outage cause.

tier-global: Graviton and instance-family selection. For a connection tier that is explicitly memory- and descriptor-bound, not CPU-bound, the memory-optimised and Graviton families are the economically decisive choice, and the cost paragraphs never mention instance selection at all.

tier-global: The cache tier. All three tracks route around the database but none names ElastiCache/Valkey or MemoryDB, and the live-event 'breaksFirst' (entitlement lookup saturating) is a textbook read-through-cache-plus-request-coalescing problem — cache the entitlement decision, coalesce the stampede, serve stale on failure. The fix is missing next to the failure.

tier-global: Load shedding and admission control concretely: token buckets, priority classes, the waiting-room/virtual-queue pattern (CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge issuing signed queue tokens). 'Panic mode: a runtime feature-flag plane' and 'load shedding as designed behaviour' are named but never specified, and they are the two mechanisms that actually save the event.

tier-global: Client-side behaviour as architecture. The track correctly says jitter and backoff are architecture, then never states the contract: capped exponential backoff with full jitter, a server-issued retry-after, and a circuit breaker. Reconnection-storm mitigation for the cellular fabric (staggered reconnect windows, server-assigned reconnect delay) is likewise named as the #1 failure and left unengineered.

tier-global: Observability under spike. Metrics pipelines are the first thing to fall over at 25M concurrent: cardinality explosion, CloudWatch PutMetricData throttling, log ingest cost. The multi-region entry counts '3x observability ingest' as cost but nobody counts it as a failure mode, and you cannot run a panic-mode decision on a dashboard that is 4 minutes stale.

tier-global: Evacuation prerequisites that drills actually expose: statically stable data-plane configuration, pre-scaled receiving-region capacity (a receiving region that must autoscale on arrival has not evacuated in 7 minutes), DNS TTLs short enough to matter, connection draining, and the rule that the failover tooling runs from a region that is never the one being evacuated.

tier-global: Cost controls and blast-radius on spend: budgets, anomaly detection, and a written teardown plan for the event fleet. A track that claims a 10–40x event-day multiple must say who turns it off and when, or the multiple becomes permanent.

tier-global: Security and tenancy at the edge: DDoS posture (Shield Advanced + WAF rate-based rules) for an announced, scheduled, globally advertised traffic event — an event everyone knows the start time of is also an event attackers know the start time of. Not mentioned once.

tier-global: Testing rigour beyond the game day: how the load generator is validated against real client behaviour (real TLS handshakes, real auth, real player manifest requests, not synthetic GETs), and for the cellular track the explicit claim 'a cell must be small enough to test at full scale' is stated but never operationalised into a cell-size formula.

tier-global: Data-layer specifics for the cellular fabric: the entry says a cell is 'a complete self-contained copy of the stack' and separately mandates 'regional write-locality with queued asynchronous cross-region writes', which are in tension. Cross-cell messaging (the actual product — user in cell A messages user in cell B) is never described, and it is the hardest part of the design.

tier-global: Migration/repartitioning mechanics: the track names 'the first time you need to split a hot cell' as a failure and then offers no mechanism (consistent hashing with virtual nodes, dual-write-and-verify, per-user migration with a read fence). Naming the failure without the mechanism is the hand-waving the brief asks to catch.

video: Requests are missing from every cost model. CloudFront bills HTTPS requests as well as GB, and segmented video is request-heavy: at 2-second parts in low-latency mode, 100,000 concurrent viewers generate on the order of 150,000+ manifest and part requests per second. The live blueprint even identifies origin request rate as failure #2 but never prices it or gives the reader a target requests/second figure.

video: Origin Shield is named once, in passing, as a thing that can be 'off' — it is never in any components list. For both the VOD and live blueprints it is the specific control that collapses origin request rate, and it is the fix for the failure the live section ranks second.

video: No edge-based authorisation. The VOD blueprint correctly identifies the entitlement API as the first thing to break under a release burst, then offers no architectural answer. CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge validating a short-lived signed token at the edge removes the per-playback-start origin call entirely. Diagnosing a failure and not putting its fix in components is the biggest structural gap in the track.

video: Nothing about capacity reservations for the mega event. 'Pre-provisioned compute with reactive autoscaling explicitly disabled' states the intent but omits the mechanisms: EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservations, warm pools, pre-raised service quotas, and load balancer pre-warming. Without these, 'pre-provisioned' is an aspiration — the blueprint's own ceiling says forecasting low IS the outage, so the buying mechanism is the load-bearing part.

video: No DRM reality. 'DRM via SPEKE (only where required)' understates what is involved: SPEKE is only the key-provider interface, you still need a licensed DRM vendor, and multi-DRM (Widevine + PlayReady + FairPlay) over CMAF requires SPEKE v2 with a different key layout than SPEKE v1. Studio licensing also dictates the encryption scheme and the output-protection rules, which drive the packaging decision upstream.

video: No ad insertion. MediaTailor, SCTE-35 markers from the contribution feed, and server-side ad insertion are absent from all three blueprints, yet for the live and mega-event cases advertising is usually the reason the event exists and SSAI materially changes both the manifest personalisation load and the CDN cache-hit rate the whole cost model depends on.

video: No quality-of-experience measurement. There is no rebuffer ratio, startup time, or playback-failure telemetry anywhere. Every operational decision the track recommends — ladder shape, latency tier, CDN steering — is unfalsifiable without client-side QoE data, and the mega-event blueprint's multi-CDN steering layer cannot function without it as its input signal.

video: No storage lifecycle for the VOD blueprint. Mezzanine sources accumulate forever and the blueprint calls storage 'noise' — S3 Intelligent-Tiering or a lifecycle policy to Glacier Instant Retrieval for mezzanine, and the cross-region transfer charge when the output bucket is not co-located with the distribution, are both missing.

video: No DVR, catch-up, or recording path in the live blueprint. Real live events need time-shift, start-over and a VOD asset afterwards; MediaPackage harvest jobs and the handoff to the VOD blueprint are not mentioned, so the two blueprints do not connect.

video: No multi-region or CDN failover for live. The live blueprint runs a single MediaPackage origin in a single region behind a single CDN, then hands off to the mega-event blueprint for multi-CDN. The gap between them — a second origin, a second CDN with health-based failover, dual MediaLive pipelines feeding separate packagers — is where most real production events actually sit, and it is unwritten.

video: No contribution detail. 'MediaConnect or an RTP/SRT push input' is listed but the choice is not made: SRT vs RTMP vs Zixi, why SRT for lossy public internet, redundant streams with SMPTE 2022-7 merge, and encoder-side failover. The blueprint's own breaksFirst ranks contribution as failure #1 and then gives the least guidance about it.

video: No per-title or content-aware encoding. The mega-event blueprint correctly identifies average delivered bitrate as a multi-million-dollar lever, then never mentions the standard technique for pulling it — per-title ladder optimisation and QVBR, which routinely cut 20-30% of delivered bits at equal quality. The lever is named and the tool is omitted.

video: No negotiated-pricing mechanics. The track repeatedly says nobody at scale pays list, but never names how: CloudFront private pricing / Savings Bundle, the 10 TB/month minimum commit threshold that qualifies for custom rates, and ISP-embedded caching. Without the entry criteria, 'negotiate' is not actionable advice.

video: No AWS service quotas anywhere. MediaLive channels per region, MediaConvert concurrent jobs, MediaPackage requests per second and CloudFront distributions per account all have defaults that bind well before the ceilings this track describes, and every one of them needs a lead-time quota request before an event.

realtime: Backpressure and flow control on the socket itself. All three tracks discuss fan-out cost and latency, none discuss what happens when a single client cannot consume as fast as you send: per-connection send-buffer high-water marks, dropping or coalescing, and the decision to disconnect a slow consumer rather than let it consume heap. The owned-connection track names slow consumers as a failure mode but gives no mechanism to prevent it.

realtime: Delivery semantics stated as a product decision. 'Message ordering and delivery guarantees (protocol, not a service)' appears as a bare component name with no content. A working architect must specify: at-least-once with client-side dedupe by message id, per-conversation monotonic sequence numbers, a gap-detection-and-resync path on reconnect, and the explicit admission that a WebSocket send is fire-and-forget until the client ACKs. Without this the serverless track's 2-hour forced disconnect silently loses messages.

realtime: The reconnect and catch-up path, which is the single most-used code path in any real chat system and is absent from all three tracks. On reconnect the client must present a last-seen cursor and receive the delta; this needs a server-side per-conversation sequence, a bounded backfill query, and a 'too far behind, do a full resync' fallback. API Gateway's 2-hour cap makes this mandatory, not optional.

realtime: Authentication and authorisation on $connect and on every subscribe. No mention of Lambda authorizers on $connect, of the fact that API Gateway WebSocket authorizers run ONLY at connect (so a token that expires mid-connection stays authorised for up to 2 hours unless you re-validate), or of per-room authorisation on subscribe. This is a security hole in the architecture as written, not an omission of detail.

realtime: Multi-tenant isolation. Nothing about tenant scoping of the connections table, the messages table, the Redis keyspace or the pub/sub channel namespace, and no cross-tenant test. A shared Valkey pub/sub spine with unnamespaced channels is a cross-tenant message leak waiting to happen.

realtime: Idempotency and the duplicate-send problem. DynamoDB Streams is at-least-once and Lambda retries, so the fan-out worker WILL re-deliver. There is no client message-id dedupe or conditional-write idempotency key anywhere in the serverless track, which means the described system visibly duplicates messages under exactly the retry storm the track predicts.

realtime: Connection-table garbage collection. The track correctly notes that 410 GoneException on ghost rows consumes throttle budget, then never prescribes the fix: a DynamoDB TTL on connection rows, a $disconnect handler that is explicitly acknowledged as unreliable (it is not guaranteed to fire), and a periodic sweep. This is the difference between the wall arriving at the stated ceiling and arriving at half of it.

realtime: Cost and mechanism of message history reads. 'DynamoDB - messages table' with 'history in the tens of millions of rows' has no access pattern: no partition key design (conversation_id + sort by sequence), no pagination model, no TTL or tiering of old messages to S3, and no read-cost estimate. History reads on a chat app are typically a larger DynamoDB line item than writes and do not appear in the cost model at all.

realtime: Mobile push handoff. 'SQS FIFO + Amazon SNS mobile push (APNs/FCM)' is listed as a component and never explained, yet it is where most real chat products break: deciding per-recipient whether they are connected (presence race), the debounce window before pushing, APNs and FCM rate and payload limits, feedback handling for dead tokens, and the fact that SNS mobile push has no delivery guarantee. Roughly half of a chat product's user-visible bugs live here.

realtime: Regional and failure-domain design. All three tracks are implicitly single-region and single-AZ-agnostic. Nothing on what happens when one AZ loses its gateway nodes, how connections re-home, whether the Valkey spine is Multi-AZ with automatic failover (and the seconds of pub/sub loss during that failover, since Redis/Valkey pub/sub is not persisted and messages published during failover are simply gone), or on any multi-region story.

realtime: Load testing and how you would ever verify these ceilings. The numbers are stated as engineering fact with no method: no mention of the difficulty of generating 500k real client connections from a load generator (ephemeral ports, file descriptors, distributed load agents), which means nobody reading this can check any of it before production does.

realtime: Observability specific to long-lived connections. IteratorAge is correctly named for the serverless track, but there is nothing on the metrics that matter for a socket fleet: connection count per node and its skew, connection age histogram, send-queue depth per connection, reconnect rate as a leading indicator, subscribe latency, and end-to-end delivery latency measured with a synthetic probe client rather than inferred from service metrics.

realtime: Cost of the alternative being recommended. The owned-connection track says two c7g.2xlarge cost ~$400 and do the same job as $1,080 of API Gateway. It omits the engineering cost that is the actual reason people choose managed: on-call for a stateful fleet, deploy tooling for connection draining, and the fact that the track's own worst failure mode (the deploy thundering herd) is a cost that exists only on the self-managed side. The build-vs-buy line is drawn on infrastructure price alone, which is the wrong comparison.

realtime: Connection draining and zero-downtime deploys, which follows directly from the thundering-herd failure the track identifies but is never answered. The mechanism (staged rolling with a hard cap on connections dropped per minute, server-initiated reconnect with jittered backoff advertised to the client, and a $connect path made cheap enough to survive a full-fleet re-establish) is the mitigation, and its absence makes the identified failure unactionable.

realtime: A decision rule for choosing between the three tracks. Three architectures are described with overlapping ranges and no stated crossover criteria: at what concurrency, what average room size, what team size and what latency SLO do you move from serverless to owned. The serverless ceiling section gestures at it via cost, but there is no explicit 'here is the number at which you migrate, and here is the migration path' — and the migration itself (running both connection layers during cutover) is the hardest part and is unmentioned.

data-path: NO INDEXING / QUERY-TUNING STAGE. The track jumps from 'one database' straight to 'buy a bigger box'. In production the cheapest and most common fix by a wide margin is a missing index, an N+1, or a bad plan. A stage-zero card - pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), index-bloat and unused-index checks, Performance Insights top-SQL - belongs BEFORE vertical-scaling, and its absence will cause readers to spend $10k/month solving a $0 problem.

data-path: NO HIGH-AVAILABILITY / FAILOVER BEHAVIOUR. Multi-AZ is named as a cost driver and never as a mechanism. Missing: actual failover times (60-120s for Multi-AZ instance deployments vs under 35s for Multi-AZ DB clusters), what happens to in-flight connections, why the app needs connection-drop retry logic and short DNS TTL/JDBC failover config, and the Multi-AZ DB CLUSTER option (two READABLE standbys, faster failover) which is completely absent from a track that discusses both HA and read scaling.

data-path: NO BACKUP / PITR / RTO-RPO STAGE. Backup retention appears only as a cost line. Missing: PITR granularity (5 minutes), how long a restore of a 5 TB database actually takes (hours, and the restored instance is slow until storage is fully hydrated), automated backups vs manual snapshots vs AWS Backup, cross-Region and cross-account copies for ransomware isolation, and a restore rehearsal. The lifecycle card mentions 'restore rehearsal' in passing but no stage owns RTO/RPO as a number.

data-path: NO SCHEMA MIGRATION / ONLINE DDL STAGE. Every stage past vertical-scaling assumes you can change a multi-TB table. Missing entirely: lock_timeout and statement_timeout as mandatory settings on migrations, ADD COLUMN with volatile defaults, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, pg_repack instead of VACUUM FULL, expand-contract migrations, and the fact that a naive ALTER on a hot table is the single most common self-inflicted production outage in Postgres.

data-path: NO MAJOR VERSION UPGRADE / END-OF-LIFE PATH. RDS standard support ends on a published schedule and rolls you onto paid Extended Support automatically. A multi-year scaling track must include the upgrade treadmill: Blue/Green for minimal-downtime major upgrades, extension-compatibility checks, and the fact that Blue/Green has real restrictions (unsupported features, and it does not cover every topology).

data-path: NO OBSERVABILITY OR CAPACITY-PLANNING BASELINE. Individual cards mention individual alarms, but nothing defines the small set of signals that tell you WHICH stage you are at: DBLoad vs vCPU on Performance Insights, MaximumUsedTransactionIDs (the wraparound countdown the vertical-scaling card invokes but never tells you to alarm on), ReplicaLag, FreeableMemory, checkpoint/WAL rate, DatabaseConnections against max_connections. Without this the track is a menu with no diagnostic.

data-path: NO BACKPRESSURE / OVERLOAD PROTECTION. The whole track scales supply and never limits demand. Missing: statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, per-tenant rate limiting, circuit breakers, queueing non-urgent writes, and load shedding. These are the difference between degradation and the total-outage cascade the very first card describes.

data-path: NO SECURITY OR MULTI-TENANCY LAYER. Encryption at rest/KMS, TLS enforcement (rds.force_ssl), IAM database authentication, least-privilege roles and - critically for anything multi-tenant, which sharding and hot-shard talk implies throughout - row-level security and tenant isolation testing. Secrets Manager appears once, in stage one, and then disappears.

data-path: NO DISASTER RECOVERY OR MULTI-REGION STAGE. Aurora Global Database is listed as a component with the parenthetical '(only if you need it)' and no criteria for when that is. Missing: RPO/RTO targets, cross-Region read replicas, managed planned failover vs unplanned, the data-residency implications already flagged in the lifecycle card, and cost.

data-path: NO MIGRATION MECHANICS BETWEEN STAGES. Several transitions are large and risky and none explain the move: RDS to Aurora (snapshot restore vs read-replica promotion vs DMS, and the downtime of each), the cutover of a sharded write path, or backfilling a purpose-built store. 'Double-write, backfill, verify, cut over' is one bullet carrying six months of work.

data-path: NO EXPLICIT DECISION CRITERIA OR ANTI-STAGE GUIDANCE. The track reads as a ladder to be climbed. It needs the inverse: the signals that say DO NOT advance (you are at 30% CPU and your problem is one query), and a per-stage 'you are here when you observe X' trigger. Related: no stage tells the reader to load-test and measure the ceiling before assuming it, so every number in the track is used as a substitute for measurement rather than a prompt for it.

migrations: No step for connection pooling infrastructure in the FIRST migration. The track correctly identifies the DB connection pool as what breaks first when you go from one box to two, then never gives the fix. RDS Proxy appears only in the Lambda block. PgBouncer/ProxySQL, pool sizing as (instances x pool_size x scale-out-max) and setting max_connections deliberately belong in single-instance-to-load-balanced-pair, where the failure is named.

migrations: No rollback plan on any step. Every block describes forward motion and what breaks; none states the abort criteria, the rollback mechanism, or the point of no return. Database engine change and single-region-to-multi-region are irreversible after cutover and the track never says so. A working architect writes the rollback before the cutover runbook.

migrations: No observability or verification gate. Nothing about establishing a baseline before the change or a specific metric that proves the change worked. 'Performance Insights + a slow query baseline captured BEFORE the change' appears once, in the read-replica block, and should be a precondition on every step. Missing: ALB TargetResponseTime / HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count, ECS deployment circuit breaker, Lambda Throttles and ConcurrentExecutions alarms, RDS DatabaseConnections.

migrations: No TLS/certificate story anywhere. ACM certificate provisioning and DNS validation, the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect listener rule, and certificate renewal across accounts and regions (a cert is regional, and CloudFront needs us-east-1) are all absent. Certificate expiry and region-scoping are a top cause of failed multi-region cutovers.

migrations: No infrastructure-as-code position. Every one of these migrations doubles infrastructure temporarily. Doing that by hand guarantees drift between the old and new shape, which is the actual mechanism behind 'the things you forgot were regional'. The track should state that the migration is the moment to get into CDK/Terraform, and that the parity checklist is a diff of two IaC states, not a wiki page.

migrations: No service-quota pre-flight. Quotas are mentioned once (new-account defaults) but the same trap hits every step: ECS tasks per service, ENIs per region, Lambda concurrency, ALB rules/targets per target group, RDS instances per account, Elastic IPs. A 'raise these before you start, they take days' list per step is cheap and prevents the most common mid-migration stall.

migrations: No stateful-session or sticky-session handling in the first step. ElastiCache is listed as a component but the track never says how to get an existing app off in-process sessions, nor mentions ALB target-group stickiness as the bridge that buys time. This is the single most common reason a first ALB rollout gets reverted.

migrations: No cost-attribution or shutdown discipline. Several steps run two environments in parallel for weeks to months; nothing covers tagging for cost allocation, a budget alarm on the migration, or the decommission step. Migrations routinely leave the old environment running for a year because nobody owned turning it off.

migrations: No data-consistency verification method beyond 'a shadow comparison harness'. For read-replica splitting and the engine change, the track needs concrete verification: row counts and checksums per table, DMS data validation tasks, and a defined tolerance for rows that legitimately differ during CDC. Without it, 'we compared and it looked fine' is the ship decision.

migrations: No security review of the new shape. Security groups moving from instance-level to ALB-plus-task-level, the IAM task-execution-role vs task-role distinction (a top-three ECS mistake), VPC endpoints vs NAT for reaching AWS APIs privately, and secrets moving out of the AMI and into Secrets Manager are all implied but never made a step.

migrations: No ECS-to-EKS or EKS mention at all, and no honest statement of when ECS/Fargate is the wrong destination. A track on migrations that presents Fargate as the container answer without naming the conditions under which a team should choose EKS (existing Kubernetes skills, multi-cloud requirement, operator ecosystem) is incomplete guidance, not an opinionated one.

migrations: No queue/async decoupling step. Every one of these shapes is request/response. The single highest-leverage migration for a system at 500-5,000 req/s is usually pulling slow work out of the request path onto SQS or EventBridge, and it is absent from the track entirely.

procedure: No IAM or identity question at all. Nobody asks who can deploy, whether production is a separate AWS account under Organizations with SCPs, whether humans get access via IAM Identity Center and SSM Session Manager instead of long-lived keys and bastion hosts, or how the application's own role is scoped. This is the single largest omission — an architecture built exactly as described has no answer for 'who can delete the database'.

procedure: No secrets question. Database credentials, third-party API keys, rotation, Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store vs environment variables. Item 6 mentions encryption and KMS but only as a compliance consequence, never as an operational necessity.

procedure: No question about deployment and rollback mechanics. Item 12 asks about IaC and item 4 mentions rolling vs blue/green in passing, but nothing asks how a bad release is detected and reverted, how database migrations are sequenced against a rolling deploy (expand/contract), or what the rollback of a migration looks like. A system built to this spec can deploy but cannot safely un-deploy.

procedure: No question about service quotas and lead time. Lambda's default 1,000 concurrent executions per region, per-region vCPU quotas for On-Demand instances, ECS task limits, SES sending limits — several of these take days to raise and are discovered during the launch spike, not before it. Item 3 discusses spikes without ever asking whether the account can physically serve one.

procedure: No data transfer cost model. Cross-AZ traffic ($0.01/GB each way), internet egress, NAT processing and VPC endpoint charges routinely become the second-largest line on a small team's bill and are invisible in an instance-sized budget. Item 11 asks for a budget number without asking what shape the traffic bill takes.

procedure: No security perimeter question: AWS WAF, Shield, rate limiting at the edge, bot traffic, and where the 429 from item 3 is actually enforced. Load shedding is discussed purely as a capacity mechanism, never as an abuse mechanism.

procedure: No observability budget or SLO definition. Item 10 says 'how much of the budget goes to observability' but nothing asks what is measured, what the SLO and error budget are, what alarms exist and what each one's runbook is, or that CloudWatch Logs ingestion at roughly $0.50/GB is itself a budget item that can exceed compute.

procedure: No restore drill. Item 5 designs backups and item 9 notes that restoring 4 TB is slow, but nothing asks when a restore was last actually performed into a throwaway instance and verified byte-for-byte. An untested backup is the assumption this track otherwise exists to eliminate.

procedure: No testing question. Nothing asks what proves a change is safe before it reaches production — functional, load and regression testing, a staging environment that resembles production, or a load test that validates the rps numbers item 2 asserts.

procedure: No VPC and network-design question: CIDR sizing and future peering collisions, public/private/isolated subnet layout, IPv6, security-group topology, and whether the database is genuinely unreachable from the internet. The track assumes a VPC exists and is correct.

procedure: No question about the stateless assumption. Sessions, file uploads, in-process caches, sticky sessions, background cron running on exactly one instance — item 2 says 'the entire stateless-tier decision' without ever asking whether the application is in fact stateless, which for an existing codebase is usually the finding that reshapes the plan.

procedure: No tagging, cost-attribution, budget-alarm or account-hygiene question. Item 11 asks for a ceiling but nothing enforces it: AWS Budgets with actions, anomaly detection, and cost allocation tags are what turn the agreed number into a control rather than a hope.

procedure: No question about domains, DNS and certificates: registrar, hosted zone, ACM issuance and the us-east-1 requirement for CloudFront, cert renewal validation. Small and boring, and it blocks a launch date more often than any item on this list.

procedure: No question about third-party dependencies in the request path — payment gateway, email/SMS provider, auth provider, LLM API — their rate limits, their outages, and whether the system degrades or fails when they are down. Item 2's 'timeouts, retries and backoff' source is cited but only aimed inward at AWS services.

premature: Named-company claims: the track makes none — no Netflix, Instagram, WhatsApp or Hotstar folklore anywhere. That is a genuine pass and is rare for material in this genre. The one company claim present (Segment/Twilio 'Goodbye Microservices') is first-party and correctly cited.

premature: A security-and-tenancy track. Twelve tracks and not one covers the premature-vs-necessary line on authorization: hand-rolled tenant filtering in application code instead of Postgres row-level security, IAM policies written with wildcards because scoping is 'premature', or KMS/Secrets Manager deferred until after an incident. The custom-auth track covers authentication and stops; authorization and tenant isolation are where the expensive failures actually are.

premature: An observability-cost track. The material recommends CloudWatch Container Insights, VPC Flow Logs into Athena, X-Ray and ADOT across four tracks and never prices any of it. CloudWatch Logs ingestion at $0.50/GB is routinely the second or third line on a startup's bill and frequently exceeds the entire compute spend the k8s track is arguing about. 'Premature observability platform (Datadog/Grafana Cloud) vs CloudWatch done properly' is the exact shape of every other track here and is absent.

premature: A capacity-and-quota track. Every ceiling in this material is stated in req/s or dollars; none mentions AWS service quotas, which is what people actually hit first: Fargate On-Demand vCPU quota (default 6 vCPU in a new account, which the k8s track's own 3-services-x-2-tasks example will approach), ALB rules per listener, ECS tasks per service, Lambda concurrency, and the fact that every one of these needs a quota increase request with lead time. An architecture that works on paper and cannot be deployed on Monday is a missing piece.

premature: A background-jobs and scheduling track. SQS plus a worker appears as a component in two tracks and is never the subject of one. The premature version (Airflow or Temporal or a Step Functions state machine for four cron jobs) versus the right version (EventBridge Scheduler into an ECS task, with a dead-letter queue and a visible last-run record) is one of the most common early over-builds and the failure mode — silent job death with no heartbeat — is exactly the kind of thing the rest of this material catches well.

premature: An environments-and-accounts track. The IaC track assumes '3-5 environments' exist but nothing addresses the premature build (a full Control Tower landing zone with eight OUs before there are ten engineers) versus the right one (two or three accounts with SCPs and an Identity Center setup). Every other track's blast-radius reasoning depends on an account structure that is never specified.

premature: Within-track: no track states a migration path. Each says 'do the simple thing until X' but none says what the move looks like when X arrives — modular monolith to first extracted service, single region to pilot light, RDS to Aurora, library retries to mesh. The value of deferring a decision depends entirely on the deferred decision still being available later, and that claim is never made or defended anywhere in the material.

premature: Within-track: no track states what it would cost to be wrong. 'Premature' arguments are asymmetric-risk arguments, and the asymmetry is never quantified. Building a mesh too early costs 1-3 engineer-months and is reversible; building event sourcing too early is, as the track itself notes, permanent. Those are different-magnitude mistakes presented in the same register.
